choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You contradicted the explicit premise stating that a spider has eight legs.

questions.explanation: Since all insects have six legs, and a spider has eight legs, the spider cannot be an insect: if it were, it would need to have exactly six legs.

questions.stem:
If a battery is dead, the flashlight will not turn on. The flashlight did not turn on.
Can we conclude the battery is dead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the flashlight could fail to turn on for another reason, such as a broken bulb or a loose connection, not just a dead battery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: a flashlight failing to turn on always means the battery is dead.
choices.rationale: You assumed a dead battery is the only reason a flashlight will not light.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: this is a valid modus tollens argument.
choices.rationale: You confused affirming the consequent with modus tollens. Modus tollens requires the flashlight turning on to conclude the battery is not dead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the flashlight actually did turn on.
choices.rationale: You disputed the premise that the flashlight did not turn on.

questions.explanation: This is "affirming the consequent" in reverse form: the premise only guarantees a dead battery prevents the flashlight from turning on, not that this is the only possible cause of failure.

questions.stem:
If a shape is a triangle, it has three sides. This shape does not have three sides.
What must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This shape is not a triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You contradicted the modus tollens inference. Lacking a required trait of triangles means the shape cannot be a triangle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: This shape has exactly three sides.
choices.rationale: You contradicted the given premise stating the shape does not have three sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing can be concluded about this shape.
choices.rationale: You overlooked modus tollens. Denying a necessary condition validly proves the shape is not a triangle.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: since having three sides is guaranteed for triangles, and this shape lacks three sides, it cannot be a triangle.

questions.stem:
All licensed drivers have passed a driving test. Juan passed a driving test. Therefore, Juan is a licensed driver.
Is this conclusion valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: passing a driving test does not guarantee being licensed; Juan could have passed the test without completing other licensing requirements, such as registration or fees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: passing a driving test always means someone is a licensed driver.
choices.rationale: You assumed passing a test is the sole condition for getting a license.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: this follows modus ponens correctly.
choices.rationale: You misidentified affirming the consequent as modus ponens. Modus ponens starts with "Juan is a licensed driver".

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because Juan never actually took a driving test.
choices.rationale: You questioned the premise facts rather than analyzing the validity of the deduction.

questions.explanation: This is "affirming the consequent." The premise only says licensed drivers have passed a test, not that everyone who passes a test automatically becomes licensed: other requirements might still apply.

questions.stem:
All fish live in water. A dolphin lives in water.
Can we conclude that a dolphin is a fish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the premise only guarantees fish live in water; it does not say everything living in water is a fish, so this conclusion does not follow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: since a dolphin lives in water, and all fish live in water, a dolphin must be a fish.
choices.rationale: You assumed living in water is an exclusive property of fish.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: this is a valid deductive conclusion using modus ponens.
choices.rationale: You misidentified affirming the consequent as modus ponens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because dolphins do not actually live in water.
choices.rationale: You disputed the factual premise that dolphins live in water.

questions.explanation: This is a category version of "affirming the consequent." "All fish live in water" does not mean "everything that lives in water is a fish": a dolphin is actually a mammal, not a fish, despite living in water.

questions.stem: Consider this argument: "All reptiles are cold-blooded. A snake is cold-blooded. Therefore, a snake is a reptile." Separately, consider: "All reptiles are cold-blooded. A snake is a reptile. Therefore, a snake is cold-blooded." Evaluate the validity of each argument.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first argument is invalid (it affirms the consequent, since "cold-blooded" does not guarantee "reptile": some fish and amphibians are also cold-blooded); the second argument is valid, since it correctly applies the trait from the category to a confirmed member of it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both arguments are valid, since they use the same two facts about reptiles.
choices.rationale: You treated argument structure as irrelevant. Premise order and direction determine validity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both arguments are invalid, since neither can be evaluated without knowing if snakes are truly reptiles.
choices.rationale: You confused deductive validity with empirical checking. Validity tests structural necessity given premises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first argument is valid, and the second is invalid, reversing the correct evaluation.
choices.rationale: You inverted valid deduction and affirming the consequent.

questions.explanation: The first argument reasons backward from a shared trait to category membership, which is invalid since other animals (like some fish and amphibians) are also cold-blooded. The second argument correctly reasons forward from confirmed category membership to a guaranteed trait, making it valid.

choices.label: D

questions.stem: If $P$ is false and $Q$ is false, what is the truth value of "$P \rightarrow Q$" (if P then Q)?

choices.label: D

questions.stem: A student reasons, "Since $P$ is false, we can't say anything about whether '$P \rightarrow Q$' is true or false." Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: formal propositional logic always assigns a definite truth value to a conditional whose "if" part is false; "$P \rightarrow Q$" is true whenever $P$ is false, no matter what $Q$ is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the truth value of a conditional cannot be determined when its "if" part is false.
choices.rationale: You applied everyday intuition instead of formal logic. In formal logic, a false antecedent guarantees the conditional is true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because conditionals are never actually true or false.
choices.rationale: You claimed conditionals lack truth values. Conditionals always evaluate to either true or false in propositional logic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: everyday intuition about conditionals always matches formal propositional logic exactly.
choices.rationale: You assumed intuition matches formal logic. Everyday usage often treats false antecedents as undefined, whereas formal logic defines them as true.

questions.explanation: Everyday intuition might suggest that "if $P$ is false, we can't say anything about the conditional," but formal propositional logic always assigns a definite truth value (true, in this case) to a conditional whose "if" part is false.

questions.stem: A student claims "$P \lor Q$" requires both $P$ and $Q$ to be true, the same requirement as "$P \land Q$." Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: "and" requires both statements to be true, but "or" requires only at least one to be true; "or" is the more lenient connective, "and" is the stricter one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: "and" and "or" always require the exact same condition to be true.
choices.rationale: You equated conjunction and disjunction. "And" requires both components true, while "or" requires only one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because "or" can never be true under any circumstance.
choices.rationale: You claimed disjunction can never be true. Disjunction is true whenever at least one component is true.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: both connectives are false whenever either statement is false.
choices.rationale: You applied the rule of conjunction to disjunction. Disjunction is only false when both components are false.

questions.explanation: Mixing up and and or is one of the most common truth-table errors. And is the stricter connective (requires both true), while or is more lenient (requires only at least one true).

questions.stem: A student evaluates "$(P \land Q) \lor R$" (with $P$ true, $Q$ false, $R$ true) by first combining $Q$ and $R$ instead of $P$ and $Q$, ignoring the parentheses grouping. What is wrong with this approach, and what is the correct final truth value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student ignored the parentheses grouping $P$ and $Q$ together; just like order of operations in math, the innermost parentheses must be evaluated first. Evaluating correctly, "$P \land Q$" is false, and "false $\lor R$" (with $R$ true) gives the correct answer of true.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The approach is correct: parentheses grouping does not affect the order of evaluation in propositional logic.
choices.rationale: You claimed parentheses do not dictate evaluation order. Parentheses determine which connective evaluates first.

choices.text: The student's approach is correct, and the final answer is false.
choices.rationale: You accepted an incorrect evaluation order that violates precedence in propositional logic.

choices.label: D

choices.rationale: You claimed compound expressions cannot be evaluated under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Evaluating combined expressions in the wrong order (ignoring parentheses grouping) produces an incorrect final truth value. Just like arithmetic order of operations, evaluate the innermost parentheses first: "$P \land Q$" first, giving false, then "false $\lor R$," giving true.

questions.stem: Author is to book as book is to ______. Is "author" the correct answer to complete this second analogy?

choices.rationale: You assumed analogy relationships are symmetric regardless of word order.

choices.rationale: You ignored directional order in relational pairs.

questions.explanation: Connected, open containers always settle to the same fluid level, regardless of their width. The water levels are the same in both the wide and narrow containers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The water speeds up in the narrow section

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water slows down in the narrow section
choices.rationale: You assumed a tighter passage restricts speed. To maintain a constant volume flow rate, fluid must speed up when cross-sectional area decreases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The water's speed stays exactly the same
choices.rationale: You assumed flow speed is independent of pipe diameter. Narrowing area forces velocity to increase to satisfy continuity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The water stops flowing entirely in the narrow section
choices.rationale: You assumed narrow pipes block steady fluid movement. Continuous incompressible flow accelerates through narrower sections.

questions.explanation: The same volume of water must pass through both sections per second. Since the narrow section has less cross-sectional area, the water must move faster to maintain the same volume flow rate.

questions.stem: Using the same narrowing pipe as before, how does the pressure in the narrow section compare to the pressure in the wide section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pressure is lower in the narrow section

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pressure is higher in the narrow section
choices.rationale: You relied on intuition that tight spaces create high pressure. Faster fluid speed in a narrow section results in lower internal pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pressure is exactly the same in both sections
choices.rationale: You assumed pressure is unaffected by flow speed. Changes in fluid speed cause corresponding changes in internal pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pressure cannot be compared without knowing the pipe's material
choices.rationale: You assumed wall material dictates fluid pressure dynamics. Speed and area changes determine internal pressure differences.

questions.explanation: The water moves faster in the narrow section. By the relationship between fluid speed and pressure (faster flow means lower pressure), the pressure in the faster-moving narrow section is lower than in the wider section.

questions.stem: Figure shows three open containers of different shapes and widths (one wide, one narrow, one medium), all connected at the bottom. Water is poured in until it settles. How do the three water levels compare?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All three containers settle at exactly the same water level

choices.label: B
choices.text: The widest container settles at the lowest level
choices.rationale: You assumed wider containers spread fluid lower. Connected open vessels balance at equal heights regardless of container shape or width.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrowest container settles at the highest level
choices.rationale: You assumed narrow columns push fluid higher. Fluid levels balance strictly by depth and atmospheric pressure equality.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each container settles at a different level, proportional to its width
choices.rationale: You assumed level varies with width. Communicating vessels equalize to a single horizontal level.

questions.explanation: Connected, open containers always settle at the same fluid level, no matter how many containers are connected or how different their widths and shapes are.

questions.stem: Figure shows a deep container of water with three marked points: Point X near the surface, Point Y at the middle depth, and Point Z at the very bottom. Rank the three points from lowest to highest pressure.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Point X (lowest), then Point Y, then Point Z (highest)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Point Z (lowest), then Point Y, then Point X (highest)
choices.rationale: You inverted the pressure ranking. Shallow points have less fluid weight above them, so Point X has the lowest pressure and Point Z has the highest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All three points have exactly equal pressure
choices.rationale: You assumed pressure is uniform throughout a fluid volume. Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point Y (lowest), then Point X, then Point Z (highest)
choices.rationale: You misordered the shallowest point X. Pressure increases continuously from top to bottom.

questions.explanation: Pressure increases steadily with depth. Point X (shallowest) has the lowest pressure, Point Z (deepest) has the highest pressure, and Point Y (middle depth) falls in between.

questions.stem: Figure shows water flowing steadily through a pipe that widens from a narrow section to a wide section. Compared to the narrow section, how does the water's speed change in the wide section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The water slows down in the wide section

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water speeds up in the wide section
choices.rationale: You assumed wider pipes increase flow velocity. Expanding cross-sectional area allows fluid to move slower while maintaining flow rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The water's speed stays exactly the same
choices.rationale: You assumed pipe width does not influence speed. Flow velocity decreases when cross-sectional area increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The water stops flowing entirely in the wide section
choices.rationale: You assumed widening halts fluid movement. Flow continues steadily at a lower speed.

questions.explanation: Since the wide section has more cross-sectional area, the same volume of water can pass through more slowly while still maintaining the same overall flow rate: the water slows down in the wide section.

questions.stem: Using the same widening pipe as before, how does the pressure in the wide section compare to the pressure in the narrow section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pressure is higher in the wide section

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pressure is lower in the wide section
choices.rationale: You assumed wider sections have lower pressure. Slower-moving fluid in a wider pipe section has higher internal pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pressure is exactly the same in both sections
choices.rationale: You ignored the relationship between fluid speed and pressure. Velocity changes cause inverse pressure changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pressure cannot be compared without knowing the flow rate
choices.rationale: You assumed relative pressure cannot be determined. The cross-sectional ratio establishes that the wider section has lower speed and higher pressure.

questions.explanation: The water moves slower in the wide section. Since slower-moving fluid exerts higher pressure, the pressure in the wide section is higher than in the narrow section.

questions.stem: A student sees a very wide container connected to a very narrow container, both open at the top, and assumes the wide container must settle at a lower water level, "since it needs to spread its water across more area." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: connected, open containers always settle at the same fluid level, no matter how different their widths are; the wide container does not settle lower just because it holds more total water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: wider containers always settle at a lower level than narrower ones.
choices.rationale: You assumed surface area lowers fluid height. Open connected containers equalize pressure by maintaining matching fluid heights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because the narrow container was filled first.
choices.rationale: You assumed filling sequence determines settled height. Fluid flows between vessels until heights balance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the two containers are not actually connected.
choices.rationale: You disputed the problem premise. The containers are connected at the bottom.

questions.explanation: A wider container does not settle at a lower level just because it "holds more water" overall: the surface level still equalizes with any connected narrower container, since pressure at the connecting point must balance out equally on both sides.

questions.stem: A student assumes that squeezing a hose nozzle to make the opening narrower will slow down the water flow, "since it's a tighter squeeze." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a narrower section of pipe causes the fluid to speed up, not slow down, in order to maintain the same overall flow volume passing through per second.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: narrower openings always slow down fluid flow.
choices.rationale: You applied intuition that tighter spaces slow movement. Decreasing opening area increases exit velocity to maintain flow rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because hose nozzles are a special exception to normal fluid behavior.
choices.rationale: You treated nozzles as an exception. Fluid acceleration through narrow openings is standard continuity behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because water cannot flow through narrow openings at all.
choices.rationale: You assumed narrow openings block flow completely. Water flows through at increased speed.

questions.explanation: Confusing this with everyday intuition (like assuming a "tighter squeeze" naturally slows things down) leads to the opposite, incorrect prediction: the fluid actually accelerates through a narrower opening, which is exactly why squeezing a hose nozzle makes the water spray faster.

questions.stem: A student reasons that the narrow, fast-flowing section of a pipe must have higher pressure than the wide section, "since it feels more forceful and energetic." Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: sections with faster movement (like narrow pipe sections) have lower pressure, not higher, following the relationship between fluid speed and pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: faster-flowing sections always have higher pressure than slower sections.
choices.rationale: You equated flow velocity with internal fluid pressure. Faster-moving fluid exerts lower internal pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because "forceful" and "high pressure" always mean the same thing.
choices.rationale: You confused kinetic impact force of a spray with internal static fluid pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because narrow pipe sections never have any measurable pressure.
choices.rationale: You claimed narrow pipes lack pressure. Moving fluids maintain measurable pressure that varies inversely with speed.

questions.explanation: Assuming a narrow, fast-flowing section must have higher pressure (since it "feels more forceful" intuitively) reverses the correct relationship between fluid speed and pressure: faster flow actually means lower pressure.

questions.stem: Figure shows four open containers of completely different shapes (round, square, triangular cross-section, and irregular), all connected at the bottom by tubes. After water settles, one container appears visually taller than the others. Does its water surface actually sit higher than the others?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: despite looking taller overall, its water surface still settles at the exact same level as the other connected containers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the visually taller container always has a higher water surface
choices.rationale: You confused container wall height with fluid level. Open connected containers equalize water surfaces to the same height.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because its cross-sectional shape is different from the others
choices.rationale: You assumed container shape alters fluid height equilibrium. Shape does not affect settled fluid level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on which container was filled with water first
choices.rationale: You assumed filling order prevents equilibrium. Fluid flows between connected vessels until levels equalize.

questions.explanation: Container height or shape does not affect the settled water surface level in a connected, open system: only the fluid level itself equalizes, regardless of how tall, wide, or oddly shaped each individual container looks.

questions.stem: Figure shows a pipe that narrows in the middle section, then widens back to its original width at the far end (wide → narrow → wide). Compare the flow speed and pressure in the middle (narrow) section to the two wide end sections.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The middle section has the fastest flow speed and the lowest pressure; both wide end sections have slower flow speed and higher pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: The middle section has the slowest flow speed and the highest pressure
choices.rationale: You inverted both speed and pressure relationships. Narrow sections have faster flow and lower pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All three sections have identical flow speed and pressure
choices.rationale: You assumed pipe width variations do not affect flow speed or pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The middle section has the fastest flow speed and the highest pressure
choices.rationale: You correctly identified faster speed but incorrectly assumed faster flow creates higher internal pressure.

questions.explanation: The narrow middle section forces the water to speed up (to maintain the same flow volume), and faster-moving fluid has lower pressure. The wider end sections allow slower flow and correspondingly higher pressure.

questions.stem: A tall, wide open container is connected at the bottom to a tall, narrow open container, forming a U-shape; water is poured in until it settles. A pipe leads from the bottom of the wide container, narrowing partway along its length before opening into the narrow container. Determine: (a) how the settled water surface levels in the wide and narrow containers compare, and (b) how the flow speed and pressure in the narrowed section of the connecting pipe compare to the wider parts of that same pipe, while water is actively flowing through it.

choices.label: A
choices.text: (a) The water surface levels are equal in both containers, regardless of width; (b) the narrowed section of the pipe has faster flow speed and lower pressure than the wider parts of the pipe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: (a) The wide container settles at a lower level than the narrow container; (b) the narrowed section has slower flow speed and higher pressure.
choices.rationale: You incorrectly assumed wider containers settle lower and narrow pipes slow down fluid flow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (a) The narrow container settles at a lower level than the wide container; (b) the narrowed section has faster flow speed and higher pressure.
choices.rationale: You incorrectly assumed narrow containers settle lower and faster flow creates higher pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (a) The water surface levels are equal in both containers; (b) the narrowed section has slower flow speed and lower pressure.
choices.rationale: You correctly identified equal levels, but incorrectly claimed fluid slows down in narrow sections.

questions.explanation: Connected, open containers always settle at the same fluid level regardless of width, so (a) the levels are equal. Within the connecting pipe, the narrowed section forces faster flow (to maintain the same flow volume) and correspondingly lower pressure than the wider sections, so (b) faster flow speed and lower pressure in the narrow section.

questions.stem: Figure shows three gears connected in a row, each meshing directly with its neighbor. The first gear turns clockwise. What direction does the third gear turn?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed every gear in a chain turns counter-clockwise. Odd-numbered gears in a linear chain turn in the same direction as the first gear.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not turn at all
choices.rationale: You assumed connected gears jam. Linear gear trains turn smoothly when properly aligned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns in both directions at once
choices.rationale: You assigned impossible dual directions. A single gear rotates in only one direction at a time.

questions.explanation: Meshing gears alternate direction: gear 1 clockwise, gear 2 counter-clockwise, gear 3 clockwise. Since gears 1 and 3 are both in odd positions, they turn in the same direction.

questions.stem: Figure shows five gears connected in a row, each meshing directly with its neighbor. The first gear turns counter-clockwise. What direction does the fifth gear turn?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You applied an even-position rule to an odd position. Gear 5 is in an odd position in the chain, so it matches gear 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not turn at all
choices.rationale: You assumed the chain locks up. An odd-numbered chain of meshing gears turns freely without jamming.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns in both directions at once
choices.rationale: You assigned impossible dual rotation directions to a single gear.

questions.explanation: Gears 1, 3, and 5 are all in odd positions, so they share the same rotation direction as gear 1. Since gear 1 turns counter-clockwise, gear 5 also turns counter-clockwise.

questions.stem: Figure shows four gears connected in a row, each meshing directly with its neighbor. The first gear turns clockwise. What direction does the fourth gear turn?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You applied the odd-position rule to an even position. Gear 4 is in an even position, so it turns opposite to gear 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not turn at all
choices.rationale: You assumed the 4-gear train jams. A linear 4-gear train rotates smoothly without locking up.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns in both directions at once
choices.rationale: You assigned opposing simultaneous rotation directions to a single gear.

questions.explanation: Gear 4 is in an even position, so it turns opposite to gear 1. Since gear 1 turns clockwise, gear 4 turns counter-clockwise.

questions.stem: Figure shows six gears connected in a row, each meshing directly with its neighbor. The first gear turns counter-clockwise. What direction does the sixth gear turn?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed gear 6 matches gear 1. Gear 6 is in an even position, so it turns opposite to gear 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not turn at all
choices.rationale: You assumed a 6-gear train locks up. Linear gear trains turn freely regardless of chain length.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns in both directions at once
choices.rationale: You assigned conflicting simultaneous rotation directions.

questions.explanation: Gear 6 is in an even position, so it turns opposite to gear 1. Since gear 1 turns counter-clockwise, gear 6 turns clockwise.

questions.stem: Figure shows a small gear with 10 teeth meshing with a large gear with 30 teeth. If the small gear completes 6 full rotations, how many full rotations does the large gear complete?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed both gears complete the same number of rotations. Larger gears have more teeth and complete fewer rotations.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You multiplied rotations by the teeth ratio instead of dividing. The larger gear completes  \times 6 \div 30 = 2$ rotations.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You miscalculated the teeth ratio. The ratio is  \div 10 = 3$, so  \div 3 = 2$ rotations.

questions.explanation: The number of teeth passing the meshing point must be equal for both gears: the small gear completes $10 \times 6 = 60$ teeth passing. The large gear (30 teeth) must also have 60 teeth pass, so it completes $60 \div 30 = 2$ rotations.

questions.stem: Figure shows a small gear with 8 teeth meshing with a large gear with 24 teeth. If the small gear completes 9 full rotations, how many full rotations does the large gear complete?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed rotation count is unaffected by gear size. The 24-tooth gear is 3 times larger, so it rotates 3 times fewer.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You multiplied rotations by 3 instead of dividing. Small-to-large gear transmission reduces rotation count ( \div 24 = 3$).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You estimated the calculation.  \times 9 = 72$ teeth passing, so  \div 24 = 3$ rotations.

questions.explanation: The small gear completes $8 \times 9 = 72$ teeth passing the contact point. The large gear (24 teeth) must also have 72 teeth pass, so it completes $72 \div 24 = 3$ rotations.

questions.stem: Figure shows three gears connected in a row. Gear 1 turns clockwise, and gear 2 (meshing directly with gear 1) turns counter-clockwise. A student assumes gear 3 (meshing directly with gear 2) must also turn counter-clockwise, "matching gear 2." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gear 3 meshes directly with gear 2, so it must turn opposite to gear 2 (clockwise), alternating back to match gear 1's direction, not continuing gear 2's direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: once a gear in the chain turns counter-clockwise, every gear after it also turns counter-clockwise.
choices.rationale: You assumed a direction persists down the chain. Meshing gears alternate direction at every step.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because gear 3 does not actually mesh with gear 2.
choices.rationale: You disputed the given meshing connection between the gears.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because gear 1 and gear 2 actually turn in the same direction.
choices.rationale: You disputed the premise that meshing gears turn in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: Assuming the third gear spins the same direction as the second (rather than correctly alternating back to match the first) is one of the most common gear-direction errors. Directly meshing gears always spin in opposite directions, so gear 3 must be opposite gear 2, which means it matches gear 1.

questions.stem: A very large gear meshes directly with a very small gear. A student assumes the large gear, because of its size, must always turn in the same direction as other large gears elsewhere in a machine, regardless of the meshing pattern. Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gear size (number of teeth) affects rotation speed, not direction; direction depends only on whether gears mesh directly (always opposite) or how many gears separate them in a chain, independent of size.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: larger gears always share the same rotation direction as each other, regardless of meshing.
choices.rationale: You assumed physical size determines rotation direction. Direction is governed entirely by meshing connections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: smaller gears always share the same rotation direction as each other, regardless of meshing.
choices.rationale: You assumed small size forces matching rotation directions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because gear size has no effect on anything mechanical.
choices.rationale: You claimed gear size has no mechanical effect. Gear size determines rotation speed and torque.

questions.explanation: A larger gear does not automatically spin the "same direction" or "opposite direction" based on its size alone. Direction is governed purely by the meshing/alternating rule; gear size only affects rotation speed.

questions.stem: A small gear with 12 teeth meshes with a large gear with 36 teeth. A student says, "the large gear obviously spins slower, so let's just guess it completes half as many rotations as the small gear," without calculating the exact teeth ratio. If the small gear completes 9 rotations, is "half as many" (4.5 rotations) the correct answer for the large gear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the exact ratio must be calculated from the actual teeth counts (36 ÷ 12 = 3, so the large gear turns 3 times slower); the small gear's $9$ rotations mean $12 \times 9 = 108$ teeth pass, so the large gear completes $108 \div 36 = 3$ rotations, not 4.5.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: "half as many rotations" is always a safe guess for any two meshing gears, regardless of their teeth counts.
choices.rationale: You relied on a random guess instead of calculating the exact ratio from teeth counts ( \div 12 = 3$).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: since the large gear is 3 times bigger, guessing half its rotations is close enough for these questions.
choices.rationale: You accepted an approximation. Mechanical calculations require exact ratios ( \div 36 = 3$).

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because gears with different teeth counts can never mesh together.
choices.rationale: You claimed gears with different teeth counts cannot mesh together.

questions.explanation: Assuming two gears "just spin at different speeds" without calculating the precise inverse ratio from their actual teeth counts leads to an incorrect answer. The correct ratio here is 3:1 (36 ÷ 12 = 3), giving 3 rotations for the large gear, not a guessed 4.5.

questions.stem: A small gear with 15 teeth meshes with a large gear with 45 teeth. If the large gear completes 4 full rotations, how many full rotations does the small gear complete?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed the smaller gear rotates at the same speed. The smaller gear has fewer teeth and must rotate faster ( \div 15 = 12$).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You multiplied by 9 instead of the 3:1 gear ratio.  \times 4 \div 15 = 12$.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You miscalculated the teeth ratio. The ratio is  \div 15 = 3$, so  \times 3 = 12$ rotations.

questions.explanation: The large gear completes $45 \times 4 = 180$ teeth passing the contact point. The small gear (15 teeth) must also have 180 teeth pass, so it completes $180 \div 15 = 12$ rotations.

questions.stem: Figure shows seven gears connected in a row, each meshing directly with its neighbor. The first gear turns clockwise. What direction does the seventh gear turn?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assigned an even-position direction to position 7. Odd positions match gear 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not turn at all
choices.rationale: You assumed a 7-gear train locks up and prevents movement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It turns in both directions at once
choices.rationale: You assigned impossible dual rotation directions to a single gear.

questions.explanation: Gear 7 is in an odd position, so it shares the same direction as gear 1. Since gear 1 turns clockwise, gear 7 also turns clockwise.

questions.stem: Figure shows four gears connected in a row. Gear 1 has 20 teeth and turns clockwise at 10 rotations per minute. Gear 2 has 10 teeth. What direction does gear 2 turn, and how many rotations per minute does it complete?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You kept the same rotation direction. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions, so gear 2 turns counter-clockwise.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You halved the speed instead of doubling it. A gear with half the teeth must spin twice as fast ( \div 10 = 20$ rpm).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You assumed identical speed and direction. Smaller meshing gears turn faster and in the opposite direction.

questions.explanation: Gear 2 meshes directly with gear 1, so it turns opposite (counter-clockwise). Since gear 1 (20 teeth) turns 10 times per minute, $20 \times 10 = 200$ teeth pass per minute; gear 2 (10 teeth) must also have 200 teeth pass per minute, so it completes $200 \div 10 = 20$ rotations per minute.

questions.stem: Figure shows a fixed pulley used to lift a 50 kg load. How much pulling force is required, and does the direction of pulling matter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 50 kg worth of force is required; only the direction of pulling changes (you can pull down to lift the load up)

choices.label: B
choices.text: 25 kg worth of force is required, since a pulley always halves the needed force
choices.rationale: You assumed all pulleys reduce force. Fixed pulleys only redirect force without offering mechanical advantage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 100 kg worth of force is required, since a fixed pulley doubles the needed force
choices.rationale: You assumed fixed pulleys double effort. Fixed pulleys redirect pulling force without changing effort magnitude.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No force is required, since pulleys eliminate the need for effort entirely
choices.rationale: You assumed pulleys eliminate work. Mechanical advantage cannot reduce required work to zero.

questions.explanation: A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force; it does not reduce the amount of force needed. The pulling force required still equals the load's weight, 50 kg worth of force.

questions.stem: Figure shows a movable pulley used to lift a 60 kg load. How much pulling force is required, and how far must the rope be pulled to lift the load by 2 meters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 30 kg of force is required, and 4 meters of rope must be pulled

choices.label: B
choices.text: 60 kg of force is required, and 2 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You treated the movable pulley as fixed. Movable pulleys halve force ( \div 2 = 30$ kg) while doubling rope distance ( \times 2 = 4$ m).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 30 kg of force is required, and 2 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You correctly halved the force but forgot distance trade-off. Halving effort requires doubling rope distance to 4 meters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 15 kg of force is required, and 8 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You applied a 4:1 mechanical advantage. A single movable pulley provides a 2:1 mechanical advantage ($ kg, $ m).

questions.explanation: A single movable pulley halves the force needed: $60 \div 2 = 30$ kg worth of force. Since force is halved, the rope must be pulled twice as far as the load moves: $2 \times 2 = 4$ meters.

questions.stem: Figure shows 2 movable pulleys working together to lift an 80 kg load. How much pulling force is required, and how far must the rope be pulled to lift the load by 3 meters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 20 kg of force is required, and 12 meters of rope must be pulled

choices.label: B
choices.text: 40 kg of force is required, and 6 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You applied a single movable pulley ratio (2:1) instead of 2 movable pulleys (4:1). Force is  \div 4 = 20$ kg and distance is  \times 4 = 12$ m.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 20 kg of force is required, and 6 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You correctly calculated force ( \div 4 = 20$ kg) but used a 2:1 distance multiplier instead of 4:1 ( \times 4 = 12$ m).

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10 kg of force is required, and 24 meters of rope must be pulled
choices.rationale: You applied an 8:1 mechanical advantage instead of 4:1 for 2 movable pulleys.

questions.explanation: With 2 movable pulleys, only one-quarter the load's weight in force is needed: $80 \div 4 = 20$ kg. The rope must be pulled four times the lifting distance: $3 \times 4 = 12$ meters.

questions.stem: A lever has a load of 100 kg placed 2 meters from the fulcrum. How much effort force is needed if applied 5 meters from the fulcrum on the other side?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You divided load by 5 instead of calculating $\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 2$. Effort is  \div 5 = 40$ kg.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You divided 100 kg by 2 instead of computing torque equilibrium ($\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 2$).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You cross-multiplied incorrectly as $\text{effort} \times 2 = 100 \times 5$. Effort pairs with effort distance.

questions.explanation: Using effort $\times$ effort distance = load $\times$ load distance: $\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 2 = 200$, so $\text{effort} = 200 \div 5 = 40$ kg.

questions.stem: A lever has a load of 90 kg placed 3 meters from the fulcrum. How much effort force is needed if applied 9 meters from the fulcrum on the other side?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You subtracted load distance from effort distance. Torque equilibrium requires $\text{effort} \times 9 = 90 \times 3 = 270$, giving $ kg.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You divided load by effort distance directly ( \div 9$). You must multiply load by load distance first ( \times 3 = 270$).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You forgot to divide total torque by effort distance ( \div 9 = 30$ kg).

questions.explanation: Using effort $\times$ effort distance = load $\times$ load distance: $\text{effort} \times 9 = 90 \times 3 = 270$, so $\text{effort} = 270 \div 9 = 30$ kg.

questions.stem: Using the same 100 kg load and 5-meter effort distance as before, if the fulcrum is moved so the load is now only 1 meter from the fulcrum (instead of 2 meters), how does the required effort change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The required effort drops from 40 kg to 20 kg, since moving the fulcrum closer to the load reduces the effort needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The required effort increases from 40 kg to 80 kg
choices.rationale: You assumed moving fulcrum closer to load increases effort. Shorter load distance reduces required effort ($\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 1 = 100 \implies 20$ kg).

choices.label: C
choices.text: The required effort stays the same at 40 kg, since only the effort distance affects the balance
choices.rationale: You ignored load distance. Torque balance depends on both load distance and effort distance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The required effort drops to 10 kg, since halving the load distance quarters the effort
choices.rationale: You quartered effort instead of halving it ( \times 1 \div 5 = 20$ kg).

questions.explanation: Recomputing: $\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 1 = 100$, so $\text{effort} = 100 \div 5 = 20$ kg. Moving the fulcrum closer to the load (from 2 m to 1 m) reduced the required effort from 40 kg to 20 kg.

questions.stem: Using the same 100 kg load and 5-meter effort distance, if the fulcrum is instead moved so the load is now 4 meters from the fulcrum (instead of 2 meters), how does the required effort change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The required effort increases from 40 kg to 80 kg, since moving the fulcrum farther from the load requires more effort

choices.label: B
choices.text: The required effort decreases from 40 kg to 20 kg
choices.rationale: You inverted the effect. Moving fulcrum farther from load increases load torque, requiring more effort ($\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 4 = 400 \implies 80$ kg).

choices.label: C
choices.text: The required effort stays the same at 40 kg
choices.rationale: You assumed load distance does not alter required effort.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The required effort increases to 400 kg
choices.rationale: You forgot to divide total torque by effort distance ( \div 5 = 80$ kg).

questions.explanation: Recomputing: $\text{effort} \times 5 = 100 \times 4 = 400$, so $\text{effort} = 400 \div 5 = 80$ kg. Moving the fulcrum farther from the load (from 2 m to 4 m) increased the required effort from 40 kg to 80 kg.

questions.stem: A student sets up a single fixed pulley to lift a 70 kg load and claims, "using this pulley makes the load easier to lift, since pulleys always reduce the force needed." Is this claim correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: only movable pulleys (attached to the load) reduce the required force; a fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force, so the full 70 kg worth of force is still needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any pulley, fixed or movable, always reduces the required force by half.
choices.rationale: You assumed fixed pulleys provide mechanical advantage. Only movable pulleys reduce required force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because this specific load happens to weigh exactly 70 kg.
choices.rationale: You assumed load weight gives fixed pulleys mechanical advantage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because fixed pulleys actually require more force than lifting without any pulley.
choices.rationale: You claimed fixed pulleys increase force. Fixed pulleys require equal force to the load weight.

questions.explanation: Assuming a single fixed pulley "makes lifting easier" in terms of force is incorrect: it only makes lifting more convenient by letting you pull in a different direction, while still requiring the full weight's worth of force.

questions.stem: A movable pulley halves the force needed to lift a 50 kg load, requiring only 25 kg of pulling force. A student assumes that since the force is halved, the rope-pulling distance must also be halved compared to how far the load rises. Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: reducing the required force always comes with a distance trade-off; a movable pulley that halves the force requires pulling the rope twice as far as the load actually rises, not half as far.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: halving the force always means halving the pulling distance as well.
choices.rationale: You ignored work conservation. Halving effort force requires doubling displacement distance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because this specific load weighs 50 kg.
choices.rationale: You tied the work trade-off strictly to the specific load value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because movable pulleys never affect rope-pulling distance at all.
choices.rationale: You claimed movable pulleys do not change distance. Movable pulleys double required rope travel.

questions.explanation: Simple machines like pulleys reduce the force needed but always require moving a correspondingly greater distance: you cannot reduce force without some distance trade-off. A movable pulley halving the force also doubles the rope distance you must pull, not halves it.

questions.stem: A student sets up the lever balance equation as "effort × load distance = load × effort distance" for a lever with a 100 kg load 2 meters from the fulcrum and effort applied 5 meters from the fulcrum. Using this (incorrect) setup, they compute effort × 2 = 100 × 5, getting effort = 250 kg. What is wrong with this approach, and what is the correct effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student cross-paired the values incorrectly; the correct equation is effort × effort distance = load × load distance, giving effort × 5 = 100 × 2, so the correct effort is 40 kg, not 250 kg.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nothing is wrong; 250 kg is the correct effort force needed.
choices.rationale: You accepted cross-paired torque equations. Effort pairs with effort arm length.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student's equation is correct, but their arithmetic is wrong; the correct effort using their equation is 200 kg.
choices.rationale: You validated an incorrect mechanical formula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lever balance equation does not apply to this scenario at all.
choices.rationale: You claimed lever balance formulas do not apply to levers.

questions.explanation: Keep effort paired with its own distance, and load paired with its own distance: do not cross-pair effort's force with the load's distance (or vice versa). The correct equation, effort × effort distance = load × load distance, gives effort × 5 = 100 × 2 = 200, so effort = 40 kg.

questions.stem: A lever balances a load using 25 kg of effort applied 8 meters from the fulcrum, against a 100 kg load. How far from the fulcrum is the load placed?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You divided $ by $ instead of $. Load distance is  \times 8 \div 100 = 2$ meters.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed load distance equals effort distance despite unequal forces.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied effort distance by ratio  \div 25$ instead of dividing ( \div 4 = 2$ meters).

questions.explanation: Using effort $\times$ effort distance = load $\times$ load distance: $25 \times 8 = 200 = 100 \times \text{load distance}$, so load distance $= 200 \div 100 = 2$ meters.

questions.stem: A lever balances a 90 kg load placed 3 meters from the fulcrum, using 15 kg of effort force. How far from the fulcrum must the effort be applied?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You divided load weight by effort force ( \div 15$) without multiplying by load distance ( \div 15 = 18$ m).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You forgot to divide total torque by effort force ( \div 15 = 18$ meters).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You estimated the calculation ( \times 3 \div 15 = 18$ meters).

questions.explanation: Using effort $\times$ effort distance = load $\times$ load distance: $15 \times \text{effort distance} = 90 \times 3 = 270$, so effort distance $= 270 \div 15 = 18$ meters.

questions.stem: How many movable pulleys, working together, are needed to reduce the required lifting force to one-eighth of the load's weight?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You calculated ^2 = 4$, which gives $\dfrac{1}{4}$ force. 3 pulleys give $\dfrac{1}{2^3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$ force.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You calculated ^4 = 16$, which gives $\dfrac{1}{16}$ force. 3 pulleys give $\dfrac{1}{8}$ force.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You used pulley count equal to denominator. Pulley count $ reduces force by $\dfrac{1}{2^n}$.

questions.explanation: Each movable pulley halves the required force again: 1 pulley gives one-half, 2 pulleys give one-quarter, and 3 pulleys give one-eighth ($\dfrac{1}{2^3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$).

questions.stem: A 120 kg load sits on a lever, 2 meters from the fulcrum. Effort is applied 6 meters from the fulcrum, but the effort itself is supplied through a rope running over a single movable pulley system, which halves the pulling force needed at the rope. What is the final pulling force required at the rope?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You calculated lever effort ( \times 2 \div 6 = 40$ kg) but omitted the movable pulley's 2:1 reduction ( \div 2 = 20$ kg).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You quartered the lever effort instead of halving it ( \div 2 = 20$ kg).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied lever effort by 2 instead of dividing ( \div 2 = 20$ kg).

questions.explanation: First, the lever balance: $\text{effort} \times 6 = 120 \times 2 = 240$, so the lever requires $240 \div 6 = 40$ kg of effort force. Since a movable pulley halves the pulling force needed, the final rope-pulling force is $40 \div 2 = 20$ kg.

questions.stem: Two different setups are used to lift the same 100 kg load. Setup A uses a lever: the load is placed 2 meters from the fulcrum, and effort is applied 8 meters from the fulcrum. Setup B uses 2 movable pulleys working together directly on the load, with no lever involved. Compare the required force in each setup, and identify which setup requires the rope or effort to travel farther for the same 2-meter lift.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both setups require the same 25 kg of force (Setup A gives $100 \times 2 \div 8 = 25$ kg; Setup B gives $100 \div 4 = 25$ kg), but Setup B requires pulling the rope farther (8 meters, since 2 movable pulleys require 4 times the lifting distance) compared to Setup A's effort-side movement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Setup A requires less force than Setup B, and both require the same travel distance.
choices.rationale: You incorrectly claimed Setup A needs less force ($ kg vs $ kg) and ignored Setup B's 8m rope travel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Setup B requires less force than Setup A, and Setup A requires a farther travel distance.
choices.rationale: You inverted force and distance comparisons between lever and pulley setups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both setups require exactly the same force and the same travel distance, with no difference at all.
choices.rationale: You ignored distance trade-offs. Setup B requires pulling 8m of rope to lift 2m.

questions.explanation: Setup A (lever): $\text{effort} \times 8 = 100 \times 2 = 200$, so effort $= 200 \div 8 = 25$ kg. Setup B (2 movable pulleys): force $= 100 \div 4 = 25$ kg, matching Setup A's force, but Setup B requires pulling the rope $2 \times 4 = 8$ meters to lift the load 2 meters, illustrating that different mechanisms can reach the same force reduction with different distance trade-offs.

questions.stem: Figure shows a spring that stretches 5 cm when a 2 kg weight is attached. How far will it stretch with an 8 kg weight?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You doubled the stretch when the weight went up four times. From 2 kg to 8 kg is a factor of four, so the stretch is $5 \times 4$.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added the new weight to the original stretch. Stretch and weight are different units and scale by multiplication, not addition.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied the stretch by the new weight directly. You must scale by the ratio of the weights, which is 4, not the new weight itself.

questions.explanation: The weight increased by a factor of $8 \div 2 = 4$. Since stretch is proportional to weight, the stretch also increases by the same factor: $5 \times 4 = 20$ cm.

questions.stem: Figure shows a spring that stretches 6 cm when a 3 kg weight is attached. How far will it stretch with a 9 kg weight?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You doubled the stretch instead of tripling it. The weight increased from 3 kg to 9 kg, which is a factor of three.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added the new weight to the original stretch. You must scale the stretch by the ratio of the weights, not add them together.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied the stretch by the new weight directly. You must scale by the ratio of the weights, which is 3, not the new weight itself.

questions.explanation: The weight increased by a factor of $9 \div 3 = 3$. Since stretch is proportional to weight, the stretch also increases by the same factor: $6 \times 3 = 18$ cm.

questions.stem: Figure shows a spring that stretches 4 cm for every 1 kg attached. How much weight is attached if the spring has stretched 20 cm?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You subtracted the unit stretch from the total stretch. You must divide the total stretch by the unit stretch to find the weight.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added the total stretch and the unit stretch together. You must divide the total stretch by the stretch per kilogram to find the weight.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You confused the unit stretch with the total weight. The spring stretches 4 cm per kg, so a 20 cm stretch requires 5 kg.

questions.explanation: Each 4 cm unit of stretch corresponds to 1 kg. Dividing the total stretch by that unit: $20 \div 4 = 5$, so 5 kg is attached.

questions.stem: Figure shows a spring that stretches 2 cm for every 1 kg attached. How much weight is attached if the spring has stretched 18 cm?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You subtracted the unit stretch from the total stretch. You must divide the total stretch by the stretch per kilogram to find the weight.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You multiplied the total stretch by the unit stretch. You must divide the total stretch by the stretch per kilogram to find the weight.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You confused the unit stretch with the total weight. The spring stretches 2 cm per kg, so an 18 cm stretch requires 9 kg.

questions.explanation: Each 2 cm unit of stretch corresponds to 1 kg. Dividing the total stretch by that unit: $18 \div 2 = 9$, so 9 kg is attached.

questions.stem: Figure shows Spring A stretching 3 cm under a 6 kg weight, and Spring B stretching 8 cm under the same 6 kg weight. Which spring is stiffer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spring A, since it stretched less under the identical weight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spring B, since it stretched more under the identical weight
choices.rationale: You assumed that a stiffer spring moves more. Stiffness is the resistance to stretching, so the stiffer spring is the one that stretches less.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both springs are equally stiff, since they hold the same weight
choices.rationale: You assumed that holding the same weight makes them equally stiff. Stiffness is determined by how much they stretch under that weight, which differs here.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither spring can be compared without knowing their exact spring constants
choices.rationale: You assumed you need the exact constants. You can compare stiffness directly by looking at which spring stretches less under the same weight.

questions.explanation: Under the identical weight, Spring A stretched less (3 cm) than Spring B (8 cm). A spring that stretches less under the same weight is stiffer.

questions.stem: Using Spring A from before (stretches 3 cm under a 6 kg weight), predict its stretch under a 12 kg weight.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You added the original weight to the stretch. You must multiply the stretch by the ratio of the new weight to the old weight.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed the stretch remains the same. Since the weight increased, the stretch must also increase proportionally.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied the stretch by the new weight directly. You must multiply by the ratio of the weights, which is 2, not 12.

questions.explanation: The scaling factor between the weights is $12 \div 6 = 2$. Applying the same factor to the stretch: $3 \times 2 = 6$ cm.

questions.stem: Figure shows Spring C stretching 4 cm under an 8 kg weight, and Spring D stretching 10 cm under the same 8 kg weight. Which spring is stiffer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spring C, since it stretched less under the identical weight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spring D, since it stretched more under the identical weight
choices.rationale: You assumed that a larger stretch means greater stiffness. Stiffness is the resistance to stretching, so the stiffer spring stretches less.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed they are equally stiff because they hold the same weight. Since they stretch different amounts under that weight, their stiffness differs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither spring can be compared without more information
choices.rationale: You assumed more data is needed. Since both springs are tested under the identical weight, you can directly compare their stretch to find which is stiffer.

questions.explanation: Under the identical 8 kg weight, Spring C stretched less (4 cm) than Spring D (10 cm), making Spring C the stiffer spring.

questions.stem: A spring stretches 4 cm under a 2 kg weight. A student assumes "every additional 2 kg simply adds another 4 cm," and uses this to predict the stretch under a 3 kg weight by rounding up to "2 lots of 2 kg," predicting $4+4=8$ cm. What is the actual stretch at 3 kg, using the correct proportional (ratio) method, and what did the student get wrong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The actual stretch is 6 cm ($3 \div 2 = 1.5$ scaling factor, so $4 \times 1.5 = 6$ cm); the student's error was adding a fixed amount per fixed weight increment instead of scaling by the true ratio, which only coincidentally matches for whole-number multiples of the original weight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The actual stretch is 8 cm, matching the student's fixed-amount reasoning exactly.
choices.rationale: You accepted the student's error of adding a fixed amount. Stretch scales proportionally by multiplication, so a 1.5 times increase in weight means a 1.5 times increase in stretch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The actual stretch is 4 cm, since only the original weight and stretch matter.
choices.rationale: You assumed the stretch does not change when the weight changes. Stretch increases proportionally as weight increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The actual stretch cannot be determined without knowing the spring's exact material.
choices.rationale: You assumed the material is needed. The ratio of stretch to weight provides all the information required to predict the new stretch.

questions.explanation: Stretch is proportional to weight (a constant ratio), not simply increased by a fixed amount each time weight increases by some fixed increment. The correct approach scales by the true ratio ($3 \div 2 = 1.5$), giving $4 \times 1.5 = 6$ cm: the student's fixed-amount reasoning only happens to work for whole-number weight multiples, not fractional ones like this.

questions.stem: Spring E stretches 9 cm under a 3 kg weight. Spring F stretches 3 cm under the same 3 kg weight. A student claims Spring E is the "stiffer" spring, reasoning that it moved (stretched) more. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a stiffer spring stretches less under the same weight, not more; Spring F, which stretched less, is actually the stiffer spring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: "stiffer" means the spring that stretches the most under a given weight.
choices.rationale: You agreed with the student's misconception that stiffness means moving more. Stiffness is resistance to stretching, so the stiffer spring moves less.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because Spring E is physically larger than Spring F.
choices.rationale: You assumed physical size determines stiffness. Stiffness is determined entirely by how much a spring stretches under a given weight, not its size.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because Spring E and Spring F are actually the same spring.
choices.rationale: You assumed the springs are identical. Since they stretch different amounts under the same weight, they must be different springs with different stiffness.

questions.explanation: It is easy to intuitively assume "stiffer" means "moves more" or "stretches more." In fact, stiffness describes resistance to stretching, so a stiffer spring is precisely the one that stretches the least for a given weight: here, Spring F, not Spring E.

questions.stem: Spring G stretches 4 cm under an 8 kg weight. Spring H stretches 4 cm under a 16 kg weight. A student claims both springs are equally stiff, since they stretched the same amount. Is this a valid comparison?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the two springs were tested under different weights, so this comparison is not valid; Spring H is actually stiffer, since it resisted stretching just as much despite carrying double the weight of Spring G.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: since both springs stretched exactly 4 cm, they must be equally stiff regardless of the weights used.
choices.rationale: You ignored the different weights. To compare stiffness, you must factor in the weight applied; Spring H held twice the weight for the same stretch, making it stiffer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because both springs are made of the same material.
choices.rationale: You assumed the material guarantees equal stiffness. The different weights required to produce the same stretch prove the springs have different stiffness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because Spring G and Spring H cannot both stretch exactly 4 cm.
choices.rationale: You assumed two springs cannot stretch the same amount. They can, but because they required different weights to do so, their stiffness is not equal.

questions.explanation: To fairly compare which spring is stiffer, the weight applied to each spring must be the same: comparing stretches under different weights does not directly reveal which spring is inherently stiffer. Spring H is actually stiffer, since it resisted stretching just as much despite a heavier weight.

questions.stem: A spring stretches 2 cm for every 1 kg attached. What is its stretch under a 7 kg weight, and what weight would cause a 21 cm stretch?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 14 cm under 7 kg; 10.5 kg would cause a 21 cm stretch

choices.label: B
choices.text: 9 cm under 7 kg; 19 kg would cause a 21 cm stretch
choices.rationale: You added the weight to the ratio instead of multiplying. You must multiply 7 kg by 2 cm/kg to find the stretch, and divide 21 cm by 2 cm/kg to find the weight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 14 cm under 7 kg; 42 kg would cause a 21 cm stretch
choices.rationale: You multiplied the 21 cm stretch by the ratio instead of dividing. To find the weight, you must divide the total stretch by the stretch per kilogram.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 7 cm under 7 kg; 10.5 kg would cause a 21 cm stretch
choices.rationale: You assumed the stretch is equal to the weight. Since the spring stretches 2 cm for every 1 kg, a 7 kg weight causes a 14 cm stretch.

questions.explanation: Using the ratio of 2 cm per kg: at 7 kg, stretch $= 2 \times 7 = 14$ cm. For a 21 cm stretch, weight $= 21 \div 2 = 10.5$ kg.

questions.stem: Figure shows Spring I stretching 7 cm under a 5 kg weight, and Spring J stretching 3 cm under the same 5 kg weight. Which spring is looser (less stiff)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spring I, since it stretched more under the identical weight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spring J, since it stretched less under the identical weight
choices.rationale: You confused looser with stiffer. A looser spring offers less resistance, so it will stretch more, not less, under the same weight.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed holding the same weight makes them equally loose. Since they stretched different amounts, one spring offers less resistance than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither spring can be classified as looser without more data
choices.rationale: You assumed you need more data. Since both were tested with the exact same weight, the one that stretched more is clearly looser.

questions.explanation: A spring that stretches more under the same weight is the looser (less stiff) one. Spring I stretched more (7 cm vs. 3 cm), so it is the looser spring.

questions.stem: Spring L stretches 4 cm under a 2 kg weight, and 10 cm under a 4 kg weight. A student claims this data is consistent with a simple proportional (Hooke's law) relationship. Check the ratios: is this claim correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the first ratio is $4 \div 2 = 2$ cm per kg, but the second ratio is $10 \div 4 = 2.5$ cm per kg; since these ratios are not equal, this spring's behavior is not simply proportional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: both stretches came from the same spring, so they must automatically be proportional.
choices.rationale: You assumed a single spring always behaves proportionally. You must check the ratios; since they differ (2 vs 2.5), the spring's behavior is not proportional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: the ratios $4 \div 2$ and $10 \div 4$ are actually equal.
choices.rationale: You miscalculated the ratios. $4 \div 2$ is 2, while $10 \div 4$ is 2.5, so the ratios are not equal and the relationship is not proportional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because a spring can never stretch different amounts under different weights.
choices.rationale: You assumed springs cannot stretch different amounts. They do, but the relationship is only proportional if the ratio of stretch to weight remains constant.

questions.explanation: To check proportionality, compute stretch-per-weight for each data point: $4 \div 2 = 2$ cm/kg and $10 \div 4 = 2.5$ cm/kg. Since these two ratios differ, the data is not consistent with a simple proportional relationship.

questions.stem: A spring stretches 5 cm under a 2 kg weight. What total weight would cause a 20 cm stretch, and how much additional weight beyond that would be needed to reach a 30 cm stretch?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 8 kg causes a 20 cm stretch; 4 kg more (12 kg total) is needed to reach 30 cm

choices.label: B
choices.text: 8 kg causes a 20 cm stretch; 10 kg more is needed to reach 30 cm
choices.rationale: You gave the difference in stretch instead of the difference in weight. The extra 10 cm of stretch requires only 4 kg more weight, since the ratio is 2.5 cm/kg.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 4 kg causes a 20 cm stretch; 2 kg more is needed to reach 30 cm
choices.rationale: You divided the stretch by 5 instead of 2.5. The ratio is $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ cm/kg, so a 20 cm stretch requires 8 kg, not 4 kg.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 8 kg causes a 20 cm stretch; 8 kg more is needed to reach 30 cm
choices.rationale: You assumed reaching 30 cm requires doubling the weight. A 30 cm stretch requires 12 kg in total, which is only 4 kg more than the 8 kg already attached.

questions.explanation: The ratio is $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ cm per kg. For 20 cm: $20 \div 2.5 = 8$ kg. For 30 cm: $30 \div 2.5 = 12$ kg. The additional weight needed beyond 8 kg is $12 - 8 = 4$ kg.

questions.stem: Spring P stretches 6 cm under a 3 kg weight. Spring Q stretches 8 cm under a 4 kg weight. Spring R stretches 5 cm under a 5 kg weight. Since these three springs were tested under three different weights, rank them from stiffest to loosest using their stretch-per-kilogram ratio.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spring R is stiffest (1 cm/kg); Springs P and Q are tied for second, equally less stiff than R (each 2 cm/kg)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spring P is stiffest, then Spring Q, then Spring R, based on their raw stretch amounts (6 cm, 8 cm, 5 cm)
choices.rationale: You ranked them by raw stretch without accounting for the different weights. You must calculate the stretch-per-kilogram ratio to compare their stiffness fairly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spring R is loosest, since it has the smallest raw stretch number
choices.rationale: You assumed a smaller raw stretch means it is looser, and you ignored the weights. A smaller stretch-per-kilogram ratio actually means a stiffer spring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three springs are equally stiff, since they were tested under different weights and cannot be compared
choices.rationale: You assumed they cannot be compared. By calculating the stretch-per-kilogram ratio for each spring, you can compare their stiffness directly despite the different weights.

questions.explanation: Since the weights differ, compare stretch-per-kilogram instead of raw stretch: Spring P is $6 \div 3 = 2$ cm/kg, Spring Q is $8 \div 4 = 2$ cm/kg, and Spring R is $5 \div 5 = 1$ cm/kg. A smaller ratio means a stiffer spring, so Spring R is stiffest, with P and Q tied for second.

questions.stem: What is the term for the single point where an object's entire weight can be thought of as concentrated, balancing perfectly in every direction?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You confused the concentration of weight with the area the object rests on. The base of support is the contact area on the ground, not a single point of balance.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You confused the balancing point of the object itself with a pivot point. A fulcrum is the external support about which a lever pivots, not the object's internal balancing point.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You confused the balance point with the critical angle of tilt. A tipping point is the threshold where an object falls over, not the point where its weight is concentrated.

questions.explanation: The center of gravity is the single point where an object's entire weight can be thought of as concentrated, balancing perfectly in every direction.

questions.stem: What is the term for the area on the ground enclosed by an object's points (or edges) of contact with the ground?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You confused the area on the ground with the single point where weight is concentrated. Center of gravity is an internal balance point, not the contact area.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You confused the resting area with a pivot point. A fulcrum is the specific point a lever rests or turns on, not the entire area enclosed by the object's feet.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You guessed a term related to levers. Load distance refers to how far a weight is from a fulcrum, not the area an object rests upon.

questions.explanation: The base of support is the area on the ground enclosed by an object's points or edges of contact with the ground, like the rectangle connecting a table's four feet.

questions.stem: Figure shows an object with an imaginary vertical line dropped straight down from its center of gravity. Under what condition does the object remain stable and not tip over?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vertical line falls within the object's base of support

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vertical line falls exactly at the center of the object's base
choices.rationale: You assumed the line must be perfectly centered. As long as the line falls anywhere within the boundaries of the base of support, the object remains stable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The object's weight is below a certain threshold
choices.rationale: You assumed stability depends on how light the object is. Stability depends on the alignment of the center of gravity with the base, not the total weight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The object's base of support is perfectly circular
choices.rationale: You assumed a specific shape is required for stability. The base of support can be any shape, as long as the vertical line from the center of gravity falls within it.

questions.explanation: An object remains stable as long as an imaginary vertical line dropped straight down from its center of gravity falls within its base of support. If that line falls outside the base of support, the object tips over.

questions.stem: Figure shows a short, wide pyramid and a tall, narrow pyramid, both the same weight and made of the same uniform material. Which one is more stable, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The short, wide pyramid, since it has both a lower center of gravity and a wider base of support

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tall, narrow pyramid, since height always improves stability
choices.rationale: You assumed being taller makes an object more stable. A taller object has a higher center of gravity, which actually makes it easier to tip over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both pyramids are equally stable, since they weigh the same
choices.rationale: You assumed equal weight means equal stability. Stability also depends heavily on the height of the center of gravity and the width of the base.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tall, narrow pyramid, since a narrower base is always more stable
choices.rationale: You assumed a narrower base is better. A narrow base means the center of gravity has less distance to shift before the object tips over.

questions.explanation: The short, wide pyramid has a lower center of gravity (since it is shorter) and a wider base of support (since it is wider). Both factors independently improve stability, making it more stable than the tall, narrow pyramid.

questions.stem: Figure shows a rectangular box being slowly tilted to one side, pivoting on one bottom edge. At what point does the box tip over rather than settling back down?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moment the vertical line from its center of gravity moves beyond the edge of the base of support it is pivoting on

choices.label: B
choices.text: As soon as the box is tilted at all, even slightly
choices.rationale: You assumed any tilt causes tipping. An object will rock back to its original position as long as its center of gravity remains over its base of support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only once the box is tilted a full 90 degrees
choices.rationale: You assumed it must fall completely flat to tip. The tipping point happens much earlier, the moment its center of gravity passes the edge it is pivoting on.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The box never tips over regardless of tilt, since it is resting on the ground
choices.rationale: You assumed resting on the ground makes it immune to tipping. Once the center of gravity is pushed past the pivot edge, gravity will pull the object over.

questions.explanation: The box remains stable as long as the vertical line from its center of gravity stays within its base of support. It tips over at the exact moment this line moves beyond the edge of the base of support it is still pivoting on.

questions.stem: A moving truck carries the same total weight of cargo, either stacked very high or spread out lower. Which loading method makes the truck more stable while turning corners?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spreading the cargo lower, since it keeps the center of gravity closer to the ground

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stacking the cargo high, since it distributes weight more evenly
