choices.rationale: You assumed stacking high distributes weight evenly. Stacking high raises the center of gravity, making the truck much more likely to tip over during a turn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both loading methods provide exactly the same stability
choices.rationale: You assumed only the total weight matters. How the weight is distributed vertically changes the center of gravity, which directly affects stability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stacking the cargo high, since a higher center of gravity always improves turning stability
choices.rationale: You assumed a higher center of gravity is better for turns. A higher center of gravity acts like a longer lever arm for tipping, making the truck less stable.

questions.explanation: Spreading cargo lower keeps the center of gravity closer to the ground, requiring a larger tilt (like from a sharp turn) before the vertical line from the center of gravity could be pushed outside the truck's base of support: making it more stable while turning.

questions.stem: A person standing with feet close together is compared to the same person standing with feet spread wider apart. Which stance is more stable against being pushed sideways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Feet spread wider apart, since it increases the base of support

choices.label: B
choices.text: Feet close together, since it lowers the center of gravity
choices.rationale: You assumed bringing feet together lowers the center of gravity. It actually narrows the base of support, making it much easier to be pushed over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both stances are equally stable against sideways pushes
choices.rationale: You assumed the width of the stance does not matter. Spreading your feet widens your base of support, meaning you can lean further before falling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Feet close together, since a narrower base is always more stable
choices.rationale: You assumed a narrower base is better. A narrow base means your center of gravity only has to shift a tiny bit sideways before you tip over.

questions.explanation: Spreading the feet wider apart increases the base of support, meaning the vertical line from the center of gravity can shift farther sideways before falling outside that base: making the wider stance more stable against sideways pushes.

questions.stem: An object has a very low center of gravity but an extremely narrow base of support. A student assumes this object must be very stable, "since only the center of gravity's height matters." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: stability depends on both the center of gravity's height and the base of support's width; an object with a low center of gravity but an extremely narrow base can still tip over easily.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: a low center of gravity alone always guarantees maximum stability, regardless of base width.
choices.rationale: You assumed the center of gravity is the only factor that matters. If the base is extremely narrow, even a low center of gravity will quickly shift outside it and cause tipping.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: base of support width has no effect on stability at all.
choices.rationale: You assumed the base of support is irrelevant. The base defines the safe zone; if it is too narrow, the object will tip over with very little tilt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because this object cannot have a center of gravity at all.
choices.rationale: You assumed an object can exist without a center of gravity. Every object with mass has a center of gravity where its weight is effectively concentrated.

questions.explanation: An object could have a low center of gravity but still be unstable if its base of support is extremely narrow; both factors must be considered together, not just one in isolation.

questions.stem: A very heavy object has a high center of gravity and a narrow base of support. A student assumes this object must be stable, "since heavier objects are always more stable." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: stability depends on the location of the center of gravity relative to the base of support, not simply on how much an object weighs; a heavy object with a high center of gravity and narrow base can still tip over easily.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: heavier objects are always more stable than lighter ones, regardless of their shape.
choices.rationale: You assumed weight alone creates stability. If that heavy weight is balanced high above a narrow base, it will still tip over very easily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because this object's weight makes its base of support automatically wider.
choices.rationale: You assumed weight changes the physical dimensions of the base. An object's weight does not automatically widen its contact area with the ground.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because heavy objects cannot have a center of gravity.
choices.rationale: You assumed heavy objects lack a center of gravity. Every object has a center of gravity, and a high one makes tipping easier regardless of weight.

questions.explanation: Stability depends on the location of the center of gravity relative to the base of support, not simply on how much an object weighs overall. A very heavy object with a high center of gravity and a narrow base can still tip over easily, despite its large weight.

questions.stem: A student says, "this box is stable," treating stability as a fixed, permanent property of the box regardless of how it is positioned. Is this the correct way to think about stability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: an object can be perfectly stable while sitting still, but become unstable once tilted enough that its center of gravity's vertical line moves outside the base of support; stability depends on the specific tilt angle, not a fixed, unchanging fact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: once an object is described as "stable," it remains stable at every possible tilt angle.
choices.rationale: You assumed stability is absolute. As soon as you tilt the object far enough, its center of gravity moves past its base, and it will fall over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: stability is a permanent property that never changes, regardless of orientation.
choices.rationale: You assumed orientation does not matter. If you turn a stable box on its pointed corner, it immediately becomes unstable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because boxes can never be considered stable under any circumstance.
choices.rationale: You assumed no box is ever stable. A box sitting flat on the ground with its center of gravity over its base is perfectly stable until disturbed.

questions.explanation: Assuming an object "is stable" as an absolute, unchanging fact (rather than "is stable at this specific tilt angle") misses that further tilting can push any object past its tipping point, given enough tilt.

questions.stem: A bottom-heavy roly-poly toy (weighted heavily at its rounded base) is pushed over onto its side. Why does it always return to standing upright?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its center of gravity is very low (concentrated near its heavy base), so the vertical line from its center of gravity quickly returns within its base of support as it rocks, pulling it back upright

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its base of support is extremely narrow, which always causes objects to return upright
choices.rationale: You assumed a narrow base helps it stand up. A narrow base usually makes an object tip over easier; it is the extremely low center of gravity that pulls this toy back up.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The toy has no center of gravity, so it cannot tip over in the first place
choices.rationale: You assumed the toy lacks a center of gravity. The reason it works is precisely because its center of gravity is heavily weighted at the very bottom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The toy is simply too light to be affected by gravity at all
choices.rationale: You assumed it ignores gravity. Gravity is exactly what pulls the heavy, rounded bottom back down against the ground.

questions.explanation: The toy's very low center of gravity, concentrated near its heavy rounded base, means the vertical line from its center of gravity stays within (or quickly returns within) its base of support as it rocks, pulling it back upright rather than tipping over completely.

questions.stem: A sports utility vehicle (SUV) has a higher center of gravity than a sports car with the same wheel base width. Which vehicle is more prone to rolling over while making a sharp turn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The SUV, since its higher center of gravity requires less tilt before the vertical line from its center of gravity could fall outside its base of support

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sports car, since lower vehicles are always more prone to rolling over
choices.rationale: You assumed being lower increases rollover risk. A lower center of gravity keeps the vertical line inside the wheelbase much better during a turn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both vehicles are equally prone to rolling over, since they share the same wheel base width
choices.rationale: You assumed only the wheelbase matters. Because the SUV is taller, its center of gravity swings out further and faster during a sharp turn than the sports car's does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither vehicle can roll over, since both have four wheels providing support
choices.rationale: You assumed four wheels guarantee stability. Any vehicle can roll over if cornering forces push its center of gravity outside the footprint of its wheels.

questions.explanation: A higher center of gravity requires less tilt before the vertical line from the center of gravity could be pushed outside the base of support (the wheel base). Since the SUV has a higher center of gravity than the sports car (with the same base width), it is more prone to rolling over.

questions.stem: A ladder with widely spread legs is compared to an identical-height ladder with legs placed close together. Which ladder is more stable against tipping sideways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ladder with widely spread legs, since it has a wider base of support

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ladder with legs close together, since a narrower base concentrates support
choices.rationale: You assumed concentrated support is better. A narrow base means even a small sideways lean will push your center of gravity outside the base, causing a fall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both ladders are equally stable, since they are the same height
choices.rationale: You assumed height is the only factor. The width of the base of support is just as critical; a wider base allows you to lean further safely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither ladder can be compared without knowing their exact weight
choices.rationale: You assumed weight determines stability. While weight matters, the geometric relationship between the center of gravity and the base of support dictates when tipping occurs.

questions.explanation: A wider base of support means the vertical line from the center of gravity can shift farther sideways before falling outside that base, making the widely-spread-leg ladder more stable against tipping sideways.

questions.stem: A box's base of support extends 3 meters from the edge it is currently pivoting on. At a certain tilt angle, the vertical line dropped from its center of gravity falls 2 meters from that same edge, still within the base. Does the box tip over at this specific angle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since 2 meters is still within the 3-meter base of support, the box remains stable at this tilt angle; it would only tip if the vertical line moved beyond the 3-meter edge

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any tilt at all causes the box to tip over immediately
choices.rationale: You assumed an object cannot tilt without falling. As long as the center of gravity remains directly over any part of the base, the object will rock back to a stable position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: since 2 meters is more than half of 3 meters, the box has already tipped
choices.rationale: You assumed it tips once it passes the halfway mark. It only tips once the center of gravity passes the very outer edge of the 3-meter base.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the box's exact weight
choices.rationale: You assumed weight changes the tipping geometry. Tipping is based purely on whether the center of gravity is over the base, regardless of how heavy the box is.

questions.explanation: The box remains stable as long as the vertical line from its center of gravity stays within its base of support. Since 2 meters is still within the 3-meter base, the box has not yet tipped: it would only tip once the line moves beyond the 3-meter edge.

questions.stem: Box P has a low center of gravity and a wide base of support. Box Q has a high center of gravity and a narrow base of support. Both boxes are gradually tilted at the same steady rate, starting from level ground. Which box tips over first, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Box Q tips over first, since both its higher center of gravity and its narrower base of support independently require less tilt before the vertical line from its center of gravity falls outside its base, compared to Box P's more favorable combination of both factors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Box P tips over first, since a lower center of gravity always causes objects to tip sooner.
choices.rationale: You assumed a lower center of gravity makes tipping easier. It actually makes it much harder, because the object must tilt further before its weight shifts outside its base.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both boxes tip over at exactly the same tilt angle, since tilt rate is the only factor that matters.
choices.rationale: You assumed the speed of tilting is all that matters. The physical dimensions (how wide the base is and how high the weight is centered) determine the exact angle they tip at.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither box will ever tip over, regardless of how far they are tilted.
choices.rationale: You assumed they are immune to tipping. Once any box is tilted far enough that its center of gravity passes its base, it will inevitably tip over.

questions.explanation: Both stability factors favor Box P: a lower center of gravity and a wider base of support each independently require a larger tilt before the vertical line from the center of gravity is pushed outside the base. Box Q, with both a higher center of gravity and a narrower base, tips over first.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes: a square, a rectangle, a rhombus, and a triangle. Which one does not belong, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The triangle, since it has only 3 sides while the other three shapes all have 4 sides

choices.label: B
choices.text: The square, since it is the only shape with equal sides
choices.rationale: You focused on equal side lengths instead of total side count. The rhombus also has four equal sides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rectangle, since it is the only shape that is not a rhombus
choices.rationale: You focused on named shape sub-types. Square, rectangle, and rhombus are all 4-sided quadrilaterals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rhombus, since it is the only shape with slanted sides
choices.rationale: You focused on visual orientation. All three 4-sided shapes share quadrilateral membership.

questions.explanation: The square, rectangle, and rhombus all have 4 sides (they are all quadrilaterals). The triangle has only 3 sides, so it is the odd-one-out.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes: a perfect circle, a square, an equilateral triangle, and an irregular, lopsided blob shape with no matching sides. Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The irregular blob, since it has no line of symmetry, while the other three shapes can all be folded so both halves match

choices.label: B
choices.text: The circle, since it is the only shape without straight sides
choices.rationale: You picked curvature instead of symmetry. The circle, square, and triangle all share reflective symmetry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The square, since it is the only shape with four equal sides
choices.rationale: You picked a side count feature that does not group the remaining three shapes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The equilateral triangle, since it is the only shape with three sides
choices.rationale: You selected a side-count rule that leaves circle and square in different categories.

questions.explanation: The circle, square, and equilateral triangle can all be folded along at least one line so both halves match exactly (they are all symmetric). The irregular blob has no such line, so it is the odd-one-out.

questions.stem: Figure shows four circles, each cut by straight lines: one circle has 1 line through the center (creating 2 regions), one has 2 lines through the center (creating 4 regions), one has 3 lines through the center (creating 6 regions), and one has 2 lines that do not pass through the center, creating 3 uneven regions. Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The circle with 2 off-center lines (3 uneven regions), since the other three all have lines through the center creating an even number of regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: The circle with 1 line through the center, since it has the fewest regions
choices.rationale: You picked the lowest quantity instead of finding the structural rule. Lines through center always create even region counts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The circle with 3 lines through the center, since it has the most regions
choices.rationale: You picked the highest quantity. The three matching circles all have center-intersecting lines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The circle with 2 lines through the center, since it has an even number of lines
choices.rationale: You counted line segments instead of region symmetry.

questions.explanation: The first three figures follow a consistent rule: lines through the center split a circle into an even number of regions (2, 4, 6). The fourth figure's off-center lines create an uneven split (3 regions), breaking that pattern.

questions.stem: Figure shows five different shapes. Four of them each contain exactly one small shaded (black) dot somewhere inside. The fifth shape contains two small shaded dots inside. Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shape with two shaded dots, since the other four all contain exactly one shaded dot, regardless of their outer shape

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whichever shape has the largest outer outline
choices.rationale: You focused on outer scale rather than internal dot count.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whichever shape has the most sides
choices.rationale: You focused on outer polygon side counts when the rule governs interior dot count.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whichever shape is positioned in the middle of the row
choices.rationale: You judged by display position instead of geometric features.

questions.explanation: Four figures share the specific feature of containing exactly one shaded dot, regardless of their outer shape. The fifth figure contains two shaded dots, breaking that count: the shared rule here is about the dot count, not the outer shape.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes: a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and a circle. Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The circle, since it is made entirely of a curved line, while the other three are made entirely of straight lines

choices.label: B
choices.text: The square, since it is the only shape with four equal sides
choices.rationale: You picked equal side lengths instead of straight versus curved lines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The triangle, since it is the only shape with three sides
choices.rationale: You focused on side count, which leaves square and rectangle un-grouped with circle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rectangle, since it is the only shape with two pairs of equal sides
choices.rationale: You picked a sub-property of 4-sided polygons.

questions.explanation: The square, triangle, and rectangle are all made entirely of straight lines. The circle is made entirely of a curved line, breaking the "straight lines only" pattern shared by the other three.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes: a pentagon (5 sides), another pentagon (5 sides), a hexagon (6 sides), and a third pentagon (5 sides). Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hexagon, since it has 6 sides while the other three shapes all have 5 sides

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first pentagon, since it appears first in the row
choices.rationale: You used row position instead of side count.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second pentagon, since it is positioned in the middle
choices.rationale: You used layout placement instead of counting polygon sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The third pentagon, since it appears last in the row
choices.rationale: You judged by array order rather than side count.

questions.explanation: Three of the shapes are pentagons, sharing a 5-side count. The hexagon has 6 sides, breaking that shared feature.

questions.stem: Figure shows four quadrilaterals: a large square rotated 45° so it looks like a diamond, a small square, a rectangle, and a triangle drawn the same size as the others. A student picks the rotated diamond-looking square as the odd-one-out, since it "looks the most different" at a glance. Is this the correct answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the rotated square still has 4 sides, matching the small square and rectangle; the triangle, with only 3 sides, is the actual odd-one-out, even though it is not the most visually unusual-looking figure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the most visually different-looking figure is always the correct odd-one-out.
choices.rationale: You judged by superficial rotation appearance. Rotating a square does not change its 4-side count.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because rotated shapes never count as quadrilaterals.
choices.rationale: You claimed rotation alters polygon classification. A square remains a 4-sided quadrilateral when rotated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the triangle and the rotated square are actually the same shape.
choices.rationale: You claimed a triangle and square are the same shape.

questions.explanation: The most visually striking figure is not always the correct odd-one-out. The rotated square still shares the true underlying rule (4 sides) with the small square and rectangle, while the "normal-looking" triangle actually breaks the rule with only 3 sides.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes: a triangle, another triangle, a third triangle, and a four-sided kite shape. A student proposes the rule "all shapes have straight sides," noting this fits three of the triangles and technically fits the kite too, so they conclude there is no odd-one-out. Is this the correct conclusion, given that the three triangles are meant to share a more specific true rule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: "all shapes have straight sides" fits all four shapes and is too broad to distinguish them; the more specific true rule is "3 sides," which the three triangles share but the four-sided kite breaks, making the kite the actual odd-one-out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: since all four shapes have straight sides, there is genuinely no odd-one-out in this group.
choices.rationale: You accepted an overly broad rule that fails to separate any shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because triangles never have straight sides.
choices.rationale: You claimed triangles do not have straight sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the broadest rule that fits all figures is always the correct one to use.
choices.rationale: You assumed broad rules take precedence. Grouping rules must isolate a specific odd-one-out.

questions.explanation: A valid shared rule must be specific enough to distinguish the true odd-one-out, not just broadly true of every figure. Settling for an overly broad rule that fits everyone (including the kite) misses the more specific rule (3 sides) that only the three triangles actually share.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes, each divided into exactly 3 regions by internal lines, and a fifth shape divided into 4 regions. Which one does not belong?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shape divided into 4 regions, since the other four are all divided into exactly 3 regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whichever shape has the most internal lines drawn
choices.rationale: You focused on line segment count instead of total enclosed regions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whichever shape has curved internal lines
choices.rationale: You evaluated line curvature instead of region count.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whichever shape is shaded differently from the rest
choices.rationale: You searched for shading differences when region count is the defining rule.

questions.explanation: Four figures share the feature of being divided into exactly 3 regions by their internal lines. The fifth figure is divided into 4 regions, breaking that shared region count.

questions.stem: Figure shows four shapes that are each both symmetric (foldable into matching halves) and have exactly 4 sides: a square, a rectangle, a rhombus, and a kite. A fifth shape is a symmetric pentagon (foldable into matching halves, but with 5 sides). Which one does not belong, and which specific shared rule does it break?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The symmetric pentagon does not belong; although it shares the symmetry feature with the other four, it breaks the "exactly 4 sides" feature, since it has 5 sides.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The symmetric pentagon does not belong, since it is the only shape that is symmetric.
choices.rationale: You inverted the symmetry property. All five shapes in the group are symmetric.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The kite does not belong, since it is the only shape that is not a common household object.
choices.rationale: You used real-world object associations instead of geometric side count.

choices.label: D
choices.text: None of the shapes belong together, since a pentagon can never be symmetric.
choices.rationale: You claimed pentagons cannot be symmetric. Regular and isosceles pentagons have lines of symmetry.

questions.explanation: This group is defined by two combined features: symmetry AND exactly 4 sides. The pentagon shares the symmetry feature but breaks the 4-sides feature, making it the odd-one-out on that specific dimension, even though it isn't wrong on every dimension.

questions.stem: A 2x2 matrix's top row shows a triangle, then the same triangle rotated 90°. The bottom row shows a square, then a blank cell. What should the blank cell show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A square rotated 90° from the first bottom-row square

choices.label: B
choices.text: A square rotated 180° from the first bottom-row square
choices.rationale: You doubled the rotation angle to 180°. The top row establishes a 90° rotation pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A triangle rotated 90°, matching the top row exactly
choices.rationale: You copied the shape from the top row instead of applying the rotation transformation to the bottom row's square.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You omitted the transformation. The row rule requires a 90° rotation.

questions.explanation: The row pattern is a 90° rotation moving left to right. Applying the same pattern to the bottom row, the blank cell should show the square rotated 90° from the first bottom-row square.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's rows show circles with an increasing number of dots: row 1 has circles with 1, 2, 3 dots; row 2 has circles with 2, 3, 4 dots; row 3 has circles with 3, 4, and a blank cell. How many dots should the blank cell have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You repeated the second cell's count instead of continuing the +1 increment to 5.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added 2 instead of 1. The constant step size across each row is +1 dot.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You repeated the first cell's count instead of advancing the row progression.

questions.explanation: Within each row, the dot count increases by 1 moving left to right. Row 3 continues $3 \to 4 \to \, ?$, so the blank cell should have $5$ dots.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's columns show a shape growing in size moving top to bottom: column 1 has small, medium, large squares. The blank cell is at the bottom of column 2, which has small and medium squares above it. What size should the blank cell's square be?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medium, repeating the cell above it
choices.rationale: You repeated the middle cell instead of completing the small to medium to large progression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Small, repeating the top of the column
choices.rationale: You restarted the sequence at small instead of following the vertical growth rule to large.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You skipped the expected large size to pick an extra-large figure.

questions.explanation: The column pattern shows size growing (small, medium, large) moving down. Column 2 follows the same rule, so its blank bottom cell should be large.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's columns show a shape's size growing (small, medium, large) moving top to bottom, while its rows show the shape's shading alternating (black, white, black) moving left to right. The blank is in the bottom-right cell. What size and shading should it have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assigned white shading. Following the row pattern (black to white to black), the right-most cell must be black.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assigned medium size. The bottom row position requires large size per the column growth rule.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You assigned small size, which belongs to the top row rather than the bottom row.

questions.explanation: Since the blank is in the bottom row, the column pattern (small → medium → large) makes its size large. Since the blank is in the right-most position of its row, the row pattern (black → white → black) makes its shading black.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's first row shows: a circle with a horizontal line, a circle with a vertical line, and a circle with both lines (a plus-sign pattern) in the third cell. The same combination rule applies to another row: a square with a diagonal line (top-left to bottom-right), a square with the other diagonal line (top-right to bottom-left), and a blank third cell. What should the third cell show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A square with both diagonal lines drawn (forming an X pattern)

choices.label: B
choices.text: A square with only the first diagonal line, repeated
choices.rationale: You repeated the first cell without combining the second diagonal line.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A blank square with no lines at all
choices.rationale: You subtracted the lines instead of combining them into an X pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A square with a horizontal and vertical line, like the circle row
choices.rationale: You copied line orientations from a different row rather than combining the diagonal lines present in this row.

questions.explanation: The combination rule from the completed first row shows the third cell combines both features from the first two cells. Applying the same logic, the third cell should show a square with both diagonal lines, forming an X.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's row shows: a triangle shaded on its left half, a triangle shaded on its right half, and a blank third cell, following the same "combination" rule established in a previous, already-completed row. What should the third cell show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A triangle shaded on both halves (fully shaded)

choices.label: B
choices.text: A triangle shaded on neither half (fully unshaded)
choices.rationale: You cleared the shading instead of combining the left and right shaded halves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A triangle shaded only on its left half, repeated
choices.rationale: You ignored the right-half shading from the second cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A triangle shaded only on its right half, repeated
choices.rationale: You ignored the left-half shading from the first cell.

questions.explanation: Following the combination rule, the third cell should combine both features from the first two cells: a triangle shaded on its left half plus one shaded on its right half combine into a fully shaded triangle.

questions.stem: A 2x2 matrix's top row shows a circle with a dot in the top position, then the same circle rotated 90° clockwise (dot now in the right position). The bottom row shows a square with a dot in the top position, then a blank cell. Where should the dot be in the blank cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The right position, matching the same 90° clockwise rotation rule

choices.label: B
choices.text: The top position, unchanged from the first bottom-row cell
choices.rationale: You left the dot un-rotated instead of applying the 90° clockwise shift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bottom position, a 180° rotation instead of 90°
choices.rationale: You rotated 180° instead of the 90° clockwise angle shown in the top row.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The left position, a counterclockwise rotation instead
choices.rationale: You rotated counterclockwise instead of matching the top row's clockwise rotation.

questions.explanation: The row pattern is a 90° clockwise rotation of the dot's position, moving left to right. Applying the same rule to the bottom row, the dot should move from the top position to the right position.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's columns show a shape's size growing (small, medium, large) moving top to bottom, while its rows show the shape's shading alternating (black, white, black) moving left to right. The blank is in the bottom-right cell. A student checks only the column pattern and answers "large" without specifying shading, assuming the row direction does not matter here. What is wrong with this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student checked only one direction; this matrix requires checking both the column pattern (for size) and the row pattern (for shading) together: the complete answer should be "large, black," not size alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nothing is wrong: size alone is always a complete answer for any figure matrix.
choices.rationale: You assumed checking one pattern dimension is sufficient for multi-rule matrices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student's approach is correct, since shading never applies to matrix questions.
choices.rationale: You claimed shading does not apply to matrices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student should have checked only the row pattern and ignored the column pattern entirely.
choices.rationale: You swapped one single-dimension approach for another instead of evaluating both row and column rules.

questions.explanation: Many matrices require checking both the row pattern and the column pattern together: solving only one direction gives an incomplete answer. Here, size follows the column direction while shading follows the row direction, so both must be checked.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's row shows a circle with a horizontal line, then a circle with a vertical line, then a blank third cell. A student assumes the third cell should follow a simple step-by-step progression (like rotating the line further), predicting a circle with a diagonal line. Given that this matrix actually uses a combination rule, is the student's prediction correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this row uses a combination rule, where the third cell combines both features from the first two cells; the correct answer is a circle with both a horizontal and vertical line (a plus-sign pattern), not a diagonal line.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: a diagonal line is always the correct continuation of a two-line pattern.
choices.rationale: You assumed a sequential angle progression applies instead of combining the horizontal and vertical lines into a plus sign.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: combination rules never apply to circles, only to squares.
choices.rationale: You claimed combination rules are limited to squares.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because circles cannot have any lines at all.
choices.rationale: You claimed circles cannot contain interior lines.

questions.explanation: Assuming the third cell should follow a simple incrementing pattern (like a figure series) when it is actually meant to combine features from the first two cells leads to a plausible but incorrect prediction. The correct answer combines both lines into a plus-sign pattern.

questions.stem: A 2x2 matrix's top row shows a triangle, then a triangle rotated 90°. Its bottom row shows a completely different shape, a pentagon, then a blank cell. A student assumes the bottom row must also use triangles, since "all rows in a matrix should use the same shapes." Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: different rows can apply the same transformation rule (like a 90° rotation) to different starting shapes; the bottom row correctly uses pentagons, and the blank cell should show a pentagon rotated 90°, not a triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: every row in a figure matrix must use the exact same shapes as every other row.
choices.rationale: You assumed all rows must feature identical geometric shapes rather than identical transformation rules.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: but only because pentagons and triangles are actually the same shape.
choices.rationale: You claimed pentagons and triangles are the same shape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the top row's shapes are also invalid.
choices.rationale: You claimed top row figures are invalid.

questions.explanation: Different rows or columns can apply the same transformation rule to different starting shapes: do not expect literally identical figures across rows, only a consistent pattern of change. Recognizing the rule (90° rotation), not memorizing specific shapes, is the key skill.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's row shows a star shaded black, then a star shaded white, then a blank third cell, with shading alternating left to right. What shading should the blank third cell have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You repeated white instead of maintaining the alternating black to white to black pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You introduced partial shading not present in the alternating binary sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You introduced an intermediate shade not matching the black and white alternation rule.

questions.explanation: The row pattern shows shading alternating (black, white) moving left to right. Continuing the alternation, the third cell should return to black.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's column shows an arrow pointing up, then the same arrow rotated 90° clockwise (pointing right), then a blank third cell, moving top to bottom. What direction should the arrow point in the blank third cell?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You reset the arrow to the top position instead of continuing the 90° clockwise rotation down.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You rotated counterclockwise instead of continuing clockwise.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You repeated the second cell's position without applying the third rotation step.

questions.explanation: The column pattern shows a 90° clockwise rotation moving top to bottom (up → right). Continuing the same rotation, the third cell's arrow should point down.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix's columns show a shape's number of sides increasing (triangle, square, pentagon) moving top to bottom, while its rows show the shape rotated further (0°, 45°, 90°) moving left to right. The blank is in the bottom-right cell. What shape and rotation should it show?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked a square (4 sides) instead of the 5-sided pentagon specified by the bottom row's growth rule.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assigned a 45° rotation, which belongs to the middle column rather than the right column.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You advanced the side count past 5 to 6 sides.

questions.explanation: Since the blank is in the bottom row, the column pattern (triangle → square → pentagon) makes its shape a pentagon. Since the blank is in the right-most column, the row pattern (0° → 45° → 90°) makes its rotation 90°.

questions.stem: A 3x3 matrix has two rules running at once. Row rule: the third cell in each row combines the line features of the first two cells (e.g., a horizontal line plus a vertical line becomes both lines together). Column rule: every shape in column 1 is shaded black, every shape in column 2 is shaded white, and every shape in column 3 is shaded black, regardless of row. Row 2 shows: a black circle with a horizontal line (column 1), a white circle with a vertical line (column 2), and a blank third cell (column 3). What should the blank third cell show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A black circle with both a horizontal and vertical line

choices.label: B
choices.text: A white circle with both lines, ignoring the column shading rule
choices.rationale: You ignored the column 3 shading rule requiring black fill.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A black circle with only a horizontal line, ignoring the row combination rule
choices.rationale: You ignored the row combination rule by omitting the vertical line.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A white circle with neither line, ignoring both rules
choices.rationale: You broke both the shading rule and the line combination rule.

questions.explanation: Two rules apply at once: the row rule combines both lines from the first two cells (horizontal + vertical = both), and the column rule fixes column 3's shading as black. Combining both gives a black circle with both a horizontal and vertical line.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three squares, each containing a single line. Square 1's line points straight up. Square 2's line points to the upper-right (a 45° clockwise turn from square 1). Square 3's line points directly right (another 45° clockwise turn from square 2). What direction should the line point in the fourth square?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You turned 90° clockwise instead of 45°. The established pattern turns 45° clockwise per step.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You reset to the start position instead of advancing 45° clockwise to lower-right.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You reversed rotation direction to counterclockwise.

questions.explanation: The line turns 45° clockwise at each step (up → upper-right → right). Continuing the same rotation from "right," the next position is lower-right.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three shapes: a triangle (3 sides), a square (4 sides), and a pentagon (5 sides). How many sides should the fourth figure have, and what shape is it?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You repeated 5 sides instead of incrementing by +1 to 6 sides.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added 2 sides instead of continuing the constant +1 side increment.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You jumped three sides ahead. The pattern adds one side each step, so the next one has six.

questions.explanation: The number of sides increases by 1 each step ($3, 4, 5, \ldots$). The fourth figure should have $6$ sides: a hexagon.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three circles: a fully black circle, then a fully white (empty) circle, then a fully black circle again. What should the fourth circle look like?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You repeated black instead of maintaining the strict black and white alternation.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You introduced partial shading not present in the binary alternating sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gray (a blend of black and white)
choices.rationale: You introduced an intermediate shade when the sequence alternates between solid black and white.

questions.explanation: The shading alternates strictly: black, white, black. Since the pattern alternates every step, the figure after "black" should return to "white."

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three triangles: a small black triangle, a medium white triangle, and a large black triangle. Predict the size and shading of the fourth triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You correctly identified extra-large size but kept black shading instead of alternating to white.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You correctly identified white shading but failed to advance size from large to extra-large.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You reset size back to small instead of continuing to extra-large.

questions.explanation: Tracking size separately (small, medium, large, increasing one step each time) gives extra-large next. Tracking shading separately (black, white, black, alternating) gives white next. Combined: extra-large, white.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three squares, each with a black dot in one corner. Square 1's dot is in the top-left corner. Square 2's dot is in the top-right corner (moved clockwise one corner). Square 3's dot is in the bottom-right corner (moved clockwise one more corner). Where should the dot be in the fourth square?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You skipped to the top-left corner instead of continuing clockwise to bottom-left.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You jumped back to top-right instead of advancing to bottom-left.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You moved the dot off the perimeter corners into the center.

questions.explanation: The dot moves one corner clockwise at each step (top-left → top-right → bottom-right). Continuing clockwise from bottom-right, the next corner is bottom-left.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three circles, each with an arrow inside. Circle 1's arrow points up. Circle 2's arrow points right (a 90° clockwise turn). Circle 3's arrow points down (another 90° clockwise turn). What direction should the arrow point in the fourth circle?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You reset to up instead of continuing 90° clockwise to left.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You jumped back to right instead of advancing to left.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You repeated down without applying the next 90° clockwise rotation.

questions.explanation: The arrow turns 90° clockwise at each step (up → right → down). Continuing clockwise from "down," the next direction is left.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three circles, each containing small dots. Circle 1 has 1 dot. Circle 2 has 2 dots. Circle 3 has 3 dots. How many dots should the fourth circle have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You added 2 dots instead of continuing the +1 dot increment.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You repeated 3 dots instead of advancing to 4 dots.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You doubled the dot count instead of adding 1.

questions.explanation: The number of dots increases by 1 each step ($1, 2, 3, \ldots$). The fourth circle should have $4$ dots.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three squares, decreasing in size: a large square, a medium square, and a small square. What size should the fourth square be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extra small (smaller than the small square)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extra large (larger than the large square)
choices.rationale: You inverted the shrinking trend to growing extra large.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You reversed the size trend back to medium.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same size as the small square
choices.rationale: You stopped shrinking and repeated the small size.

questions.explanation: The size decreases by one step each time (large, medium, small). Continuing this shrinking pattern, the fourth square should be extra small.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three stars: a small black star, a medium white star, and a large black star. A student predicts the fourth figure should be "extra-large, black," tracking only the size feature and assuming shading stays the same as figure 3. What is wrong with this prediction, and what should the fourth figure actually be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student ignored the shading feature, which alternates (black, white, black); tracking both features separately, the fourth figure should be extra-large and white, not extra-large and black.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student's prediction is correct, since shading always matches the previous figure once size changes.
choices.rationale: You assumed shading stops alternating when size changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student's prediction is correct, but only because shading is irrelevant in this series.
choices.rationale: You claimed shading is irrelevant when both size and shading vary systematically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither size nor shading can be predicted from this series.
choices.rationale: You claimed multi-feature series cannot be predicted.

questions.explanation: A figure series can change several features at once: missing that both size and shading are changing leads to only half-correct predictions. Size continues growing (extra-large), and shading continues alternating (white after black).

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three squares, each with a dot in one corner. Square 1's dot is top-left. Square 2's dot is bottom-left (moved counterclockwise one corner). Square 3's dot is bottom-right (moved counterclockwise one more corner). A student assumes the dot must now move clockwise for the fourth square, predicting bottom-left again. Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the established direction is counterclockwise (top-left → bottom-left → bottom-right), so the fourth square's dot should continue counterclockwise to top-right, not switch direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the dot should always reverse direction after two steps.
choices.rationale: You assumed rotation direction reverses after two steps without evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: the dot should return to bottom-left, since patterns commonly repeat every two steps.
choices.rationale: You assumed a 2-step oscillation pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the dot cannot move to any corner other than top-left.
choices.rationale: You claimed dots are restricted from moving to top-right.

questions.explanation: Carefully confirm the established rotation direction by comparing at least two consecutive steps rather than assuming a direction switch. Here, the dot consistently moves counterclockwise, so it should continue to top-right next.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three circles with shading: 25% filled, 50% filled, 75% filled. A student assumes this is a cumulative pattern and predicts the fourth circle should be 100% filled. Given that the actual series repeats as 25%, 50%, 75%, 25%, 50%, 75%, ..., is the student's prediction correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this is a repeating cycle, not a steadily cumulative pattern; after 75%, the cycle restarts at 25%, not continuing to 100%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the shading always increases steadily without ever restarting.
choices.rationale: You assumed steady cumulative growth instead of observing the repeating cycle rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: 100% filled is the correct next step in this specific series.
choices.rationale: You applied a linear cumulative rule to a cycling sequence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because circles cannot be partially shaded.
choices.rationale: You claimed partial shading is impossible.

questions.explanation: Not every changing feature increases steadily forever: some patterns cycle back to an earlier state after reaching a certain point. Here, the series explicitly cycles (25%, 50%, 75%, 25%, ...), so the fourth figure returns to 25%, not 100%.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three triangles, each with a dot near one corner. Triangle 1's dot is near the top corner. Triangle 2's dot is near the bottom-left corner (moved clockwise). Triangle 3's dot is near the bottom-right corner (moved clockwise again). Where should the dot be in the fourth triangle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Near the top corner, completing one full clockwise cycle around the triangle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Near the bottom-left corner, repeating triangle 2
choices.rationale: You repeated the second corner position instead of completing the 3-corner cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Near the bottom-right corner, repeating triangle 3
choices.rationale: You repeated the third corner position without advancing clockwise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the center of the triangle
choices.rationale: You moved the dot away from the corners into the interior center.

questions.explanation: A triangle has three corners. The dot moves clockwise, one corner per step (top → bottom-left → bottom-right). After all three corners, the fourth figure completes the cycle back at the top corner.

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of three figures, each changing in three ways at once: figure 1 is a small black triangle rotated with its point up; figure 2 is a medium white square rotated with its point (top corner) to the right (a 90° clockwise turn from the triangle's orientation, and the shape gained one side); figure 3 is a large black pentagon rotated with its point pointing down (another 90° clockwise turn, and the shape gained one more side). Predict the size, shading, side count, and rotation of the fourth figure.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extra-large, white, 6 sides (hexagon), point rotated to the left (a further 90° clockwise turn)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extra-large, black, 6 sides (hexagon), point rotated to the left
choices.rationale: You correctly tracked size, sides, and rotation but failed to alternate shading to white.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Large, white, 5 sides (pentagon), point pointing down
choices.rationale: You repeated figure 3's size, sides, and rotation, changing only shading.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extra-large, white, 5 sides (pentagon), point rotated up
choices.rationale: You failed to advance side count to 6 and misrotated the point orientation.

questions.explanation: Tracking each feature separately: size grows one step (extra-large); shading alternates (black, white, black, so white next); sides increase by 1 each step (3, 4, 5, so 6 next); rotation turns 90° clockwise each step (up, right, down, so left next).

questions.stem: Figure shows a row of four squares, each with a dot in a corner and a number of small lines along one edge: square 1 has a dot in the top-left corner and 1 line; square 2 has a dot in the top-right corner (moved clockwise) and 2 lines; square 3 has a dot in the bottom-right corner (moved clockwise again) and 3 lines; square 4 has a dot in the bottom-left corner (moved clockwise again) and 4 lines. If the series continues for one more figure (figure 5), where should the dot be, and how many lines should there be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Top-left corner (completing one full clockwise cycle), with 5 lines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottom-left corner, repeating figure 4, with 5 lines
choices.rationale: You repeated the corner position of figure 4 instead of completing the 4-corner cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Top-left corner, with 4 lines, repeating the line count
choices.rationale: You correctly cycled the dot position but failed to advance the line count to 5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You skipped to top-right instead of returning to top-left after 4 steps.

questions.explanation: The dot completes one clockwise corner move per figure; after 4 figures (one full cycle of 4 corners), it returns to the top-left corner for figure 5. Separately, the line count increases by 1 each figure ($1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots$), so figure 5 should have 5 lines.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded exactly in half (vertically, left side onto right side). A small triangular notch is cut out of the folded paper, entirely within one layer (not on the fold line itself). How many notches appear when the paper is fully unfolded?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed 1 fold produces 1 notch. One fold creates 2 layers, yielding ^1 = 2$ notches.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You doubled the layer count. One fold creates 2 layers (^1 = 2$).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You added the fold count to the cut count instead of calculating ^{\text{folds}}$.

questions.explanation: One fold means the cut passes through 2 layers, so unfolding reveals $2^1 = 2$ notches.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded in half vertically, then folded in half again horizontally (into a quarter-square). A small circular hole is cut through all the folded layers at once. How many holes appear when fully unfolded?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You assumed 2 folds produce 2 holes. Two folds create ^2 = 4$ layers, yielding 4 holes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You applied a 3-fold formula (^3 = 8$) to a 2-fold problem.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You assumed all layers fold over the same spot without multiplying.

questions.explanation: Two folds mean the cut passes through $2^2 = 4$ layers, so unfolding reveals 4 holes.

questions.stem: A rectangular paper is folded in half three separate times (each fold halving it again). A cut is made through all the layers at once. How many holes appear when fully unfolded?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You multiplied 3 folds by 2 layers per fold ( \times 2 = 6$) instead of using exponential growth ^3 = 8$.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed the hole count equals the fold count.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You applied a 4-fold formula (^4 = 16$) to a 3-fold scenario.

questions.explanation: Three folds mean $2^3 = 8$ layers are cut through simultaneously, so unfolding reveals 8 separate holes.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded in half vertically, then folded in half again horizontally (into a quarter-square). A small circular hole is cut near the corner where all the folded edges meet (the center of the original square). Where will the resulting holes appear when unfolded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four small holes, one in each quadrant, all positioned near the center of the original square

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four small holes, one in each quadrant, all positioned near the four outer corners of the original square
choices.rationale: You placed the holes at the outer corners. Cutting near the all-folds intersection clusters the 4 holes near the center.

choices.label: C
choices.text: One single hole at the exact center, with no other holes elsewhere
choices.rationale: You merged the holes into a single center hole. A cut near the corner produces 4 distinct holes near the center.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four holes scattered randomly with no symmetric relationship to each other
choices.rationale: You ignored reflection symmetry. Unfolded cuts form symmetric patterns across fold axes.

questions.explanation: Since the cut is positioned at the center corner (where all folds meet), each of the 4 layers corresponds to one of the 4 quadrants, and unfolding reveals 4 small holes, each mirrored close to the center point in its own quadrant.

questions.stem: Using the same two-fold setup as before (folded into a quarter-square), a notch is cut this time along the outer edge of the folded paper, far from the center corner where the folds meet. Where will the resulting holes appear when unfolded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four notches, one along each outer edge/corner region of the original square, symmetric about both fold lines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four notches, all clustered near the exact center of the original square
choices.rationale: You placed outer-edge cuts near the center. Cuts on the outer edge remain near the outer edges when unfolded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single connected notch spanning the entire outer edge of the square
choices.rationale: You assumed outer cuts merge into one giant continuous notch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two notches only, since the cut is far from one of the fold lines
choices.rationale: You halved the hole count based on distance from fold lines.

questions.explanation: Since the cut is on the outer edge (far from the fold-meeting corner), reflecting it across both fold lines places the four resulting holes near the four outer edges of the original square, not near the center.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded exactly in half (vertically, left side onto right side). A triangular notch is cut exactly on the folded edge (the fold line itself), at the vertical midpoint. What does the unfolded paper look like?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single diamond-shaped hole straddling the center fold line, not two fully separate notches

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two completely separate triangular notches, one on each side of the fold line
choices.rationale: You treated a cut on the fold line as two separate holes. A cut on a fold line merges across the line into one connected diamond shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No hole at all, since cutting on the fold line does not go through any paper
choices.rationale: You claimed cutting a fold line produces no hole.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four separate notches, since cutting on a fold line doubles the usual count
choices.rationale: You quadrupled the hole count for a single fold cut.

questions.explanation: A cut positioned exactly on a fold line typically becomes a single connected shape straddling that line once unfolded, rather than the usual number of fully separate holes.

questions.stem: A paper is folded in half twice (into a quarter-square), giving 4 layers. A cut is made that crosses one of the fold lines directly, rather than sitting entirely within one layer's interior. A student predicts this will still produce exactly 4 fully separate holes when unfolded, using the standard $2^{\text{folds}}$ formula. Is this prediction correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a cut that crosses a fold line directly gets reflected across that fold line, merging what would otherwise be separate holes into fewer, larger connected shapes, rather than 4 fully separate holes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the $2^{\text{folds}}$ formula always applies regardless of where the cut is positioned relative to the fold lines.
choices.rationale: You assumed cut position does not affect whether holes merge across fold lines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: cuts crossing fold lines always produce more holes than the formula predicts, not fewer.
choices.rationale: You claimed crossing fold lines increases the total hole count.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because cuts can never cross a fold line.
choices.rationale: You claimed paper cuts cannot cross fold lines.

questions.explanation: If the cut crosses a fold line directly (rather than sitting entirely within one folded layer's interior), unfolding may connect what would otherwise be separate holes into one continuous connected shape, changing the expected count.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded in half four separate times (each fold halving it again). A cut is made through all the layers at once, entirely within one layer's interior. How many holes appear when fully unfolded?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You used a 3-fold calculation (^3 = 8$) for a 4-fold process (^4 = 16$).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You assumed 4 folds produce 4 holes ( \times 1 = 4$).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied 4 folds by 3 instead of evaluating ^4 = 16$.

questions.explanation: Four folds mean $2^4 = 16$ layers are cut through simultaneously, so unfolding reveals 16 separate holes.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded in half once (vertically). A small notch is cut entirely within the interior of the folded layer, away from the fold line and away from the paper's outer edges. How many separate notches appear when unfolded, and are they connected or fully separate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 fully separate notches, one mirrored on each side of the fold line

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1 connected notch straddling the fold line
choices.rationale: You treated an interior cut as a fold-line cut. Cuts away from fold lines remain fully separate.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You doubled the result of a single fold (^1 = 2$).

choices.label: D
choices.text: No notches, since the cut is not on the fold line or an outer edge
choices.rationale: You claimed interior cuts produce no holes when unfolded.

questions.explanation: A cut positioned away from all fold lines becomes multiple separate holes, one per layer. With one fold (2 layers), unfolding reveals 2 fully separate notches, mirrored across the fold line.

questions.stem: A square paper is folded in half vertically, then folded in half again horizontally (into a quarter-square). A notch is cut near one specific corner of the folded quarter-square, not the corner where both folds meet, and not along an outer edge, but the corner diagonally opposite the all-folds corner. Predict how many notches appear when unfolded, and their general position.

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4 notches, one in each quadrant, each mirrored to the position diagonally opposite the center within its own quadrant

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 notches, all clustered at the exact center of the original square
choices.rationale: You placed the notches at the center. The cut was made at the outer opposite corner, so notches cluster in outer corners.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 notches only, since this corner is not the all-folds corner
choices.rationale: You halved the hole count because the cut was away from the all-folds corner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1 notch, since cuts away from the all-folds corner do not get mirrored
choices.rationale: You claimed cuts away from the center do not mirror across fold axes.

questions.explanation: Regardless of which specific point on the folded shape is cut, two folds always produce $2^2 = 4$ holes when the cut is away from any fold line. Each hole is mirrored into its own quadrant at the position corresponding to where the cut was made on the folded shape.

questions.stem: Two square papers are each folded twice into a quarter-square (4 layers). On paper 1, a notch is cut near the all-folds center corner. On paper 2, an identical-sized notch is cut near the outer edge, far from the center. Both papers are then unfolded. Do the two papers end up with the same hole count, the same hole positions, or neither?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both papers end up with the same hole count (4 holes each, since both used 2 folds), but different hole positions: paper 1's holes cluster near the center, while paper 2's holes appear near the outer edges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both papers end up with the same hole count and the same hole positions, since both used the same number of folds and the same notch size.
choices.rationale: You assumed cut location on the folded paper does not affect unfolded hole positions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two papers end up with different hole counts, since cut position affects the total number of holes.
choices.rationale: You claimed cut location changes the number of layers cut through.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither paper produces any holes, since folding twice cancels out any cut made afterward.
choices.rationale: You claimed folding cancels out paper cuts.

questions.explanation: The number of folds determines the hole count ($2^{\text{folds}}$), independent of where exactly the cut is placed (as long as it's away from any fold line). But the specific position of the cut on the folded shape determines where each of those holes ends up once unfolded, so the count matches, but the positions differ.

questions.stem: A rectangular paper is folded in half vertically (fold A), then folded in half again horizontally (fold B), then folded in half a third time along a diagonal (fold C). A small triangular notch is cut through all the layers at once, entirely within one layer's interior, away from any fold line. Determine: (a) how many notches appear when fully unfolded, and (b) in what order the folds should be undone to correctly trace each notch's final position.

choices.label: A
choices.text: (a) $2^3 = 8$ notches; (b) undo fold C first (the most recently made fold), then fold B, then fold A last, reflecting the cut's position at each step in that reverse order.

choices.label: B
choices.text: (a) 3 notches, one per fold; (b) undo the folds in the same order they were made: A, then B, then C.
choices.rationale: You miscounted holes as equal to folds and used forward unfolding order instead of reverse order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (a) 6 notches; (b) the order of undoing folds does not matter for the final positions.
choices.rationale: You miscalculated ^3$ as 6 and claimed unfolding order does not matter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (a) 8 notches; (b) undo fold A first, then B, then C, following the original folding order.
choices.rationale: You correctly calculated 8 notches but failed to reverse the unfolding order.

questions.explanation: Three folds mean $2^3=8$ layers are cut through, producing 8 notches. To correctly trace each notch's position, folds must be undone in reverse order, the most recently made fold (C) first, then B, then A, reflecting the cut's position across the correct fold line at each step.

questions.stem:
Statement: "All employees who complete the training program will receive a performance bonus."
Which assumption is necessary for this statement to hold true?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bonuses will double for senior employees next year
choices.rationale: You picked a future compensation change not required for the current statement to hold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-participating staff members will face penalty
choices.rationale: You assumed non-participants are punished. The statement only addresses rewards for participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Training programs are conducted outside city limits
choices.rationale: You introduced an irrelevant geographic requirement.

questions.explanation: The statement assumes that completing the training program is an achievable goal, enabling employees to earn the bonus.

questions.stem:
Statement: "The city council increased public transit routes to reduce traffic congestion during peak hours."
Which assumption underlies the council's decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased transit reduces private car usage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Traffic congestion will vanish completely within two days
choices.rationale: You assumed an extreme and instant elimination of traffic rather than a reasonable reduction mechanism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public transit fare rates will decrease by fifty percent
choices.rationale: You introduced an unstated pricing assumption not required for transit expansion to lower car usage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City residents dislike walking to nearby municipal offices
choices.rationale: You introduced an irrelevant pedestrian behavioral preference.

questions.explanation: The council's decision assumes that expanding transit routes encourages commuters to use public transit instead of private cars, reducing traffic.

questions.stem:
Statement: "Premise 1: Every civil servant must pass an ethics exam. Premise 2: Maria passed the ethics exam."
Which conclusion logically follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maria satisfied one requirement for civil service

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maria is automatically appointed to a senior executive director role
choices.rationale: You assumed passing one exam guarantees an immediate senior job appointment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maria scored highest among all examination test takers nationwide
choices.rationale: You assumed top rank performance when the premise states only that she passed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maria is exempt from all future annual official evaluation tests
choices.rationale: You inferred future testing exemptions not stated in the premises.

questions.explanation: Passing the ethics exam fulfills one mandatory requirement, but does not guarantee an immediate senior appointment or top score.

questions.stem:
Statement: "If it rains heavily, the outdoor community assembly will be moved indoors. The assembly was held indoors."
Which conclusion is valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rain was a possible reason for moving indoors

choices.label: B
choices.text: It definitely rained heavily during assembly hours
choices.rationale: You committed the fallacy of affirming the consequent. Moving indoors could have occurred for other reasons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The outdoor venue was destroyed by severe winds
choices.rationale: You inferred extreme physical destruction not supported by the premises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Community members refused to attend outdoor events
choices.rationale: You inferred member refusal without premise evidence.

questions.explanation: Holding the assembly indoors could be due to rain, but moving indoors could also happen for other unstated reasons.

questions.stem:
Statement: "Company X replaced all paper invoices with digital billing to cut processing costs."
What assumption is made by Company X?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Digital billing costs less than paper processing

choices.label: B
choices.text: All customers prefer receiving digital billing receipts monthly
choices.rationale: You assumed customer preference drives cost reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paper invoices will be banned nationwide by government decree
choices.rationale: You assumed an external legal ban motivated the company's decision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Processing digital receipts requires zero electrical energy consumption
choices.rationale: You assumed digital billing requires zero energy, which is impossible and unnecessary for net savings.

questions.explanation: Replacing paper with digital billing to cut costs assumes that processing digital bills incurs lower total expenses than paper invoicing.

questions.stem:
Statement: "No unregistered vehicles are allowed inside the government compound. Vehicle A is parked inside."
Which conclusion must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vehicle A is a registered vehicle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vehicle A belongs to the department head
choices.rationale: You inferred specific ownership not indicated by the registration rule.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You introduced an irrelevant vehicle age feature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vehicle A has electric power features
choices.rationale: You introduced an irrelevant engine type attribute.

questions.explanation: Since unregistered vehicles are barred, any vehicle parked inside must be registered.

questions.stem:
Statement: "All department supervisors must hold a master's degree. Elena is not a department supervisor."
Which conclusion is valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elena may or may not hold a master's degree

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elena definitely does not hold any master's degree credential
choices.rationale: You committed denying the antecedent. Non-supervisors can also possess master's degrees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elena is disqualified from holding any public office job title
choices.rationale: You inferred general job disqualification beyond the supervisor requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elena will be appointed supervisor next month by executive vote
choices.rationale: You assumed a future appointment contrary to her current status.

questions.explanation: Holding a master's degree is a requirement for supervisors, but non-supervisors may still hold master's degrees.

questions.stem:
Statement: "Strict waste segregation reduced landfill volume in Municipality Y by thirty percent."
What is assumed by this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Waste segregation contributed to volume reduction

choices.label: B
choices.text: All residents produce zero non-recyclable waste products daily
choices.rationale: You assumed an extreme zero-waste threshold rather than a 30% reduction contribution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landfills in Municipality Y will close next year permanently
choices.rationale: You inferred complete and permanent landfill closure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recycling facilities generate huge net financial profits yearly
choices.rationale: You introduced financial profitability assumptions unrelated to volume reduction.

questions.explanation: Attributing the thirty percent drop to strict waste segregation assumes a causal link between segregation efforts and volume reduction.

questions.stem:
Statement: "All candidates who score above 80% pass the examination. Juan scored 85%."
Which conclusion is certain?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juan scored highest in his class
choices.rationale: You assumed Juan was top rank when the premise only guarantees he passed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juan is guaranteed a job offer
choices.rationale: You inferred employment guarantees beyond passing the test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juan will retake the test soon
choices.rationale: You inferred a retake despite Juan successfully passing.

questions.explanation: Since 85% exceeds the 80% passing threshold, Juan necessarily passed the examination.

questions.stem:
Statement: "To reduce paper usage, the department instituted electronic recordkeeping."
Which assumption underlies this action?

choices.label: B
choices.text: All paper records will be destroyed today permanently
choices.rationale: You assumed immediate destruction of historical paper records.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Computer hardware systems never experience technical errors
choices.rationale: You assumed zero technical failure, which is unrequired for reducing paper usage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees prefer reading computer screens over printed sheets
choices.rationale: You assumed user media preferences drive paper savings.

questions.explanation: Adopting electronic recordkeeping to reduce paper usage assumes that digital filing consumes less paper overall.

questions.stem:
Statement: "Only licensed engineers may approve building plans. Mark approved the building plans for Project A."
Which conclusion is valid?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You inferred project ownership rather than engineering credentials.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You introduced an unstated geographic location.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Project A cost millions of pesos
choices.rationale: You introduced an unstated financial cost.
