questions.explanation: Because only licensed engineers can approve building plans, Mark must be a licensed engineer to have approved them.

questions.stem:
Statement: "Solar panel installation decreased monthly electricity bills for School Z."
What is the underlying assumption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Solar energy replaced paid grid electricity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electricity rates dropped nationwide this month significantly
choices.rationale: You attributed the savings to external rate drops, which would negate the solar panel's causal role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: School Z turned off all air conditioning units completely
choices.rationale: You assumed air conditioning shutdown rather than solar generation caused the savings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: School Z operates only during daytime operating hours
choices.rationale: You assumed daytime-only operation instead of solar substitution.

questions.explanation: Attributing lower electric bills to solar panels assumes that generated solar power substituted for utility grid electricity.

questions.stem: Which plant tissue forms the outer covering, protecting the plant and controlling gas exchange and water loss?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the tissue that moves water and sugar around the plant. Vascular tissue
is the plant's transport system, not its outer covering.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the tissue that fills most of the plant's body. Ground tissue handles
photosynthesis and storage. It sits inside, not on the surface.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked one type of vascular tissue. Xylem carries water upward from the roots.
It does not form the plant's outer covering.

questions.explanation: Dermal tissue forms the plant's outer covering, like skin, protecting it and controlling gas exchange and water loss.

questions.stem: Which vascular tissue carries water and minerals upward from the roots to the rest of the plant?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the tissue that carries sugar, not water. Phloem moves sugars from
the leaves to wherever the plant needs them. Water is xylem's job.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the plant's outer covering. Dermal tissue protects the surface and
controls gas exchange. It does not transport water.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the filler tissue. Ground tissue handles photosynthesis and storage.
It does not carry water up from the roots.

questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots, made of dead cells that act like hollow pipes.

questions.stem: Which vascular tissue carries sugars made through photosynthesis to wherever the plant needs energy or storage?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the tissue that carries water, not sugar. Xylem moves water upward
from the roots through dead, hollow cells. Sugar distribution is phloem's job.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the plant's outer covering. Dermal tissue protects the surface. It
does not carry sugars.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the bulk tissue. Ground tissue stores and uses energy, but it does
not transport sugars around the plant. That is phloem's job.

questions.explanation: Phloem carries sugars (food made through photosynthesis) throughout the plant, made of living cells, unlike the dead cells of xylem.

questions.stem: Which plant tissue makes up most of a plant's body, filling the space between dermal and vascular tissue, and handles photosynthesis, storage, and support?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the outer skin layer. Dermal tissue covers the surface. It does not
fill the body or handle photosynthesis and storage.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked one part of the transport system. Xylem is a tube inside the stem
that carries water. It does not make up most of the plant's body.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the other part of the transport system. Phloem carries sugars. It
does not fill the bulk of the plant's body.

questions.explanation: Ground tissue makes up most of a plant's body, filling the space between dermal and vascular tissue, handling photosynthesis, storage, and support.

questions.stem: A gardener notices a plant's stem transporting water from its roots to its topmost leaves, while a separate set of cells in the same stem transports sugar made in the leaves down toward the roots. Which tissue transports the water, and which transports the sugar?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Xylem transports the water upward; phloem transports the sugar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phloem transports the water upward; xylem transports the sugar.
choices.rationale:
You swapped them. Phloem carries sugar, not water. Xylem carries water, not
sugar. Their jobs are the opposite of what you chose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Xylem transports both the water and the sugar.
choices.rationale:
You gave xylem both jobs. Xylem only carries water upward through dead cells.
Sugar needs living phloem cells to move it around the plant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ground tissue transports both the water and the sugar.
choices.rationale:
You picked the filler tissue. Ground tissue does not transport anything around
the plant. Transport is the job of the vascular tissues: xylem and phloem.

questions.explanation: Water traveling upward from roots to leaves is the job of xylem. Sugar traveling from the leaves (where it is made) to the roots is the job of phloem.

questions.stem: A student claims phloem carries water upward from the roots, and xylem carries sugar throughout the plant. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this swaps their jobs; xylem carries water upward from the roots, while phloem carries sugar throughout the plant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: phloem always carries water, and xylem always carries sugar.
choices.rationale:
You agreed with the swap. Phloem carries sugar, not water. Xylem carries water,
not sugar. The student's claim has both tissues doing the wrong job.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because neither tissue transports any substance.
choices.rationale:
You said neither tissue transports anything, which is wrong. Both xylem and
phloem are transport tissues. Xylem moves water; phloem moves sugar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: xylem and phloem are simply two different names for the same tissue.
choices.rationale:
You said they are the same tissue. They are two distinct tissues with different
cell types and different jobs. Xylem uses dead cells for water; phloem uses
living cells for sugar.

questions.explanation: These two terms are frequently swapped. Anchor them with their cell type: xylem is made of dead, hollow cells for water transport, while phloem is made of living cells actively distributing sugar (food).

questions.stem: What term describes a plant's directional growth response to light?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the growth response to gravity, not to light. Gravitropism describes
how roots grow down and stems grow up in response to gravity.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the growth response to touch. Thigmotropism is what makes a vine's
tendril curl around a fence post. Light is a different stimulus.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked a reproductive process. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from
one flower part to another. It has nothing to do with directional growth.

questions.explanation: Phototropism is a plant's directional growth response to light.

questions.stem: What term describes a plant's directional growth response to gravity?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the growth response to light. Phototropism describes how a stem
bends toward a window. Gravity is a different stimulus.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the growth response to touch. Thigmotropism is what makes tendrils
curl around objects they contact. Gravity is a different stimulus.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked a reproductive process. Fertilization is when a sperm cell joins an
egg cell. It has nothing to do with directional growth in response to gravity.

questions.explanation: Gravitropism is a plant's directional growth response to gravity.

questions.stem: A climbing vine's tendrils are observed curling tightly around a fence post after making physical contact with it. What tropism does this demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Positive thigmotropism, a growth response to touch

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive phototropism, a growth response to light
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to light. The stimulus here is physical contact with
the post, not light. Growth toward a touch stimulus is thigmotropism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative gravitropism, a growth response to gravity
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to gravity. Gravitropism explains why stems grow up
and roots grow down. The tendril is responding to the fence post it touched.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negative thigmotropism, a growth response to touch
choices.rationale:
You got the right tropism but the wrong direction. The tendril grew toward and
around the post, not away from it. Moving toward the stimulus is positive.

questions.explanation: Thigmotropism is a plant's growth response to touch or physical contact. The tendril curling toward and around the fence post (the stimulus) is positive thigmotropism.

questions.stem: A plant's stem is observed bending and growing toward a nearby window, in the direction of the incoming light. What is this tropic response called?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You got the right tropism but the wrong direction. Negative means growing away
from the stimulus. The stem is growing toward the light, which is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to gravity. Gravitropism explains why stems grow up
and roots grow down. The stimulus here is light, not gravity.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to gravity with the wrong direction. The stem is
responding to light, not gravity. Growth away from gravity is negative
gravitropism, which describes roots.

questions.explanation: Stems typically show positive phototropism, growing toward the light stimulus.

questions.stem: A plant's roots are observed growing downward and away from a light source shining from one side of the pot. What is this tropic response called?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You got the right tropism but the wrong direction. Positive means growing
toward the light. The roots are growing away from the light source.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to gravity. The roots are also showing positive
gravitropism (growing down), but the question asks about the response to
the light source specifically.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the response to gravity in the wrong direction. Negative gravitropism
means growing against gravity, which is what stems do. The question asks about
the roots' response to the light source.

questions.explanation: Roots typically show negative phototropism, growing away from light, while also independently showing positive gravitropism by growing downward with gravity.

questions.stem: A student observes a stem growing toward a light source and concludes that the plant's roots must also grow toward the light, since it is "the same plant responding to the same stimulus." Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: roots and stems typically show opposite tropic responses to the same stimulus; while stems show positive phototropism (toward light), roots typically show negative phototropism (away from light).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: every part of a plant always responds identically to the same stimulus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because roots cannot respond to light at all.
choices.rationale:
You said roots ignore light entirely. Roots can respond to light. They typically
show negative phototropism, growing away from it, not zero response.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: since stems and roots are directly connected, they must grow in the same direction.
choices.rationale:
You said physical connection forces the same response. Being connected does not
mean the same response. Roots and stems are connected and still grow in opposite
directions in response to light.

questions.explanation: A common error is assuming the whole plant responds the same way to a stimulus. In reality, roots and stems often show opposite tropic responses: stems grow toward light (positive phototropism) while roots grow away from it (negative phototropism).

questions.stem: What is the term for pollen (containing the plant's male sex cells) being transferred from the male part of a flower to the female part of a flower?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the next step. Fertilization is when the sperm cell from pollen
actually joins with an egg cell. Pollination is just the transfer of pollen
to the flower's female part.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked a tropism. Gravitropism is a plant's growth response to gravity.
It has nothing to do with pollen transfer.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the process where a seed sprouts into a new plant. Germination
comes after fertilization. It is not about pollen transfer between flower parts.

questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, often carried by wind, insects, or other animals.

questions.stem: What is the term for a male sex cell from pollen joining with a female egg cell inside a flower's ovule, forming a zygote?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the step before. Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the
flower's female part. Fertilization is the actual joining of sperm and egg
cells that happens afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked a tropism. Thigmotropism is a plant's growth response to touch.
It has nothing to do with sex cells joining.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the spreading of seeds away from the parent plant. Dispersal
happens after fertilization and seed formation. It is not the joining of
sex cells.

questions.explanation: Fertilization is the joining of a male sex cell from pollen with a female egg cell, forming a zygote that develops into a plant embryo.

questions.stem: A description states only that a bee deposited pollen onto the female part of a flower, with no mention of any sex cells joining together afterward. Is this description best classified as pollination, fertilization, or both?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pollination only: pollination is just the transfer of pollen; fertilization requires the additional step of a sperm cell actually fusing with an egg cell, which is not mentioned here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fertilization only, since any contact between pollen and a flower counts as fertilization.
choices.rationale:
You said contact with pollen is fertilization. It is not. Fertilization requires
a sperm cell to fuse with an egg cell inside the ovule. Pollen landing on the
flower is only pollination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both pollination and fertilization, since one step always implies the other has already happened.
choices.rationale:
You said pollination implies fertilization has also occurred. It does not.
Pollination can happen without fertilization following. The description mentions
no joining of sex cells, so only pollination is described.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither, since depositing pollen does not relate to plant reproduction.
choices.rationale:
You said pollen transfer is unrelated to reproduction. It is the first step.
Pollination is the start of plant sexual reproduction, even before fertilization.

questions.explanation: A description of only pollen landing on a flower's female part (without mentioning any joining of sex cells) is describing pollination alone. Fertilization requires the additional step of a sperm cell fusing with an egg cell, which happens afterward.

questions.stem: A seedling is planted sideways in a pot. After several days, regardless of its sideways starting position, what is the most likely outcome for its root and stem, and which tropism explains it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The root will curve to grow downward (positive gravitropism), and the stem will curve to grow upward (negative gravitropism), since gravity is the stimulus and roots and stems typically respond oppositely to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both the root and the stem will curve to grow downward, since both parts respond identically to gravity.
choices.rationale:
You said both parts grow downward. Roots grow down (positive gravitropism) but
stems grow up (negative gravitropism). They respond to gravity in opposite
directions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither the root nor the stem will change direction, since gravity does not affect plant growth.
choices.rationale:
You said gravity has no effect. Gravity is a key stimulus for plant growth.
Gravitropism causes roots to grow down and stems to grow up, whatever
direction the seedling starts in.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The root will curve upward, and the stem will curve downward, reversing the typical gravitropic response.
choices.rationale:
You reversed the typical responses. Roots grow downward (positive gravitropism)
and stems grow upward (negative gravitropism). Your answer has each part doing
the other's job.

questions.explanation: This is gravitropism: the root grows downward, in the same direction as gravity (positive gravitropism), while the stem grows upward, against gravity (negative gravitropism): the typical gravitropic pattern regardless of the seedling's starting orientation.

questions.stem:
Which part of the cell is called its "control center" because it holds
the cell's DNA and directs its activities?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that makes energy, not the one that runs the
cell. The mitochondrion breaks down glucose into ATP. It does not
store DNA or give the cell its instructions.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that builds proteins. The ribosome reads
instructions from the DNA, but it does not store DNA or direct the
cell's activities.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that packages and ships proteins. The Golgi
apparatus handles proteins after they are made. It does not store DNA
or control the cell.

questions.explanation:
The nucleus stores the DNA and controls what the cell does. The other
organelles listed do not hold the cell's DNA.

questions.stem:
Which organelle is known as the "powerhouse of the cell" because it
breaks down glucose to produce ATP?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that builds proteins. The ribosome links
amino acids together to make proteins, not ATP.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that stores DNA and controls the cell. The
nucleus directs what the cell does, but it does not break down
glucose for energy.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that stores water, nutrients, or waste. The
vacuole holds things inside the cell but does not produce ATP.

questions.explanation:
Mitochondria break down glucose and release energy as ATP, the fuel
the cell uses to do work. Ribosomes build proteins, not energy.

questions.stem:
Which structure builds proteins by following instructions copied from
the cell's DNA?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that packages proteins after they are built.
The Golgi apparatus modifies and ships proteins. It does not build
them by reading DNA.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that makes energy. The mitochondrion breaks
down glucose into ATP. It does not build proteins by reading DNA
instructions.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the barrier that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
The cell membrane acts as a gate but does not build proteins.

questions.explanation:
Ribosomes read copied DNA instructions and link amino acids together
to build proteins. The Golgi apparatus packages proteins afterward:
it does not build them.

questions.stem:
A cell organelle modifies, sorts, and packages proteins, then ships
them to where they are needed inside or outside the cell. Which
organelle is this?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that helps build and process proteins. The
rough ER works earlier in the pipeline. It does not package proteins
and send them to their destination.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that stores DNA and gives instructions. The
nucleus controls the cell but does not package or ship proteins.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that makes ATP. The mitochondrion releases
energy from glucose. It does not sort or package proteins for
shipping.

questions.explanation:
The Golgi apparatus works like a packaging and shipping center for the
cell. The rough ER helps build proteins earlier in the process, but it
does not package and ship them.

questions.stem:
Which structure is covered in ribosomes and helps build and process
proteins?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the other type of endoplasmic reticulum. The smooth ER
has no ribosomes on its surface and builds lipids, not proteins.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that packages and ships proteins. The Golgi
apparatus handles proteins after the rough ER has finished processing
them.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that breaks down waste and old cell parts.
The lysosome is a cleanup unit, not a protein-building structure.

questions.explanation:
The rough ER is named for the ribosomes dotting its surface, and those
ribosomes build proteins. The smooth ER has no ribosomes and builds
lipids instead.

questions.stem:
Which structure acts as a thin, flexible barrier that controls which
substances enter and leave the cell?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the rigid outer layer found in plant cells. The cell wall
gives the cell its shape and support. It does not control which
substances pass through.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the fluid inside the cell that holds the organelles. The
cytoplasm is not a barrier and does not control what enters or
leaves.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked a structure inside the nucleus that makes ribosomes. The
nucleolus is not a barrier and does not select substances entering
or leaving the cell.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is found in animal cells but NOT in plant
cells?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked a structure found in plant cells, not animal cells. The
cell wall gives plants their rigid shape. Animal cells do not have
one.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked a structure found in plant cells, not animal cells.
Chloroplasts do photosynthesis. Animal cells lack them entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked a structure found in plant cells, not animal cells. The
central vacuole stores water and keeps the plant firm. Animal cells
do not have one.

questions.explanation:
Animal cells typically have a centrosome, which helps organize cell
division. Cell wall, chloroplast, and central vacuole are the three
structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is NOT one of the three structures unique to
plant cells?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked one of the three plant-only structures. The cell wall is
found in plants but not animal cells. It is part of the set the
question asks about.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked one of the three plant-only structures. Chloroplasts make
food for the plant through photosynthesis. They are not found in
animal cells.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked one of the three plant-only structures. The central
vacuole stores water and helps keep plants firm. Animal cells do not
have one.

questions.explanation:
Lysosomes are typically found in animal cells, where they break down
waste. Cell wall, chloroplast, and central vacuole are the three
plant-only structures.

questions.stem:
A cell observed under a microscope has a rigid outer wall, a large
water-filled sac, and small green structures inside. Is this most
likely a plant cell or an animal cell?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the wrong cell type. Animal cells have no rigid outer
wall, no large central water sac, and no green structures. All three
clues point to a plant cell.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot be either type of cell
choices.rationale:
You said neither type matches, but all three clues are plant-only
structures. A rigid wall is a cell wall, the sac is a central
vacuole, and the green structures are chloroplasts.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You said both cell types are equally possible, but animal cells lack
cell walls, central vacuoles, and chloroplasts. Three plant-only
clues rule out the animal cell.

questions.explanation:
A rigid wall matches the cell wall, the water-filled sac matches the
central vacuole, and the green structures match chloroplasts. All
three clues are plant-only structures, so this is a plant cell.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart diffusion and osmosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Osmosis is specifically the movement of water; diffusion can involve any particle, including water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diffusion is specifically the movement of water; osmosis can involve any particle.
choices.rationale:
You have the two terms swapped. Osmosis is the specific case and it
only describes water. Diffusion is the broader term that covers any
particle moving from high to low concentration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmosis requires energy; diffusion does not.
choices.rationale:
You added an energy requirement that is not there. Both osmosis and
diffusion move particles from high to low concentration on their own,
without the cell spending energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffusion only happens in animal cells; osmosis only happens in plant cells.
choices.rationale:
You applied a cell-type restriction that does not exist. Both
processes happen in all living cells, not in one type only.

questions.explanation:
Osmosis is a special case of diffusion that applies only to water.
Diffusion is the broader term and can describe any particle moving
from high to low concentration. Neither process needs energy.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart diffusion and active transport?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration and needs no energy; active transport moves particles from low to high concentration and needs energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diffusion needs energy and moves particles from low to high concentration; active transport needs no energy.
choices.rationale:
You reversed both descriptions. Diffusion needs no energy and moves
particles from high to low. Active transport needs energy and moves
particles from low to high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both processes always move particles from low to high concentration.
choices.rationale:
You applied the active transport rule to diffusion. Diffusion follows
the concentration gradient, moving from high to low concentration on
its own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Active transport only happens in plant cells.
choices.rationale:
You added a cell-type restriction that is not true. Active transport
happens in all living cells that need to move substances against a
concentration gradient.

questions.explanation:
Diffusion follows the concentration gradient (high to low) on its own.
Active transport pushes particles against the gradient (low to high),
which always requires the cell to spend energy.

questions.stem:
A red blood cell is placed in a solution with a lower solute
concentration than the inside of the cell. What is the most likely
result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water moves into the cell, and it may swell or burst.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water moves out of the cell, and it shrinks.
choices.rationale:
You described what happens in a hypertonic solution. The surrounding
solution here has less solute than the cell, so water is pulled into
the cell, not out of it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No water moves, and the cell stays the same size.
choices.rationale:
You described isotonic conditions. This solution has a lower solute
concentration than the cell, so water does move, and it moves
inward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cell wall prevents any change.
choices.rationale:
You applied a plant cell feature to a red blood cell. Animal cells
have no cell wall, so nothing stops water from moving in and
swelling the cell.

questions.explanation:
A solution with lower solute concentration than the cell is
hypotonic. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, which
here is inside the cell, so the cell swells and may even burst.

questions.stem:
A red blood cell is placed in a salt solution, and the cell shrinks
and shrivels. What type of solution was it most likely placed in?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the solution where the cell swells, not shrinks. In a
hypotonic solution, water moves into the cell because the outside
has less solute than the inside.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the solution where the cell stays the same size. In an
isotonic solution, water moves in and out at the same rate and the
cell does not change shape.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked a term that describes pH, not the relationship between
solute concentrations. Tonicity is about how much solute is on each
side of the membrane, not whether the solution is acidic or basic.

questions.explanation:
The cell shrank, so water moved out of it. Water leaves a cell when
the surrounding solution has a higher solute concentration than the
cell: that solution is called hypertonic.

questions.stem:
A red blood cell is placed in a solution with the same solute
concentration as the inside of the cell. What happens to the cell's
size?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You described what happens in a hypotonic solution. A hypotonic
solution has less solute outside than inside, so water moves in.
This solution has equal solute on both sides.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You described what happens in a hypertonic solution. A hypertonic
solution has more solute outside than inside, so water moves out.
This solution is equal on both sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It splits into two smaller cells.
choices.rationale:
You described cell division, which is a separate process driven by
the cell cycle. A change in surrounding solute concentration does
not cause a cell to divide.

questions.explanation:
Equal solute concentration inside and outside is called isotonic.
Water still moves in and out, but at the same rate in both
directions, so the cell's size does not change.

questions.stem:
Put the following steps of protein production and shipping in the
correct order.
1. Golgi apparatus packages the protein for shipping
2. Ribosome builds the protein
3. Rough endoplasmic reticulum processes the protein

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You put the Golgi apparatus first. The Golgi packages proteins at the
end, not the beginning. The ribosome builds the protein first, then
the rough ER processes it, and then the Golgi ships it.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You started with the rough ER. The ribosome builds the protein before
the rough ER ever touches it. Packaging by the Golgi comes last, not
first.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You skipped the rough ER. The ribosome builds the protein first, but
the rough ER must process it before the Golgi can package and ship
it.

questions.explanation:
A ribosome builds the protein first. The rough ER, covered in
ribosomes, then helps process it. Last, the Golgi apparatus packages
and ships the finished protein.

questions.stem:
A cell normally uses active transport to keep pumping a nutrient into
itself, even though the nutrient is already more concentrated inside
than outside. If the cell suddenly runs out of ATP, what will most
likely happen to the movement of that nutrient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The nutrient will stop being pumped in and may start leaking back out along its concentration gradient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nutrient will keep moving into the cell at the same rate.
choices.rationale:
You assumed the transport continues without fuel. Active transport
needs ATP to push substances against the concentration gradient.
Without ATP, the pump stops.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nutrient will be pumped in even faster.
choices.rationale:
You predicted the opposite of what happens. The pump needs ATP to
run. With no ATP, it cannot move the nutrient at all, let alone
faster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nutrient will convert into a different substance.
choices.rationale:
You described a chemical reaction, not a transport process. Losing
ATP stops the pump. It does not change the chemical identity of the
nutrient being transported.

questions.explanation:
Active transport needs ATP to move a substance against its
concentration gradient. Without ATP, the cell cannot keep pumping the
nutrient in, and it may drift back out toward the lower
concentration, following ordinary diffusion instead.

questions.stem: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, water, and light energy as raw materials. What are its two products?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You listed the raw materials, not the products. Carbon dioxide and
water go into photosynthesis. Glucose and oxygen come out of it.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked outputs of cellular respiration, not photosynthesis. ATP
is made when the cell breaks down glucose. Photosynthesis makes
glucose and oxygen.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You got one product right but swapped the other. Glucose is a
product of photosynthesis, but carbon dioxide is one of its raw
materials. The second product is oxygen.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis combines carbon dioxide, water, and light energy to produce glucose (the plant's food) and oxygen (released as a byproduct).

questions.stem: Cellular respiration uses glucose and oxygen as raw materials. What are its products?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You listed the raw materials of cellular respiration, not the
products. Glucose and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide, water, and ATP
come out.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You named a raw material of cellular respiration, not a product.
Oxygen is consumed during respiration. The products are carbon
dioxide, water, and ATP.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You described inputs of photosynthesis, not outputs of cellular
respiration. Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release
ATP, carbon dioxide, and water.

questions.explanation: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, and usable energy stored as ATP.

questions.stem: In which organelle does photosynthesis take place?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle for cellular respiration, not
photosynthesis. The mitochondrion breaks down glucose into ATP.
The chloroplast is the one that uses sunlight to make glucose.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that stores DNA and controls the cell. The
nucleus does not capture sunlight or make glucose. Photosynthesis
happens in the chloroplast.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that builds proteins. The ribosome reads
DNA instructions to make proteins. Photosynthesis happens in the
chloroplast.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis happens inside the chloroplast, using chlorophyll to capture sunlight.

questions.stem: In which organelle does cellular respiration mainly take place?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle for photosynthesis, not cellular
respiration. The chloroplast captures sunlight to make glucose.
The mitochondrion breaks down glucose to make ATP.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that stores DNA and controls the cell. The
nucleus does not break down glucose. Cellular respiration happens
mainly in the mitochondrion.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the organelle that builds proteins. The ribosome reads
DNA instructions to link amino acids. Cellular respiration happens
in the mitochondrion.

questions.explanation: Cellular respiration mainly happens inside the mitochondrion, which is why it is often called the cell's "powerhouse."

questions.stem: A student examines a green, disc-shaped organelle under a microscope. Which process does this organelle perform?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Photosynthesis, since this describes a chloroplast.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cellular respiration, since this describes a mitochondrion.
choices.rationale:
You named the wrong organelle. A mitochondrion is bean-shaped with
folded inner membranes and is not green. A green, disc-shaped
organelle is a chloroplast, which does photosynthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You split the function between both processes, but a single organelle
does one job. The green, disc-shaped chloroplast does photosynthesis.
The mitochondrion does cellular respiration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither: this organelle does not perform any energy process.
choices.rationale:
You said the organelle has no energy role, but the chloroplast is
central to energy capture. It uses chlorophyll to convert sunlight
into glucose through photosynthesis.

questions.explanation: A green, disc-shaped organelle matches the chloroplast, whose green color comes from chlorophyll, and which performs photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A student examines a bean-shaped organelle with folded inner membranes under a microscope. Which process does this organelle perform?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cellular respiration, since this describes a mitochondrion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Photosynthesis, since this describes a chloroplast.
choices.rationale:
You named the wrong organelle. Photosynthesis happens in a
chloroplast, which is green and disc-shaped. The one described here
has no pigment and a folded interior.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You split the function between both processes, but each organelle
does one job. The bean-shaped mitochondrion does cellular
respiration. The chloroplast does photosynthesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither: this organelle does not perform any energy process.
choices.rationale:
You said the organelle has no energy role, but the mitochondrion is
the cell's main energy-releasing structure. It breaks down glucose
into ATP through cellular respiration.

questions.explanation: A bean-shaped organelle with folded inner membranes matches the mitochondrion, which performs cellular respiration.

questions.stem: Why does the oxygen that animals breathe in ultimately come from plants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Photosynthesis in plants produces oxygen as a byproduct while making glucose, which animals then use in cellular respiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Animals produce their own oxygen internally, unrelated to plants.
choices.rationale:
You said animals make their own oxygen, but animals cannot produce
oxygen. They consume it during cellular respiration and get it from
the oxygen plants release during photosynthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plants absorb oxygen from animals and store it for later use.
choices.rationale:
You reversed the direction. Plants release oxygen as a byproduct of
photosynthesis. Animals breathe that oxygen in. Plants do not
absorb and store oxygen from animals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen is created directly by the Sun, unrelated to any living process.
choices.rationale:
You removed living things from the oxygen cycle entirely. The Sun
provides the energy for photosynthesis, but the oxygen is made by
plants, not by the Sun directly.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen as a byproduct of making glucose. This oxygen becomes available for animals (and plants themselves) to use as a raw material in cellular respiration.

questions.stem: A student claims, "Plants only perform photosynthesis; only animals perform cellular respiration." Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: plants perform both photosynthesis (to make food) and cellular respiration (to use that food for energy), just like animal cells.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: plants never need ATP energy, unlike animals.
choices.rationale:
You said plants do not need ATP, but every living cell needs ATP to
do work. Plant cells use cellular respiration to convert their own
glucose into ATP energy just like animal cells do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: plants only perform cellular respiration, never photosynthesis.
choices.rationale:
You kept the error but reversed it. Plants do perform photosynthesis.
That is how they make glucose. They also perform cellular respiration
to convert that glucose into usable ATP.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: only animal cells contain mitochondria.
choices.rationale:
You said plant cells lack mitochondria, but that is not true. Plant
cells have both chloroplasts and mitochondria. They use the
mitochondria to perform cellular respiration.

questions.explanation: Plant cells need ATP energy just as much as animal cells do. To get it, they also perform cellular respiration, breaking down some of the glucose they produced through photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A student writes an equation with "light energy" as one of the inputs, but labels it cellular respiration. Is this labeling correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: an equation with light energy as an input describes photosynthesis, not cellular respiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: light energy is always an input for cellular respiration.
choices.rationale:
You accepted the label, but light energy is not an input for cellular
respiration. Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and oxygen to
release ATP. Light energy is an input for photosynthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because light energy is never used by any biological process.
choices.rationale:
You got the label wrong but gave the wrong reason. Light energy is
used by a biological process. Photosynthesis uses it to make
glucose. That is why the equation describes photosynthesis, not
cellular respiration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: photosynthesis and cellular respiration use identical inputs.
choices.rationale:
You said the two processes share the same inputs, but they do not.
Photosynthesis needs light energy, carbon dioxide, and water.
Cellular respiration needs glucose and oxygen.

questions.explanation: Light energy is a defining input of photosynthesis. Cellular respiration's defining output is ATP energy, not an input of light: mixing these up reverses the two equations.

questions.stem: A student says the mitochondrion is where photosynthesis happens, since it is also involved in energy production. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the chloroplast performs photosynthesis; the mitochondrion performs cellular respiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: both processes happen in the mitochondrion.
choices.rationale:
You put photosynthesis in the mitochondrion, but that is wrong. The
mitochondrion performs cellular respiration. Photosynthesis happens
in the chloroplast, which contains chlorophyll to capture sunlight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because neither organelle is involved in energy production.
choices.rationale:
You said neither organelle handles energy, but that is the opposite
of the truth. The mitochondrion releases energy through cellular
respiration. The chloroplast captures energy through photosynthesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the mitochondrion is simply another name for the chloroplast.
choices.rationale:
You treated the two as the same organelle, but they are different.
The chloroplast is green, disc-shaped, and does photosynthesis.
The mitochondrion is bean-shaped and does cellular respiration.

questions.explanation: Chloroplasts (found only in plant-type cells) capture light energy for photosynthesis. Mitochondria (found in nearly all cells) release energy from glucose through cellular respiration: different organelles, different processes.

questions.stem: A student lists oxygen as one of the products of cellular respiration. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: cellular respiration consumes oxygen as a raw material; it does not produce it. Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: cellular respiration always produces oxygen as a byproduct.
choices.rationale:
You accepted oxygen as a product, but cellular respiration consumes
oxygen, it does not make it. Oxygen is used to break down glucose.
The products are carbon dioxide, water, and ATP.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: cellular respiration produces glucose instead of oxygen.
choices.rationale:
You got the verdict right but named the wrong product. Cellular
respiration does not produce glucose. It breaks glucose down into
carbon dioxide, water, and ATP.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: both photosynthesis and cellular respiration produce oxygen.
choices.rationale:
You said both processes release oxygen, but cellular respiration
consumes oxygen as a raw material. Only photosynthesis releases
oxygen as a byproduct.

questions.explanation: Cellular respiration uses oxygen as an input to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water as byproducts. Oxygen is strictly consumed here, not produced: it is photosynthesis that produces oxygen.

questions.stem: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related to each other?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are essentially opposite processes: the products of one are the raw materials the other needs, and vice versa.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are identical processes that happen in the same organelle.
choices.rationale:
You said both processes are the same, but they are opposites.
Photosynthesis builds glucose and releases oxygen. Cellular
respiration breaks glucose down and consumes oxygen. They also
happen in different organelles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are completely unrelated processes with no shared substances.
choices.rationale:
You said the two processes share nothing, but they are directly
linked. The glucose and oxygen that photosynthesis produces are
exactly what cellular respiration needs as inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cellular respiration is simply an early stage of photosynthesis.
choices.rationale:
You put cellular respiration inside photosynthesis, but they are
separate processes in separate organelles. Cellular respiration
breaks down the glucose that photosynthesis already made.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis's products (glucose and oxygen) are exactly what cellular respiration needs as reactants, and respiration's products (carbon dioxide and water) are exactly what photosynthesis needs: making them mirror-image processes.

questions.stem: Identify the missing product in this equation, and name the process it represents: $6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{light energy} \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + \, ?$

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You named a raw material of this equation as its product. Carbon
dioxide appears on the left side as an input. The missing product
is oxygen gas, and the equation describes photosynthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the product of cellular respiration, not photosynthesis.
ATP is released when glucose breaks down. This equation shows
glucose being built, not broken down, so the missing product is
oxygen gas.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You named a raw material as the missing product. Water appears on
the left side as an input. The equation is photosynthesis, but the
missing product is oxygen gas, not water.

questions.explanation: This equation matches photosynthesis (carbon dioxide, water, and light energy combining to form glucose). The complete equation also produces oxygen gas ($6O_2$) as the other product.

questions.stem: A plant cell is observed performing photosynthesis during the day while sunlight is available. At the same time, is this plant cell also performing cellular respiration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes: plant cells perform cellular respiration continuously, alongside photosynthesis, to convert some of their own glucose into usable ATP energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No: plant cells only perform cellular respiration at night, never during the day.
choices.rationale:
You restricted cellular respiration to nighttime, but plant cells
need ATP energy all day, every day. Cellular respiration runs
continuously in plant cells, even while photosynthesis is also
happening.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: plant cells never perform cellular respiration at all.
choices.rationale:
You said plant cells skip cellular respiration entirely, but plant
cells need ATP just as much as animal cells do. They get it by
performing cellular respiration in their mitochondria.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only because the plant has stopped photosynthesizing for the day.
choices.rationale:
You said photosynthesis and cellular respiration cannot happen at the
same time, but they can and do. During the day, plant cells run
both processes simultaneously in different organelles.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis happens mainly during the day, but cellular respiration happens continuously in plant cells, just like in animal cells, since plant cells constantly need ATP energy for their own life processes.

questions.stem: A skin cell divides to repair a small cut, producing two new skin cells that are genetically identical to the original. Is this mitosis or meiosis?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the division type used to make sex cells. Meiosis
produces four genetically different cells with half the normal
chromosome number. Body repair uses mitosis, which keeps the
chromosome number the same and produces identical copies.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You said both processes apply, but only one fits. Meiosis makes sex
cells with half the chromosomes. Mitosis makes identical copies for
growth and repair. This scenario matches mitosis alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither: this is not a form of cell division
choices.rationale:
You said no cell division is happening, but the scenario describes a
cell producing two daughter cells. That is cell division. The
correct type is mitosis.

questions.explanation: Producing two genetically identical daughter cells for growth or repair is exactly what mitosis does.

questions.stem: A reproductive organ produces sperm cells for sexual reproduction. Is this process mitosis or meiosis?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the division type used for growth and repair. Mitosis
makes two identical copies with the full chromosome number. Sex
cells need half the normal chromosome number, so meiosis is used
instead.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You said both processes apply, but sex cells are made only by
meiosis. Mitosis would give each sperm the full chromosome count,
which would double the offspring's chromosomes at fertilization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither: sperm cells are not produced through cell division
choices.rationale:
You said sperm cells are not made by cell division, but they are.
Meiosis divides a parent cell to produce four sperm cells, each
with half the normal chromosome number.

questions.explanation: Meiosis is used specifically to make sex cells (sperm and egg cells) for sexual reproduction.

questions.stem: A human cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. How many daughter cells result, and how many chromosomes does each have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You described mitosis, not meiosis. Mitosis produces 2 cells with
the full chromosome number. Meiosis produces 4 cells, each with
half: 23 chromosomes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You got the cell count right but not the chromosome count. Meiosis
halves the chromosomes in each daughter cell. Four cells with 46
each would mean no halving occurred.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You got the chromosome count right but not the cell count. Meiosis
goes through two rounds of division and always produces 4 daughter
cells, not 2.

questions.explanation: Meiosis always produces 4 daughter cells, each with half the original chromosome number: $\dfrac{46}{2} = 23$.

questions.stem: A cell with 20 chromosomes undergoes mitosis. How many daughter cells result, and how many chromosomes does each have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You described meiosis, not mitosis. Meiosis produces 4 cells with
half the chromosomes. Mitosis produces 2 cells, each with the full
chromosome number unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You got the cell count right but halved the chromosomes. Mitosis
does not reduce the chromosome number. Each daughter cell gets a
complete copy of all 20 chromosomes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You described the meiosis cell count but with the mitosis chromosome
number. Mitosis produces 2 daughter cells, not 4, and each keeps
the full 20 chromosomes.

questions.explanation: Mitosis always produces 2 daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the original cell: no halving occurs.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis do chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the first phase. Prophase is when chromosomes condense
into visible structures and the nuclear membrane breaks down.
Lining up at the center happens later, in metaphase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase after lineup. Anaphase is when sister
chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite ends. The lineup at
the center happens just before this, in metaphase.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the final phase. Telophase is when two new nuclei form
before the cell splits. The lineup at the center happens much
earlier, in metaphase.

questions.explanation: Metaphase is defined by chromosomes lining up along the cell's center, attached to spindle fibers from opposite sides.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis does the copied DNA condense into visible chromosomes, and the nuclear membrane breaks down?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase when chromosomes line up at the center.
Metaphase comes after the chromosomes have already condensed.
Condensing and nuclear membrane breakdown both happen in prophase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase when sister chromatids separate. Anaphase
comes after condensing and after the nuclear membrane has already
broken down. Both events happen in prophase.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the last phase, when new nuclei form and the cell splits.
Telophase is the end of mitosis. Condensing and nuclear membrane
breakdown happen at the beginning, in prophase.

questions.explanation: Prophase is defined by DNA condensing into visible chromosomes and the breakdown of the nuclear membrane.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis do the sister chromatids separate and get pulled to opposite ends of the cell?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the first phase. Prophase is when chromosomes condense
and the nuclear membrane breaks down. Sister chromatids do not
separate until anaphase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase when chromosomes line up at the center.
Separation of sister chromatids comes right after the lineup, in
anaphase.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the last phase. By telophase, the chromatids have
already separated and reached opposite ends. The separation itself
happens in anaphase.

questions.explanation: Anaphase is defined by the separation of sister chromatids, pulled toward opposite ends of the cell.

questions.stem: During which phase of mitosis do two new nuclei form, one at each end of the cell, before the cell splits in two?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You picked the first phase. Prophase is when the original nucleus
breaks down, not when new nuclei form. New nuclei appear at the
end of mitosis, in telophase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase when chromosomes line up at the center.
Metaphase is the middle of mitosis. Two new nuclei form near the
end, in telophase.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You picked the phase when chromatids separate. After anaphase
delivers the chromosomes to opposite ends, telophase forms a new
nucleus around each set.

questions.explanation: Telophase is defined by the formation of two new nuclei, followed by the cell splitting into two separate cells.

questions.stem: A student says mitosis produces four daughter cells, since it is a form of cell division like meiosis. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: mitosis produces two daughter cells; meiosis is the process that produces four.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: both mitosis and meiosis produce four daughter cells.
choices.rationale:
You applied meiosis's cell count to both processes. Meiosis goes
through two division rounds to produce four cells. Mitosis goes
through one round and produces two.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: mitosis actually produces one daughter cell.
choices.rationale:
You got the verdict right but the number wrong. Mitosis produces
two daughter cells, not one. One cell divides into two identical
copies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: mitosis always produces more daughter cells than meiosis.
choices.rationale:
You said mitosis produces more daughter cells than meiosis, but it
is the opposite. Mitosis produces two. Meiosis produces four. Meiosis
goes through two rounds of division.

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two identical daughter cells. Meiosis, used to make sex cells, produces four. This is one of the most commonly swapped facts between the two processes.

questions.stem: A student assumes meiosis, like mitosis, produces daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: meiosis shuffles genetic material between chromosome pairs, so its four daughter cells are genetically different from each other and from the parent cell.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: meiosis always produces identical daughter cells, just like mitosis.
choices.rationale:
You applied the mitosis outcome to meiosis. Mitosis copies DNA
without shuffling it, so its cells are identical. Meiosis shuffles
genetic material between chromosome pairs, producing four different
cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because meiosis produces no daughter cells at all.
choices.rationale:
You got the verdict right but the reason is wrong. Meiosis does
produce daughter cells. It produces four of them. They are
genetically different from each other because of shuffling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: genetic differences only appear after fertilization, never during meiosis itself.
choices.rationale:
You placed the genetic variation at fertilization, but it starts
during meiosis. The shuffling of chromosome pairs in meiosis is
itself a major source of genetic variation, before any fertilization
occurs.

questions.explanation: Unlike mitosis, meiosis includes genetic shuffling between chromosome pairs, which is a major source of variation: the four resulting cells are not identical to each other or to the parent.

questions.stem: A student assumes that when a sperm cell and egg cell combine during fertilization, the offspring ends up with double the normal chromosome number. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: each sex cell already carries half the normal chromosome number, so combining two returns the total to the normal full number, not double.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: fertilization always doubles the chromosome number beyond the normal count.
choices.rationale:
You accepted the doubling idea, but meiosis exists precisely to
prevent it. Sex cells each carry half the normal number so that
combining two gives back the correct full number.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: fertilization actually results in zero chromosomes.
choices.rationale:
You got the verdict right but the reason is wrong. Fertilization
does not eliminate chromosomes. It combines the chromosomes from
both sex cells to produce the normal full number.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: this is why each new generation has more chromosomes than the last.
choices.rationale:
You said chromosomes accumulate each generation, but that would
make reproduction impossible over time. Meiosis halves the count
in sex cells so fertilization restores the same number every
generation.

questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number in each sex cell specifically so that combining a sperm and egg cell restores the normal full chromosome count, not doubles it.

questions.stem: A description of a dividing cell jumps directly from chromosomes condensing (prophase) to two new nuclei forming (telophase), with no mention of the chromosomes lining up or separating. Does this correctly describe mitosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a valid description of mitosis must include all four phases, in order: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: mitosis can skip phases as long as the cell still divides in the end.
choices.rationale:
You said phases can be skipped, but mitosis is a fixed sequence.
Chromosomes must line up in metaphase before they can separate in
anaphase. Neither step can be left out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because telophase must come before prophase.
choices.rationale:
You got the verdict right but reversed the order. Prophase is first
and telophase is last. The description skipped metaphase and
anaphase, not put telophase first.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: metaphase and anaphase are optional steps in mitosis.
choices.rationale:
You said metaphase and anaphase are optional, but they are not. The
chromosomes must line up in metaphase and separate in anaphase.
Both are required steps in the correct order.

questions.explanation: All four phases of mitosis must occur in order. A description that skips metaphase and anaphase is missing required steps and does not correctly describe the full process.

questions.stem: Why must sex cells (sperm and egg) have half the normal chromosome number, rather than the full number like other body cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: So that when a sperm cell and egg cell combine during fertilization, their chromosome counts add back up to the normal full number.

choices.label: B
choices.text: So that the resulting offspring will have fewer chromosomes than either parent.
choices.rationale:
You said the goal is to reduce the offspring's chromosomes, but
the goal is to keep the count normal. Half plus half equals the
full number. The offspring ends up with the same count as each
parent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: So that sex cells can divide faster than regular body cells.
choices.rationale:
You replaced the chromosome-number reason with a speed argument,
but division speed is not why sex cells have half the number. The
reason is to make sure the chromosome count stays correct after
fertilization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no specific reason; it is simply a coincidence of biology.
choices.rationale:
You said the halving is random, but it is not. It is the direct
result of meiosis, which exists so that two sex cells can combine
and still give the offspring the correct chromosome number.

questions.explanation: If sex cells carried the full chromosome number, offspring would end up with double the normal amount after fertilization. Halving the number in each sex cell keeps the combined total correct.

questions.stem:
Put the four phases of mitosis in the correct order.
1. Anaphase
2. Telophase
3. Prophase
4. Metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You put anaphase before metaphase. Chromosomes must line up in
metaphase before they can be pulled apart in anaphase. The correct
order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You started with metaphase and put prophase second. Prophase is
always first. Chromosomes must condense before they can line up.
The correct order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You put telophase before anaphase. The chromatids must separate in
anaphase first, then the new nuclei form in telophase. The correct
order is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

questions.explanation: The correct order is Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (remembered as "PMAT: Prepare, Middle, Apart, Two").

questions.stem: A sperm cell with 23 chromosomes fertilizes an egg cell with 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does the resulting offspring have?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale:
You kept only one sex cell's count. Fertilization combines the
chromosomes from both. Adding 23 from the sperm and 23 from the
egg gives 46 chromosomes total.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale:
You doubled the full count. The sperm contributes 23 and the egg
contributes 23. Together they add up to 46, which is the normal
human chromosome number, not 92.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale:
You halved instead of added. Fertilization combines chromosomes.
The sperm's 23 and the egg's 23 are added together to give the
offspring 46 chromosomes.

questions.explanation: Fertilization combines the chromosomes from both sex cells: $23 + 23 = 46$, restoring the normal full chromosome number.

questions.stem: Every living thing is made of one or more of what basic unit?
questions.explanation: Cellular organization is a core characteristic of life: every living thing is made of one or more cells, the basic building blocks of life.

questions.stem: What characteristic of life describes an organism keeping its internal conditions stable even when the outside environment changes, like sweating to cool down on a hot day?
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions despite changes in the external environment.

questions.stem: What characteristic of life describes an organism producing new individuals of the same kind?
questions.explanation: Reproduction is the ability to produce new individuals of the same kind, either asexually or sexually.

questions.stem: What characteristic of life describes living things gradually changing traits, over many generations, that help them survive and reproduce better in their environment?
questions.explanation: Adaptation through evolution describes gradual trait changes across generations that improve survival and reproduction in a given environment.

questions.stem: A mushroom absorbs nutrients from decaying wood to fuel its activities. Which characteristic of life does this directly demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Using energy absorbed from the environment (nutrients from decaying wood) is metabolism.

questions.stem: A mushroom releases spores that grow into new mushrooms. Which characteristic of life does this directly demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Producing new individuals (new mushrooms, via spores) is reproduction.

questions.stem: A virus can reproduce, but only after hijacking a host cell's internal machinery: outside of a host cell, it is completely inactive. Does this fact alone make a virus fully alive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: reproduction is only one characteristic; a virus still lacks cells and independent metabolism, which most biologists require for something to be fully alive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the ability to reproduce, on its own, is enough to be classified as fully alive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: viruses cannot reproduce under any circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: since it can reproduce inside a host, it counts the same as any living cell.

questions.explanation: A single characteristic is never enough. Viruses fail the "made of cells" and "independent metabolism" requirements, which is why most biologists classify them as borderline, not fully alive.

questions.stem: Most biologists do not classify viruses as fully "living," even though viruses can reproduce and evolve. Why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Viruses are not made of cells and cannot carry out metabolism or maintain homeostasis on their own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Viruses cannot reproduce or evolve at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viruses are too small to be studied by biologists.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viruses only exist in humans, not in other organisms.

questions.explanation: Viruses show some characteristics of life (reproduction, evolution) but fail others (no cells, no independent metabolism or homeostasis), placing them at the border between living and non-living.

questions.stem: A car engine "consumes" gasoline and produces motion, which might resemble metabolism. Is a car engine considered living?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: it is not made of cells, cannot reproduce itself, and cannot maintain homeostasis, grow, or adapt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: consuming fuel for energy is enough to be classified as living.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because it does not produce any motion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: any machine that uses fuel is considered alive.

questions.explanation: Resembling one characteristic (using energy) is not enough. The engine fails every other requirement: no cells, no reproduction, no homeostasis, no growth, no adaptation, so it is non-living.

questions.stem: A crystal in a mineral solution grows larger over time by adding more material in a repeating pattern. Is the crystal considered living?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this growth is just repeated chemical bonding, not cellular growth, and the crystal cannot reproduce, respond to stimuli, or maintain homeostasis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: growing larger over time is enough to be classified as living.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because crystals are too small to be alive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: any object that grows is automatically living.

questions.explanation: Resembling one characteristic (growth) is not enough. The crystal fails every other requirement, so it is non-living, despite appearing to "grow."

questions.stem: A fire spreads across a field, consuming fuel (plant material and oxygen) for energy and growing larger. A student argues the fire must be alive, since it grows and uses energy. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the fire cannot reproduce itself, does not maintain homeostasis, and is not made of cells; resembling growth and energy use alone is not enough.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: anything that grows and consumes energy is alive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because fire cannot spread across a field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: fire reproduces by spreading to new fuel sources.

questions.explanation: Fire mimics "growth" (spreading) and "metabolism" (consuming fuel for energy), but it fails the other characteristics of life: it has no cells, cannot reproduce itself, and cannot maintain homeostasis. It is non-living.

questions.stem: A rock rolls down a hill after being pushed. A student describes this as the rock "responding to a stimulus." Is this a correct use of the term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: response to stimuli means an organism actively reacting in a controlled, biological way, not simply obeying gravity or physical forces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any movement caused by an outside force counts as response to stimuli.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because rocks are too large to respond to anything.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: gravity is itself considered a biological stimulus.

questions.explanation: True response to stimuli involves an organism actively reacting, like a plant growing toward light or an animal fleeing danger, not an object simply obeying gravity or another physical force.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart asexual and sexual reproduction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asexual reproduction involves one parent producing offspring; sexual reproduction involves two parents combining genetic material.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Asexual reproduction always involves two parents; sexual reproduction always involves one parent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both types of reproduction always require exactly two parents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Asexual reproduction only happens in plants; sexual reproduction only happens in animals.

questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction (like a bacterium splitting in two) involves a single parent. Sexual reproduction involves two parents combining their genetic material.

questions.stem: An organism is observed to be made of cells, uses chemical reactions to obtain energy, maintains stable internal conditions, grows over time, produces offspring, reacts to changes in its environment, and shows trait changes across generations. Based on this full description, should it be classified as alive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes: it demonstrates all seven characteristics of life together, meeting the requirement for being classified as alive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No: demonstrating all seven characteristics together actually disqualifies something from being alive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the organism's exact species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the reproduction and growth characteristics matter; the rest are irrelevant.

questions.explanation: An organism showing all seven characteristics of life together (cellular organization, metabolism, homeostasis, growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, and adaptation) meets the full requirement to be classified as alive.

questions.stem: A pond, with its fish, plants, water, and mud all interacting together in one specific area, is best described as what?
questions.explanation: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and their non-living environment in a specific area, like a pond.

questions.stem: A large-scale grouping of many ecosystems that share a similar climate and similar types of plants and animals, such as a desert or tropical rainforest, is called what?
questions.explanation: A biome is a much larger-scale grouping of ecosystems that share a similar climate and similar plant and animal life, like a desert, rainforest, grassland, or tundra.

questions.stem: Arrange these into a correct food chain, from producer to top predator: a hawk, grass, a frog, a grasshopper.
questions.explanation: Grass (producer) is eaten by the grasshopper (primary consumer), which is eaten by the frog (secondary consumer), which is eaten by the hawk (tertiary consumer).

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk, which trophic level does the grass occupy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary consumer, the second trophic level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secondary consumer, the third trophic level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tertiary consumer, the fourth trophic level

questions.explanation: Grass makes its own food through photosynthesis, making it the producer, the first trophic level in the chain.

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk, which trophic level does the frog occupy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Secondary consumer, the third trophic level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary consumer, the second trophic level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tertiary consumer, the fourth trophic level

questions.explanation: The frog eats the grasshopper (a primary consumer), making the frog a secondary consumer, the third trophic level.

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk, which trophic level does the hawk occupy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tertiary consumer, the fourth (top) trophic level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secondary consumer, the third trophic level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary consumer, the second trophic level

questions.explanation: The hawk eats the frog (a secondary consumer), and since nothing eats the hawk in this chain, it is the tertiary consumer, the top trophic level.

questions.stem: A trophic level of producers contains 10,000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is passed on to the primary consumers?
questions.explanation: The 10% rule means only 10% of energy passes to the next level: $10{,}000 \times 0.10 = 1{,}000$ kilocalories.

questions.stem: A trophic level of producers contains 10,000 kilocalories of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy is available to the secondary consumers (two trophic levels up from producers)?
questions.explanation: Apply the 10% rule one level at a time: $10{,}000 \times 0.10 = 1{,}000$ kilocalories reach the primary consumers, then $1{,}000 \times 0.10 = 100$ kilocalories reach the secondary consumers. Multiplying by 10% only once and skipping straight to the secondary consumers is a common mistake.

questions.stem: A diagram shows a hawk eating both frogs and snakes, snakes eating both frogs and mice, and frogs eating both grasshoppers and crickets: many overlapping, interconnected feeding relationships. Is this best described as a food chain or a food web?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A food web, since it shows many interconnected, overlapping food chains rather than one simple straight-line sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A food chain, since food chains always include more than four organisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: this diagram does not describe feeding relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A biogeochemical cycle, since energy is moving between organisms.

questions.explanation: A food chain is a single, straight-line sequence. Once multiple predators share prey, or one predator eats several prey types, the diagram is showing a food web: the more realistic, interconnected picture.

questions.stem: Which biogeochemical cycle involves carbon moving between the atmosphere (as carbon dioxide), living things (through photosynthesis and respiration), and long-term storage like fossil fuels?
questions.explanation: The carbon cycle moves carbon between the atmosphere, living things, and long-term storage such as fossil fuels.

questions.stem: What is the term for the process, carried out mainly by certain bacteria, that converts nitrogen gas in the air into a usable form for plants?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation is carried out mainly by certain bacteria, converting atmospheric nitrogen gas into a usable form, like ammonia or nitrates, that plants can absorb.
