questions.explanation: On the right, $CO_2$ contributes 2 oxygen atoms and $2H_2O$ contributes 2 more, totaling 4. Since each $O_2$ molecule supplies 2 oxygen atoms, a coefficient of 2 gives $2 \times 2 = 4$ oxygen atoms on the left, matching the right side.

questions.stem: Balance this equation by finding the correct coefficient for $Fe$: $\_\_Fe + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe_2O_3$
questions.explanation: The right side has $2 \times 2 = 4$ iron atoms (from $2Fe_2O_3$). To match, $Fe$ needs a coefficient of 4 on the left. (Checking oxygen: $3 \times 2 = 6$ on the left, and $2 \times 3 = 6$ on the right: also balanced.)

questions.stem: A student tries to balance an equation containing $H_2O$ by changing it to $H_2O_2$ instead of adding a coefficient in front of it. Is this a valid way to balance the equation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: changing a subscript creates an entirely different substance (hydrogen peroxide), not a balanced version of water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: subscripts and coefficients can be adjusted interchangeably to balance an equation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: as long as the total atom count comes out even on both sides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because $H_2O_2$ does not really exist.

questions.explanation: Only coefficients (numbers in front of a formula) may be changed to balance an equation. Changing the subscript inside a formula changes the substance's identity entirely: $H_2O_2$ is hydrogen peroxide, a completely different compound from water.

questions.stem: A student adjusts an equation's coefficients until nitrogen atoms match on both sides, then declares the equation balanced without checking hydrogen. Is this equation confirmed to be balanced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: every element's atom count must match on both sides, not just nitrogen; hydrogen still needs to be checked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: matching just one element is enough to confirm the whole equation is balanced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: hydrogen automatically balances whenever nitrogen does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because nitrogen itself was checked incorrectly.

questions.explanation: An equation is balanced only when every single element matches on both sides. Stopping after checking just one element (like nitrogen) can miss an imbalance in another element (like hydrogen).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart synthesis and decomposition reactions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Synthesis combines multiple substances into one product; decomposition breaks one substance into multiple products.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Synthesis breaks one substance into multiple products; decomposition combines multiple substances into one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both reaction types always involve exactly the same number of reactants and products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Synthesis only happens with elements; decomposition only happens with compounds.

questions.explanation: These are mirror-image reactions: synthesis is many merging into one, and decomposition is one splitting into many. Checking which side of the arrow has more separate substances tells them apart.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart single replacement and double replacement reactions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Single replacement has one free element swapping into a compound; double replacement has two compounds trading their parts with each other.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single replacement always involves two compounds; double replacement always involves one free element.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both reaction types are identical, just with different names.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single replacement only happens with metals; double replacement only happens with nonmetals.

questions.explanation: If only one reactant is a lone element and the other is a compound, it is single replacement. If both reactants are already compounds and simply trade partners, it is double replacement.

questions.stem: Why must a chemical equation be balanced, with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because matter cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction (the Law of Conservation of Mass).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because chemical equations are only a stylistic convention with no physical meaning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because unbalanced equations are illegal to write on an exam.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because only reactions with equal numbers of reactants and products actually occur.

questions.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Mass says atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction: every atom present in the reactants must still be accounted for in the products, which is exactly what a balanced equation shows.

questions.stem: Balance this equation by finding the correct coefficient for $Al$: $\_\_Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3$
questions.explanation: The right side has $2 \times 2 = 4$ aluminum atoms (from $2Al_2O_3$). To match, $Al$ needs a coefficient of 4. (Checking oxygen: $3 \times 2 = 6$ on the left, and $2 \times 3 = 6$ on the right: also balanced.)

questions.stem: Classify this reaction: $2KClO_3 \rightarrow 2KCl + 3O_2$
questions.explanation: One compound ($KClO_3$) breaks apart into two different simpler substances ($KCl$ and $O_2$). Even though it produces two separate products instead of just one, this is still a single substance splitting apart: decomposition.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 5 liters at a pressure of 3 atm. If the pressure is increased to 15 atm at the same temperature, what is the new volume? (Boyle's Law: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$)
questions.explanation: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$: $(3)(5) = (15)(V_2)$, so $15 = 15V_2$, giving $V_2 = 1$ liter. Pressure went up 5 times, so volume shrank to one-fifth.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 4 liters at 200 K. If it is heated to 400 K at constant pressure, what is the new volume? (Charles's Law: $\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{4}{200} = \dfrac{V_2}{400}$. Cross multiplying: $4 \times 400 = 200 \times V_2$, so $V_2 = 8$ liters. Doubling the temperature doubled the volume.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds gas at 2 atm and 250 K. If it is heated to 500 K, what is the new pressure? (Gay-Lussac's Law: $\dfrac{P_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{T_2}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{2}{250} = \dfrac{P_2}{500}$. Cross multiplying: $2 \times 500 = 250 \times P_2$, so $P_2 = 4$ atm. Doubling the temperature doubled the pressure.

questions.stem: A container holds 3 liters of gas with 2 moles present. If 6 moles are present instead, at the same pressure and temperature, what is the new volume? (Avogadro's Law: $\dfrac{V_1}{n_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{n_2}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{V_2}{6}$. Cross multiplying: $3 \times 6 = 2 \times V_2$, so $V_2 = 9$ liters. Tripling the moles tripled the volume.

questions.stem: A gas has a pressure of 2 atm, a volume of 4 liters, and a temperature of 200 K. If the pressure changes to 4 atm and the temperature changes to 400 K, find the new volume using the combined gas law: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{(2)(4)}{200} = \dfrac{(4)(V_2)}{400}$. Cross multiplying: $8 \times 400 = 200 \times 4 \times V_2$, so $3200 = 800V_2$, giving $V_2 = 4$ liters. Pressure doubling (which alone would halve volume) and temperature doubling (which alone would double volume) cancel out.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 10-liter container at a pressure of 3 atm and a temperature of 300 K? (Use $R = 0.0821 \, \text{L·atm/(mol·K)}$.)
A student plugs a temperature of 25°C directly into a gas law formula without converting it. Is this safe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: all gas law formulas require temperature in kelvin; the student must add 273 to convert first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Celsius and kelvin can be used interchangeably in gas law formulas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because 25°C is too low a temperature for gas laws to apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: only pressure and volume need consistent units, not temperature.

questions.explanation: Gas law formulas depend on kelvin specifically, since zero kelvin truly means no thermal energy. Using Celsius directly (especially without converting) breaks the proportional relationships these laws rely on.

questions.stem: A student assumes that squeezing a gas into a smaller volume will decrease its pressure, treating pressure and volume as directly related. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle's Law); squeezing a gas into less space increases its pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: pressure and volume always increase or decrease together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because temperature is not held constant.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: this is exactly what Boyle's Law states.

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law describes an inverse relationship: at constant temperature, decreasing volume increases pressure, not the other way the student assumed.

questions.stem: A problem describes a gas whose pressure, volume, and temperature all change together, with the amount of gas staying fixed. A student tries to solve it using only Boyle's Law. Is this the right approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since temperature is also changing, the combined gas law is needed, not Boyle's Law alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Boyle's Law can always be used regardless of how many quantities change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the ideal gas law should be used instead, since three quantities are changing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as pressure and volume are correctly identified.

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law only accounts for pressure and volume, assuming temperature stays fixed. Since temperature is also changing here, the combined gas law (which merges all three relationships) is required.

questions.stem: A problem gives a single set of values for pressure, volume, moles, and temperature, all at one moment, with no "before and after" comparison. Which law should be used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Ideal Gas Law ($PV = nRT$), since it handles a single snapshot in time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Combined Gas Law, since it always applies whenever all quantities are given.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Boyle's Law, since pressure and volume are both given.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Avogadro's Law, since moles are given.

questions.explanation: The Combined Gas Law compares two different states (before and after a change) for a fixed amount of gas. Since this problem describes only one single moment (with moles included), the Ideal Gas Law is the correct choice.

questions.stem: A gas is compressed into a smaller volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases, since pressure and volume are inversely related at constant temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It decreases, since pressure and volume move in the same direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact volume.

questions.explanation: Boyle's Law describes an inverse relationship between pressure and volume at constant temperature: shrinking the volume raises the pressure.

questions.stem: A gas is heated at constant pressure. What happens to its volume?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases, since volume and temperature are directly related at constant pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It decreases, since heating always shrinks a gas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact temperature.

questions.explanation: Charles's Law describes a direct relationship between volume and temperature at constant pressure: heating the gas makes it expand.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated. What happens to its pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases, since pressure and temperature are directly related at constant volume.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It decreases, since heating always lowers pressure in a sealed container.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It stays exactly the same, since the container is rigid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the exact temperature.

questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac's Law describes a direct relationship between pressure and temperature at constant volume: heating a sealed, rigid container raises its internal pressure.

questions.stem: A sealed, rigid container holds gas at 2 atm and 27°C. If it is heated to 327°C, what is the new pressure? (Remember to convert to kelvin first.)
questions.explanation: Convert to kelvin: $27°C + 273 = 300$ K, and $327°C + 273 = 600$ K. Using Gay-Lussac's Law: $\dfrac{2}{300} = \dfrac{P_2}{600}$, giving $P_2 = 4$ atm.

questions.stem: A problem gives a gas's pressure, volume, temperature, and number of moles, all measured at one specific moment, with no described change from one condition to another. Which gas law directly relates all four quantities at once?
questions.explanation: The Ideal Gas Law ($PV = nRT$) relates pressure, volume, moles, and temperature all at once, without needing a "before and after" comparison: exactly the situation described here.

questions.stem: Which scientist proposed that atoms are simple, indivisible solid spheres, with no internal parts?
questions.explanation: Dalton's early model pictured atoms as tiny solid balls, like billiard balls, with nothing inside them.

questions.stem: Which scientist proposed the "plum pudding model," with negative electrons scattered throughout a positively charged material?
questions.explanation: After discovering the electron, Thomson pictured it embedded in a positive "pudding," like plums scattered through pudding.

questions.stem: Which scientist proposed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its center, with electrons orbiting around it?
questions.explanation: Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed a small, dense, positive nucleus, replacing Thomson's model with electrons orbiting this central nucleus.

questions.stem: Which scientist proposed that electrons can only occupy certain fixed, specific energy levels around the nucleus, like rungs on a ladder?
questions.explanation: Bohr refined Rutherford's model by proposing fixed energy levels, which explained why atoms absorb and release light only at specific wavelengths.

questions.stem: Which scientist developed the modern model describing electrons as existing in "clouds" of probability rather than on fixed orbital paths?
questions.explanation: Schrödinger's quantum mechanical model describes regions where an electron is more or less likely to be found, rather than a fixed path. This is the model chemists still use today.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most of the fired particles passed straight through the thin gold foil without deflecting. What did this result reveal about the atom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An atom is mostly empty space.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An atom has no charge at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An atom is a solid, indivisible sphere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electrons are scattered evenly throughout the atom.

questions.explanation: Since most particles encountered nothing solid in their path, this showed that atoms are mostly empty space, not solid all the way through.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, a small number of fired particles bounced back sharply instead of passing through. What did this result reveal about the atom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its center.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The atom has no nucleus at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The atom is completely empty, with nothing inside it.

questions.explanation: A sharp bounce could only happen if the fired particles collided with something extremely small, dense, and positively charged: this revealed the existence of a concentrated nucleus.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart Thomson's model and Rutherford's model?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thomson's electrons are scattered throughout a positive material; Rutherford's electrons orbit a separate, concentrated nucleus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thomson's model has a nucleus; Rutherford's model has no nucleus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both models describe electrons orbiting a central nucleus in the exact same way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thomson's model came after Rutherford's and replaced it.

questions.explanation: Thomson pictured electrons embedded throughout the positive "pudding," with no separate nucleus. Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed a separate, concentrated nucleus that electrons orbit around, which is the key difference exams test.

questions.stem: Which scientist is credited with discovering the electron itself?
questions.explanation: Thomson discovered the electron years before Rutherford's gold foil experiment. Rutherford's experiment revealed the nucleus, not the electron, which Thomson had already found.

questions.stem: A student says Bohr's fixed-orbit model is the current, scientifically accepted model of the atom. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Schrödinger's electron cloud (quantum mechanical) model is the current accepted model.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Bohr's model is still the current accepted model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: Rutherford's nuclear model is the current accepted model.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: Dalton's solid sphere model is the current accepted model.

questions.explanation: Bohr's neat, fixed-orbit picture is a useful simplification, but it was later replaced by Schrödinger's electron cloud model, which better matches experimental evidence and is still used today.

questions.stem: If Thomson's plum pudding model had been correct, what result would you expect from firing particles at a thin gold foil?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All particles would pass through with only slight, even deflection, since there is no concentrated dense region to bounce off of.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most particles would bounce straight back, since the positive "pudding" fills the entire atom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All particles would be absorbed and stop completely inside the foil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The particles would pass through only if they were negatively charged.

questions.explanation: Since Thomson's model spreads the positive charge evenly through the whole atom, there is no small, dense region to cause a sharp bounce: only mild, even deflection would be expected. The actual sharp bounces observed proved this model wrong.

questions.stem: What problem did Bohr's model solve that Rutherford's original nuclear model could not explain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Why atoms absorb and release light only at specific, predictable wavelengths, not a continuous range.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Why atoms are mostly empty space.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Why the nucleus is positively charged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Why electrons have a negative charge.

questions.explanation: Rutherford's model let electrons orbit at any distance, which could not explain why atoms only give off light at very specific amounts of energy. Bohr's fixed energy levels explained this, since jumping between levels releases only specific, predictable amounts of light energy.

questions.stem:
Put these atomic models in the correct historical order, from earliest to most recent.
1. Rutherford's nuclear model
2. Dalton's solid sphere model
3. Schrödinger's electron cloud model
4. Thomson's plum pudding model
5. Bohr's fixed energy level model
questions.explanation: The order is Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear) → Bohr (fixed energy levels) → Schrödinger (electron cloud). Each model was built from testing and improving on the one before it.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence directly overturned Thomson's plum pudding model and led to Rutherford's nuclear model instead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gold foil experiment's sharp-angle bounces, which Thomson's evenly spread-out positive charge could not explain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The discovery of the electron itself, which Thomson had not yet known about.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The observation that atoms absorb light only at specific wavelengths.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The realization that atoms are made of more than one element.

questions.explanation: Thomson's model spreads positive charge evenly through the atom, so it predicted only mild, even deflection: never a sharp bounce. The gold foil experiment's sharp bounces could only happen if the positive charge were concentrated in one small, dense spot, which is exactly what overturned Thomson's model.

questions.stem: Pure oxygen gas ($O_2$) is made of only one type of atom. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: An element is made of only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Oxygen gas fits this exactly.

questions.stem: Table salt ($NaCl$) is made of sodium and chlorine chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: A compound is two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Table salt is always one sodium atom for every one chlorine atom, so it is a compound.

questions.stem: A glass of lemonade contains water, sugar, and lemon juice combined in amounts that can be adjusted to taste. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: A mixture is two or more substances physically combined in amounts that can vary. Since the sugar and lemon juice can be added in different amounts, lemonade is a mixture.

questions.stem: Saltwater looks completely uniform, with no visible particles of salt floating in it. A student concludes it must be a compound. Is the student correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because the ratio of salt to water can vary, which makes it a mixture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because it looks completely uniform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because saltwater has no fixed composition, so it cannot be classified at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because salt and water cannot be separated once combined.

questions.explanation: Looking uniform does not make something a compound. A compound must have a fixed ratio of elements. Since you can dissolve more or less salt in the same water, saltwater is a mixture, even though it looks smooth and even.

questions.stem: An ice cube is left on a table and turns into a puddle of water. Name this phase change.
questions.explanation: Melting is the change from solid to liquid. Ice (solid) turning into water (liquid) is melting.

questions.stem: Water vapor touches a cold glass window and turns into liquid droplets on the surface. Name this phase change.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid. Water vapor (gas) turning into droplets (liquid) is condensation.

questions.stem: A block of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) placed in a room slowly disappears into a misty gas, without ever forming a puddle of liquid. Name this phase change.
questions.explanation: Sublimation is the change from solid directly to gas, skipping the liquid phase entirely. Since the dry ice never becomes liquid, this is sublimation, not evaporation.

questions.stem: On a very cold morning, water vapor in the air turns directly into ice crystals (frost) on a car window, without first forming liquid water. Name this phase change.
questions.explanation: Deposition is the change from gas directly to solid, skipping the liquid phase. Frost forming straight from water vapor is deposition.

questions.stem: Is melting an endothermic or an exothermic phase change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothermic, because the substance absorbs energy to break apart its ordered solid structure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exothermic, because the substance releases energy as it becomes a liquid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothermic, because the substance releases energy as it becomes more ordered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exothermic, because no energy is involved in melting.

questions.explanation: Melting moves a substance from a more ordered state (solid) to a less ordered one (liquid). Becoming less ordered always requires absorbing energy, which makes melting endothermic.

questions.stem: Is freezing an endothermic or an exothermic phase change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exothermic, because the substance releases energy as it becomes a more ordered solid.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothermic, because the substance absorbs energy as it becomes a solid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exothermic, because the substance absorbs energy to form a solid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endothermic, because freezing always requires added heat.

questions.explanation: Freezing moves a substance from a less ordered state (liquid) to a more ordered one (solid). Becoming more ordered always releases energy, which makes freezing exothermic.

questions.stem: "Iron is attracted to a magnet." Is this a physical property or a chemical property?
questions.explanation: A physical property can be observed without changing what the substance is made of. Being attracted to a magnet does not turn iron into a different substance, so it is a physical property.

questions.stem: "Iron can react with oxygen and moisture to form rust." Is this describing a chemical property or a chemical change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemical property, because it describes something the iron could do, not something that has already happened.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemical change, because rust has already formed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physical property, because rusting only affects the iron's surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physical change, because no new substance is involved.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes a potential reaction, what iron *could* do, not an event that already occurred. A description of what a substance is capable of doing is a chemical property. If the sentence said "this nail has rusted," that would describe an actual event, a chemical change.

questions.stem: A nail that was left outside for a month is now covered in a reddish-brown coating and has become brittle. Is this a chemical property or a chemical change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemical change, because a new substance (rust) has actually formed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemical property, because it describes how iron generally behaves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physical change, because the nail's shape is different.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physical property, because the coating can be seen.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes something that has already happened: the iron reacted with oxygen and moisture to form rust, a new substance with different properties. An event that has already occurred, producing a new substance, is a chemical change.

questions.stem: A sheet of paper is torn into several pieces. Is this a physical change or a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Tearing paper changes its shape and size, but it is still made of the same paper: no new substance is formed. That makes it a physical change.

questions.stem: A student claims that boiling water into steam creates a new substance, since steam looks and behaves so differently from liquid water. Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student is wrong: boiling is a phase change, and phase changes never create a new substance, only a new physical state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student is correct: steam is chemically different from liquid water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student is wrong, but only because steam is actually a mixture, not a pure substance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is correct, since boiling requires heat, and any change that requires heat is a chemical change.

questions.explanation: Phase changes only change how tightly packed and ordered the particles are: they never change what the substance actually is. Both liquid water and water vapor (steam) are still $H_2O$. Needing heat does not by itself make a change chemical; several phase changes need heat and are still physical changes.

questions.stem: A student burns a small piece of paper. It turns into ash and smoke while releasing noticeable heat. Which pair correctly describes this event?
questions.explanation: Burning paper produces new substances (ash, smoke, gases) that are different from paper, so it is a chemical change. Since the reaction releases heat instead of absorbing it, it is also exothermic.

questions.stem: A cup of black coffee has no visible grounds or separate parts floating in it. Is this mixture homogeneous or heterogeneous?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the mixture type that has visibly distinct parts or layers. Black coffee has a uniform appearance throughout.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked a pure substance formed when elements chemically bond together. Coffee is a physical blend of water and dissolved compounds.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked a fundamental substance made of only one kind of atom. Coffee contains many distinct chemical compounds mixed together.

questions.explanation: A homogeneous mixture looks completely uniform, with no visible separate parts. Since the coffee shows no separate parts, it is homogeneous.

questions.stem: A bowl of vegetable soup clearly shows separate chunks of carrots, potatoes, and celery. Is this mixture homogeneous or heterogeneous?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the mixture type that looks completely uniform throughout. Vegetable soup has visibly separate ingredients and layers.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked a pure substance joined by chemical bonds. Vegetable soup is a physical mixture whose components retain their identities.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked a basic chemical substance that cannot be broken down further. Soup is a physical combination of many different compounds.

questions.explanation: A heterogeneous mixture has visible separate parts. Since the vegetable chunks can clearly be seen, the soup is heterogeneous.

questions.stem: Clean air is a uniform blend of gases with no visible separate parts. Is this mixture homogeneous or heterogeneous?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the classification for mixtures with visible parts or separate phases. Clean air looks uniform and evenly mixed throughout.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked a substance formed by chemically bonded elements. Air is a physical mixture of separate gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked a single pure substance of one atomic type. Air is a mixture containing several different gases.

questions.explanation: Since the gases in clean air blend together with no visible separate parts, it is a homogeneous mixture.

questions.stem: A bucket of dry sand mixed with small gravel stones shows clearly distinct particles of different sizes. Is this mixture homogeneous or heterogeneous?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the term for a uniform blend with no visible differences. Sand and gravel remain clearly distinct from each other.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked a material made of only one type of element or compound. Sand and gravel are a physical mixture of distinct mineral grains.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked a substance formed by chemical bonding between elements. Mixing sand and gravel is a physical process without chemical bonds.

questions.explanation: Since the sand and gravel particles remain visibly distinct and unevenly distributed, this is a heterogeneous mixture.

questions.stem: A student needs to separate sand from a sand-and-water mixture. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the technique used to separate dissolved liquids by boiling point. Sand is an insoluble solid that can be filtered much faster.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the method used to separate dissolved solutes like pigments. Undissolved sand particles are easily trapped with a simple filter.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the method that boils away the liquid. Filtration is faster and lets you keep both the sand and liquid water.

questions.explanation: Filtration uses a material with tiny holes that let the liquid pass through while trapping solid particles. Since sand does not dissolve in water, filtration easily traps it.

questions.stem: A student wants to recover the salt from saltwater and does not need to keep the water afterward. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the method for trapping undissolved solids. Salt dissolves into particles far too small for a liquid filter to trap.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the method used to separate mixtures of colored dyes based on attraction. Evaporation is the standard way to recover a dissolved solid.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the process that cools and collects evaporated liquid vapor. Since you do not need the water, simple evaporation saves time.

questions.explanation: Evaporation heats the mixture until the liquid turns to vapor and escapes, leaving the dissolved solid behind. Since the water does not need to be collected, simply letting it evaporate away is enough.

questions.stem: A student wants to separate alcohol from an alcohol-water mixture and needs to keep both liquids afterward. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the method that lets boiled vapor escape into the air. Distillation cools and collects that vapor so you keep both liquids.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the method for solid-liquid mixtures. Alcohol and water are completely dissolved together and pass right through a filter.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the technique used to analyze component pigments in tiny samples. Distillation is designed for collecting bulk liquid mixtures.

questions.explanation: Distillation heats the mixture so the substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first, then cools that vapor back into a liquid and collects it separately. This is the only technique here that captures both liquids instead of letting one escape.

questions.stem: A student wants to find out whether a sample of black ink is really a single pure dye or a blend of several different colored dyes. Which technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the method for trapping insoluble solids. Ink dyes are dissolved liquids or tiny particles that pass through filter paper.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the method that leaves all dissolved solids together in one pile. It cannot separate individual dyes from one another.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the technique for separating liquids by boiling points. Chromatography separates dissolved pigments along a paper strip.

questions.explanation: Chromatography separates the different components of a mixture based on how strongly each one is attracted to a moving liquid versus a fixed material. If the ink is really several dyes, they will separate into visible bands of different colors.

questions.stem: A student uses evaporation to try to separate an alcohol-water mixture, planning to keep both liquids. Why does this approach fail?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaporation lets the vapor escape into the air instead of collecting it, so the more volatile liquid is lost rather than recovered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evaporation only works on solids, never on liquid mixtures.
choices.rationale: You picked a rule that is incorrect because liquids can evaporate. The failure occurs because the escaped vapor is not condensed or saved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evaporation destroys the chemical identity of both liquids.
choices.rationale: You picked a statement implying a chemical reaction occurs. Evaporation is a physical change that leaves chemical structures intact.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evaporation requires a stationary phase that alcohol-water mixtures do not have.
choices.rationale: You picked a requirement that applies to chromatography. Evaporation depends on heat and vapor pressure, not a stationary phase.

questions.explanation: Evaporation simply lets the vapor escape into the air: it never captures it. To keep both liquids, the vapor must be cooled and collected, which is exactly what distillation does that evaporation does not.

questions.stem: A student tries to use filtration to separate salt that is fully dissolved in water. Why does this approach fail?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Filtration only traps undissolved solid particles; a fully dissolved solid has broken into particles too small for the filter to catch.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filtration only works on gases, never on liquids.
choices.rationale: You picked an incorrect limitation. Filtration is widely used on liquids to trap insoluble solids like sand or coffee grounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salt is a compound, so it cannot be separated by any physical method.
choices.rationale: You picked a statement that confuses physical mixtures with chemical bonds. Saltwater is a mixture that can be separated physically by evaporation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Filtration only works if the mixture is heterogeneous, and dissolved salt makes the water homogeneous, so filtration is unrelated to that idea.
choices.rationale: You picked an explanation with flawed logic. Homogeneous mixtures like saltwater cannot be filtered because the solute particles are dissolved.

questions.explanation: Filtration relies on solid particles being too large to pass through the filter's tiny holes. Once salt fully dissolves, its particles become far too small to trap, so evaporation or distillation is needed instead.

questions.stem: A student assumes that because saltwater looks completely uniform (homogeneous), it must be impossible to separate back into salt and water. Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: homogeneous mixtures can still be separated, for example with evaporation or distillation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: homogeneous mixtures can never be physically separated.
choices.rationale: You picked a choice that confuses visual appearance with chemical bonding. Homogeneous mixtures can be separated by physical methods like distillation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because saltwater is actually a compound, not a mixture.
choices.rationale: You picked a classification error. Saltwater is a physical mixture of sodium chloride and water, not a single chemical compound.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: only heterogeneous mixtures can be separated using physical methods.
choices.rationale: You picked a rule that excludes solutions. Homogeneous mixtures can easily be separated using phase changes like boiling or evaporating.

questions.explanation: Looking uniform (homogeneous) only describes appearance: it says nothing about whether a mixture can be separated. Saltwater can still be separated by evaporation or distillation, even though it looks completely smooth.

questions.stem: A mixture of two liquids is heated during distillation. Liquid A has a lower boiling point than Liquid B. Which liquid evaporates and gets collected first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liquid A, because substances with lower boiling points evaporate at lower temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Liquid B, because higher boiling points evaporate first.
choices.rationale: You picked the liquid that requires more thermal energy to boil. The component with the lower boiling point always vaporizes first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both evaporate at exactly the same time.
choices.rationale: You picked an option that ignores differences in physical properties. Distinct boiling points cause liquids to boil off one after the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither evaporates until the mixture reaches its freezing point.
choices.rationale: You picked the phase transition where liquids freeze into solids. Vaporization occurs when heating toward boiling points.

questions.explanation: During distillation, the substance with the lower boiling point turns to vapor first as the mixture is heated, so it is the first one collected after cooling.

questions.stem: During paper chromatography, one dye in a black ink sample travels much farther up the paper than another dye. What does this tell us about the faster-traveling dye?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is less strongly attracted to the paper (stationary phase) and more easily carried by the moving liquid (mobile phase).

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is heavier than the slower dye.
choices.rationale: You picked mass as the primary factor. Chromatography separates components based on solubility and phase attraction, not weight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has a higher boiling point than the slower dye.
choices.rationale: You picked a property relevant to distillation. Chromatography depends on molecular attraction between stationary and mobile phases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not actually part of the original ink mixture.
choices.rationale: You picked an option that treats separated dyes as external contaminants. Every band on the paper came directly from the original ink sample.

questions.explanation: In chromatography, components that are less strongly attracted to the stationary phase (the paper) get carried farther by the mobile phase (the moving liquid). Traveling farther means weaker attraction to the paper.

questions.stem: A fruit salad contains clearly visible pieces of mango, banana, and apple. Is this mixture homogeneous or heterogeneous?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the term for mixtures with a single uniform appearance. Fruit salad has distinct pieces of different fruits throughout.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked a pure substance formed by chemical bonds. Fruit salad is a physical combination of fruit pieces that keep their identities.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked a single chemical substance made of one atom type. Fruit salad is a mixture containing many different organic compounds.

questions.explanation: Since the different fruit pieces remain visibly separate and unevenly distributed, the fruit salad is a heterogeneous mixture.

questions.stem: A community wants to turn muddy river water (water with visible dirt and other dissolved impurities) into safe drinking water. Which two techniques, used in order, would best accomplish this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Filtration first to remove the visible dirt, then distillation to purify the water further by removing dissolved impurities.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked paper chromatography, which is a analytical laboratory method for micro-samples, not a bulk water purification process.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the steps in reverse. Boiling muddy water directly ruins distillation equipment with thick mud before filtration happens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Filtration alone is enough; no second step is needed.
choices.rationale: You picked a single step that only catches solid dirt. Filter paper cannot stop dissolved minerals or contaminants.

questions.explanation: Filtration removes the undissolved solid dirt, since it is too large to pass through the filter. But dissolved impurities remain in the water even after filtering, so distillation is still needed afterward to collect only the purified water vapor.

questions.stem: Find the molar mass of water ($H_2O$), given hydrogen's atomic mass is about 1 g/mol and oxygen's is about 16 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Water has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. Add each atom's contribution: $(2 \times 1) + (1 \times 16) = 2 + 16 = 18$ g/mol.

questions.stem: Find the molar mass of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$), given carbon's atomic mass is about 12 g/mol and oxygen's is about 16 g/mol.
questions.explanation: $CO_2$ has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. Add each atom's contribution: $12 + (2 \times 16) = 12 + 32 = 44$ g/mol.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 54 grams of water (molar mass 18 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass: $\dfrac{54 \text{ g}}{18 \text{ g/mol}} = 3$ mol.

questions.stem: How many individual molecules are in 3 moles of water?
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of moles by Avogadro's number: $3 \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 1.8066 \times 10^{24}$ molecules.

questions.stem: How many individual molecules are present in 45 grams of water (molar mass 18 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: First convert grams to moles: $\dfrac{45 \text{ g}}{18 \text{ g/mol}} = 2.5$ mol. Then convert moles to particles: $2.5 \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 1.5055 \times 10^{24}$ molecules.

questions.stem: A student tries to convert a given mass in grams directly into a number of particles, without finding moles first. Is this a valid shortcut?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: grams and particles are never directly convertible; moles must always be the middle step.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: grams and particles can always be converted directly using Avogadro's number alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: as long as the substance is a compound, not an element.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because Avogadro's number only applies to gases.

questions.explanation: Molar mass connects grams to moles, and Avogadro's number connects moles to particles: these are two different conversion factors. Skipping the mole step mixes them up and produces a badly wrong answer.

questions.stem: A student calculates water's molar mass as 17 g/mol, using only 1 g/mol for hydrogen without multiplying by its subscript. What is the correct molar mass, and what mistake was made?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 18 g/mol: the student forgot to multiply hydrogen's atomic mass by its subscript of 2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 17 g/mol: the student's calculation is already correct.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 18 g/mol: the student forgot to multiply oxygen's atomic mass by a subscript.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 16 g/mol: oxygen's mass alone is the correct molar mass.

questions.explanation: Water has 2 hydrogen atoms, so hydrogen's contribution must be $2 \times 1 = 2$ g/mol, not just 1 g/mol. The correct total is $2 + 16 = 18$ g/mol: always check each element's subscript before adding.

questions.stem: An element's atomic mass on the periodic table and its molar mass share the same number. Are these two quantities measuring the exact same thing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: atomic mass describes a single atom in atomic mass units, while molar mass describes one mole of atoms in grams.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: they are identical in every way, including units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: atomic mass is always larger than molar mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for elements, never for compounds.

questions.explanation: The numeric value transfers directly, but atomic mass (in amu) describes one tiny atom, while molar mass (in g/mol) describes an entire mole of that same substance: very different scales for different purposes.

questions.stem: A student uses 6 x 10^23 instead of the more precise 6.022 x 10^23 for Avogadro's number in a multi-step calculation, without being told to round. Is this a safe practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: using a rounded version of Avogadro's number without instruction can throw off the final answer, especially in multi-step problems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Avogadro's number is always rounded to one significant figure on exams.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because Avogadro's number should actually be 6.022 x 10^24.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: rounding never affects the accuracy of mole calculations.

questions.explanation: Unless a problem explicitly says to round, using the full value $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ keeps multi-step calculations accurate and matching the intended answer choice.

questions.stem: Find the molar mass of sodium chloride ($NaCl$), given sodium's atomic mass is about 23 g/mol and chlorine's is about 35.5 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Add each atom's contribution: $23 + 35.5 = 58.5$ g/mol.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 117 grams of sodium chloride (molar mass 58.5 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass: $\dfrac{117 \text{ g}}{58.5 \text{ g/mol}} = 2$ mol.

questions.stem: How many individual formula units are present in 117 grams of sodium chloride (molar mass 58.5 g/mol)?
questions.explanation: First convert grams to moles: $\dfrac{117 \text{ g}}{58.5 \text{ g/mol}} = 2$ mol. Then convert moles to particles: $2 \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 1.2044 \times 10^{24}$ formula units.

questions.stem: Glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$) has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms, and 6 oxygen atoms. Using atomic masses of about 12 g/mol for carbon, 1 g/mol for hydrogen, and 16 g/mol for oxygen, find glucose's molar mass.
questions.explanation: Add each element's contribution: $(6 \times 12) + (12 \times 1) + (6 \times 16) = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180$ g/mol.

questions.stem: A sample's mass, in grams, is smaller than its substance's molar mass. Without doing the full division, what can you conclude about the number of moles present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is less than 1 mole present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is more than 1 mole present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing can be concluded without doing the division.

questions.explanation: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass. If the mass (the numerator) is smaller than the molar mass (the denominator), the result of the division must be less than 1.

questions.stem: A nucleus ejects a particle identical to a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons). What type of decay is this?
questions.explanation: A particle identical to a helium nucleus is, by definition, an alpha particle. Emitting it is alpha decay.

questions.stem: A neutron inside a nucleus transforms into a proton, ejecting an electron in the process. What type of decay is this?
questions.explanation: Beta decay happens when a neutron transforms into a proton, ejecting an electron (the beta particle) in the process.

questions.stem: A nucleus releases pure energy as a high-energy ray, with no change to its atomic number or mass number. What type of decay is this?
questions.explanation: Gamma decay releases pure energy (a gamma ray) with no change to the atomic number or mass number, usually alongside alpha or beta decay.

questions.stem: An atom with atomic number 88 and mass number 226 undergoes alpha decay. Find the resulting atomic number and mass number.
questions.explanation: Alpha decay decreases mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2: mass $226 - 4 = 222$; atomic number $88 - 2 = 86$. (This describes radium-226 decaying into radon-222.)

questions.stem: An atom with atomic number 15 and mass number 32 undergoes beta decay. Find the resulting atomic number and mass number.
questions.explanation: Beta decay increases atomic number by 1, while mass number stays essentially the same: atomic number $15 + 1 = 16$; mass number stays 32. (This describes phosphorus-32 decaying into sulfur-32.)

questions.stem: Inside a nuclear power plant reactor, a large uranium nucleus splits apart into two smaller nuclei. What nuclear process is this?
questions.explanation: Fission is a large, heavy nucleus splitting apart into two or more smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy: the process used in nuclear power plants.

questions.stem: Inside the Sun, two small hydrogen nuclei combine to form one larger helium nucleus. What nuclear process is this?
questions.explanation: Fusion is two small, light nuclei combining to form one larger nucleus, releasing an even greater amount of energy than fission: the process that powers the Sun.

questions.stem: A student calculates the result of alpha decay by decreasing only the atomic number by 2, leaving the mass number unchanged. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: alpha decay decreases both the mass number (by 4) and the atomic number (by 2).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: alpha decay only ever changes atomic number.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: alpha decay only changes mass number, not atomic number.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: no numbers change during alpha decay.

questions.explanation: Alpha decay ejects a particle with 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so it reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2: the student's calculation missed the mass number change entirely.

questions.stem: A student describes the Sun's hydrogen-to-helium process as "fission," reasoning that fission and fusion are interchangeable terms. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the Sun's process, joining small nuclei together, is fusion; fission is a large nucleus splitting apart.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: fission and fusion always describe the exact same process.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the Sun's process is actually gamma decay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the Sun performs fission, not fusion.

questions.explanation: Fission splits a large nucleus apart; fusion joins small nuclei together. The Sun combines hydrogen nuclei into helium, which is fusion, not fission.

questions.stem: A student assumes that since gamma decay causes no change to atomic number or mass number, the resulting nucleus must have transformed into a different element. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gamma decay releases only energy; the element stays exactly the same before and after.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: gamma decay always transforms the nucleus into a new element.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because gamma decay does not actually involve the nucleus at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: any radioactive decay always changes the element.

questions.explanation: Unlike alpha and beta decay, gamma decay does not change the atomic number or mass number: it simply releases excess energy as the nucleus settles into a more stable state, with the element staying the same.

questions.stem: A student assumes gamma rays must be the "weakest" and easiest to block, since gamma decay causes no elemental change. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gamma rays are actually the most penetrating type of radiation discussed here, requiring thick lead or concrete to block.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: gamma rays are the weakest and easiest to block, stopped by ordinary paper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: beta particles are actually the most penetrating.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: "no elemental change" always means "less penetrating radiation."

questions.explanation: "No elemental change" is unrelated to penetrating power. Gamma rays are in fact the hardest of the three to shield against, needing thick lead or concrete, unlike alpha (stopped by paper) or beta (stopped by foil).

questions.stem: Rank alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays from weakest to strongest penetrating power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three have exactly the same penetrating power.

questions.explanation: Alpha particles are stopped by paper (weakest), beta particles need aluminum foil, and gamma rays need thick lead or concrete (strongest): an increasing order of penetrating power.

questions.stem: An atom with atomic number 90 and mass number 230 undergoes alpha decay twice in a row. Find the final atomic number and mass number.
questions.explanation: Each alpha decay decreases atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4. After the first: atomic number $90-2=88$, mass number $230-4=226$. After the second: atomic number $88-2=86$, mass number $226-4=222$.

questions.stem: Comparing a fission reaction (a large uranium nucleus splitting apart) and a fusion reaction (small hydrogen nuclei combining), which process generally releases a greater amount of energy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fusion generally releases even more energy than fission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fission generally releases even more energy than fusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both processes always release exactly the same amount of energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither fission nor fusion releases any usable energy.

questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion, joining small nuclei together, releases an even greater amount of energy than fission: this is why the Sun (powered by fusion) generates such enormous energy output.

questions.stem: An element is shiny, conducts electricity well, and tends to lose electrons in reactions. It is found on the left and center of the periodic table. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: Metals are shiny, good conductors, and tend to lose electrons. Their position on the left and center of the table confirms this classification.

questions.stem: An element is a poor conductor of electricity and tends to gain electrons in reactions. It is found on the right side of the periodic table. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: Nonmetals are poor conductors and tend to gain electrons. Their position on the right side of the table confirms this classification.

questions.stem: An element has properties between a metal and a nonmetal and is useful as a semiconductor in electronics. It is found along the staircase boundary of the periodic table. How should it be classified?
questions.explanation: Metalloids sit along the staircase boundary between metals and nonmetals, with in-between properties that make them useful as semiconductors.

questions.stem: Two elements are found in the same vertical column of the periodic table but in different rows. What can you predict about their chemical behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They likely behave similarly, since elements in the same group share the same number of valence electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They likely behave very differently, since being in different rows means they have nothing in common.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They must be the exact same element.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nothing can be predicted from column position alone.

questions.explanation: Elements in the same group (column) share the same number of valence electrons, which largely determines chemical behavior. This is exactly why the table is organized by columns.

questions.stem: Sodium and chlorine are both in period 3, with sodium in group 1 and chlorine in group 17. Which atom has the larger atomic radius?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sodium, because atomic radius decreases moving left to right across a period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlorine, because atomic radius increases moving left to right across a period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both are exactly the same size, since they are in the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sodium, because it has more electron energy levels.

questions.explanation: Across a period, atomic radius shrinks from left to right as more protons pull the electrons in closer. Sodium sits farther left than chlorine, so it is the larger atom.

questions.stem: Lithium (period 2) and potassium (period 4) are both in group 1. Which one requires more energy to remove an electron?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lithium, because ionization energy decreases going down a group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potassium, because ionization energy increases going down a group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both require exactly the same amount of energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Potassium, because it has a larger atomic radius.

questions.explanation: Ionization energy decreases going down a group, since outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus and are held less tightly. Lithium, higher up in the group, has the greater ionization energy.

questions.stem: Fluorine (period 2) and iodine (period 5) are both in group 17. Which atom has the larger atomic radius?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iodine, because atomic radius increases going down a group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorine, because atomic radius increases going down a group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both are exactly the same size, since they are in the same group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iodine, because it has a higher electronegativity.

questions.explanation: Atomic radius increases going down a group, since each row adds a new electron energy level. Iodine, lower in the group, is the larger atom.

questions.stem: Oxygen (period 2) and sulfur (period 3) are both in group 16. Which atom has the higher electronegativity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oxygen, because electronegativity decreases going down a group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sulfur, because electronegativity increases going down a group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both have exactly the same electronegativity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sulfur, because it has a smaller atomic radius.

questions.explanation: Electronegativity follows the same pattern as ionization energy: it decreases going down a group. Oxygen, higher in the group, has the higher electronegativity.

questions.stem: Carbon and nitrogen are both in period 2, with carbon in group 14 and nitrogen in group 15. Which atom has the higher ionization energy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nitrogen, because ionization energy increases moving left to right across a period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon, because ionization energy decreases moving left to right across a period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both have exactly the same ionization energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbon, because it has a larger atomic radius.

questions.explanation: Ionization energy increases moving left to right across a period, as electrons are held more tightly. Nitrogen, farther right than carbon, has the higher ionization energy.

questions.stem: Ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity all generally increase toward the upper-right corner of the periodic table. Where is atomic radius the largest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Toward the lower-left corner of the table: the opposite direction from the other three trends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Toward the upper-right corner, the same direction as the other three trends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exactly in the center of the table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atomic radius does not follow any position-based trend.

questions.explanation: Atomic radius is the one major trend that runs in reverse: it grows largest toward the lower-left of the table, while the other three trends grow largest toward the upper-right.

questions.stem: Which set of properties all increase together toward the upper-right corner of the periodic table?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ionization energy, electronegativity, and atomic radius

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atomic radius, electron affinity, and electronegativity

questions.explanation: Ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity all increase toward the upper right. Atomic radius is the exception, increasing toward the lower left instead.

questions.stem: Two elements share neither the same period nor the same group, for example, one sits diagonally from the other. Can a single straightforward trend rule (like "left to right" or "top to bottom") be applied directly to compare them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: comparing elements that share neither a period nor a group requires combining both trends carefully, and the result is not always obvious.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the "left to right" rule always applies regardless of row.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: the "top to bottom" rule always applies regardless of column.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No comparison is ever possible unless the elements share a period or group.

questions.explanation: The simple period and group trend rules only apply directly when two elements share a period or a group. Diagonal neighbors require reasoning about both trends together, since neither rule applies on its own.

questions.stem: A student assumes that all metalloids behave in exactly the same way, since they all sit along the same staircase boundary. Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: metalloids fall along a spectrum of properties between metals and nonmetals, not one identical behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: all metalloids have identical chemical and physical properties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: because metalloids are not actually related to each other at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as they are in the same period.

questions.explanation: Metalloids share the general trait of being useful as semiconductors, but their properties still vary along the staircase: they are not all identical to each other.

questions.stem: Between a metal on the left side of a period and a nonmetal on the right side of the same period, which is more likely to have the higher electron affinity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The nonmetal, since nonmetals tend to gain electrons more readily and electron affinity generally increases left to right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The metal, since metals generally have higher electron affinity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both have exactly the same electron affinity, regardless of period position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither: electron affinity does not relate to metal or nonmetal character.

questions.explanation: Electron affinity generally increases left to right across a period, and nonmetals (right side) tend to gain electrons more readily than metals (left side), matching this trend.

questions.stem: Magnesium is in period 3, group 2. Calcium is in period 4, group 2. Chlorine is in period 3, group 17. Which of these three atoms has the smallest atomic radius?

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three are the same size.

questions.explanation: Magnesium and chlorine share period 3, and radius shrinks left to right, so chlorine (far right) is smaller than magnesium. Magnesium and calcium share group 2, and radius grows going down, so magnesium (higher up) is smaller than calcium. Since chlorine is smaller than magnesium, and magnesium is smaller than calcium, chlorine is the smallest of the three.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons an $s$ orbital can hold?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the electron capacity of a set of $p$ orbitals. An $s$ orbital holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the electron capacity of a $d$ subshell. Single $s$ orbitals hold at most 2 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the electron capacity of an $f$ subshell. An $s$ orbital holds only up to 2 electrons.

questions.explanation: An $s$ orbital holds up to 2 electrons: the smallest capacity of the four orbital types.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons a $p$ orbital can hold?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the capacity of an $s$ orbital. A $p$ subshell contains three orbitals and holds 6 electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the capacity of a $d$ subshell. A $p$ subshell holds a maximum of 6 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the capacity of an $f$ subshell. A $p$ subshell can hold up to 6 electrons.

questions.explanation: A $p$ orbital (a set of three sub-orbitals) holds up to 6 electrons in total.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons a $d$ orbital can hold?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You picked the maximum capacity of an $s$ orbital. A $d$ subshell has five orbitals that hold 10 electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You picked the capacity of a $p$ subshell. A $d$ subshell holds up to 10 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You picked the capacity of an $f$ subshell. A $d$ subshell has five orbitals holding up to 10 electrons.

questions.explanation: A $d$ orbital (a set of five sub-orbitals) holds up to 10 electrons in total.

questions.stem: Nitrogen has an atomic number of 7. Write its electron configuration.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You counted 9 total electrons instead of 7. Subtract 2 to account for nitrogen having only 7 electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You placed 3 electrons into the 2s orbital. Remember that $s$ orbitals hold a maximum of 2 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You assigned 8 total electrons instead of 7. Nitrogen has an atomic number of 7 so $2p$ receives 3.

questions.explanation: Fill the lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s holds 2, 2s holds 2, leaving $7 - 2 - 2 = 3$ for 2p. Adding the superscripts confirms the total: $2 + 2 + 3 = 7$.

questions.stem: Oxygen has an atomic number of 8. Write its electron configuration.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You wrote the configuration for 10 electrons (neon). Oxygen has only 8 electrons, so $2p$ holds 4.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You put 4 electrons into the 2s orbital. The $s$ subshell can only hold up to 2 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You wrote the configuration for 7 electrons (nitrogen). Oxygen has 8 electrons, so $2p$ requires 4.

questions.explanation: Fill 1s with 2 and 2s with 2, leaving $8 - 2 - 2 = 4$ for 2p. Adding the superscripts confirms the total: $2 + 2 + 4 = 8$.

questions.stem: Which orbital fills first: the 4s orbital or the 3d orbital?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 4s orbital, because it has slightly lower energy than 3d at this point, even though its leading number is larger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 3d orbital, because 3 is a smaller number than 4.
choices.rationale: You assumed principal quantum numbers strictly dictate energy. Orbitals fill by total energy, and 4s has lower energy than 3d.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both fill at exactly the same time.
choices.rationale: You assumed degenerate orbital energies. 4s and 3d have different energy levels, so 4s fills before 3d.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither fills before the other; 3d is skipped entirely.
choices.rationale: You picked an option that ignores standard electron configurations. 3d fills immediately after 4s is full.

questions.explanation: The Aufbau principle fills orbitals by increasing energy, not simply by increasing leading number. The 4s orbital has slightly lower energy than 3d at this point in the periodic table, so it fills first: this is why potassium's configuration ends in $4s^1$, not $3d^1$.

questions.stem: A student writes the configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^8$ for an atom. Is this a valid electron configuration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a $p$ orbital can never hold more than 6 electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: as long as the total adds up correctly.
choices.rationale: You ignored subshell capacity rules. A $p$ subshell cannot hold more than 6 electrons regardless of atomic total.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: because the $2s$ orbital should come after $2p$.
choices.rationale: You reversed the energy ordering. 2s has lower energy than 2p and fills before 2p in valid configurations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: $p$ orbitals can hold up to 8 electrons.
choices.rationale: You confused subshell capacity with the octet rule. A $p$ subshell holds 6 electrons, not 8.

questions.explanation: Each orbital type has a fixed maximum capacity, and $p$ can never exceed 6 electrons. A superscript of 8 on a $p$ orbital is impossible, no matter what the total electron count is.

questions.stem: Three electrons must be placed into a set of three separate $p$ orbitals of the same energy. Which arrangement correctly follows Hund's Rule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each of the three orbitals gets exactly one electron.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two electrons pair up in one orbital, leaving one orbital completely empty.
choices.rationale: You paired electrons prematurely. Hund's Rule requires placing one electron per degenerate orbital before pairing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All three electrons pair up in a single orbital.
choices.rationale: You placed 3 electrons in one orbital, violating Pauli Exclusion and Hund's Rule. Orbitals hold at most 2 electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any arrangement is equally correct, since the total electron count is the same either way.
choices.rationale: You assumed orbital distribution does not affect energy. Unpaired parallel spins minimize electron repulsion.

questions.explanation: Hund's Rule says electrons fill each available same-energy orbital singly before any orbital receives a second electron. With three electrons and three empty orbitals available, each orbital should get exactly one electron.

questions.stem: Can two electrons occupying the same orbital have the same spin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the Pauli Exclusion Principle requires the two electrons in one orbital to have opposite spins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: spin direction does not matter within a single orbital.
choices.rationale: You ignored quantum number restrictions. Pauli Exclusion states two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: an orbital can never hold two electrons at all.
choices.rationale: You set orbital capacity to one. Orbitals can hold up to two electrons if their spins are paired opposite.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as the orbital is an $s$ orbital.
choices.rationale: You exempted s orbitals from spin rules. Pauli Exclusion applies equally to all orbital types.

questions.explanation: The Pauli Exclusion Principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, and requires those two to have opposite spins. Two electrons with the same spin cannot share the same orbital.

questions.stem: An atom has the electron configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^3$. What is its atomic number?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You likely miscounted the electrons in $2p$ or $3p$. Adding $2+2+6+2+3$ gives 15 electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added extra electrons to the total. Summing all superscripts $2+2+6+2+3$ equals 15.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You counted only the valence shell electrons ($3s^2 3p^3$). Atomic number requires counting all electrons.

questions.explanation: Add up all the superscripts: $2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15$. Since this is a neutral atom, its atomic number equals its total electron count, 15 (phosphorus).

questions.stem: An atom has the electron configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^3$. How many electrons are in its outermost energy level?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You counted only the electrons in the $3p$ subshell. Outermost electrons include both $3s$ and $3p$ ($2+3=5$).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You gave the total atomic number of the atom. The outermost energy level (n=3) contains 5 valence electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You stated the maximum octet capacity instead of counting the $3s^2 3p^3$ valence electrons.

questions.explanation: The outermost energy level is level 3 (from the $3s$ and $3p$ terms). Adding their superscripts: $2 + 3 = 5$.

questions.stem: Neutral sodium (atomic number 11) has the configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^1$. What is the correct electron configuration for the sodium ion $Na^+$?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You gave the configuration for neutral sodium. The 1+ ion loses its single outer electron from $3s$.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You added an electron as if it were an anion ($Na^-$). Positive ions lose electrons.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You removed two electrons instead of one. $Na^+$ loses only 1 electron to reach 10 total.

questions.explanation: $Na^+$ has lost one electron compared to neutral sodium, leaving $11 - 1 = 10$ electrons. Removing the single $3s$ electron from neutral sodium's configuration leaves $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6$: do not just copy the neutral atom's configuration without adjusting for the charge.

questions.stem: An atom has the electron configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^6\ 4s^2\ 3d^5$. What is its atomic number?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You miscounted the sum of superscripts. Adding $2+2+6+2+6+2+5$ gives an atomic number of 25.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You stopped counting at $4s^2$ and ignored the 5 electrons in the $3d$ subshell.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You added 10 extra electrons to the total. Summing the given superscripts yields 25.

questions.explanation: Add up every superscript: $2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 25$. This is manganese, whose configuration fills $4s$ before $3d$, following the established energy order.

questions.stem: An ion has the electron configuration $1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6$ and a charge of 1+. What is the atomic number of its neutral parent atom?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You gave the electron count of the ion rather than the neutral parent atom. Add 1 electron back to find atomic number 11.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You subtracted 1 electron from the ion count. A 1+ charge means the neutral atom had one MORE electron.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You added 2 electrons instead of 1. A 1+ ion lost only a single electron relative to its neutral atom.

questions.explanation: The ion has $2 + 2 + 6 = 10$ electrons. Since it lost one electron to reach a 1+ charge, the neutral atom must have had $10 + 1 = 11$ electrons, giving an atomic number of 11 (sodium).

questions.stem: A solution contains 3 moles of $NaCl$ dissolved in enough water to make 6 liters of solution. Find the molarity.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You inverted the fraction by dividing 6 liters by 3 moles. Molarity requires moles divided by liters.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: You took the number of moles without dividing by the 6 liters of solution volume.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: You multiplied 3 moles by 6 liters instead of dividing moles by liters of solution.

questions.explanation: Molarity equals moles of solute divided by liters of solution: $\dfrac{3 \text{ mol}}{6 \text{ L}} = 0.5$ M.

questions.stem: A solution is made by dissolving 2 moles of sugar into 4 kilograms of water. Find the molality.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: You divided 4 kilograms by 2 moles. Molality is moles of solute divided by kilograms of solvent.
