choices.text: Yes: solid rock can never flow under any circumstances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the mantle is actually liquid, not solid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the mantle only flows once it becomes a gas.

questions.explanation: Students think "solid" must mean "completely rigid and unmoving." The mantle's slow flow, similar to thick toffee, is exactly what drives the plates on Earth's surface: being solid and flowing slowly are not contradictions.

questions.stem: Which layer, made mostly of liquid iron and nickel, generates Earth's magnetic field as it flows?
questions.explanation: The outer core is made mostly of liquid iron and nickel; its flow around Earth's center is what generates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.stem: Which layer, at the very center of Earth, is made of iron and nickel and stays solid despite being the hottest layer of all?
questions.explanation: The inner core, at Earth's very center, is made of iron and nickel and is the hottest layer, yet stays solid due to extreme pressure.

questions.stem: The inner core has the highest temperature of any layer inside Earth, yet it is solid, while the cooler outer core above it is liquid. What explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The inner core experiences the greatest pressure in all of Earth, since it is squeezed by the weight of every layer above it, forcing its iron and nickel atoms to stay locked in a solid arrangement despite the extreme heat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inner core is actually cooler than the outer core, which is why it stays solid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inner core is made of a completely different material than the outer core, which happens to have a higher melting point.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Temperature has no effect on whether a layer is solid or liquid.

questions.explanation: Temperature alone would suggest the hottest layer should be most likely to melt, but the inner core also experiences the greatest pressure of any layer, squeezed by the weight of everything above it: this immense pressure keeps it solid despite the extreme heat.

questions.stem: A choice claims "the inner core must be liquid, since it is the hottest layer inside Earth." Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: higher pressure can keep a layer solid even at extreme temperature; the inner core is solid despite being the hottest layer, due to the crushing pressure at Earth's center.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the hottest layer inside Earth is always liquid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the inner core is not actually the hottest layer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: pressure has no effect on whether a layer is solid or liquid.

questions.explanation: This choice ignores the role of pressure. The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet stays solid because of the crushing pressure at Earth's center: temperature alone does not determine whether a layer is solid or liquid.

questions.stem: List Earth's four main layers in order, starting from the outermost layer and ending at the very center.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crust, outer core, mantle, inner core

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mantle, crust, outer core, inner core

choices.label: D
choices.text: Crust, mantle, inner core, outer core

questions.explanation: From the surface inward: the crust (outermost), then the mantle, then the liquid outer core, and finally the solid inner core at the very center.

questions.stem: Which of Earth's four layers takes up the largest share of Earth's total volume?
questions.explanation: The mantle, at roughly 2,880 km thick, makes up most of Earth's volume: by far the largest of the four layers.

questions.stem: Scientists cannot dig down to directly observe Earth's outer core, yet they are confident it is liquid. How do they know this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Certain earthquake waves cannot travel through liquid material, and scientists observed these waves disappearing on the far side of the planet from certain earthquakes, forming a "shadow" region only explainable by a liquid layer inside Earth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scientists have sent underwater cameras directly into the outer core to observe it visually.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The outer core's liquid state was directly measured using deep drilling equipment that reached the core.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Earthquake waves have no relationship to determining whether a layer is solid or liquid.

questions.explanation: Certain earthquake waves can only travel through solid material. When these waves disappeared in a "shadow" region on the opposite side of the planet from certain earthquakes, it revealed a liquid layer blocking them: evidence for the liquid outer core.

questions.stem: A certain type of earthquake wave can only travel through solid material and cannot pass through liquid. Based on this, would this wave type be able to pass through the outer core?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since the outer core is liquid, this wave type would be blocked and unable to pass through it, creating a shadow region where the wave does not arrive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: this wave type can pass through any material, solid or liquid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: since the outer core is actually solid, not liquid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the outer core does not actually exist.

questions.explanation: Since this wave type cannot travel through liquid, and the outer core is liquid, the wave is blocked there: creating the shadow region that first revealed the outer core's liquid state to scientists.

questions.stem: What causes Earth's magnetic field?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The flow of liquid, metallic material in the outer core

choices.label: B
choices.text: The solid rock of the mantle

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thin crust at Earth's surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: The solid inner core alone, without any flow

questions.explanation: Earth's magnetic field is generated by the flow of liquid iron and nickel in the outer core, moving around Earth's center.

questions.stem: A question describes a region of land with crust about 70 km thick and labels it "oceanic crust." Is this labeling correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: crust about 70 km thick describes continental crust (found under land); oceanic crust, found under the oceans, is much thinner, only about 5 km.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: oceanic crust is always about 70 km thick.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because continental crust does not actually exist.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: continental and oceanic crust are always the same thickness.

questions.explanation: A question describing land areas versus ocean floor is testing which crust type is thicker. Continental crust (under continents) is roughly 70 km thick, while oceanic crust (under oceans) is only about 5 km thick.

questions.stem: An earthquake occurs, and scientists observe that a certain wave type (one that only travels through solid material) fails to reach detectors on the exact opposite side of Earth, while a different wave type (one that can travel through both solid and liquid) does reach those detectors, though bent from its expected path. What can scientists conclude about Earth's interior from this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is a liquid layer inside Earth (the outer core) that blocks the solid-only wave entirely, while bending the path of the wave that can travel through both solid and liquid material.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Earth's interior must be entirely solid, since one wave type still reached the detectors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earth's interior must be entirely liquid, since one wave type failed to arrive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This wave pattern provides no information about Earth's interior structure.

questions.explanation: A wave that only travels through solid material failing to reach the far side of the planet, combined with a wave that travels through both solid and liquid bending along the way, together indicate a liquid layer inside Earth: direct seismic evidence for the liquid outer core.

questions.stem: What is a naturally occurring, solid substance with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure called?
questions.explanation: A mineral is a naturally occurring, solid substance with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure.

questions.stem: What is a mix of one or more minerals stuck together called?
questions.explanation: A rock is simply a mix of one or more minerals stuck together.

questions.stem: The Mohs hardness scale, used to measure mineral hardness, ranges from which two numbers?
questions.explanation: The Mohs hardness scale ranges from 1 (very soft, like talc) to 10 (very hard, like diamond).

questions.stem: Mineral A can scratch Mineral B, but Mineral B cannot scratch Mineral A. Mineral C can scratch both A and B. Rank the three minerals from softest to hardest.
questions.explanation: Since A can scratch B, A is harder than B. Since C can scratch both A and B, C is the hardest of the three. Order from softest to hardest: B, A, C.

questions.stem: What is the term for the color of a mineral's powder, made by rubbing it on an unglazed tile?
questions.explanation: Streak is the color of a mineral's powder, made by rubbing it on an unglazed tile, and is more reliable than the mineral's outer color.

questions.stem: The mineral pyrite looks golden on the outside but leaves a dark greenish-black powder when scratched on an unglazed tile. A student identifies pyrite as "golden-colored" based on this streak test. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the dark greenish-black powder is pyrite's streak, which can be very different from its golden outer color; streak, not outer color, is what the scratch test reveals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the streak test always reveals the mineral's outer color.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because pyrite does not actually have a streak.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: pyrite's streak and outer color are always identical.

questions.explanation: A question describing "the color left behind when scratched on a tile" is asking about streak, not the visible outer color of the whole mineral sample. Pyrite looks golden outside but leaves a dark greenish-black streak.

questions.stem: What term describes how a mineral's surface reflects light, grouped mainly as metallic (shiny, like metal) or non-metallic (dull, glassy, pearly)?
questions.explanation: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light, grouped mainly as metallic or non-metallic.

questions.stem: A mineral breaks along smooth, flat planes because of weaker bonds in that direction. What is this property called, as opposed to breaking in a rough, irregular way?
questions.explanation: Cleavage is breaking along smooth, flat planes due to weaker bonds in that direction; fracture is breaking in a rough, irregular way with no flat planes.

questions.stem: Which rock type forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens?
questions.explanation: Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens.

questions.stem: Lava cools very quickly on a volcano's surface, forming a rock with small or no visible crystals, such as basalt or obsidian. If the same magma had instead cooled slowly underground, what would the resulting igneous rock most likely look like?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It would have large, visible crystals, since slow cooling underground gives crystals more time to grow, forming a rock like granite.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It would look identical, since cooling speed has no effect on crystal size.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It would have no crystals at all, since underground cooling always prevents crystal formation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It would turn into a sedimentary rock instead of an igneous rock.

questions.explanation: Cooling speed determines crystal size: cooling slowly underground gives crystals more time to grow large (like granite), while cooling quickly at the surface produces small or no crystals (like basalt or obsidian).

questions.stem: Which rock type forms when small pieces of rock, sand, shells, or other debris pile up in layers and get pressed and cemented together over time?
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rock forms when sediment (small pieces of rock, sand, shells, or other debris) piles up in layers and gets pressed and cemented together over a long time.

questions.stem: Which rock type forms when an existing rock is changed by intense heat and pressure underground, without fully melting?
questions.explanation: Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by intense heat and pressure underground, without fully melting, rearranging its minerals into a new texture.

questions.stem: A student claims that metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock completely melts and then re-hardens. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: metamorphic rock forms without fully melting; heat and pressure change the rock's minerals and texture while it stays essentially solid. A rock that fully melts and re-forms describes the igneous process instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: metamorphic rock always forms by completely melting and re-hardening.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because metamorphic rock never involves heat or pressure at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: igneous and metamorphic rock form through the exact same melting process.

questions.explanation: Heat and pressure change a rock's minerals and texture while it stays essentially solid: this is the metamorphic process. A choice describing "rock that melts and re-forms" describes the igneous process (via magma), not metamorphism.

questions.stem: Classify this rock-forming process: layers of sand and shell fragments are compressed and cemented together over thousands of years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: None of the three rock types

questions.explanation: Sand and shell fragments compressing into layers over time is the defining process of sedimentary rock formation.

questions.stem: Classify this rock-forming process: limestone is squeezed by intense heat and pressure deep underground and turns into marble, without melting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: None of the three rock types

questions.explanation: Limestone transforming into marble under heat and pressure, without melting, is the defining process of metamorphic rock formation.

questions.stem: A student memorized only one path through the rock cycle (igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic) and assumes every rock must always follow this exact order. Is this assumption correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: any rock type can become any other rock type given the right process; a metamorphic rock can weather directly into sediment, or an igneous rock can be metamorphosed directly without ever becoming sedimentary first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: every rock must pass through igneous, then sedimentary, then metamorphic, in that exact order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because sedimentary rock can never become metamorphic rock.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the rock cycle has a single fixed starting point and ending point.

questions.explanation: Students sometimes memorize only one path and assume it always goes in that order. In reality, the rock cycle has no fixed sequence: any rock type can become any other rock type, and there is no required starting or ending point.

questions.stem: Describe the correct order of a path through the rock cycle that turns granite (an igneous rock) into marble (a metamorphic rock), passing through a sedimentary stage in between: weathering into sediment, granite exposed at the surface, heat and pressure transformation, compressing into sedimentary rock.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granite exposed at the surface, weathering into sediment, compressing into sedimentary rock, heat and pressure transformation into marble

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heat and pressure transformation into marble, granite exposed at the surface, weathering into sediment, compressing into sedimentary rock

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granite exposed at the surface, compressing into sedimentary rock, weathering into sediment, heat and pressure transformation into marble

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weathering into sediment, granite exposed at the surface, heat and pressure transformation, compressing into sedimentary rock

questions.explanation: Granite, exposed at the surface, weathers into sediment particles; these particles compress and cement into a sedimentary rock like limestone; buried underground, heat and pressure then transform it, without melting, into marble.

questions.stem: A geologist finds an unknown mineral sample. It can be scratched by a steel knife (hardness about 5.5) but can itself scratch glass (hardness about 5.5 as well, roughly tied). Its outer color is silvery, but rubbing it on an unglazed tile produces a black powder. Which two properties did the geologist use to gather the most reliable identifying clues, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hardness (compared against known reference materials like a steel knife and glass) and streak (the black powder), since streak is more reliable than outer color, which can vary due to surface impurities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the mineral's outer silvery color, since color alone is always sufficient for identification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only luster, since hardness and streak provide no useful identifying information.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleavage and fracture, since the scenario describes breaking patterns rather than hardness or color.

questions.explanation: Hardness is tested by comparing scratch resistance against reference materials, and streak (the tile-powder color) is more reliable than a mineral's outer color, which can be affected by surface impurities: these are the two properties the geologist actually used here.

questions.stem: About how many years ago does the Big Bang theory say the universe began?
questions.explanation: The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, when it started expanding from one incredibly hot, tiny point.

questions.stem: Which physicist first proposed the Big Bang theory, in 1927, using Einstein's equations for gravity?
questions.explanation: Georges Lemaître first proposed the Big Bang theory in 1927, two years before Hubble's observation provided strong supporting evidence.

questions.stem: In 1929, which astronomer found that almost every distant galaxy is moving away from Earth, faster the farther away it is?
questions.explanation: Edwin Hubble's 1929 observation that distant galaxies are moving away from Earth, faster with distance, provided strong evidence for the Big Bang theory.

questions.stem: Why does Hubble's observation, that distant galaxies are moving away from Earth faster the farther away they are, support the idea that the universe began from one tiny point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If everything is flying apart from each other today, then tracing this motion backward in time means everything must have been squeezed together in one place long ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shows that galaxies are being pulled toward Earth by gravity, proving Earth is the center of the universe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that the universe has always been the same size, with no expansion at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proves that space itself is shrinking over time.

questions.explanation: If distant galaxies are moving away from us today, and faster the farther they are, then running this motion backward in time implies everything was once squeezed together at a single starting point: direct evidence for an expanding universe.

questions.stem: What is the name for the faint glow of leftover heat radiation, discovered in 1965 by Penzias and Wilson, coming from every direction in the sky?
questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background, discovered in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, is the leftover heat from the Big Bang, cooled down over billions of years.

questions.stem: A student claims the cosmic microwave background is "the light from the first stars." Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the cosmic microwave background is leftover heat radiation from the hot, early universe itself; stars had not even formed yet when this radiation was released.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the cosmic microwave background is exactly the light given off by the very first stars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the cosmic microwave background does not actually exist.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: all radiation detected from the sky comes from stars.

questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background comes from a much earlier, hotter stage of the universe, before any stars had formed: it is the cooled-down leftover heat from the Big Bang itself, not starlight.

questions.stem: A choice credits Edwin Hubble with "inventing" the Big Bang theory in 1929. Is this accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Georges Lemaître first proposed the Big Bang theory in 1927; Hubble's 1929 observation of galaxies moving apart provided strong supporting evidence for a theory that already existed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Hubble was the first person to propose the Big Bang theory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because no one proposed the Big Bang theory before 1965.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Lemaître and Hubble proposed the theory together in the same year.

questions.explanation: Lemaître proposed the theory in 1927, using Einstein's equations for gravity. Hubble's contribution, two years later, was the observational evidence, not the original proposal of the theory itself.

questions.stem: A student pictures the Big Bang as an explosion that happened at one specific location in space, with matter flying outward into empty space that already existed around it. Is this an accurate picture of the Big Bang?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the Big Bang was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once; there was no empty space "outside" the expansion for matter to fly into.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the Big Bang was exactly like a bomb exploding at a single point in pre-existing space.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the Big Bang never actually happened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: space existed first, and matter later expanded to fill it from one corner.

questions.explanation: Students often imagine the Big Bang like a bomb exploding at one location. In reality, space itself stretched out everywhere at once: there was no pre-existing empty space outside the expansion for matter to fly into.

questions.stem: What is the name for the hypothesis explaining that the Sun and planets formed from one giant, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust?
questions.explanation: The nebular hypothesis explains that the Sun and planets formed from one giant, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust called a nebula.

questions.stem: Arrange these events of the nebular hypothesis in the correct order: planets form from clumps in the disk; the cloud collapses and spins faster; the center becomes hot enough to ignite as the Sun; a giant cloud of gas and dust exists.

choices.label: A
choices.text: A giant cloud of gas and dust exists, the cloud collapses and spins faster, the center ignites as the Sun, planets form from clumps in the disk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The center ignites as the Sun, a giant cloud of gas and dust exists, planets form from clumps, the cloud collapses and spins faster.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planets form from clumps in the disk, a giant cloud of gas and dust exists, the cloud collapses and spins faster, the center ignites as the Sun.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A giant cloud of gas and dust exists, planets form from clumps in the disk, the cloud collapses and spins faster, the center ignites as the Sun.

questions.explanation: The nebular hypothesis sequence: a giant, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust (nebula) exists → gravity pulls it inward, causing it to collapse and spin faster → the center becomes hot and dense enough to ignite as the Sun → leftover material in the disk clumps together to form the planets.

questions.stem: According to the nebular hypothesis, why does the collapsing cloud of gas and dust spin faster and faster as it gets smaller?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The same principle that makes a spinning ice skater speed up when pulling their arms in applies to the shrinking cloud: as its material moves closer to the center, its spin speeds up.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An outside force from a nearby star pushes the cloud to spin faster.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cloud only spins faster because it is losing mass to outer space.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cloud's spin speed has no relationship to its size.

questions.explanation: As the cloud collapses under gravity and its material moves closer to the center, it spins faster: the same principle that makes a spinning ice skater speed up when pulling their arms inward.

questions.stem: According to the nebular hypothesis, why do all the planets in the solar system orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane and in the same direction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All the planets formed from clumps of material within the same flattened, spinning disk that surrounded the young Sun, so they inherited that disk's flat shape and spin direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each planet formed completely independently, and it is a coincidence that they all orbit in the same plane.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Sun's gravity forces every planet into the same plane regardless of how or where it formed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The planets originally orbited in random directions, and later collisions randomly aligned them.

questions.explanation: As the original spinning cloud collapsed, it flattened into a wide disk. Since all the planets formed from clumps of material within that same flat, spinning disk, they ended up orbiting the Sun in nearly the same plane and direction.

questions.stem: An answer choice describes a giant, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsing to form a star and planets, but labels this process "the Big Bang." Is this labeling correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this description matches the nebular hypothesis, which explains the formation of a solar system, not the Big Bang, which explains the origin of the entire universe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the Big Bang and the nebular hypothesis describe the exact same process at every scale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because clouds of gas and dust never collapse to form stars.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: any process involving gas, dust, and collapse is automatically the Big Bang.

questions.explanation: These are two different scales of "beginning." A spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsing into a star and planets describes the nebular hypothesis (solar system formation), not the Big Bang (the origin of the whole universe).

questions.stem: A question describes the motion and expansion of galaxies across the universe. Which theory should you think of first: the Big Bang theory or the nebular hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Big Bang theory, since it explains the origin and expansion of the whole universe, including galaxies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nebular hypothesis, since it explains the motion of any object in space.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both theories equally, since they describe identical processes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither theory, since galaxy motion is unrelated to either theory.

questions.explanation: If a question mentions "galaxies" or "the universe," think Big Bang theory. If it mentions "planets" or "the Sun," think nebular hypothesis: the two theories explain different scales of "beginning."

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the idea that the universe is still expanding today: the leftover heat detected in every direction of the sky, or the observation that distant galaxies are moving away faster the farther they are?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The observation that distant galaxies are moving away faster the farther they are, since this directly shows space is still stretching apart right now, while the leftover heat is stronger evidence for a hot beginning rather than ongoing expansion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The leftover heat detected in every direction of the sky, since it directly measures how fast galaxies are currently moving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both pieces of evidence are equally irrelevant to whether the universe is still expanding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither piece of evidence relates to the Big Bang theory in any way.

questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background (leftover heat) is strong evidence for a hot beginning, but Hubble's observation of galaxies moving away, faster with distance, is the direct evidence that space is still expanding today.

questions.stem: What are the large pieces of Earth's rigid outer shell, which slowly move over the softer mantle beneath, called?
questions.explanation: Tectonic plates are the large pieces of Earth's rigid outer shell (crust and the rigid top of the mantle) that slowly move over the softer, slowly-flowing mantle beneath them.

questions.stem: In 1915, which scientist proposed continental drift, the idea that all continents were once joined together as one giant landmass called Pangaea?
questions.explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1915, using evidence like matching coastlines, rock layers, and fossils across now-separated continents.

questions.stem: In 1959, which scientist proposed seafloor spreading, explaining that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and pushes older seafloor away?
questions.explanation: Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in 1959, providing the moving force that Wegener's continental drift theory was missing.

questions.stem: Identical fossils of an ancient reptile are found both on the eastern coast of South America and the western coast of Africa, two continents now separated by a wide ocean. How does this support Wegener's continental drift theory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If South America and Africa were once joined as a single landmass (Pangaea), the reptile could have lived and spread across it; after the continents drifted apart, the same fossil species would end up found on both, now-separated continents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reptile must have swum across the ocean separately to reach both continents.

choices.label: C
choices.text: This fossil pattern actually contradicts continental drift, since the continents are now far apart.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fossils provide no evidence about how continents were arranged in the past.

questions.explanation: Wegener proposed that all continents were once joined as Pangaea. If South America and Africa were once connected, a land-dwelling reptile could have lived and spread across the single joined landmass, explaining why the same fossil species is found on both continents after they drifted apart.

questions.stem: A choice claims Wegener's continental drift theory was immediately and widely accepted by scientists in 1915. Is this accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Wegener's theory was doubted for decades because he could not explain what force moved the continents; only after seafloor spreading was discovered in 1959 did the full theory of plate tectonics become widely accepted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: scientists universally accepted continental drift as soon as Wegener proposed it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because Wegener's evidence, like matching fossils and coastlines, was completely wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Wegener had already discovered seafloor spreading himself in 1915.

questions.explanation: Wegener's theory was doubted for decades because he could not explain the moving force behind continental drift. Only after Harry Hess's seafloor spreading supplied that missing piece did the full theory of plate tectonics become widely accepted.

questions.stem: At which type of plate boundary do two plates move apart from each other, with magma rising to fill the gap and create new crust?
questions.explanation: A divergent boundary is where two plates move apart, with magma rising to fill the gap and create new crust: exactly what happens at mid-ocean ridges.

questions.stem: At which type of plate boundary do two plates move toward each other and collide, sometimes causing one plate to be pushed underneath the other?
questions.explanation: A convergent boundary is where two plates move toward each other and collide; if one plate is denser, it gets pushed underneath the other in a process called subduction.

questions.stem: At which type of plate boundary do two plates slide past each other sideways, without creating or destroying crust?
questions.explanation: A transform boundary is where two plates slide past each other sideways, without creating or destroying crust; friction here builds up stress that releases suddenly as earthquakes.

questions.stem: Two plates are sliding sideways past each other, causing frequent strong earthquakes but no new mountains or volcanoes. What type of plate boundary is this?
questions.explanation: Sideways sliding motion, without creating or destroying crust, describes a transform boundary. Since crust is neither created nor destroyed here, no new volcanoes or mountain ranges typically form; the frequent earthquakes come from built-up friction releasing suddenly.

questions.stem: A student assumes every convergent boundary produces the exact same outcome, regardless of which plates are involved. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the outcome depends on plate density; if one plate is much denser (typically oceanic crust), it sinks beneath the other in subduction, but if both plates are similar in density (often two continental plates), they crumple upward into a mountain range instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: every convergent boundary always produces subduction, regardless of plate density.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: every convergent boundary always produces a mountain range, regardless of plate density.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because convergent boundaries never involve two colliding plates.

questions.explanation: Not every convergent boundary looks the same. If one plate is much denser, it sinks beneath the other (subduction), often creating volcanoes above it. If both plates are similar in density, neither sinks, and they crumple upward into a mountain range instead.

questions.stem: What is a crack in Earth's crust where rock on either side has moved, and which produces an earthquake when built-up stress along it suddenly releases?
questions.explanation: A fault is a crack in Earth's crust where rock on either side has moved. When built-up stress along a fault suddenly releases, the ground shakes as an earthquake.

questions.stem: Which type of seismic wave is the fastest, arriving first at a seismograph station, and can travel through both solids and liquids?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both P and S waves equally

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither type of wave can travel through liquid

questions.explanation: P waves (primary waves) are the fastest seismic waves, always arriving first, and can travel through both solids and liquids.

questions.stem: Which type of seismic wave is slower than P waves and can only travel through solids, not liquids?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both P and S waves equally

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither type of wave can travel through solids

questions.explanation: S waves (secondary waves) are slower than P waves and can only travel through solids, not liquids.

questions.stem: A choice claims "S waves are faster than P waves and can travel through both solids and liquids," swapping the two wave types' properties. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this reverses the properties; P waves are actually faster and travel through both solids and liquids, while S waves are slower and travel through solids only.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: S waves are indeed faster and can travel through both solids and liquids.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because neither P waves nor S waves can travel through solids.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: P waves and S waves have identical speed and travel through identical materials.

questions.explanation: A common wrong answer swaps these properties. Anchor the memory device: P comes first (faster) and passes through everything (solids and liquids); S comes second (slower) and cannot travel through liquid at all.

questions.stem: A seismograph station records the P wave from an earthquake arriving several seconds before the S wave. Why does a larger time gap between the two waves indicate a greater distance to the earthquake's origin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since P waves travel faster than S waves, the farther the earthquake's origin is from the station, the more time the faster P wave gains over the slower S wave during the journey, producing a longer arrival gap.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The time gap actually has no relationship to the earthquake's distance from the station.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A larger time gap means the earthquake's origin is closer to the station, not farther away.

choices.label: D
choices.text: S waves always arrive before P waves, and a larger gap means the earthquake was weaker.

questions.explanation: P waves travel faster than S waves and always arrive first. The farther the earthquake's origin, the more time the faster P wave gains over the slower S wave, so a longer arrival gap indicates a greater distance: this is how scientists pinpoint an earthquake's location.

questions.stem: At which two types of plate boundaries do most volcanoes form?
questions.explanation: Volcanoes most often form at convergent boundaries (where subducting plates melt and produce rising magma) and at divergent boundaries (where magma rises to fill the gap between separating plates).

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands are a volcanic island chain located in the middle of a tectonic plate, far from any plate boundary. A student claims this is impossible, since "all volcanoes form at plate boundaries." Is this claim correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a hotspot is a place where magma rises from deep within the mantle, independent of any plate boundary, and can create volcanic islands like the Hawaiian Islands even in the middle of a plate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the Hawaiian Islands must actually sit exactly on a plate boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes: all volcanoes, without exception, form only at plate boundaries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No: but only because the Hawaiian Islands are not actually volcanic in origin.

questions.explanation: Most volcanoes do form at convergent or divergent boundaries, but a hotspot's magma source comes from deep within the mantle and is not tied to any plate boundary: this is exactly how the Hawaiian Islands formed in the middle of a plate.

questions.stem: At a convergent boundary between an oceanic plate and a continental plate, the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate. Why does the oceanic plate sink rather than the continental plate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The oceanic plate is denser than the continental plate, so in subduction, the denser plate is pushed underneath the less dense one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The continental plate is always denser, so it should sink instead, but friction prevents this.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plate density has no role in determining which plate sinks during subduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both plates always sink equally at every convergent boundary.

questions.explanation: In subduction, the denser plate, typically oceanic crust, is pushed underneath the less dense plate. This is why oceanic plates commonly sink beneath continental plates at convergent boundaries.

questions.stem: Scientists first discovered that Earth's outer core is liquid partly by observing that S waves from earthquakes disappear on the far side of the planet, forming a "shadow zone." Why does this observation reveal the outer core's liquid state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since S waves can only travel through solids and not liquids, their disappearance in a shadow zone on the far side of Earth indicates a liquid layer (the outer core) blocking them from passing through.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S waves travel through both solids and liquids equally, so their disappearance must be caused by something other than the outer core.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P waves, not S waves, are the type of wave that reveals information about the outer core.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shadow zone shows that the outer core is solid, not liquid.

questions.explanation: S waves cannot travel through liquid. Their disappearance in a shadow zone on the far side of the planet, relative to an earthquake, is explained by a liquid layer (the outer core) blocking them: connecting the P/S wave rule directly to the evidence for Earth's liquid outer core.

questions.stem: A region sits where two continental plates are slowly colliding, with neither plate sinking beneath the other. Nearby, seismographs also detect a location where P waves consistently arrive shortly before S waves, and a separate volcanic island chain sits far from any mapped plate boundary. Identify: (a) the landform most likely produced by the colliding continental plates, (b) what the P-S wave gap tells scientists, and (c) what most likely explains the isolated volcanic island chain.

choices.label: A
choices.text: (a) A mountain range, since neither continental plate is dense enough to subduct; (b) the size of the gap indicates the earthquake's distance from the station; (c) a hotspot, since the island chain is unrelated to any plate boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: (a) A deep ocean trench from subduction; (b) the gap indicates the earthquake's magnitude; (c) the island chain must actually sit on an undiscovered plate boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (a) A mountain range; (b) the gap has no scientific use; (c) volcanic islands can only form at convergent boundaries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (a) A new ocean forming between the plates; (b) the gap indicates wind speed at the surface; (c) the island chain formed from a meteor impact.

questions.explanation: Two colliding continental plates of similar density crumple upward into a mountain range rather than subducting. The P-S wave arrival gap indicates distance to the earthquake's origin, since P waves gain more lead time over longer distances. An isolated volcanic island chain far from any boundary is best explained by a hotspot, where magma rises from deep within the mantle independent of plate edges.

questions.stem: What is the process called when heat from the Sun turns liquid water into water vapor, which rises into the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Evaporation is when heat from the Sun turns liquid water (mostly from the oceans) into water vapor, which rises into the atmosphere.

questions.stem: What is the process called when rising water vapor cools and turns back into tiny liquid water droplets, forming clouds?
questions.explanation: Condensation is when water vapor rises and cools, turning back into tiny liquid water droplets that form clouds: the opposite process of evaporation.

questions.stem: What is the process called when cloud droplets combine and grow heavy enough to fall back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail?
questions.explanation: Precipitation is when cloud droplets combine and grow heavy enough to fall back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

questions.stem: What is the process called when plants release water vapor into the air through their leaves?
questions.explanation: Transpiration is when plants release water vapor into the air through their leaves; evaporation and transpiration together are sometimes called "evapotranspiration."

questions.stem: A student believes "transpiration" refers to any water vapor rising from soil or bodies of water, the same as general evaporation. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: transpiration specifically refers to water vapor released from plants through their leaves, distinct from evaporation off soil or water bodies; the two are combined into the term "evapotranspiration" precisely because they are different processes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: transpiration and evaporation are simply two different names for the exact same process.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because plants do not release any water vapor at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: transpiration only applies to water evaporating from soil, never from plants.

questions.explanation: Some students confuse transpiration with general evaporation from soil or water bodies. Transpiration is specifically the plant-based release of water vapor through leaves, which is why it is paired with evaporation as "evapotranspiration" when discussing total water vapor sources.

questions.stem: After a heavy rainstorm, some water soaks slowly into the soil, while the rest flows quickly over the ground surface into a nearby river. Identify which process is which.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water soaking into the soil is infiltration; water flowing over the surface into the river is runoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water soaking into the soil is runoff; water flowing over the surface into the river is infiltration.

questions.explanation: Water soaking slowly into the soil is infiltration (which feeds groundwater). Water flowing over the surface into a river is runoff. Both can happen to the same rainfall at the same time.

questions.stem: What is the term for precipitation that soaks into the soil, feeding groundwater?
questions.explanation: Infiltration is precipitation that soaks into the soil, feeding groundwater.

questions.stem: What is the term for precipitation that flows over the surface into streams, rivers, and eventually back to the ocean?
questions.explanation: Runoff is precipitation that flows over the surface into streams, rivers, and eventually back to the ocean.

questions.stem: A choice describes condensation as "liquid water turning into water vapor, rising into the atmosphere," swapping it with evaporation's description. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this describes evaporation, not condensation; condensation is the opposite process, water vapor cooling and turning back into liquid droplets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: condensation and evaporation describe the exact same liquid-to-gas process.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because neither evaporation nor condensation actually occurs in the water cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: condensation always describes liquid turning into gas.

questions.explanation: These are opposite processes, and questions often swap their descriptions. If the process is warming water into vapor, it is evaporation; if it is cooling vapor into visible droplets or clouds, it is condensation.

questions.stem: Water vapor rises from the ocean surface, cools as it rises higher into the atmosphere, and turns back into tiny liquid droplets that form a cloud. Which stage of the water cycle does "turning back into tiny liquid droplets" describe?
questions.explanation: Water vapor (a gas) turning into liquid droplets, forming clouds, is condensation: the opposite of evaporation.

questions.stem: About what percentage of all the water on Earth is held in the oceans?
questions.explanation: Oceans hold about 96% of all the water on the planet, far more than lakes, rivers, or any other water source.

questions.stem: A choice claims that freshwater lakes and rivers hold most of Earth's water, more than the oceans. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the ocean holds about 96% of Earth's water; freshwater lakes and rivers hold only a small fraction in comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: freshwater lakes and rivers hold the vast majority of Earth's water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because oceans do not actually contain any water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: oceans and freshwater lakes hold exactly equal amounts of water.

questions.explanation: A choice suggesting that lakes or rivers are the largest water reservoir is incorrect. The vast majority of Earth's water, and nearly all of it that is liquid, is contained within the salty oceans.

questions.stem: Why does most of the water vapor found in Earth's atmosphere come from the ocean rather than from lakes, rivers, or plants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Since evaporation depends on the amount of exposed water surface heated by the Sun, and the ocean covers the vast majority of Earth's surface (holding about 96% of all its water), the ocean's enormous surface area makes it by far the largest source of evaporation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lakes, rivers, and plants do not produce any water vapor at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ocean is the only water source cool enough to allow evaporation to occur.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The amount of water vapor produced has no relationship to the surface area of the water source.

questions.explanation: Since evaporation depends on the amount of exposed water surface heated by the Sun, the ocean's enormous surface area (and the fact that it holds about 96% of Earth's water) makes it by far the largest source of water vapor, even though lakes, rivers, and plant transpiration also contribute.

questions.stem: What term describes ocean water's saltiness, distinguishing it from most water in lakes and rivers?
questions.explanation: Ocean water is saline (salty), unlike most water in lakes and rivers.

questions.stem: Ocean water is layered based on two main factors. What are they?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depth and sunlight only, unrelated to temperature

questions.explanation: Ocean water has layers based on temperature and density: warmer, sunlit water near the surface, and colder, denser water in the deep ocean, where sunlight cannot reach.

questions.stem: What drives ocean currents, and why are they important for redistributing heat around the planet?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ocean currents are driven by wind, differences in water density, and Earth's rotation; as they constantly move, they help redistribute heat from warmer to cooler regions around the planet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ocean currents are driven entirely by the Moon's gravity, unrelated to wind or density.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ocean currents do not move at all; ocean water stays in a fixed position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ocean currents have no effect on the distribution of heat around the planet.

questions.explanation: Ocean water constantly moves in currents, driven by wind, differences in water density, and Earth's rotation, which help redistribute heat around the planet.

questions.stem: Heat from the Sun warms a large stretch of ocean, sending water vapor rising into the sky. High in the atmosphere, the vapor cools and forms clouds, which later release heavy rain over a mountainous region. Some of this rain seeps into the ground, and the rest flows down the mountainside into a river that eventually reaches the sea. Identify, in order, the water cycle stages this scenario describes.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaporation (ocean water rising as vapor), condensation (vapor cooling into clouds), precipitation (rain falling), and both infiltration (seeping into ground) and runoff (flowing into the river) occurring together

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condensation, evaporation, infiltration, and precipitation, in that order

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only evaporation and precipitation occur in this scenario; infiltration and runoff are unrelated concepts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Runoff, precipitation, condensation, and evaporation, in that order

questions.explanation: This scenario traces the full cycle: evaporation (ocean water heated into vapor), condensation (vapor cooling into cloud droplets), precipitation (rain falling on the mountains), and finally infiltration and runoff occurring together, since some rain soaks into the soil while the rest flows over the surface toward the sea.

questions.stem: What is the short-term condition of the air at a specific place and time, such as today's temperature, rain, or wind, called?
questions.explanation: Weather is the short-term condition of the air at a specific place and time, like today's temperature, rain, or wind.

questions.stem: What is the long-term average pattern of weather in a region over many years called?
questions.explanation: Climate is the long-term average pattern of weather in a region over many years, like a personality, compared to weather's daily "mood."

questions.stem: "It is raining heavily in Manila right now." Is this statement describing weather or climate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Weather, since it describes conditions right now, at one specific time

choices.label: B
choices.text: Climate, since it describes a general, long-term pattern

questions.explanation: This statement describes conditions right now, at one specific time and place: this is weather, not climate.

questions.stem: "The Philippines generally has a hot and humid climate with two main seasons." Is this statement describing weather or climate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Climate, since it describes a general, long-term pattern over many years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weather, since it describes conditions right now

questions.explanation: This statement describes a general, long-term pattern over many years: this is climate, not weather.

questions.stem: A person argues, "It was unusually cold this week, so global warming must not be real." Is this a valid argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a single short-term weather event does not disprove a long-term climate trend measured over decades; weather and climate operate on very different timescales.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any single cold week is enough to disprove long-term climate trends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because cold weather never actually occurs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: weather and climate always match each other exactly, day to day.

questions.explanation: A choice might describe "unusually cold weather this week" as proof that "the climate is not warming." But a single weather event, hot or cold, does not disprove a long-term climate trend measured over decades: weather is short-term and local, while climate is a long-term average.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric layer, up to about 10 km high, is the lowest layer, where almost all weather (clouds, rain, storms) happens?
questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer, up to about 10 km high, where almost all weather happens and where we live and breathe.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric layer, from about 10 km to 50 km high, contains the ozone layer that absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation?
questions.explanation: The stratosphere, from about 10 km to 50 km high, contains the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric layer, from about 50 km to 85 km high, is the coldest layer, and is where most meteors burn up?
questions.explanation: The mesosphere, from about 50 km to 85 km high, is the coldest atmospheric layer, and it is where most meteors burn up.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric layer, from about 85 km to 600 km high, has very high measured temperatures despite its extremely thin air?
questions.explanation: The thermosphere, from about 85 km to 600 km high, has very high measured temperatures, though its air is too thin to feel warm to a person.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric layer is the outermost layer, fading gradually into outer space, and where satellites orbit?
questions.explanation: The exosphere is the outermost atmospheric layer, fading gradually into outer space, where satellites orbit.

questions.stem: Arrange Earth's five atmospheric layers in order from the ground up: exosphere, mesosphere, stratosphere, thermosphere, troposphere.
questions.explanation: From the ground up: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere: remembered with "Tall Storms Make Thin Exits."

questions.stem: A commercial airplane cruises at an altitude where nearly all storm clouds are already below it, and this layer also contains the ozone layer that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Which atmospheric layer is this closest to?
questions.explanation: "Nearly all storm clouds below it" suggests this layer is above the troposphere (where weather happens), and "contains the ozone layer" is a direct match to the stratosphere.

questions.stem: A choice describes the thermosphere as "literally warm to the touch for an astronaut," citing its very high measured temperature. Is this description accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: although the thermosphere has high measured temperatures, its air is so thin that there is not enough matter to transfer that heat to a person or object, so it would not feel warm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: anyone in the thermosphere would feel intensely warm due to its high temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the thermosphere actually has a very low temperature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: temperature always directly determines how warm something feels, regardless of air density.

questions.explanation: Temperature measures how fast particles move, but with so few particles in the thin thermosphere, there is not enough matter to transfer that heat to a person or object: a choice describing the thermosphere as literally "warm to the touch" misunderstands this thin-air effect.

questions.stem: A choice describes the ozone layer's job as "producing the oxygen that living things breathe." Is this an accurate description of the ozone layer's role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the ozone layer's specific, testable job is absorbing most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, not producing breathable oxygen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the ozone layer's main job is producing oxygen for living things to breathe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the ozone layer does not exist within the stratosphere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the ozone layer and oxygen production are the exact same process.

questions.explanation: Some choices confuse the ozone layer's protective role with unrelated atmospheric functions. Its specific, testable job is shielding Earth's surface from the Sun's most harmful UV rays, not producing oxygen.

questions.stem: What is the name for the southwest monsoon in the Philippines, roughly from June to October, bringing hot, humid weather and frequent typhoons?
questions.explanation: Habagat is the southwest monsoon, roughly from June to October, bringing hot, humid weather, frequent heavy rainfall, and the most frequent destructive typhoons.

questions.stem: What is the name for the northeast monsoon in the Philippines, roughly from November to April, bringing cooler, drier weather?
questions.explanation: Amihan is the northeast monsoon, roughly from November to April, bringing cooler, drier weather with generally little rainfall in much of the country.

questions.stem: During a certain month, the Philippines experiences a prevailing wind from the southwest, hot and humid weather, and an active typhoon warning. Which monsoon season is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Habagat (southwest monsoon), roughly June through October

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amihan (northeast monsoon), roughly November through April

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both Habagat and Amihan occur simultaneously

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither monsoon; this describes an unrelated weather pattern

questions.explanation: A southwest wind with hot, humid conditions and frequent typhoons describes habagat, the southwest monsoon, running roughly from June to October.

questions.stem: A student describes a month with cooler, drier weather and a prevailing northeast wind, but labels this season "Habagat." Is this labeling correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: cooler, drier weather with a northeast wind describes Amihan, not Habagat; Habagat is the hot, rainy, typhoon-prone southwest monsoon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: Habagat always describes cooler, drier, northeast-wind conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because neither Habagat nor Amihan involves wind direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Habagat and Amihan are simply two different names for the same season.

questions.explanation: These two Filipino terms are easy to confuse under time pressure. Anchor them by season type: if the description mentions frequent typhoons and humidity from the southwest, it must be Habagat; cooler, drier weather from the northeast is Amihan.

questions.stem: What is a powerful, rotating tropical storm system with very strong winds and heavy rain, most common during the Habagat season, called?
questions.explanation: A typhoon is a powerful, rotating tropical storm system with very strong winds and heavy rain, most common during the Habagat season.

questions.stem: Why does the buildup of greenhouse gases, like carbon dioxide, in the atmosphere cause global warming?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Greenhouse gases trap heat from the Sun in the atmosphere, similar to how a greenhouse traps warmth, causing a long-term rise in Earth's average temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greenhouse gases block sunlight from reaching Earth's surface entirely, cooling the planet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greenhouse gases have no relationship to Earth's average temperature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenhouse gases only affect temperature in the stratosphere, not at Earth's surface.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide trap heat from the Sun in the atmosphere, similar to how a greenhouse traps warmth: this buildup is a major cause of global warming, the long-term rise in Earth's average temperature.

questions.stem: A news report says, "This year's typhoon was unusually strong." A separate scientific report says, "Average global temperatures have risen over the past century, and sea levels are slowly rising as a result." Which report describes a weather event, and which describes climate change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "This year's typhoon was unusually strong" describes a weather event; "average global temperatures have risen over the past century" describes climate change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both reports describe the same kind of event: a weather event.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both reports describe the same kind of event: climate change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "This year's typhoon" describes climate change, while the temperature report describes a weather event.

questions.explanation: "This year's typhoon" describes a single storm at a specific time, a weather event. "Average global temperatures have risen over the past century" describes a long-term shift measured over many decades, climate change.

questions.stem: In September, the Philippines experiences a strong typhoon with a prevailing southwest wind, hot and humid conditions, and heavy rainfall. Meteorologists also note that global average temperatures this decade are measurably higher than the previous decade's average. Using what you know about weather, climate, and monsoons, identify: (a) which monsoon season this typhoon belongs to, and (b) whether the September typhoon alone proves long-term climate change is happening.

choices.label: A
choices.text: (a) Habagat, the southwest monsoon (roughly June–October); (b) no, a single typhoon is a short-term weather event, and the actual evidence for long-term climate change comes from the measured rise in average temperatures across decades, not any single storm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: (a) Amihan, the northeast monsoon; (b) yes, one strong typhoon is sufficient proof of long-term climate change on its own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: (a) Habagat, the southwest monsoon; (b) yes, any single weather event, no matter how ordinary, directly proves long-term climate trends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: (a) Amihan, the northeast monsoon; (b) no, weather events and climate change are entirely unrelated concepts.

questions.explanation: A southwest wind with hot, humid, typhoon conditions in September identifies Habagat. The typhoon itself is a short-term weather event and does not alone prove climate change; the decade-over-decade temperature rise is the actual long-term climate evidence.

questions.stem: A 5 kg object experiences a net force of 20 N. Find its acceleration. (Use $F_{net} = ma$.)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{m} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4$ m/s².

questions.stem: An 8 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². Find the net force acting on it.
A net force of 50 N causes an object to accelerate at 2 m/s². Find the object's mass.
questions.explanation: $m = \dfrac{F_{net}}{a} = \dfrac{50}{2} = 25$ kg.

questions.stem: Which of Newton's laws states that an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion, unless acted on by a net external force?
questions.explanation: This is Newton's First Law, also called the Law of Inertia: an object resists changes to its state of motion unless a net force acts on it.

questions.stem: Which of Newton's laws states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Law of Conservation of Momentum

questions.explanation: This is Newton's Third Law: action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on two different objects.

questions.stem: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's Third Law, which pair of forces are true action-reaction partners?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The book pushing down on the table, and the table pushing up on the book.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The book's weight and the normal force, both acting on the book.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The table's weight and the floor's normal force on the table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no true action-reaction pair in this scenario.

questions.explanation: True Newton's Third Law pairs act on two different objects: here, the book pushes down on the table, and the table pushes back up on the book with an equal, opposite force.

questions.stem: A heavy crate requires a push of 200 N to just begin sliding, but only 150 N to keep it sliding at constant speed once moving. Which value is the maximum static friction, and which is the kinetic friction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 200 N is the maximum static friction; 150 N is the kinetic friction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 150 N is the maximum static friction; 200 N is the kinetic friction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both values represent kinetic friction at different speeds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both values represent static friction at different speeds.

questions.explanation: The force needed to just start the crate moving overcomes the maximum static friction (200 N). The lower force needed to keep it moving at constant speed matches the kinetic friction (150 N), which is typically less than the maximum static friction.

questions.stem: A student says the weight and normal force acting on a resting book form a Newton's Third Law action-reaction pair, since they are equal and opposite. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: both forces act on the same object (the book), which makes them a balanced-force pair (First Law), not a Third Law action-reaction pair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any two equal and opposite forces are automatically a Third Law pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: weight and normal force are never equal in any situation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only when the book is accelerating.

questions.explanation: Third Law pairs always act on two different objects. Weight and normal force both act on the same book: they happen to balance (a First Law equilibrium), which is a separate fact from Third Law pairing.

questions.stem: A student assumes that doubling an object's mass, while keeping the net force the same, will double its acceleration. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: mass and acceleration are inversely related in Newton's Second Law; doubling the mass halves the acceleration instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: doubling the mass always doubles the acceleration for the same force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: doubling the mass has no effect on acceleration at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: mass and acceleration are directly related.

questions.explanation: $F_{net} = ma$ means $a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{m}$. For a fixed force, increasing mass decreases acceleration: doubling the mass halves the acceleration, it does not double it.

questions.stem: A student assumes that once an object is sliding, kinetic friction becomes negligible and can safely be ignored. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: kinetic friction is roughly constant once sliding begins and can be strong enough to eventually stop the object if no other force keeps pushing it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: kinetic friction always becomes zero once an object starts sliding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because kinetic friction increases the longer an object slides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: friction only matters before an object starts moving.

questions.explanation: Kinetic friction continues to act on a sliding object, opposing its motion. Without a continued applied force, a sliding object will eventually decelerate to a stop due to this friction.

questions.stem: A student assumes the normal force on an object always equals its weight ($mg$), in every situation. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the normal force equals weight only on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces acting; it must be recalculated in other situations, like on an incline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the normal force always equals $mg$, regardless of the surface or other forces.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the normal force is always greater than weight in every situation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for objects that are not accelerating.

questions.explanation: Normal force only equals $mg$ when the surface is horizontal and no other vertical forces are involved. On an incline, or with an additional applied force, the normal force must be found from the actual vertical force balance in that specific situation.

questions.stem: What is the formula for an object's weight?
questions.explanation: Weight is the force of gravity pulling an object downward, calculated as mass times the acceleration due to gravity: $W = mg$.

questions.stem: A 10 kg object is pushed with an applied force of 50 N, while friction opposes its motion with a force of 20 N. Find the object's acceleration.
questions.explanation: The net force is the applied force minus the opposing friction: $50 - 20 = 30$ N. Then $a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{m} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ m/s².

questions.stem: A box sits at rest on a flat, horizontal table, with no other forces applied. Which forces should appear on its free body diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Weight (pulling down) and normal force (pushing up), equal in magnitude since the box is not accelerating.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only weight, since the table does not exert any force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only normal force, since the box has no weight while resting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weight, normal force, and friction, even though the box is not sliding or being pushed.

questions.explanation: With nothing else pushing or pulling the box, only weight and normal force act on it. Since the box is at rest (not accelerating), these two forces must be equal and opposite, balancing each other.

questions.stem: A box rests on a ramp inclined at an angle, rather than on a flat horizontal surface. Does the normal force on the box still equal its full weight, $mg$?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: on an incline, the normal force is less than the full weight, since only part of the weight presses directly into the ramp's surface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the normal force always equals $mg$, regardless of the surface's angle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the normal force is always greater than the full weight on an incline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only if the box is sliding down the ramp.

questions.explanation: On an incline, weight has a component pressing into the surface and a component along the surface. Only the perpendicular component is balanced by the normal force, making it less than the box's full weight: normal force must be recalculated from the actual geometry, not assumed equal to $mg$.

questions.stem: Two electric charges are moved to twice their original distance apart. By what factor does the force between them change? (Use Coulomb's Law, $F = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 1/4 of the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 1/2 of the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 2 times the original force.

questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law is an inverse-square law: doubling the distance divides the force by $2^2 = 4$.

questions.stem: Two electric charges are moved to three times their original distance apart. By what factor does the force between them change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 1/9 of the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 1/3 of the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 3 times the original force.

questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law is an inverse-square law: tripling the distance divides the force by $3^2 = 9$.

questions.stem: A circuit has a resistance of 10 ohms and a current of 2 amperes flowing through it. Find the voltage. (Use $V = IR$.)
A circuit has a voltage of 24 volts and a current of 3 amperes. Find the resistance.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $V = IR$: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8$ ohms.

questions.stem: A circuit has a voltage of 15 volts and a resistance of 5 ohms. Find the current.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $V = IR$: $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$ amperes.

questions.stem: In a series circuit with two light bulbs, one bulb suddenly burns out. What happens to the other bulb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It also goes dark, since the burned-out bulb breaks the single shared path.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It stays lit, unaffected by the other bulb.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the resistances.

questions.explanation: In a series circuit, all components share one single path. Breaking that path (by one bulb burning out) stops current from flowing anywhere in the circuit.

questions.stem: In a parallel circuit with two light bulbs, one bulb suddenly burns out. What happens to the other bulb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It stays lit, since each bulb has its own separate branch.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It also goes dark, since both bulbs share a single path.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes dimmer but stays lit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the resistances.

questions.explanation: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own independent branch. If one branch breaks, the other remains a complete, separate path, so its bulb stays lit.

questions.stem: Two like electric charges (both positive, or both negative) are brought near each other. Do they attract or repel?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: like charges have no effect on each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on their distance apart.

questions.explanation: Like charges repel (push apart), following the same pattern as magnetic poles.

questions.stem: A positive charge and a negative charge are brought near each other. Do they attract or repel?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: opposite charges have no effect on each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on their distance apart.

questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract (pull together).

questions.stem: A student assumes doubling the distance between two charges simply halves the electric force between them. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Coulomb's Law is an inverse-square law, so doubling the distance divides the force by $2^2=4$, not by 2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: force is inversely proportional to distance directly, not distance squared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: doubling the distance actually doubles the force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for charges of the same sign.

questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law has distance squared in the denominator, exactly like Newton's law of gravitation. Skipping the squaring step (dividing by 2 instead of 4) is a common error.

questions.stem: A student assumes current is the same across every branch in a parallel circuit, since current stays the same in a series circuit. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: in a parallel circuit, voltage is the same across each branch, but current splits between branches; only in series circuits is current the shared quantity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: current is always the same everywhere, in both series and parallel circuits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: in a parallel circuit, neither current nor voltage is shared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only when all branches have equal resistance.

questions.explanation: Series and parallel circuits share different quantities: series circuits share the same current (with voltage splitting), while parallel circuits share the same voltage (with current splitting). Mixing these up is one of the most common circuit errors.

questions.stem: A student assumes that one burned-out bulb always causes an entire circuit to stop working, regardless of circuit type. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
