choices.text: No: this is only true for series circuits; in parallel circuits, other branches keep working independently even if one bulb burns out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any broken component always stops the entire circuit, regardless of type.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: broken components never affect any part of a circuit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only in circuits with more than two bulbs.

questions.explanation: Only series circuits fail entirely when one component breaks, since they share a single path. Parallel circuits (like household wiring) keep other branches working independently.

questions.stem: A student uses their left hand instead of their right hand to apply the right-hand rule for a current-carrying wire. Will this give the correct magnetic field direction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: using the left hand reverses the result, giving the opposite (incorrect) magnetic field direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: either hand gives the same correct result.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the wire must be curved for the rule to apply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the right-hand rule works regardless of which hand is used.

questions.explanation: The right-hand rule specifically requires the right hand: thumb pointing in the current's direction, with curled fingers showing the magnetic field's direction. Using the left hand gives the mirror-image (incorrect) direction.

questions.stem: A straight wire carries current flowing directly upward. Using the right-hand rule, in which direction does the magnetic field circle around the wire, viewed from above (looking down along the direction of current flow)?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly outward from the wire, not circling at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: Directly along the wire, parallel to the current

questions.explanation: Pointing the right thumb upward (the current's direction), the curled fingers circle counterclockwise around the wire when viewed from above.

questions.stem: In a house, if one lamp burns out, the other outlets and lights in the house keep working normally. What does this tell you about how household wiring is typically arranged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Household wiring is typically parallel, since each outlet or light has its own independent branch.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Household wiring is typically series, since all components share one single path.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Household wiring alternates between series and parallel randomly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This behavior does not depend on how the wiring is arranged.

questions.explanation: Since other lights and outlets keep working when one bulb burns out, this shows each component has its own independent branch: the defining behavior of a parallel circuit, which is why household wiring is typically parallel.

questions.stem: An object has a mass of 300 g and a volume of 150 cm³. Find its density. (Use $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$.)
questions.explanation: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{300}{150} = 2$ g/cm³.

questions.stem: An object has a density of 0.8 g/cm³. It is placed in water, which has a density of 1.0 g/cm³. Will the object float or sink?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Float, since its density is less than water's density.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sink, since its density is less than water's density.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stay perfectly suspended, neither floating nor sinking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the object's shape.

questions.explanation: An object less dense than the surrounding fluid floats. Since 0.8 g/cm³ is less than water's 1.0 g/cm³, the object floats.

questions.stem: An object has a density of 1.2 g/cm³. It is placed in water, which has a density of 1.0 g/cm³. Will the object float or sink?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sink, since its density is greater than water's density.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Float, since its density is greater than water's density.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stay perfectly suspended, neither floating nor sinking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the object's mass.

questions.explanation: An object denser than the surrounding fluid sinks. Since 1.2 g/cm³ is greater than water's 1.0 g/cm³, the object sinks.

questions.stem: A solid block, fully submerged in water, displaces 250 cm³ of water. Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. Find the buoyant force on the block. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: Mass of displaced water: $(1)(250) = 250$ g $= 0.25$ kg. Weight (buoyant force): $W = mg = (0.25)(9.8) = 2.45$ N.

questions.stem: What is the formula for pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure is force spread over an area: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$.

questions.stem: According to Bernoulli's Principle, what happens to a fluid's pressure as its speed increases?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pressure stays exactly the same.

questions.explanation: Bernoulli's Principle describes an inverse relationship: as a fluid's speed increases, its pressure decreases.

questions.stem: Air moves faster over the curved top of an airplane wing than beneath its flatter bottom. Using Bernoulli's Principle, explain why this creates lift.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster air above the wing has lower pressure; slower air below has higher pressure, and the higher pressure below pushes the wing up more than the lower pressure above pushes it down.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster air above the wing has higher pressure, directly pushing the wing upward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wing's shape has no effect on air pressure at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lift is caused entirely by the airplane's engines, not by air pressure differences.

questions.explanation: By Bernoulli's Principle, faster-moving air has lower pressure. The pressure difference between the slower (higher-pressure) air below and faster (lower-pressure) air above creates a net upward force: lift.

questions.stem: A student calculates the buoyant force on a submerged brass block by using the brass's own density, instead of the water's density. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Archimedes' Principle uses the density of the displaced fluid (water), not the density of the submerged object itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: buoyant force always depends on the submerged object's own density.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: buoyant force does not depend on density at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as the object is denser than the fluid.

questions.explanation: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid, calculated using the fluid's own density and the displaced volume, not any property of the submerged object itself.

questions.stem: A student assumes a massive steel ship must sink, since steel is much denser than water, while a small pebble would float since it is "so small." Is this reasoning correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: floating and sinking depend on overall average density compared to the fluid, not size or mass alone; the ship's hollow shape gives it a low average density, letting it float, while a small solid steel pebble would sink.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: larger objects always sink regardless of their shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because ships are not really made of steel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: smaller objects always float regardless of their material.

questions.explanation: A ship's hollow, air-filled shape gives it a low overall average density, even though its material (steel) is much denser than water. Size and mass alone cannot predict floating or sinking: the object's overall average density relative to the fluid is what matters.

questions.stem: A student assumes that faster-moving fluid has higher pressure than slower-moving fluid. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Bernoulli's Principle states the opposite: faster-moving fluid has lower pressure, not higher.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: faster-moving fluid always has higher pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only for fluids moving through a narrow pipe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: this is exactly what causes airplane lift.

questions.explanation: Reversing Bernoulli's actual relationship (faster means lower pressure) would incorrectly predict a downward force on an airplane wing instead of the real upward lift force that keeps planes flying.

questions.stem: A student assumes water pressure is the same at every depth in a swimming pool. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: pressure increases with depth, since deeper water must support the weight of all the water above it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: fluid pressure never changes with depth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: pressure actually decreases with depth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: pressure only depends on the pool's total volume, not depth.

questions.explanation: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, since fluid deeper down supports the weight of the fluid above it. Treating pressure as constant throughout a container ignores this depth dependence.

questions.stem: An object has a mass of 450 g and a volume of 500 cm³. Find its density, and determine whether it would float or sink in water (density 1.0 g/cm³).
questions.explanation: $\rho = \dfrac{450}{500} = 0.9$ g/cm³. Since 0.9 is less than water's density (1.0), the object would float.

questions.stem: A block, fully submerged in water, displaces 400 cm³ of water. Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. Find the buoyant force on the block. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: Mass of displaced water: $(1)(400) = 400$ g $= 0.4$ kg. Weight (buoyant force): $W = mg = (0.4)(9.8) = 3.92$ N.

questions.stem: A block of solid steel sinks in water, but a steel ship of much greater total mass floats. What explains this apparent contradiction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ship's hollow, air-filled shape gives it a much lower overall average density than solid steel, making its average density less than water's, unlike the solid block.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ships are not actually made of steel, unlike the solid block.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water becomes less dense around large objects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ship's greater mass alone is what allows it to float.

questions.explanation: Floating depends on overall average density, not the density of the raw material alone. The ship's hollow shape spreads its steel mass across a much larger volume, lowering its average density below water's, even though solid steel itself is much denser than water.

questions.stem: Two objects are moved to three times their original distance apart. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 1/9 of the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 1/3 of the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 3 times the original force.

questions.explanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: tripling the distance divides the force by $3^2 = 9$.

questions.stem: Two objects are moved to twice their original distance apart. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 1/4 of the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 1/2 of the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 2 times the original force.

questions.explanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: doubling the distance divides the force by $2^2 = 4$.

questions.stem: Two objects are moved to four times their original distance apart. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 1/16 of the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 1/4 of the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 1/8 of the original force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It becomes 4 times the original force.

questions.explanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: increasing the distance 4 times divides the force by $4^2 = 16$.

questions.stem: Which of Kepler's laws states that planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun at one focus?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kepler's Second Law (Law of Equal Areas)

questions.explanation: Kepler's First Law states that orbits are ellipses, not perfect circles, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center.

questions.stem: Which of Kepler's laws states that a line connecting a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kepler's Second Law (Law of Equal Areas)

questions.explanation: Kepler's Second Law describes equal areas swept in equal times, which is why planets move faster near the Sun and slower far from it.

questions.stem: Which of Kepler's laws relates the square of a planet's orbital period to the cube of its average distance from the Sun?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kepler's Second Law (Law of Equal Areas)

questions.explanation: Kepler's Third Law states $T^2 \propto r^3$: period squared is proportional to distance cubed.

questions.stem: A planet is at perihelion (closest to the Sun) at one point in its orbit, and at aphelion (farthest from the Sun) at another. At which point does the planet move faster?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perihelion, since a planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aphelion, since a planet moves faster when farther from the Sun.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The planet moves at the same speed at both points.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speed cannot be compared between these two points.

questions.explanation: By Kepler's Second Law, to sweep equal areas in equal times, a planet must travel faster when close to the Sun (perihelion) and slower when far away (aphelion).

questions.stem: Planet A's orbital period is 3 times longer than Planet B's period. Using Kepler's Third Law, by what factor is Planet A's distance cubed greater than Planet B's distance cubed?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The same, since distance is unrelated to period.

questions.explanation: Since $T^2 \propto r^3$, if Planet A's period is 3 times Planet B's, then period squared is $3^2=9$ times greater, meaning distance cubed must also be 9 times greater.

questions.stem: A student assumes tripling the distance between two masses divides the gravitational force between them by 3. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gravity is an inverse-square law, so tripling the distance divides the force by $3^2=9$, not 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: force is inversely proportional to distance directly, not distance squared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: tripling the distance actually multiplies the force by 3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for very large masses.

questions.explanation: Newton's law of gravitation has distance squared in the denominator. Skipping the squaring step and dividing by the plain distance factor (3 instead of 9) is the most common error with this law.

questions.stem: A student believes planetary orbits are perfect circles with the Sun at the exact center. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Kepler's First Law states orbits are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus, not the exact center of a circle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: all planetary orbits are perfect circles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the Sun is not actually involved in planetary orbits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Kepler's First Law confirms circular orbits.

questions.explanation: While some orbits are nearly circular, the technically correct shape described by Kepler's First Law is an ellipse, with the Sun positioned at one focus rather than the exact center.

questions.stem: A student assumes a planet moves at the same constant speed throughout its entire elliptical orbit. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Kepler's Second Law shows orbital speed changes throughout an elliptical orbit, faster near the Sun and slower far away.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: all planets move at one constant speed throughout their orbit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only for orbits that are perfect circles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Kepler's laws do not address orbital speed at all.

questions.explanation: Only a perfectly circular orbit would have constant speed. Real elliptical orbits have varying speed, as described by Kepler's Second Law.

questions.stem: A student assumes Kepler's Third Law means a planet's period is directly proportional to its distance (not involving any exponents). Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: Kepler's Third Law relates period squared to distance cubed ($T^2 \propto r^3$), not a simple direct proportion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: period and distance are directly, simply proportional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: Kepler's Third Law actually relates period cubed to distance squared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: Kepler's Third Law has no exponents involved.

questions.explanation: Ignoring the actual exponents (period squared, distance cubed) and treating the relationship as a simple direct proportion leads to significantly wrong comparisons, especially for orbits with very different periods.

questions.stem: How do Kepler's contribution and Newton's contribution to understanding planetary motion relate to each other?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kepler discovered the observed pattern of how planets move; Newton later explained the underlying physical cause (gravitation) behind that pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newton discovered the pattern first, and Kepler later explained the physical cause behind it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kepler and Newton discovered completely unrelated, separate laws about planetary motion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newton's laws replaced and disproved Kepler's laws entirely.

questions.explanation: Kepler's three laws were based on careful observation, describing how planets move. Newton later showed that all three laws follow naturally from his law of universal gravitation combined with the laws of motion.

questions.stem: The distance between two masses is halved. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes 4 times the original force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes 2 times the original force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes 1/2 of the original force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It becomes 1/4 of the original force.

questions.explanation: Halving the distance means the denominator $r^2$ becomes $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ of its original value, so the force becomes $4$ times larger (dividing by a smaller number gives a bigger result).

questions.stem: What quantity describes the rate of change of velocity?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is defined as the rate at which velocity itself changes over time.

questions.stem: What quantity describes the rate of change of displacement?
questions.explanation: Velocity is defined as the rate at which displacement (position) changes over time.

questions.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 5 m/s² for 4 seconds. Find its final velocity. (Use $v = v_0 + at$.)
A ball rolls with an initial velocity of 3 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. Find how far it travels. (Use $d = v_0t + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$.)
A rock is dropped from a cliff (initial velocity = 0) and falls for 4 seconds before hitting the ground. Find how far it fell. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $d = v_0t + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$.)
A rock is dropped from a cliff (initial velocity = 0) and falls for 4 seconds. Find its velocity just before impact. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $v = v_0 + at$.)
A car traveling at 5 m/s accelerates at 3 m/s² over a distance of 40 m. Find its final velocity, without using time. (Use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad$.)

A problem gives initial velocity, acceleration, and distance, but does not mention time at all, and does not ask for it. A student tries to use $v = v_0 + at$ anyway. Is this the right equation to use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since time is neither given nor needed, $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad$ should be used instead, since it excludes time entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: $v = v_0 + at$ can always be used regardless of which variables are given.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: $d = v_0t + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$ should be used instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: time can simply be assumed to equal 1 second in this case.

questions.explanation: Each kinematic equation excludes exactly one of the five variables. Since time is absent here, the equation that excludes time ($v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ad$) is the correct choice, avoiding the need to solve for an unknown that isn't needed.

questions.stem: A problem says a ball is "dropped" from a height. A student leaves the ball's initial velocity as an unknown variable to solve for. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: "dropped" means the initial velocity is already known to be 0, not an unknown to solve for.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: "dropped" gives no information about initial velocity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: "dropped" means the final velocity is 0, not the initial velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: initial velocity must always be solved for separately.

questions.explanation: Descriptive phrases like "dropped," "starts from rest," or "initially at rest" all directly tell you that $v_0 = 0$: this is given information, not an unknown.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight upward, with "up" chosen as the positive direction. A student uses a positive value for gravity's acceleration in the equations, since it is being treated as a general given value. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: if up is positive, gravity (which always pulls down) must be entered as a negative acceleration to keep the signs consistent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: gravity should always be entered as a positive number, regardless of the chosen direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the ball was thrown, not dropped.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: sign conventions do not matter as long as the magnitude is correct.

questions.explanation: Once "up" is chosen as positive, every quantity must follow that convention consistently. Since gravity always pulls downward, it must be negative in this setup: mixing a positive initial velocity with a positive gravity would create contradictory signs.

questions.stem: A student assumes a bowling ball will hit the ground before a tennis ball if both are dropped together from the same height, since the bowling ball is heavier. Is this correct (ignoring air resistance)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: in free fall, all objects accelerate at the same rate g, regardless of mass, so both would hit the ground at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: heavier objects always fall faster in free fall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the tennis ball would actually hit the ground first instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only if the objects are dropped from very high altitudes.

questions.explanation: Mass does not appear anywhere in the free fall kinematic equations. Ignoring air resistance, a heavy bowling ball and a light tennis ball dropped together from the same height hit the ground at exactly the same time.

questions.stem: A car traveling at 30 m/s decelerates at 5 m/s² for 4 seconds. Find its velocity after those 4 seconds. (Use $v = v_0 + at$, with deceleration as a negative acceleration.)
A ball is thrown straight upward with an initial velocity of 15 m/s. Taking "up" as positive (so gravity is $-9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$), find its velocity after 1 second.
questions.explanation: $v = v_0 + at = 15 + (-9.8)(1) = 15 - 9.8 = 5.2$ m/s. The ball is still moving upward, but has slowed down due to gravity.

questions.stem: A bowling ball and a tennis ball are dropped together, at the same instant, from the same height, with air resistance considered negligible. Which one reaches the ground first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neither: both reach the ground at exactly the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bowling ball, since it is heavier.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tennis ball, since it is lighter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on the exact height of the drop.

questions.explanation: In free fall, mass does not affect acceleration: every object accelerates downward at the same rate $g$, so both balls hit the ground simultaneously when dropped together from the same height.

questions.stem: A light ray hits a flat mirror at an angle of incidence of 40° (measured from the normal). Find the angle of reflection.
questions.explanation: The law of reflection states the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 40°.

questions.stem: A light ray hits a flat mirror at an angle of incidence of 55° (measured from the normal). Find the angle of reflection.
questions.explanation: The law of reflection states the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 55°.

questions.stem: A concave mirror (curving inward, like the inside of a spoon) brings parallel light rays together. Is it converging or diverging?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: mirrors do not affect light direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on the color of light.

questions.explanation: Concave mirrors bring parallel light rays together toward a focus point, making them converging mirrors.

questions.stem: A convex lens (thicker in the middle) bends light rays together toward a focus point. Is it converging or diverging?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: lenses do not affect light direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on the color of light.

questions.explanation: Convex lenses (thicker in the middle) bring light rays together toward a focus point, making them converging lenses.

questions.stem: A convex mirror (curving outward, like the back of a spoon) spreads parallel light rays apart. Is it converging or diverging?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: mirrors do not affect light direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on the color of light.

questions.explanation: Convex mirrors spread parallel light rays apart, making them diverging mirrors.

questions.stem: A concave lens (thinner in the middle) spreads light rays apart, and is used to correct nearsightedness. Is it converging or diverging?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: lenses do not affect light direction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on the color of light.

questions.explanation: Concave lenses (thinner in the middle) spread light rays apart, making them diverging lenses.

questions.stem: What does the law of reflection state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The angle of incidence is always greater than the angle of reflection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light always bends when it reflects off a surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Light travels at the same speed in every medium.

questions.explanation: The law of reflection states that the angle at which light hits a surface (angle of incidence) equals the angle at which it bounces off (angle of reflection).

questions.stem: What term describes light bending as it passes from one medium into another, like from air into water?
questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it crosses into a different medium, caused by a change in speed at the boundary.

questions.stem: Arrange the following from longest to shortest wavelength: X-rays, radio waves, visible light, gamma rays.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radio waves, visible light, X-rays, gamma rays

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gamma rays, X-rays, visible light, radio waves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Visible light, radio waves, gamma rays, X-rays

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radio waves, gamma rays, X-rays, visible light

questions.explanation: The full electromagnetic spectrum runs (longest to shortest): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray. From this list: radio waves, then visible light, then X-rays, then gamma rays.

questions.stem: Within the visible light spectrum, which color has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, matching the "r" at the start of the roygbiv mnemonic (ordered longest to shortest).

questions.stem: Within the visible light spectrum, which color has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Violet has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum, matching the "v" at the end of the roygbiv mnemonic (ordered longest to shortest).

questions.stem: A student assumes that since concave mirrors converge light, concave lenses must also converge light. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the concave/convex rule flips for lenses; concave lenses actually diverge light, while convex lenses converge it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: concave always means converging, for both mirrors and lenses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: concave lenses do not affect light at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: mirrors and lenses always behave identically for the same shape.

questions.explanation: For mirrors, concave converges and convex diverges. For lenses, this pattern reverses: convex lenses converge, and concave lenses diverge. Always check whether the device is a mirror or a lens before applying the rule.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart reflection and refraction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, staying in the same medium; refraction is light bending as it passes into a different medium.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reflection is light bending into a new medium; refraction is light bouncing off a surface.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reflection and refraction are just two different names for the exact same phenomenon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refraction only happens with mirrors; reflection only happens with lenses.

questions.explanation: Reflection keeps light in the same medium, simply bouncing off a surface. Refraction involves light actually crossing into a different medium and bending due to the change in speed.

questions.stem: A student assumes visible light makes up most of the electromagnetic spectrum, since it is the only part we can see and think about regularly. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: visible light is only a tiny slice of the full electromagnetic spectrum, bordered by infrared and ultraviolet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: visible light makes up the majority of the electromagnetic spectrum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the electromagnetic spectrum consists only of visible light and nothing else.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: radio waves and X-rays are actually part of visible light.

questions.explanation: Visible light occupies only a narrow band of the full electromagnetic spectrum. Most electromagnetic radiation (radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays) is invisible to human eyes.

questions.stem: A student says violet light has a longer wavelength than red light, since violet appears at the "high energy" end people associate with bigger numbers. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: red has the longest wavelength in the visible spectrum, and violet has the shortest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: violet always has a longer wavelength than red.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: red and violet actually have the exact same wavelength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: wavelength and energy always increase together in the same direction as this student assumes for violet.

questions.explanation: Red has the longest wavelength in visible light, and violet has the shortest: the opposite of what the student assumed. The roygbiv mnemonic lists colors from longest to shortest wavelength.

questions.stem: Find the momentum of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s. (Use $p = mv$.)
A 0.5 kg ball traveling at 10 m/s is caught and brought to a complete stop in 0.2 seconds. Find the magnitude of the average force exerted to stop it.
questions.explanation: Change in momentum: $\Delta p = 0 - (0.5)(10) = -5$ kg·m/s. Force: $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t} = \dfrac{-5}{0.2} = -25$ N, so the magnitude is 25 N.

questions.stem: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg cart, and the two carts stick together after the collision. Find their combined velocity afterward.
questions.explanation: Total momentum before: $(3)(4) + (1)(0) = 12$ kg·m/s. Combined mass after: $3+1=4$ kg. So $12 = 4v$, giving $v = 3$ m/s.

questions.stem: Two identical billiard balls collide and bounce apart. Measurements show both the total momentum and the total kinetic energy are the same before and after the collision. Classify this collision.
questions.explanation: An elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy. Since both were measured to be conserved here, this is an elastic collision.

questions.stem: Two carts collide and momentum is conserved, but the total kinetic energy after the collision is less than before (some energy converted to heat and sound). Classify this collision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A collision where momentum was not conserved

questions.explanation: An inelastic collision conserves momentum but not kinetic energy: some kinetic energy converts into other forms like heat or sound.

questions.stem: A student applies a kinetic energy conservation equation to a real-world car crash where the cars crumple and stick together. Is this appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: only elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; a crash where cars crumple and stick together is a perfectly inelastic collision, which does not conserve kinetic energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: kinetic energy is always conserved in every type of collision.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because momentum is also not conserved in this crash.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as momentum is also conserved.

questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in all closed-system collisions, but kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions. A real-world crash where objects crumple and stick together is inelastic, so kinetic energy is not conserved.

questions.stem: A moving cart collides with a stationary cart, and they stick together. A student calculates the combined mass afterward using only the moving cart's mass, leaving out the stationary cart's mass. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the combined mass after sticking together must include both objects' masses, even the one that started at rest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: a stationary object's mass does not need to be included after a collision.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: only the stationary cart's mass should be used instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: mass only matters for the object that was originally moving.

questions.explanation: Even though the stationary cart contributed zero momentum before the collision, its mass still becomes part of the combined moving mass afterward. Leaving it out of the "after" total is a common and costly error.

questions.stem: A question asks for the impulse delivered during a collision, and a student reports only the peak force value, without considering the time of contact. Is this a complete answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: impulse equals force multiplied by time (or the total change in momentum), not the force value alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: impulse and force are the exact same quantity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: impulse only depends on time, never on force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as the force value given is the average force.

questions.explanation: Impulse ($J = Ft$) requires both the force and the time over which it acts. Reporting force alone omits the time component and does not answer what was actually asked.

questions.stem: Two carts move directly toward each other before colliding. A student adds their momenta as two positive numbers, ignoring that they move in opposite directions. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since momentum is a vector, one cart's momentum must be treated as negative (opposite direction) in the total.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: momentum is always added as positive values, regardless of direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because one of the carts must actually be stationary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: direction only matters for velocity, not momentum.

questions.explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity. When two objects move toward each other, their momenta point in opposite directions, so one must be assigned a negative sign relative to the other before adding them.

questions.stem: A 2000 kg truck moves at 3 m/s. A 500 kg car moves at 12 m/s. Compare their momenta.

choices.label: A
choices.text: They have exactly the same momentum, 6000 kg·m/s each.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The truck has more momentum, since it has more mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The car has more momentum, since it moves faster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their momenta cannot be compared without knowing their directions.

questions.explanation: Truck: $p = (2000)(3) = 6000$ kg·m/s. Car: $p = (500)(12) = 6000$ kg·m/s. A heavy object moving slowly can have the same momentum as a light object moving fast.

questions.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg cart, and they stick together. Find their combined velocity afterward.
questions.explanation: Total momentum before: $(2)(6) + (4)(0) = 12$ kg·m/s. Combined mass: $2+4=6$ kg. So $12 = 6v$, giving $v = 2$ m/s.

questions.stem: A force of 15 N acts on an object for 3 seconds. Find the impulse delivered. (Use $J = Ft$.)
questions.explanation: $J = Ft = (15)(3) = 45$ kg·m/s (equivalently, N·s).

questions.stem: A 2 kg cart moves at +5 m/s. A 3 kg cart moves at -4 m/s (toward the first cart, in the opposite direction). They collide and stick together. Find their combined velocity afterward.
questions.explanation: Total momentum before: $(2)(5) + (3)(-4) = 10 - 12 = -2$ kg·m/s. Combined mass: $2+3=5$ kg. So $-2 = 5v$, giving $v = -0.4$ m/s (moving in the second cart's original direction).

questions.stem: A car's airbag deploys during a collision, extending the time over which the passenger's momentum changes to zero, compared to hitting a hard dashboard directly. Why does this reduce injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For the same total change in momentum, a longer time reduces the average force needed, lowering the impact on the passenger's body.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The airbag reduces the total change in momentum the passenger experiences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The airbag has no effect on force, only on the passenger's final velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The airbag works by making the passenger's mass smaller during the collision.

questions.explanation: Impulse ($J=Ft$) for a given momentum change is fixed; stretching out the time $t$ over which it happens reduces the force $F$ needed to produce that same change, which is exactly why airbags and padded surfaces reduce injury.

questions.stem: "The car traveled 50 km." Is this a scalar or a vector statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scalar, since no direction is given.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vector, since a distance is mentioned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: this statement has no magnitude either.

questions.explanation: A scalar has only magnitude, no direction. Since no direction is mentioned, "50 km" alone is a scalar (distance).

questions.stem: "The car traveled 50 km north." Is this a scalar or a vector statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vector, since a direction (north) is specified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scalar, since a distance is mentioned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: this statement has no magnitude.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both, since it also could be considered speed.

questions.explanation: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Since "north" specifies a direction, this is a vector statement (displacement).

questions.stem: "The temperature is 30°C." Is this a scalar or a vector quantity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scalar, since temperature has magnitude only, no direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vector, since temperature can rise or fall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: temperature is not a physics quantity.

questions.explanation: Temperature has only a magnitude (how hot or cold) with no associated direction, making it a scalar.

questions.stem: A runner jogs completely around a circular track and ends up exactly back at the starting point. Compare the runner's total distance traveled to their total displacement.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The distance is a large positive number (the full circumference), while the displacement is zero, since the runner ended up exactly where they started.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both the distance and the displacement are zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both the distance and the displacement equal the full circumference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The displacement is larger than the distance in this situation.

questions.explanation: Distance is the total path length traveled (a scalar), which is large here. Displacement is the straight-line change in position (a vector), which is zero since the start and end points are the same.

questions.stem: A hiker walks 6 km east, then 8 km north. Find the magnitude of the hiker's total displacement.
questions.explanation: The two vectors are perpendicular, so use the Pythagorean theorem: $R^2 = 6^2 + 8^2 = 36 + 64 = 100$, so $R = 10$ km.

questions.stem: A hiker walks 5 km east, then 12 km north. Find the magnitude of the hiker's total displacement.
questions.explanation: The two vectors are perpendicular, so use the Pythagorean theorem: $R^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169$, so $R = 13$ km.

questions.stem: Two tug-of-war teams pull on a rope. Team A pulls with 500 N to the left; Team B pulls with 350 N to the right. Find the net force and its direction.
questions.explanation: Since the forces are opposite, subtract the smaller from the larger: $500 - 350 = 150$ N. The net force takes the direction of the larger force, Team A's direction (left).

questions.stem: A force of 20 N is applied at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. ($\cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sin 30° = \dfrac{1}{2}$)
questions.explanation: $V_x = 20\cos30° = 20 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3$ N. $V_y = 20\sin30° = 20 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 10$ N.

questions.stem: A force of 8 N is applied at an angle of 60° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. ($\cos 60° = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $\sin 60° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$)
questions.explanation: $V_x = 8\cos60° = 8 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 4$ N. $V_y = 8\sin60° = 8 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.9$ N.

questions.stem: A student adds a 3 km eastward displacement and a 4 km northward displacement directly, getting a total of 7 km. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since the vectors are perpendicular, not in the same direction, the Pythagorean theorem must be used instead, giving 5 km.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: 7 km is the correct combined displacement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the correct answer is 1 km, found by subtracting instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: vector magnitudes can always be added directly, regardless of direction.

questions.explanation: Vector magnitudes can only be added directly when the vectors point in the exact same direction. Since 3 km and 4 km here are perpendicular, the Pythagorean theorem gives the correct combined magnitude: $\sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 5$ km, not 7 km.

questions.stem: A problem measures a vector's angle from the vertical axis instead of the usual horizontal axis. A student still assumes cosine always gives the horizontal component and sine always gives the vertical component. Is this assumption safe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: when the angle is measured from the vertical instead, the sine and cosine roles for the components swap compared to the usual convention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: cosine always gives the horizontal component no matter how the angle is measured.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: sine and cosine are never used when the angle is measured from the vertical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: the components do not depend on which axis the angle is measured from.

questions.explanation: Which trig function applies to which component depends on which side of the triangle the angle is measured from. Sketching the actual triangle and identifying the adjacent and opposite sides relative to the given angle is necessary before applying sine or cosine.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells apart a scalar and a vector quantity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scalar has both magnitude and direction; a vector has magnitude only.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both scalars and vectors always require a direction to be specified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scalars and vectors are just two different names for the same kind of quantity.

questions.explanation: Scalars (like mass, time, distance) carry only size. Vectors (like displacement, velocity, force) carry both size and a specific direction.

questions.stem: Two forces act on an object: 800 N pushing right, and 800 N pushing left. Find the net force.
questions.explanation: Since the forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, subtracting gives $800 - 800 = 0$ N: the forces completely cancel out.

questions.stem: A vector has a horizontal component of 6 units and a vertical component of 8 units. Find the magnitude of the original vector.
questions.explanation: The horizontal and vertical components form a right triangle with the original vector as the hypotenuse: $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36+64} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ units.

questions.stem: A metal pan handle becomes hot through direct contact with the heated pan. What heat transfer mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Conduction is heat transfer through direct contact between particles, typically through a solid, like a metal handle.

questions.stem: The Sun's heat reaches Earth across the vacuum of space, with no physical medium in between. What heat transfer mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers heat through electromagnetic waves and requires no physical medium at all: exactly how sunlight warms Earth through empty space.

questions.stem: Warm air near a heater rises and circulates around a room, carrying heat with it. What heat transfer mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Convection transfers heat through the movement of a fluid itself, as warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler, denser fluid sinks.

questions.stem: Which law of thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other?
questions.explanation: The Zeroth Law establishes this transitive property of thermal equilibrium, which is what makes thermometers work.

questions.stem: Which law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms or transferred?
questions.explanation: The First Law is the law of conservation of energy applied specifically to heat and work.

questions.stem: Which law of thermodynamics states that heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse without external work?
questions.explanation: The Second Law describes the natural direction of spontaneous heat flow: always hot to cold, unless external work forces it the other way.

questions.stem: Which law of thermodynamics states that as temperature approaches absolute zero, a system's entropy (disorder) approaches a minimum value?
questions.explanation: The Third Law describes the behavior of entropy as temperature approaches absolute zero (0 Kelvin).

questions.stem: Find the heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 3 kg of water by 5°C, given water's specific heat capacity is 4186 J/(kg·°C). (Use $Q = mc\Delta T$.)
41,860 J of heat energy raises the temperature of 2 kg of water by an unknown amount. Given water's specific heat capacity is 4186 J/(kg·°C), find the temperature change.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $Q = mc\Delta T$: $\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{mc} = \dfrac{41860}{(2)(4186)} = \dfrac{41860}{8372} = 5°C$.

questions.stem: A student describes warm air circulating around a heated room as "conduction," since heat is moving from one place to another. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the actual bulk movement of the air itself makes this convection, not conduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: any heat transfer through air is always conduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: this is actually radiation, since air is a gas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: conduction and convection are interchangeable terms.

questions.explanation: Conduction is direct particle-to-particle contact, typically through solids, with no bulk fluid movement. Since the air itself is physically moving and circulating, this is convection.

questions.stem: A refrigerator moves heat from its cold interior to the warmer room outside. A student says this violates the second law of thermodynamics. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the refrigerator uses electrical work (via its compressor) to force this backward flow; the second law only forbids this happening spontaneously, without work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: moving heat from cold to hot always violates the second law, with no exceptions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because refrigerators do not actually move heat at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: refrigerators are a well-known exception that breaks the laws of physics.

questions.explanation: The second law forbids heat flowing spontaneously from cold to hot, but a refrigerator forces this flow using external work from its compressor: this does not violate the law, since the flow is not spontaneous.

questions.stem: A student assumes a substance with a higher specific heat capacity changes temperature more easily (faster) than one with a lower specific heat capacity. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a higher specific heat capacity means the substance resists temperature change, requiring more energy for the same temperature increase; a lower specific heat means faster temperature change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: higher specific heat capacity always means faster temperature change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: specific heat capacity has no relationship to how quickly temperature changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for substances heated by radiation.

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity measures resistance to temperature change. A high specific heat capacity (like water's) means a substance needs more energy to change temperature by a given amount, so it heats up and cools down more slowly, not faster.

questions.stem: A student uses a specific heat capacity given in J/(g·°C) directly with a mass value given in kilograms, without converting either one. Is this safe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: mixing grams-based specific heat with a kilogram mass (without converting) throws off the final answer by a factor of 1000.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: specific heat capacity units automatically adjust for any mass unit used.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because specific heat capacity cannot be measured in J/(g·°C).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: grams and kilograms can always be used interchangeably in any formula.

questions.explanation: The mass units used in $Q=mc\Delta T$ must match the mass units in the specific heat capacity's own units. Mixing grams-based specific heat with a kilogram mass without converting introduces a factor-of-1000 error.

questions.stem: A hot cup of coffee is left on a table in a cooler room. Using the second law of thermodynamics, explain what happens to the coffee's temperature over time.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coffee gradually cools down, since heat flows spontaneously from the hotter coffee to the cooler room, never the reverse without added work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The coffee gradually gets hotter, drawing heat spontaneously from the cooler room air.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coffee's temperature stays exactly the same indefinitely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The coffee's temperature change cannot be predicted by the second law.

questions.explanation: Since the coffee is hotter than the surrounding air, heat flows spontaneously from the coffee to the room, cooling the coffee down. The reverse (coffee spontaneously heating up) would require heat flowing from cold to hot, which the second law forbids without external work.

questions.stem: Two identical pans, one filled with water and one filled with cooking oil (which has a lower specific heat capacity than water), are heated with the same amount of energy for the same amount of time. Which one reaches a higher temperature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The oil, since its lower specific heat capacity means the same energy input causes a larger temperature increase.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water, since its higher specific heat capacity means it heats up faster.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both reach exactly the same temperature, since the energy input and time are equal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither changes temperature, since both are liquids.

questions.explanation: A lower specific heat capacity means less energy is needed to raise a substance's temperature by a given amount. Since oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water, the same energy input causes a greater temperature rise in the oil.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a table with a horizontal velocity of 4 m/s and takes 0.6 seconds to hit the floor. Find the horizontal distance it travels.
questions.explanation: Horizontal motion has constant velocity (no horizontal acceleration): $x = v_xt = (4)(0.6) = 2.4$ m.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a table with a horizontal velocity of 4 m/s and takes 0.6 seconds to hit the floor. Find the height of the table. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: Vertically, the ball starts with $v_{y0}=0$: $y = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(0.6)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(0.36) = 1.764$ m.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Find its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components. ($\cos 30° = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sin 30° = \dfrac{1}{2}$)
questions.explanation: $v_{x0} = 40\cos30° = 40 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6$ m/s. $v_{y0} = 40\sin30° = 40 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 20$ m/s.

questions.stem: A projectile has an initial vertical velocity component of 20 m/s. Find how long it takes to reach its highest point. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $v_y = v_{y0} - gt$.)
questions.explanation: At maximum height, $v_y = 0$: $0 = 20 - 9.8t$, so $t = \dfrac{20}{9.8} \approx 2.04$ s.

questions.stem: A satellite moves at a constant speed in a perfectly circular orbit around Earth. Is the satellite accelerating?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes: its direction is constantly changing, even though its speed stays the same.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No: since its speed never changes, it cannot be accelerating.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: acceleration only applies to objects speeding up or slowing down in a straight line.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only because satellites always eventually change speed.

questions.explanation: Velocity is a vector with both speed and direction. Even at constant speed, the satellite's direction keeps changing as it curves around the orbit, which means its velocity, and therefore its acceleration, is nonzero.

questions.stem: In uniform circular motion, which direction does the centripetal acceleration point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Toward the center of the circle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Away from the center of the circle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tangent to the circle, in the direction of motion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Directly opposite the direction of motion

questions.explanation: Centripetal acceleration always points toward the center of the circular path, which is what keeps the object curving instead of flying off in a straight line.

questions.stem: A student calculates a projectile's horizontal distance using $x = v_xt + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, applying gravity to the horizontal motion. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: gravity affects only the vertical component; horizontal velocity stays constant, so $x = v_xt$ is the correct formula.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: gravity affects horizontal and vertical motion equally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: horizontal motion should use $x = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ alone instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for projectiles launched at exactly 45°.

questions.explanation: In ideal projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), horizontal velocity never changes, since no horizontal acceleration acts. Only the vertical motion includes a $\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ term.

questions.stem: A student assumes an object moving at constant speed around a circle has zero acceleration, since "constant speed" sounds like "no change." Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: constant speed is not the same as constant velocity; the changing direction alone produces a real, nonzero centripetal acceleration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: constant speed always means zero acceleration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because the object is also changing speed in this scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: acceleration only depends on speed, never on direction.

questions.explanation: Acceleration depends on velocity, a vector that includes direction. Even without any speed change, a continuously changing direction (as in circular motion) still produces acceleration.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched at 25 m/s at 40° above the horizontal. A student plugs the full 25 m/s directly into both the horizontal equation $x = vt$ and the vertical free-fall equations, without splitting it into components first. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the launch velocity must first be split into horizontal ($v_0\cos\theta$) and vertical ($v_0\sin\theta$) components before applying either equation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the full launch speed can be used directly in both directions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: only the vertical equation needs the launch speed split into components.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: splitting into components is only needed when the angle is greater than 45°.

questions.explanation: Only the correct component belongs in each direction's equation: the horizontal component in the horizontal equation, and the vertical component in the vertical equations. Using the full launch speed in both directions produces an incorrect result.

questions.stem: A projectile's launch angle is measured from the horizontal. A student uses sine to find the horizontal component and cosine to find the vertical component. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: when the angle is measured from the horizontal, cosine gives the horizontal component and sine gives the vertical component, the reverse of what the student used.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: sine always gives the horizontal component regardless of how the angle is measured.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: both components should use the same trig function.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: cosine and sine can be swapped freely without changing the result.

questions.explanation: When the angle is measured from the horizontal, cosine corresponds to the horizontal (adjacent) component and sine corresponds to the vertical (opposite) component. Swapping them produces a projectile that behaves as if launched at a very different angle.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a cliff with a horizontal velocity of 5 m/s and falls for 2 seconds before landing. Find the horizontal distance traveled.
questions.explanation: Horizontal motion has constant velocity: $x = v_xt = (5)(2) = 10$ m.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a cliff with a horizontal velocity of 5 m/s and falls for 2 seconds before landing. Find the height of the cliff. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: Vertically, the ball starts with $v_{y0}=0$: $y = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(4) = 19.6$ m.

questions.stem: A projectile launched at an angle reaches the very top of its path. What is its vertical velocity at that exact moment, and is its horizontal velocity also zero?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vertical velocity is momentarily zero; horizontal velocity is unchanged and still nonzero.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both vertical and horizontal velocity are zero at the peak.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vertical velocity is at its maximum at the peak; horizontal velocity is zero.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither vertical nor horizontal velocity changes at any point during flight.

questions.explanation: At the peak, the projectile momentarily stops moving up or down (vertical velocity = 0), but since gravity never acts horizontally, the horizontal velocity stays exactly the same as it was at launch.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched with an initial vertical velocity component of 14.7 m/s, and lands at the same height it was launched from. Using $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and the fact that the time to fall back down equals the time to rise, find the projectile's total time in the air.
questions.explanation: Time to reach the peak: $t_{up} = \dfrac{14.7}{9.8} = 1.5$ s. Since the time falling back down equals the time rising (same launch and landing height), total flight time is $1.5 \times 2 = 3$ s.

questions.stem: What is the SI base unit for length?
questions.explanation: The meter (m) is the SI base unit for length.

questions.stem: What is the SI base unit for mass?
questions.explanation: The kilogram (kg) is the SI base unit for mass.

questions.stem: What is the SI base unit for time?
questions.explanation: The second (s) is the SI base unit for time.

questions.stem: What is the SI base unit for amount of substance?
questions.explanation: The mole (mol) is the SI base unit for amount of substance.

questions.stem: Convert 350 centimeters to meters.
questions.explanation: $350 \text{ cm} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ m}}{100 \text{ cm}} = 3.5$ m.

questions.stem: Convert 5000 meters to kilometers.
questions.explanation: $5000 \text{ m} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ km}}{1000 \text{ m}} = 5$ km.

questions.stem: Convert a speed of 90 kilometers per hour into meters per second.
questions.explanation: $90 \dfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \dfrac{1000 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ km}} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ h}}{3600 \text{ s}} = \dfrac{90000}{3600} = 25$ m/s.

questions.stem: Convert a speed of 54 kilometers per hour into meters per second.
questions.explanation: $54 \dfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \dfrac{1000 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ km}} \times \dfrac{1 \text{ h}}{3600 \text{ s}} = \dfrac{54000}{3600} = 15$ m/s.

questions.stem: The formula for force is $F = ma$. Mass has units of kg; acceleration has units of $m/s^2$. What are the resulting units of force?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the units directly: $kg \times \dfrac{m}{s^2} = kg \cdot m/s^2$, a combination given its own name, the newton.

questions.stem: A student converts 250 cm to meters by multiplying $250 \text{ cm} \times \dfrac{100 \text{ cm}}{1 \text{ m}}$. Is this conversion factor arranged correctly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this leaves units of cm²/m, a nonsense result, since the unwanted "cm" does not cancel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: this arrangement correctly cancels the centimeters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because 250 cm cannot be converted to meters at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: any arrangement of the conversion factor gives the same correct answer.

questions.explanation: The conversion factor must place the unwanted unit (cm) so it cancels: on the bottom, matching the "cm" on top of the starting value. Placing "cm" on top instead leaves a leftover, nonsense unit and a wildly incorrect number.

questions.stem: A student plugs a distance in kilometers directly into a formula alongside a time measured in seconds, without converting either value first. Is this a valid approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: every value going into a formula must share compatible units; the distance or time must be converted first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: formulas automatically adjust for mismatched units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because kilometers cannot be used in any formula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: as long as the final answer is rounded correctly.

questions.explanation: Mixing incompatible units within the same calculation (like kilometers with seconds, without converting) produces a meaningless result. All values must be converted to a consistent unit system first.

questions.stem: Convert 2 square meters ($m^2$) to square centimeters ($cm^2$).
questions.explanation: Since area is length times length, the conversion factor must also be squared: $1 \text{ m}^2 = (100 \text{ cm})^2 = 10{,}000 \text{ cm}^2$. So $2 \text{ m}^2 = 2 \times 10{,}000 = 20{,}000 \text{ cm}^2$.

questions.stem: Convert 3 cubic meters ($m^3$) to cubic centimeters ($cm^3$).
questions.explanation: Since volume is length cubed, the conversion factor must also be cubed: $1 \text{ m}^3 = (100 \text{ cm})^3 = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ cm}^3$. So $3 \text{ m}^3 = 3 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 3{,}000{,}000 \text{ cm}^3$.

questions.stem: While solving a problem for speed, a student's final answer comes out with units of seconds per meter (s/m) instead of the expected meters per second (m/s). What does this most likely indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conversion factor was likely set up backwards (upside down) somewhere in the calculation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student's numeric answer is definitely still correct, since units do not affect correctness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Speed can be correctly expressed in either m/s or s/m interchangeably.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The formula for speed does not actually involve units at all.

questions.explanation: Tracking units throughout a calculation is a built-in error check. Ending up with the inverted unit (s/m instead of m/s) is a strong signal that a conversion factor was flipped upside down somewhere along the way.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. Find its speed. (Use $v = f\lambda$.)
A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. Find its wavelength.
questions.explanation: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{170} = 2$ m.

questions.stem: A wave travels at 300 m/s with a wavelength of 5 m. Find its frequency.
questions.explanation: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{300}{5} = 60$ Hz.

questions.stem: Sound travels through air to reach your ears. Is sound a mechanical wave or an electromagnetic wave?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mechanical, since it requires a medium (like air) to travel through.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electromagnetic, since it can travel through a vacuum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: sound is not a wave at all.

questions.explanation: Sound requires a physical medium like air to travel: it cannot travel through a vacuum, making it a mechanical wave.

questions.stem: Light travels from the Sun through the vacuum of space to reach Earth. Is light a mechanical wave or an electromagnetic wave?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electromagnetic, since it requires no medium and can travel through a vacuum.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mechanical, since it requires a medium like air.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither: light is not a wave at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both, depending on the distance traveled.

questions.explanation: Light travels through empty space with no medium needed, making it an electromagnetic wave.

questions.stem: What is the term for the distance between two consecutive identical points on a wave, such as crest to crest?
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive identical points on a wave, like from one crest to the next.

questions.stem: In a wave where particles move perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel, what type of wave is this?
questions.explanation: A transverse wave has particles moving perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, like light or a shaken rope.

questions.stem: In a wave where particles move back and forth parallel to the wave's direction of travel, creating compressions and stretches, what type of wave is this?
questions.explanation: A longitudinal wave has particles moving parallel to the wave's direction, creating compressions and stretches: this is how sound travels.

questions.stem: A sound source moves toward a stationary observer. What happens to the observed frequency (pitch)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases (higher pitch), since the source moving toward the observer compresses the wave crests closer together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It decreases (lower pitch), since the source is getting closer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It stays exactly the same, since the source's actual frequency has not changed.

questions.explanation: This is the Doppler effect: a source moving toward an observer compresses the wave crests reaching them, increasing the observed frequency and pitch.

questions.stem: A sound source moves away from a stationary observer. What happens to the observed frequency (pitch)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It decreases (lower pitch), since the source moving away stretches out the wave crests reaching the observer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases (higher pitch), since the source is getting farther.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It stays exactly the same, since the source's actual frequency has not changed.

questions.explanation: This is the Doppler effect: a source moving away from an observer stretches out the wave crests reaching them, decreasing the observed frequency and pitch.

questions.stem: A movie shows an explosion producing a loud sound in the vacuum of outer space. Is this physically realistic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: sound is a mechanical wave and requires a medium like air; with no matter to vibrate in a vacuum, there would be no sound at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: sound can travel through a vacuum just like light.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because explosions cannot happen in space at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: loud sounds are always audible regardless of the medium.

questions.explanation: Sound requires a physical medium to travel through, unlike electromagnetic waves such as light. With no air (or any matter) in a vacuum, there is nothing to vibrate, so no sound could actually be heard.

questions.stem: A student describes sound waves as transverse waves, since sound is a familiar kind of wave. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: sound waves are longitudinal, with air particles compressing and stretching along the same direction the sound travels, not moving side to side.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: sound waves are transverse, like light waves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: sound waves are electromagnetic, not transverse or longitudinal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: all mechanical waves are transverse.

questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave: air particles move back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, creating compressions and stretches, unlike a transverse wave's side-to-side particle motion.

questions.stem: A student assumes an approaching sound source makes the sound waves travel faster through the air, causing the higher pitch heard. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: the wave's actual speed through the medium stays constant; only the observed frequency changes, due to the wave crests bunching together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the Doppler effect works by physically speeding up the sound waves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: the wave's speed actually decreases as the source approaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: pitch and wave speed are always the same thing.

questions.explanation: The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency and pitch, not the actual wave speed through the medium. The wave crests simply bunch together (from the source's motion), which is perceived as a higher frequency.

questions.stem: A student assumes a sound source moving toward an observer results in a lower pitch, reasoning that "closer sounds are usually softer and lower." Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: a source moving toward an observer results in a higher observed pitch, not lower, which is why an approaching ambulance siren sounds higher, not lower.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: approaching sources always sound lower in pitch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: pitch does not change based on relative motion at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: but only for very quiet sounds.

questions.explanation: Reversing the Doppler direction (assuming approaching means lower pitch) contradicts everyday experience: an ambulance siren clearly rises in pitch as it approaches, not falls.

questions.stem: An ambulance drives past a stationary listener, siren blaring the whole time. Describe the sequence of pitch changes the listener hears, from before the ambulance arrives to after it passes.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pitch sounds higher than the siren's true pitch while approaching, then drops to lower than the true pitch once it has passed and is moving away.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pitch sounds lower while approaching, then rises higher once it has passed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pitch stays exactly the same throughout, since the siren's true frequency never changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pitch becomes silent right as the ambulance passes, then returns to normal.

questions.explanation: While approaching, the source's motion compresses the sound waves, raising the observed pitch above the siren's true pitch. Once it passes and moves away, the waves stretch out, lowering the observed pitch below the true pitch: the classic Doppler shift pattern.

questions.stem: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done. (Use $W = Fd$.)
Find the kinetic energy of a 4 kg object moving at 5 m/s. (Use $KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.)
Find the gravitational potential energy of a 3 kg book held 4 m above the ground. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and $PE = mgh$.)
A 5 kg object starts from rest at the top of a frictionless slide, 2 m high. Find its speed at the bottom. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.)
questions.explanation: $PE_i = mgh = (5)(9.8)(2) = 98$ J, which all converts to kinetic energy: $98 = \dfrac{1}{2}(5)v^2 = 2.5v^2$, so $v^2 = 39.2$ and $v \approx 6.26$ m/s.

questions.stem: A motor does 300 J of work in 5 seconds. Find its power output. (Use $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$.)
An object's speed is doubled, while its mass stays the same. A student assumes its kinetic energy also just doubles. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: since velocity is squared in the kinetic energy formula, doubling speed actually quadruples the kinetic energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: doubling speed always exactly doubles kinetic energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: doubling speed actually halves the kinetic energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: mass and velocity affect kinetic energy in the same simple way.

questions.explanation: $KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ squares the velocity term. Doubling $v$ means $v^2$ becomes 4 times larger, so kinetic energy quadruples, not just doubles.

questions.stem: A person holds a heavy box perfectly still above the ground, exerting a large upward force for several minutes. How much work is done on the box?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zero work, since the box does not move (no displacement in the direction of the force).

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large amount of work, proportional to how long the box is held.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Work equal to the box's weight alone, regardless of time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negative work, since the person is resisting gravity.

questions.explanation: Work requires displacement in the direction of the force. Since the box is not moving at all, no work is done on it, even though real physical effort is being exerted to hold it still.

questions.stem: A problem describes a block sliding down a ramp with noticeable friction, but a student applies $KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f$ directly, assuming no energy is lost. Is this valid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: this simple conservation equation assumes no friction; with friction present, some mechanical energy converts to heat and is not accounted for in this equation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: the equation applies regardless of whether friction is present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No: but only because gravity does not act during sliding motion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: friction has no effect on mechanical energy at all.

questions.explanation: The equation $KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f$ only holds when no energy is lost to friction or air resistance. With friction present, some energy converts to heat, so the simple form does not directly apply.

questions.stem: Two machines each do 1000 J of work. Machine A finishes in 2 seconds; Machine B finishes in 10 seconds. A student says both machines have the same power, since they did the same amount of work. Is this correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No: power depends on the rate work is done; Machine A (faster) has higher power than Machine B, even though both did the same total work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes: power and work always match whenever the total work is equal.

choices.label: C
