choices.text: No: but only because Machine B actually did more total work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes: time does not affect power in any situation.

questions.explanation: Power measures how quickly work is done ($P = W/t$), not just the total amount. Machine A does the same work in less time, giving it a higher power output than Machine B.

questions.stem: An object's kinetic energy starts at 50 J. A net force does 200 J of work on it. Find the object's final kinetic energy. (Use the work-energy theorem: $W_{net} = KE_f - KE_i$.)
questions.explanation: $W_{net} = KE_f - KE_i$, so $200 = KE_f - 50$, giving $KE_f = 250$ J.

questions.stem: A 4 kg object has 72 J of kinetic energy. Find its velocity.
Object A and Object B have the same mass. Object A moves at twice the speed of Object B. Compare their kinetic energies.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Object A has 4 times the kinetic energy of Object B.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Object A has 2 times the kinetic energy of Object B.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Object A has the same kinetic energy as Object B.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Object A has half the kinetic energy of Object B.

questions.explanation: Since kinetic energy depends on velocity squared, doubling the speed (with the same mass) quadruples the kinetic energy: $(2v)^2 = 4v^2$.

questions.stem: A motor has a power output of 200 W and runs for 10 seconds. Find the total work done.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$ gives $W = Pt = (200)(10) = 2000$ J.

questions.stem: A pendulum swings back and forth. At its lowest point, it moves at maximum speed; at its highest points on each side, it is momentarily still. Describe its energy at a point partway between the lowest and highest points (ignoring friction and air resistance).

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mix of both kinetic and potential energy, with the total mechanical energy staying the same throughout the swing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All kinetic energy, with zero potential energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All potential energy, with zero kinetic energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zero total energy at every point of the swing.

questions.explanation: At the lowest point, all energy is kinetic; at the highest points, all energy is potential. At any point in between, the energy is a mix of both, but the total (kinetic plus potential) stays constant throughout, by conservation of energy.

questions.stem: An object is dropped from rest and falls a height $h$ on a frictionless path, reaching a speed of 14 m/s at the bottom. Find $h$. (Use $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ and energy conservation.)
questions.explanation: By conservation of energy, $mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $h = \dfrac{v^2}{2g} = \dfrac{14^2}{2(9.8)} = \dfrac{196}{19.6} = 10$ m.

lessons.title: Building a CSE Vocabulary
lessons.summary: Strategies for memorizing high-frequency CSE vocabulary words.

children.text: Vocabulary is one of the most heavily tested areas in the CSE. The Civil Service Commission tests your ability to understand the meaning of words in context — not just memorize definitions. This means the best approach combines wide reading with deliberate review.

Spaced repetition works by reviewing words at increasing intervals — right before you're about to forget them. This forces your brain to retrieve the memory, which strengthens it each time. Cramming the night before floods short-term memory but leaves almost no trace a week later.
These words appear repeatedly across past CSE exams:
— lasting a very short time (syn: fleeting, transient, momentary)
— showing great attention to detail (syn: thorough, precise, painstaking)
— open to more than one interpretation (syn: unclear, vague, equivocal)
— well-meaning and kindly (syn: charitable, generous, altruistic)

Instead of learning one word at a time, study synonym clusters. Knowing that ephemeral, fleeting, transient, and momentary all mean roughly the same thing multiplies your vocabulary four-fold for the same study effort. When you see any one of them in a question, you recognize the whole family.

lessons.title: Synonyms and Antonyms
lessons.summary: How to identify synonyms and antonyms quickly under exam conditions.

children.text: CSE synonym and antonym questions ask you to pick the word closest in meaning — or most opposite — to the underlined word. Speed matters here: you'll have less than a minute per question in the actual exam.

When you don't know the target word, start by eliminating the choices you're sure are wrong. If you can narrow it down to two, the odds are now 50-50 instead of 25%. In synonym questions, watch for traps: choices that sound similar to the target word but mean something different (e.g., 'prescribe' vs. 'proscribe').
Many English words share Latin and Greek roots. Recognizing a root lets you make educated guesses on unfamiliar words:
These opposite pairs have appeared frequently in past CSE exams: loquacious ↔ taciturn, candid ↔ evasive, frugal ↔ extravagant, diligent ↔ indolent, obscure ↔ prominent.

lessons.title: Reading Context Clues
lessons.summary: Use the surrounding sentence to unlock unfamiliar words without memorizing every definition.

children.text: Context clue questions give you a sentence and ask for the meaning of one underlined word. Even if you've never seen the word, the sentence itself gives you enough information to answer correctly — if you know where to look.
The sentence restates the word's meaning. "The senator was loquacious — he talked endlessly during every session." → loquacious = talks a lot.
A word like 'but', 'however', or 'unlike' signals the opposite meaning. "Unlike her gregarious sister, Maria was reticent at parties." → reticent = quiet/shy.
Examples reveal the category. "Fauna such as tamaraws, tarsiers, and eagles are endemic to the Philippines." → fauna = animals.
General tone and logic point toward the meaning. "After the grueling 12-hour exam, she was utterly enervated." → enervated = drained/exhausted.

When you encounter an unknown word while reading — in the news, in books, anywhere — resist looking it up immediately. First, guess the meaning from context. Then check. This builds the skill you'll need under exam pressure, when a dictionary isn't an option.

lessons.title: Duties and Prohibited Acts under RA 6713
lessons.summary: Understand the statutory duties, response deadlines, prohibited acts, and gift rules under RA 6713.

children.text: Section 5 and Section 7 of RA 6713 establish statutory duties, response deadlines, prohibited acts, and gift rules for public officials and employees.
Respond within 15 working days from receipt of any request or letter sent by the public. Failure to act within 15 working days is a ground for administrative action.
Written requests must be acknowledged within 15 working days.
Written actions must contain no more than three initials or signatures.
Public officers must submit an annual performance report to their superiors within 45 working days from the end of the year.
Public documents must be accessible and readily available for inspection during office hours, except those officially classified as confidential.
Section 7 of RA 6713 prohibits public officials and employees from engaging in specific transactions:
Having a direct or indirect financial interest in any transaction requiring official approval from their office.
Owning, controlling, managing, or accepting employment in a private enterprise regulated or supervised by their office, unless authorized by law.
Engaging in private practice that conflicts with official functions. Private practice is prohibited for 1 year after separation from service regarding any matter before their former office.
Recommending any person to a position in a private enterprise that has regular or pending transactions with their office.
Disclosing or misusing confidential or classified information for private interest or undue advantage.
Soliciting or accepting gifts, favors, loans, or anything of monetary value in connection with official duties.
Recognized exceptions to the gift rule include:
Unsolicited gifts of nominal or insignificant value not given in anticipation of a favor.
Gifts from family members on special occasions with no pecuniary expectation.
Nominal donations from persons with no pending transaction.
Foreign government souvenirs of nominal value.
Travel grants entirely outside the country where appropriate.
#1: Deadline to Act on Public Requests

A citizen submits a written request for official information to a government office on May 2. Under Section 5 of RA 6713, within how many working days must the office act on or respond to the request?
Identify the statutory deadline for acting on public requests under Section 5.
Section 5 requires public officials and employees to act on letters and requests from the public.
The statutory deadline is within 15 working days from receipt of the request.
Failure to act within 15 working days is a ground for administrative disciplinary action.
Therefore, the office must act on the request within 15 working days.

A former bureau chief resigns from government service to enter private law practice. For how long after separation from service is the former official prohibited from practicing before their former office on pending matters?
Apply the post-employment conflict-of-interest restriction under Section 7.
Section 7 prohibits private practice that conflicts with official functions.
After separation from service, private practice regarding any matter before the former office is prohibited for 1 year.
Therefore, the restriction lasts for exactly 1 year after separation.
#3: Maximum Number of Signatures on Official Documents
To reduce bureaucratic delay, Section 5 sets a maximum limit on signatures or initials for written actions. What is the maximum allowed number of signatures or initials?
Recall the efficiency rule under Section 5.
Section 5 specifies rules to simplify administrative procedures.
Written actions must contain not more than three initials or signatures.
Therefore, the maximum limit is three initials or signatures.

lessons.title: Norms of Conduct for Public Officials
lessons.summary: Learn the eight statutory norms of conduct under RA 6713 that govern all public officials and employees.

children.text: Republic Act No. 6713, also known as the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, was approved on February 20, 1989 and took effect on March 25, 1989.
Section 4 of RA 6713 sets forth eight specific norms of conduct that every public official and employee must observe at all times.

Public officials and employees shall always uphold the public interest over and above personal interest. All government resources and powers of their offices must be used efficiently, effectively, honestly, and economically, particularly to avoid wastage of public funds and revenues.

Public officials and employees shall perform and discharge their duties with the highest degree of excellence, professionalism, intelligence, and skill. They shall enter public service with utmost devotion and dedication to duty.
Public officials and employees shall remain true to the people at all times. They must act with justness and sincerity, without discrimination, and respect the rights of others.
Public officials and employees shall provide service to everyone without unfair discrimination, regardless of party affiliation or preference.
Public officials and employees shall extend prompt, courteous, and adequate service to the public, and communicate clearly.
Public officials and employees shall at all times be loyal to the Republic and to the Filipino people.

Public officials and employees shall commit themselves to the democratic way of life and values, maintain the principle of public accountability, uphold the Constitution, and put loyalty to country above loyalty to persons or party.

Public officials and employees and their families shall lead modest lives appropriate to their position and income. They shall not indulge in extravagant or ostentatious display of wealth in any form.
#1: Total Count of Statutory Norms of Conduct
A civil service review question asks how many statutory norms of conduct are defined in Section 4 of RA 6713. What is the total count?
Recall the official list of norms in Section 4 of RA 6713.
Section 4 enumerates the norms of conduct in statutory order.

The list contains: Commitment to public interest, Professionalism, Justness and sincerity, Political neutrality, Responsiveness to the public, Nationalism and patriotism, Commitment to democracy, and Simple living.
Count the listed norms: exactly 8 norms.

A government employee processes applications for public permits without bias, giving equal service to supporters of all political parties. Which statutory norm of conduct is the employee demonstrating?
Match the behavior to the appropriate norm under Section 4.
Providing service to everyone without unfair discrimination regardless of party affiliation is the definition of political neutrality.
Political neutrality is the fourth norm of conduct under Section 4.
Therefore, the employee is demonstrating political neutrality.
A public officer avoids ostentatious displays of wealth and leads a modest lifestyle appropriate to their official income. Which norm of conduct requires this lifestyle?
Identify the norm governing personal lifestyle and display of wealth.
The eighth norm under Section 4 requires public officials to lead modest lives appropriate to their position and income.
It prohibits indulging in extravagant or ostentatious displays of wealth.
This norm is titled Simple living.

lessons.title: Penalties and Enforcement under RA 6713
lessons.summary: Understand the statutory penalties and administrative enforcement mechanisms under Section 11 of RA 6713.

children.text: Section 11 of RA 6713 specifies statutory penalties and administrative enforcement mechanisms for violations of the Code of Conduct.
Fine not exceeding six months' salary, suspension not exceeding one year, or removal from office, depending on the gravity of the offense.
Imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to P5,000, or both, along with possible disqualification from holding public office.
Penalties of a fine up to P25,000.
Private individuals who participate as co-principals, accomplices, or accessories face the same penalties and are tried jointly with the public official.
Where another law imposes a heavier penalty, the heavier penalty shall apply.
An administrative violation is sufficient cause for removal from office on its own, regardless of whether criminal prosecution is instituted.
#1: Penalties for Prohibited Acts under Sections 7, 8, or 9
A public official violates Section 7 by taking outside employment in a regulated private business without authorization. What maximum criminal penalties under Section 11 of RA 6713 can be imposed?
Apply the statutory penalty for Sections 7, 8, and 9 violations under Section 11.
Section 11 provides specific penalties for violations of Sections 7, 8, or 9.
The maximum criminal penalties are imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to P5,000, or both, plus possible disqualification from public office.
Therefore, the maximum penalties are up to five years imprisonment and/or a P5,000 fine.
A private businessman collaborates with a government officer to secure an unauthorized financial benefit. Can the private businessman be penalized under Section 11 of RA 6713?
Review the rule on private individuals in Section 11.
Private individuals who act as co-principals, accomplices, or accessories to a violation face the same penalties as the public official.
They are tried jointly with the public official.
Therefore, the private businessman can be tried jointly and faces the same penalties under RA 6713.
An administrative investigation finds a public officer guilty of violating RA 6713, but no criminal case has been filed in court. Can the officer be removed from service administratively?
Check the rule on administrative independence.
Under Section 11, an administrative violation is sufficient cause for removal on its own.
Administrative removal does not require a prior or concurrent criminal prosecution.
Therefore, the officer can be removed administratively even without a criminal court case.

lessons.title: SALN Filing, Public Access, and Divestment
lessons.summary: Learn the rules and deadlines for Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) filing and divestment under RA 6713.

children.text: Section 8 of RA 6713 requires public officials and employees to file a sworn Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) and disclosure of business interests and financial connections.
Includes the official, their spouse, and unmarried children under eighteen years of age living in their household.
Must disclose relatives in government service up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity.
Within 30 days, reckoned from the first day of service.
On or before April 30, reckoned as of the end of the preceding year.
Within 30 days, reckoned from the last day of service.
Secretary of the Senate or House:
Clerk of Supreme Court / Court Administrator:
Cabinet members, undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, foreign service officers, and heads of GOCCs.
Regional and local officials, state university employees.
All other public officers and employees.
SALN documents become available for public inspection after 10 working days, and remain available for 10 years after which they are destroyed unless needed in an ongoing investigation.
A conflict of interest must be resolved by resigning from a private position within 30 days or divesting shareholdings within 60 days from assumption of office or occurrence of conflict.
#1: SALN Filing Deadline on Assumption of Office
A newly appointed government employee starts working on June 1. By what deadline must the employee file their initial Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN)?
Identify the specific SALN deadline for assumption of office under Section 8 of RA 6713.
Under RA 6713, an initial SALN must be filed upon assumption of office.
The deadline is within 30 days, reckoned from the first day of service.
Therefore, the employee must file the initial SALN within 30 days of their first day of service.

A newly appointed bureau director owns shares in a private firm regulated by their new office and serves on its board. What are the legal deadlines for resigning the board position and divesting the shareholdings?
Apply the divestment timeframes specified in RA 6713.
Conflict of interest must be resolved by resigning private positions and divesting shareholdings.
The official must resign from the private board position within 30 days.
The official must divest shareholdings within 60 days.
Therefore, the deadlines are 30 days for resignation and 60 days for divestment.
#3: Public Access and Document Retention Period
A journalist requests to inspect the SALN of a local official filed 8 years ago. How many days after filing does a SALN become accessible to the public, and how long is it retained?
Review the public availability and retention rules under RA 6713.
SALN documents become available for public inspection after 10 working days from filing.
Filed SALN documents remain available for public inspection for 10 years.
Because 8 years is within the 10-year retention window, the document is still retained and publicly accessible.

lessons.title: Environmental Protection Concepts
lessons.summary: Understand key operational concepts including segregation at source, waste diversion, ECC, and disaster risk reduction.

children.text: Key operational environmental protection principles and concepts examined in Civil Service tests include:
The mandatory practice of separating different categories of waste (biodegradable, recyclable, non-recyclable, special) at the point of generation.
The activity of keeping solid waste out of disposal facilities through reduction, reuse, recycling, and composting.
A document issued by the DENR certifying that a proposed project has complied with the Environmental Impact Statement System under PD 1586.
The paradigm shift formalized under RA 10121 prioritizing proactive risk assessment and mitigation over reactive post-disaster response.
A household sorts its kitchen waste, paper, and plastic containers into separate trash bins before garbage collection. Which environmental concept does this practice demonstrate?
Match the practice to its environmental concept.
Segregation at source means separating waste at the location where it is produced rather than sorting it later at a central disposal facility.
Sorting materials into separate bins at home is separation at the point of generation.
Therefore, this practice demonstrates segregation at source.
A community composting program turns organic waste into fertilizer, reducing the total amount of waste sent to landfills. What environmental management principle does this describe?
Identify the process of keeping waste out of landfills.
Waste diversion is the practice of keeping solid waste out of disposal facilities through reduction, reuse, recycling, and composting.
Turning organic waste into fertilizer prevents that material from entering landfills.
Therefore, this process describes waste diversion.

Before starting construction on a major commercial development, a developer must obtain a specific certificate from the DENR confirming compliance with the Environmental Impact Statement System. What is this certificate called?
Identify the document required under PD 1586.
Under Presidential Decree 1586, projects undergoing environmental impact assessment require official clearance before proceeding.
The required document issued by the DENR is the Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC).
Therefore, the required document is an Environmental Compliance Certificate.

lessons.title: Philippine Environmental Laws
lessons.summary: Overview of key Philippine environmental protection statutes, Republic Acts, and governing agencies.

children.text: Key Philippine environmental laws examined in the Civil Service exam include several landmark Republic Acts, Presidential Decrees, and primary governing executive agencies.
Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 (segregation at source, waste diversion, ban on open dumpsites).
Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999 (air quality standards, emission limits, ban on municipal waste incineration).
Philippine Clean Water Act of 2004 (water quality management, wastewater discharge permits).
Climate Change Act of 2009 (creates Climate Change Commission, national framework strategy).
Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 (creates NDRRMC, shift to risk reduction).
Environmental Impact Statement System (requires Environmental Compliance Certificate / ECC).
Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (preservation of protected species).
National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act (designation of protected areas).
Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR):
The lead executive department enforcing most environmental laws.
Attached to the Office of the President under RA 9729.
#1: Matching Waste Management to Republic Act Number
A municipality is establishing a mandatory waste segregation program and banning open dumpsites. Under which Republic Act is this solid waste management framework enacted?
Match the subject of ecological solid waste management to its statutory title and number.
RA 9003 is the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000.
Therefore, the waste segregation program is mandated under RA 9003.
#2: Identifying the Law Governing Disaster Risk Reduction
Which law shifted the Philippine disaster management framework from reacting after disasters to disaster risk reduction and management?
Identify the act that established the modern disaster risk framework.
RA 10121 is the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010.
It created the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC).
It established the paradigm shift from post-disaster response to proactive risk reduction.
#3: The Lead Agency for Environmental Laws
Which executive department serves as the lead agency responsible for enforcing most Philippine environmental laws?
Recall the lead environmental regulatory body.
The Climate Change Commission is attached to the Office of the President under RA 9729 for climate strategy.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) is the primary lead agency enforcing most environmental statutes, including clean air, clean water, and solid waste regulations.
Therefore, the lead agency is the DENR.

lessons.title: Human Rights Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Understand the core concepts of human rights and the constitutional basis of the Commission on Human Rights.

children.text: Human rights are inherent rights possessed by all human beings, without discrimination based on nationality, place of residence, sex, national or ethnic origin, color, religion, language, or any other status.
Human rights law primarily binds the state and its organs in their treatment of individuals at all times, during both peacetime and conflict.
Serves as the primary domestic constitutional protection of fundamental civil and political liberties in the Philippines.
An independent national human rights institution created under
Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights)
#1: Constitutional Basis of the Commission on Human Rights
A student is asked which article of the 1987 Constitution creates the Commission on Human Rights. Is it Article III, Article IX, or Article XIII?
Match the institution to its constitutional source.
Article III is the Bill of Rights.
Article IX covers the Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA).
Article XIII is titled Social Justice and Human Rights, which creates the Commission on Human Rights.
Therefore, the Commission on Human Rights is created under Article XIII.
#2: Scope of Human Rights Law Application
Does human rights law apply only during peacetime, or does it bind the state at all times?
Recall the core application rules of human rights law.
Human rights law governs the state's obligations to individuals.
It applies continuously at all times, including during peacetime and times of conflict.
Therefore, human rights law binds the state at all times.
Which article of the Philippine Constitution serves as the primary domestic guarantee of individual civil and political rights?
Identify the primary domestic constitutional bill of rights.
Article III of the 1987 Constitution is the Bill of Rights.
It contains 22 sections establishing fundamental civil and political liberties.
Therefore, Article III is the primary domestic guarantee of individual rights.

lessons.title: Humanitarian Law vs Human Rights Law
lessons.summary: Understand the key distinctions in scope, applicability, and bound entities between International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights Law.

children.text: Understanding the distinction between International Human Rights Law (HRL) and International Humanitarian Law (IHL) is a central concept in Civil Service examinations.
Applies at all times, during both peacetime and situations of armed conflict.
Primarily places legal duties and obligations upon state authorities regarding their treatment of people.
to an armed conflict, including both state armed forces and non-state armed groups.

International Humanitarian Law seeks to limit the effects of armed conflict by protecting persons who are not or are no longer participating in hostilities, and by restricting the means and methods of warfare.

During an armed conflict, a non-state armed group claims that international law does not apply to them because they are not a state government. Does International Humanitarian Law bind non-state armed groups in a conflict?
Examine the scope of bound entities under International Humanitarian Law (IHL).
Human rights law primarily binds state authorities.
International Humanitarian Law applies in armed conflict and binds all parties to the conflict.
All parties include both state armed forces and non-state armed groups.
Therefore, IHL binds the non-state armed group.
A government agency is updating its peacetime administrative procedures. Does International Humanitarian Law apply to routine peacetime administration?
Determine the trigger for the application of IHL.
International Humanitarian Law applies specifically during situations of armed conflict.
Human rights law applies at all times, including peacetime.
Because there is no armed conflict, IHL does not apply to routine peacetime administration.
Therefore, only human rights law governs peacetime state conduct.
#3: Distinguishing Bound Parties and Temporal Scope
An exam question asks for the key difference between Human Rights Law and International Humanitarian Law regarding when they apply and who they bind. Which statement is correct?
Compare the temporal scope and bound entities of both bodies of law.
Human Rights Law applies at all times and primarily binds the state.
International Humanitarian Law applies during armed conflict and binds all parties to the conflict.
Therefore, IHL is specifically the law of armed conflict binding all participating parties, while HRL binds the state at all times.

lessons.title: Article XI: Accountability of Public Officers and Impeachment
lessons.summary: Learn the closed lists of impeachable officers and grounds for impeachment under Article XI of the 1987 Constitution.

children.text: Article XI, Section 1 states that public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must at all times be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives.
Under Article XI, Section 2, only the following public officials may be removed from office by impeachment:
The Members of the Supreme Court
The Members of the Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA)
Closed List of Grounds for Impeachment
Article XI, Section 2 restricts the grounds for impeachment exclusively to:
All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not through impeachment.
A petition seeks to remove a Regional Trial Court judge from office through impeachment. Is a Regional Trial Court judge an impeachable officer under Article XI?
Check the closed list of impeachable officers under Article XI, Section 2.
The closed list includes: President, Vice-President, Members of the Supreme Court, Members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman.
Trial court judges are not included in this closed list.
Therefore, a trial court judge is not an impeachable officer and must be removed through regular legal processes instead.
A member of a Constitutional Commission is accused of betrayal of public trust. Is this a valid ground for impeachment under Article XI?
Verify the ground against the closed list of constitutional grounds.
The six exclusive grounds are: culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, and betrayal of public trust.
Betrayal of public trust is explicitly listed as item six.
Therefore, betrayal of public trust is a valid constitutional ground for impeachment.
Which official is NOT subject to removal by impeachment under Article XI?
(A) The Ombudsman (B) A Member of the Supreme Court (C) A Cabinet Secretary
Compare each title against the five impeachable offices.
The Ombudsman is on the closed list.
Members of the Supreme Court are on the closed list.
Cabinet Secretaries are not on the closed list.
Therefore, a Cabinet Secretary is not subject to removal by impeachment.

lessons.title: Article III: The Bill of Rights
lessons.summary: Understand the 22 sections of Article III of the 1987 Constitution protecting civil, political, and accused rights.

children.text: Article III of the 1987 Constitution is the Bill of Rights. It contains exactly
that safeguard individual liberties against state infringement.
Sections 1 to 11 establish core civil and political guarantees:
Due process of law and equal protection of the laws.
Security against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Freedom of speech, expression, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning government for redress of grievances.
Free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship.
Liberty of abode and changing the same, and freedom of travel.
Right of the people to information on matters of public concern.
Right to form associations, unions, or societies.
Free access to courts and adequate legal assistance.
Sections 12 to 22 safeguard persons accused of crimes:
Rights under custodial investigation, including the right to remain silent and to competent counsel.
Right to bail, except for offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua when evidence of guilt is strong.
Presumption of innocence, right to be heard, right to counsel, and right to speedy, impartial trial.
Privilege of the writ of habeas corpus.
Right to speedy disposition of cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies.
Freedom from political detention and involuntary servitude.
Prohibition of excessive fines and cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment.
Freedom from imprisonment for debt or non-payment of a poll tax.
Absolute prohibition of ex post facto laws and bills of attainder.
#1: Total Number of Sections in the Bill of Rights
A student reviewing Article III of the 1987 Constitution needs to know how many sections make up the Bill of Rights. What is the exact number of sections?
Recall the official section count of Article III.
Article III of the 1987 Constitution is the Bill of Rights.
Therefore, the Bill of Rights contains exactly 22 sections.
A question asks which group of sections in Article III covers the rights of the accused, such as protection against self-incrimination and double jeopardy. Which section range is correct?
Divide Article III into its two main functional groups.
Sections 1 to 11 establish civil and political rights, such as free speech and due process.
Sections 12 to 22 establish protections for accused persons, such as bail, presumption of innocence, and protection against double jeopardy.
Therefore, Sections 12 to 22 protect the accused.
A citizen is threatened with jail time for failing to pay a personal financial debt. Does Article III allow imprisonment for non-payment of debt?
Check the specific protections under Article III.
Article III explicitly forbids imprisonment for debt or non-payment of a poll tax.
This protection is found in the second group of sections protecting individuals from improper state detention.
Therefore, the state cannot imprison a citizen for non-payment of a debt.

lessons.title: The 1987 Constitution: Articles in Outline
lessons.summary: Overview of the 18 articles of the 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines.

children.text: The 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines consists of a Preamble and 18 distinct Articles.
Introduces the aspirations, ideals, and devotion of the sovereign Filipino people.
Declaration of Principles and State Policies
Constitutional Commissions (A. Common Provisions, B. Civil Service Commission, C. Commission on Elections, D. Commission on Audit)
Education, Science and Technology, Arts, Culture and Sports
Knowing which article corresponds to each major constitutional area is a fundamental requirement of Civil Service examinations.
#1: Identifying the Article for Public Officer Accountability
A citizen wants to read the constitutional rules on impeachable officers and public accountability. Which article of the 1987 Constitution should the citizen review?
Match the subject to the article outline.
Article III covers the Bill of Rights.
Article XI covers Accountability of Public Officers.
Therefore, the citizen should review Article XI.
A student is asked to count the total number of distinct articles in the 1987 Constitution, excluding the Preamble. What is the total count?
Recall the structure of the Constitution.
The Constitution begins with a Preamble.
The Preamble is followed by Article I through Article XVIII.
Which specific main article and sub-part of the 1987 Constitution establish the Civil Service Commission?
Locate the Civil Service Commission within the constitutional structure.
Article IX covers the Constitutional Commissions.
Article IX is divided into four sub-parts: A (Common Provisions), B (Civil Service Commission), C (Commission on Elections), and D (Commission on Audit).
The Civil Service Commission is established under Article IX-B.

lessons.title: Article IX-B: The Civil Service Commission
lessons.summary: Understand the composition, qualifications, appointment, and tenure of the Civil Service Commission under Article IX-B.

children.text: Article IX, Section B of the 1987 Constitution establishes the Civil Service Commission as the central personnel agency of the Philippine Government.
Must possess proven capacity for public administration.
not have been candidates for any elective position in the election immediately preceding
President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments
A student is asked how many members make up the Civil Service Commission under Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution. What is the composition?
The Civil Service Commission consists of a Chairman and two Commissioners.
Therefore, the Commission is composed of a Chairman and two Commissioners.
An applicant for Civil Service Commissioner ran as a candidate in the local elections held last year. Is this applicant qualified for appointment under Article IX-B?
Check the disqualification rules for elective candidates.
Article IX-B requires that appointees must not have been candidates for any elective position in the election immediately preceding their appointment.
Since the applicant ran in the immediately preceding election, the applicant is disqualified.
Therefore, the applicant cannot be appointed to the Civil Service Commission.
A Commissioner completes a full seven-year term on the Civil Service Commission. Can the President reappoint this Commissioner for a second seven-year term?
Review the appointment and tenure rules under Article IX-B.
Members are appointed by the President with consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years.
Article IX-B explicitly specifies that appointments are without reappointment.
Therefore, the Commissioner cannot be reappointed for another term.

lessons.title: Modifiers (Identifying Misplaced and Dangling Modifiers)
lessons.summary: Learn how to spot and fix modifiers that are placed too far from the word they describe or that describe nothing at all.

children.text: is a word, phrase, or clause that describes another word in the sentence. For a sentence to be clear, a modifier must sit close to the word it describes.
is a modifier placed too far from the word it is meant to describe, which accidentally makes it seem to describe a different word instead, often creating a confusing or silly meaning.

"She almost drove her kids to school every day" (meaning: she almost never drove them) versus "She drove her kids to school almost every day" (meaning: she drove them most days). Moving "almost" changes the entire meaning, because it now modifies a different word.
is a modifier that has nothing logical to describe at all, usually because the sentence never actually states who or what is performing the action described by the modifier.

, the trees looked beautiful.": this sentence says the trees were walking down the street, since "walking down the street" has nothing else to logically attach to. The sentence never states who was walking.
Identify and fix the error: "The waiter served the pasta to the customer covered in cheese."
As written, "covered in cheese" sits right after "customer," making it sound like the customer is covered in cheese, not the pasta.
Move the modifier closer to the word it should describe, "pasta."
Corrected sentence: "The waiter served the customer the pasta
Identify and fix the error: "After finishing the marathon, a warm bath felt amazing."
"After finishing the marathon" needs a person who finished the marathon, but the sentence's actual subject is "a warm bath": baths cannot run marathons.
Add the correct subject right after the modifier so it has something logical to describe.
felt that a warm bath was amazing." (Or: "After
finished the marathon, a warm bath felt amazing.")

Choose the sentence with no misplaced or dangling modifier: (A) "Driving through the mountains, the scenery amazed the tourists." (B) "Driving through the mountains, the tourists were amazed by the scenery."
In (A), "driving through the mountains" has nothing logical to attach to: the scenery cannot drive.
In (B), "driving through the mountains" correctly attaches to "the tourists," who are capable of driving.
#4: Spotting a Meaning Change from Modifier Placement
Explain the difference in meaning between: (A) "Only she gave him the answer." (B) "She gave only him the answer."
In (A), "only" modifies "she," implying that she (and no one else) gave him the answer.
In (B), "only" modifies "him," implying that he (and no one else) received the answer from her.
Moving the single word "only" changes exactly who the sentence is emphasizing, showing how sensitive meaning is to a modifier's placement.
The "who or what" test for dangling modifiers.
After reading an introductory modifier phrase, ask "who or what is doing this action?" Then check if that exact person or thing appears immediately after the comma. If not, the modifier is dangling.
Read the modifier next to its nearest noun.
For misplaced modifiers, check what noun sits closest to the modifier phrase; if that noun does not logically match the intended meaning, the modifier needs to move.
Words like "only," "just," "almost," and "even" are easy to misplace.
These small modifiers can attach to almost any word nearby, so always double-check they sit directly before the specific word they are meant to limit or emphasize.
#1: Assuming the Modifier Describes the Nearest Noun by Default
Check what the modifier logically should describe, not just whichever noun happens to sit closest.
Test-makers deliberately place an unrelated noun right next to a modifier phrase to create a silly or confusing misplaced-modifier sentence, hoping you won't notice the mismatch.
#2: Missing a Dangling Modifier That "Sounds Fine" at First Read
Slow down and ask specifically who or what is performing the introductory action: if the sentence's actual subject cannot logically do that action, it is dangling.

Sentences like "After finishing the marathon, a warm bath felt amazing" can sound smooth on a quick read, but a bath cannot finish a marathon. Always check the literal logic, not just the sentence's overall flow.
#3: Forgetting That Small Words Like "Only" Can Be Misplaced Too
Modifiers are not just long phrases: single words like
can also be misplaced, changing meaning subtly.

"She only ate vegetables" (meaning: eating, not any other activity, was all she did) is subtly different from "She ate only vegetables" (meaning: vegetables, and nothing else, was what she ate). Exams sometimes test this small-word placement specifically.

lessons.title: Parallelism / Parallel Structure
lessons.summary: Learn how to keep matching parts of a sentence in the same grammatical form for clarity and balance.

children.text: ) means that similar parts of a sentence (items in a list, choices joined by "or," or ideas linked by "and") should all use the same grammatical form.
." All three items are "-ing" words (gerunds), so the list is parallel and reads smoothly.
." This list mixes forms: two "-ing" words and one "to + verb" phrase. This breaks parallelism and sounds awkward, even though each individual item is grammatically fine on its own.
, word pairs that connect two balanced parts:
. Whatever grammatical form follows the first word of the pair must be matched by the same form after the second word.
to save money." Both halves use "to + verb." "She wanted
to save money" breaks this matching pattern.
Identify and fix the parallelism error: "The coach told the team to run faster, jumping higher, and to try harder."
The list mixes forms: "to run" (to + verb), "jumping" (-ing), and "to try" (to + verb).
Change "jumping" to match the "to + verb" pattern used by the other two items.
Corrected sentence: "The coach told the team
to run faster, to jump higher,
Identify and fix the parallelism error: "The festival was not only fun but also it was educational."
After "not only," the sentence uses the adjective "fun." After "but also," it awkwardly uses a full clause, "it was educational," instead of matching with just the adjective "educational."
Match the second half's form to the first half's form (a plain adjective).
Corrected sentence: "The festival was not only

Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure: (A) "The manual explains how to install the software, updating it, and troubleshoot common errors." (B) "The manual explains how to install the software, update it, and troubleshoot common errors."
In (A), the list mixes "install" (base verb), "updating" (-ing), and "troubleshoot" (base verb).
In (B), all three items ("install," "update," and "troubleshoot") use the same base verb form.
Identify and fix the parallelism error: "Reading a book is more relaxing than to watch television."
The comparison mismatches "reading" (-ing form) with "to watch" (to + verb form).
Match the second half's form to the first half's form.
Corrected sentence: "Reading a book is more relaxing than
Scan the list for matching endings.
For any list joined by "and" or "or," quickly check whether each item ends the same way (all "-ing," all "to + verb," all plain nouns, and so on).
With correlative conjunctions, cover up everything except the two matched parts.
Read only what comes right after "either/or," "not only/but also," or "both/and" and check that both halves share the identical grammatical form.
In comparisons using "than" or "as," check both sides of the comparison
for matching form, the same way you would check a list.
#1: Missing a Parallelism Break Hidden in a Long Sentence
Break a long sentence down into its individual list items or paired halves, and check each one's form separately.
Long, complex sentences can hide a parallelism error in the middle, especially when the mismatched item is not the last one in the list. Always check every item, not just the first and last.
#2: Assuming Each Item Only Needs to Be Grammatically Correct on Its Own
Parallel structure requires matching form across all items, even if each individual item would be fine as a standalone sentence.
"She enjoys hiking and to swim": both "hiking" and "to swim" are perfectly correct phrases individually, but placed together in a list, their mismatched forms break parallelism.
#3: Forgetting That Correlative Conjunctions Need Matching Forms on both Sides
Whatever word or phrase form immediately follows the first half of a correlative pair (
) must be echoed by the same form after the second half (
A sentence like "He wanted either to win or winning" breaks this rule; both halves need the same form: "either

lessons.title: Parts of Speech / Bahagi ng Pananalita
lessons.summary: Learn the eight parts of speech in English and Filipino and how to identify the job each word plays in a sentence.

children.text: Every word in a sentence has a job. The
categories that describe what job a word is doing.
: names a person, place, thing, or idea (
: replaces a noun so you do not repeat it (
: shows an action or a state of being (
: describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb, often answering how, when, where, or how much (
: shows the relationship between a noun and another word, often location or time (
In Filipino, these are called the
(interjection). The categories match one-to-one with the English list; only the language of the example words changes.
The same word can be a different part of speech depending on how it is used in a sentence. In "I need a
is a noun (a thing). In "I will
is a verb (an action). Always check the word's job in that specific sentence, not just its usual meaning.
," identify the part of speech of the italicized words.
"Diligent" describes the noun "student," telling us what kind of student she is: this is an adjective.
"Quickly" describes the verb "finished," telling us how she finished: this is an adverb.
Identify the part of speech of the word "light" in each sentence: (a) "Turn on the
(a) "Light" names a thing (a lamp or its glow): Noun.
(b) "Light" shows an action (to ignite something): Verb.
(c) "Light" describes the bag, telling us its weight: Adjective.
The same word changes its part of speech depending on the job it does in each sentence.
Tukuyin ang bahagi ng pananalita ng salitang may salungguhit: Ang
na sundalo ay nagtanggol sa kanyang bayan.
Ang salitang "matapang" ay naglalarawan sa pangngalang "sundalo."
Ang bahagi ng pananalita na naglalarawan sa isang pangngalan ay tinatawag na
Choose the correct preposition to complete the sentence: The keys are
the drawer. (A) on, (B) inside, (C) between, (D) above.
The question needs a word that shows the location of the keys relative to the drawer.
"On" would mean the keys are resting on top of the drawer's surface, not stored within it.
"Between" needs two separate objects to compare, and "above" means higher than, not contained within.
"Inside" correctly shows the keys are contained within the drawer. The answer is "inside."

For any unfamiliar word, ask: does it name something (noun), replace a name (pronoun), show an action (verb), describe a noun (adjective), or describe a verb/adjective (adverb)? Answering this question fast solves most identification items.
Adverbs answer "how," "when," "where," or "how much." If you can replace the describing word with "how" and the sentence still makes sense as a question, it is likely an adverb.
This is a helpful hint, not an absolute rule: words like "friendly" end in "-ly" but are actually adjectives (describing a noun, like a
#1: Classifying a Word by Its Meaning Instead of Its Function
Check the word's role in this specific sentence: the same word can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another.
Words like "light," "run," and "study" can be nouns or verbs depending on how they are used. Test-makers often build questions around exactly this kind of shifting word.
Not every word ending in "-ly" is an adverb, and not every adverb ends in "-ly."
"Friendly," "lovely," and "lonely" all end in "-ly" but are adjectives, since they describe nouns (a
neighbor). Meanwhile, adverbs like "fast," "well," and "often" do not end in "-ly" at all. Always check the word's job, not just its ending.
Prepositions connect a noun to the rest of the sentence (showing location, time, or relationship). Conjunctions connect two grammatically equal parts (like two clauses or two nouns).

Words like "before," "after," and "since" can function as either a preposition ("before dinner") or a conjunction ("before we left"), depending on whether they are followed by just a noun phrase or by a full clause with its own subject and verb.

lessons.title: Phrases and Clauses (Independent vs. Dependent)
lessons.summary: Learn the difference between a phrase and a clause, and how to tell independent clauses apart from dependent ones.

children.text: is a group of words that works together but does not have both a subject and a verb: "in the morning," "running quickly," "the tall building." A phrase cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
does have both a subject and a verb. There are two kinds.
has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought. It can stand alone as its own sentence: "The rain stopped." (subject: rain; verb: stopped; complete thought)

(also called a subordinate clause) also has a subject and a verb, but it does not express a complete thought on its own. It depends on an independent clause to make sense. Dependent clauses usually begin with a word like
: "Because the rain stopped" has a subject (rain) and a verb (stopped), but it leaves you asking "...then what?" It cannot stand alone.
Combining an independent clause with a dependent clause makes a complete, correct sentence: "
, we went outside." The dependent clause borrows the independent clause's completeness.
Identify whether each group of words is a phrase or a clause: (a) "under the old bridge"; (b) "the cat slept."
(a) "Under the old bridge" has no subject or verb of its own: Phrase.
(b) "The cat slept" has a subject ("cat") and a verb ("slept"): Clause.
Identify whether each clause is independent or dependent: (a) "Although she was tired"; (b) "She finished her homework."
(a) "Although she was tired" has a subject ("she") and a verb ("was"), but the word "although" makes it an incomplete thought; it needs more information: Dependent.
(b) "She finished her homework" has a subject, a verb, and expresses a complete thought on its own: Independent.
Combine the dependent clause "Because the store was closed" with an appropriate independent clause to form a complete sentence.
The dependent clause "Because the store was closed" needs a complete thought to attach to, answering the implied question "...so what happened?"
A correct combination: "Because the store was closed,
The dependent clause borrows completeness from the independent clause that follows it.
Identify the error in this sentence: "Although the teacher explained the lesson twice."
This is a dependent clause standing alone, with no independent clause attached.
It has a subject ("teacher") and a verb ("explained"), but the word "although" leaves the thought incomplete: the reader is left wondering what happened as a result.
This is a sentence fragment, a common error. A correction adds an independent clause: "Although the teacher explained the lesson twice,
Check for a subject and a verb first.
If a group of words lacks either one, it is automatically a phrase, not a clause: no further analysis needed.
at the start of a clause are strong signals that it is dependent, since these words specifically set up an incomplete thought that needs another clause to finish it.
Read the clause by itself. If it sounds complete and makes sense on its own, it is independent. If it leaves you asking "...then what?" or "...so?", it is dependent.
#1: Mistaking a Long Phrase for a Clause
A phrase can be long and still lack a subject-verb pair: length does not make something a clause.

"Walking slowly along the crowded street toward the old market" is a long phrase, but it still has no subject performing a clearly stated action as its own main verb in a complete sentence: it needs an independent clause to complete the thought.
#2: Treating a Dependent Clause as a Complete Sentence
A dependent clause has a subject and verb, but the subordinating word (

Writing "Because she was late." as a standalone sentence is a common sentence fragment error, even though it technically contains a subject and verb. It needs to be attached to an independent clause to be complete.
#3: Forgetting the Comma When a Dependent Clause Comes First
When a dependent clause starts the sentence, it is usually followed by a comma before the independent clause begins.

"Because it was raining, we stayed inside" needs the comma after the dependent clause. If the order is reversed ("We stayed inside because it was raining"), no comma is typically needed before the dependent clause.

lessons.title: Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement
lessons.summary: Learn how to match a pronoun correctly with the noun it replaces in number and gender.

children.text: is the noun a pronoun replaces or refers back to. "Maria forgot
umbrella": "Maria" is the antecedent, and "her" is the pronoun replacing it.
means the pronoun must match its antecedent in number (singular or plural) and gender, when applicable.
book." (singular antecedent, singular pronoun) versus "The girls lost
The same tricky situations from subject-verb agreement apply here too, since pronouns must agree the same way verbs do.
) are singular, so the pronoun replacing them should also be singular: "Everyone must bring

, in strict formal grammar) own lunch." In everyday and even much modern formal usage, "their" is now widely accepted as a gender-neutral singular pronoun, but exams that test strict traditional grammar rules may still expect "his or her."
) are usually singular when acting as one unit: "The team celebrated
own snacks." Compound antecedents joined by
match the closer antecedent: "Neither the coach nor the players brought
) come in three sets depending on their role in the sentence:
is gender-neutral. It means "he" or "she" with no separate word for each, so a Filipino sentence never has to choose "his or her." The pronoun must still agree in number:
for many. Match the number carefully, since exams often swap
Choose the correct pronoun: Each of the students must submit
essay by Friday, according to strict formal grammar rules.
"Each" is a singular indefinite pronoun, even though it refers to a group of students.
Under strict, traditional grammar rules tested on formal exams, a singular antecedent needs a singular pronoun.
The correct answer is "his or her": "Each of the students must submit
Choose the correct pronoun: The company announced
"Company" is a collective noun, referring to one organization acting as a single unit.
The correct pronoun is "its" (singular): "The company announced
Choose the correct pronoun: Liza and Carlo finished
"Liza and Carlo" is a compound antecedent joined by "and," making it plural.
The correct pronoun is "their": "Liza and Carlo finished
Identify the problem with this sentence: "When Mrs. Santos spoke to Anna, she seemed upset."
The pronoun "she" could refer to either Mrs. Santos or Anna: it is unclear which one seemed upset.
This is called an ambiguous (unclear) antecedent, a common sentence-correction error on exams.
A clearer version names the person directly: "When Mrs. Santos spoke to Anna, Anna seemed upset."
Confirm whether the antecedent is singular or plural before choosing the pronoun; this catches most errors quickly.
Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one, -thing are always singular antecedents
, the same rule used for subject-verb agreement.
If a sentence has two nouns of the same gender before a pronoun, check whether it is clear which one the pronoun refers to; if not, the sentence has an ambiguous antecedent error.
#1: Using a Plural Pronoun for a Singular Indefinite Antecedent
are singular antecedents under strict formal grammar rules.
Everyday speech often uses "they/their" for these words, but grammar-focused exam questions typically expect the traditionally "correct" singular form ("his or her") when testing this specific rule.
#2: Assuming Collective Nouns Need Plural Pronouns
usually take a singular pronoun ("its"), since they act as one unit.
victory" breaks strict agreement rules; the grammatically consistent choice is "
If a pronoun could refer to more than one noun in the sentence, the antecedent is unclear: this is a common sentence-correction error.

Exam questions often ask you to identify or fix a sentence where "she," "he," "it," or "they" could logically point to two different nouns. The fix is usually to replace the confusing pronoun with the specific noun it should refer to.

lessons.title: Punctuation and Capitalization Rules
lessons.summary: Learn the key rules for using commas, semicolons, apostrophes, and capital letters correctly.

children.text: Commas separate items, ideas, and extra information within a sentence.
Use a comma between items in a list of three or more: "I bought apples, bananas, and oranges."
Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (
) that joins two independent clauses: "She studied hard,
Use a comma after an introductory phrase or dependent clause: "
Use commas to set off non-essential information (extra details you could remove without changing the sentence's core meaning): "My brother,

connects two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction: "The rain stopped; the sun came out." A semicolon can also separate items in a list when those items already contain commas: "We visited Manila, Philippines; Tokyo, Japan; and Seoul, Korea."
: joining two independent clauses with only a comma and no conjunction ("The rain stopped, the sun came out."). This needs a semicolon, a coordinating conjunction, or a period instead.
) or mark a contraction, where letters are omitted (
" (possessive, no apostrophe, meaning "belonging to it") versus "
Capitalize the first word of every sentence, proper nouns (specific names of people, places, organizations:
), titles used directly before a name (
, but lowercase "the president" when used generally), and the first word of a direct quotation.
Identify and fix the error: "The concert was amazing, everyone stayed until the end."
Two independent clauses ("The concert was amazing" and "everyone stayed until the end") are joined by only a comma: this is a comma splice.
Fix it by adding a coordinating conjunction, using a semicolon, or splitting into two sentences.
everyone stayed until the end." (or: "The concert was amazing; everyone stayed until the end.")
Choose the correct word: The company announced
The sentence needs a word showing possession (the product line belonging to the company), not a contraction.
Choose the correctly punctuated sentence: (A) "She wanted to travel; because she loved adventure." (B) "She loves reading; she visits the library every weekend."
In (A), "because she loved adventure" is a dependent clause, not an independent one: a semicolon should only join two independent clauses.
In (B), both "she loves reading" and "she visits the library every weekend" are independent clauses, correctly joined by a semicolon.
Choose the correctly capitalized sentence: (A) "We met the President of the company yesterday." (B) "We met President Reyes of the company yesterday."
In (A), "president" is used generally (not directly before a specific name), so it should be lowercase.
In (B), "President" is used directly before the specific name "Reyes," so capitalizing it is correct.
The correct sentence is (B). ("We met the president of the company yesterday" would be the corrected version of (A).)
Read each side of a semicolon as its own sentence.
If both sides can stand alone as complete sentences, the semicolon is used correctly. If either side cannot stand alone, use a comma with a conjunction instead, or restructure the sentence.
Whenever you see "it's," try replacing it with "it is" or "it has." If the sentence still makes sense, "it's" is correct. If not, use "its" instead.
Capitalize titles only directly before a name.
"Doctor Santos" (capitalized, directly before the name) versus "the doctor examined the patient" (lowercase, used generally, no specific name attached).
Two independent clauses joined by only a comma (with no conjunction) is a comma splice error: one of the most common punctuation mistakes tested.
"She finished her homework, she went to bed" needs a conjunction ("and"), a semicolon, or a period between the two complete thoughts.
"Its" (no apostrophe) shows possession. "It's" (with apostrophe) is a contraction for "it is" or "it has."
This is one of the most frequently tested punctuation confusions in English exams, precisely because the two words sound identical when spoken.
#3: Using a Semicolon to Join an Independent Clause with a Dependent Clause
A semicolon should only connect two independent clauses, each capable of standing alone as its own sentence.

"She wanted to travel; because she loved adventure" is incorrect, since "because she loved adventure" cannot stand alone. A comma (without a semicolon) is typically used to attach a dependent clause like this instead.
Capitalize a title only when it comes directly before a specific person's name. When used generally (without a name attached), keep it lowercase.

"We met the President" (used generally, referring to the role, without stating a specific name right there) should typically be lowercase "president," while "We met President Reyes" (directly before a specific name) is correctly capitalized.

lessons.title: Redundancy and Double Negatives
lessons.summary: Learn how to spot and fix wordy, repetitive phrases and sentences that accidentally cancel out their own meaning with two negatives.

children.text: happens when a sentence repeats the same idea using extra, unnecessary words. Good writing says something once, clearly.

" are all redundant: the italicized word already implies the meaning of the word next to it, making one of the two words unnecessary. "Advance warning" is redundant because a warning is, by definition, something given in advance; simply "a warning" already carries that meaning.
Redundancy is not about a sentence being grammatically wrong: it is about a sentence being unnecessarily wordy, saying the same thing twice.
uses two negative words in the same clause, which in standard English grammar actually cancels out to form a positive meaning, even though the speaker usually intends a negative meaning.

money" technically means "I do have money" in strict grammar logic (two negatives canceling out), even though the speaker likely means "I have no money at all." Standard English avoids this by using only one negative word per clause: "I
Common negative words to watch for:
. Using two of these in the same clause creates a double negative.
Identify and fix the redundancy: "Please give us your honest and truthful opinion."
"Honest" and "truthful" mean essentially the same thing, so using both is redundant.
Keep only one of the two words.
Identify and fix the error: "She doesn't want no help with the project."
"Doesn't" and "no" are both negative words in the same clause, creating a double negative.
Change one of the two negative words to a non-negative equivalent.
Choose the sentence without redundancy: (A) "The two of them collaborated together on the mural." (B) "The two of them collaborated on the mural."
"Collaborated" already means "worked together," so adding "together" repeats the same idea.
Sentence (A) is redundant; sentence (B) says the same thing without the unnecessary repetition.
Identify the error: "I can't hardly hear you from over here."
"Can't" and "hardly" are both negative words (hardly means "almost not"), even though "hardly" does not look like an obvious negative at first glance.
Using both together creates an unintended double negative, technically meaning the opposite of what is intended.
hear you from over here." (removing "can't" and keeping just "hardly," which already carries the intended negative meaning on its own)
For redundancy, ask "does removing this word change the meaning?"
If a word or phrase can be deleted without losing any actual information, it is likely redundant.
function as negatives even though they do not contain "not" or "no" directly: pairing any of these with another negative word creates a double negative.
Read the sentence literally, ignoring intended tone.
To catch a double negative, mentally cancel out the two negative words as if solving a simple sign problem, and check whether the literal resulting meaning matches what the sentence is trying to say.
#1: Missing Redundancy Because Each Word Seems Fine Alone
Check whether two words or phrases in the same sentence repeat the same idea, even if each one is a perfectly normal word by itself.

"Advance planning," "final outcome," and "unexpected surprise" all pair a word with another word that already implies its meaning. Neither word is wrong on its own: the problem is using them together.
These three words function as negatives in standard grammar, even though they do not look like typical negative words (
"I can't hardly wait" is a common everyday expression, but it is technically a double negative in strict grammar terms, since "can't" and "hardly" are both negative.
#3: Assuming a Double Negative Always "Sounds" Wrong
Some double negatives sound natural in casual speech but are still grammatically flagged as errors on formal exams.
Phrases like "I don't have no time" are common in relaxed conversation, but formal grammar exams expect the corrected, single-negative form: "I don't have

lessons.title: Sentence Structure (Simple, Compound, Complex, Compound-Complex)
lessons.summary: Learn how to classify sentences by the number and type of clauses they contain.

children.text: English sentences fall into four structural types, based on how many independent and dependent clauses they contain.

has exactly one independent clause and no dependent clause. "The dog barked." It can still have a compound subject or verb ("The dog and the cat barked and ran"), but it remains simple as long as there is only one clause overall.
has two or more independent clauses, joined by a coordinating conjunction (
the cat ran." Each half could stand alone as its own complete sentence.
has one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause. "
, the cat ran." The dependent clause ("Because the dog barked") cannot stand alone; it depends on the independent clause ("the cat ran") to form a complete thought.
combines both structures: it has two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. "
, the cat ran, and it hid under the bed." Here, "Because the dog barked" is dependent, while "the cat ran" and "it hid under the bed" are two independent clauses joined by "and."
Sa Filipino: Uri ng Pangungusap Ayon sa Kayarian
Filipino uses the same four structures, with these names:
(compound): two independent thoughts joined by a coordinating conjunction like
. "Umuwi ang bata ngunit naiwan ang bag niya."
(complex): one independent clause plus a dependent one, joined by a subordinating conjunction like
(compound-complex): two or more independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause. "Umuwi ang bata at natulog agad dahil pagod na siya."
Classify this sentence: "The teacher and her students prepared and rehearsed the play."
Despite having a compound subject ("teacher and students") and a compound verb ("prepared and rehearsed"), there is only one clause overall (one complete thought, no dependent clause attached).
This is a simple sentence, since compound subjects/verbs alone do not create additional clauses.
Classify this sentence: "She wanted to travel abroad, but she could not afford the airfare."
"She wanted to travel abroad" and "she could not afford the airfare" are both independent clauses (each could stand alone as its own sentence).
They are joined by the coordinating conjunction "but."
Classify this sentence: "Although the storm was severe, the town suffered minimal damage."
"Although the storm was severe" is a dependent clause (cannot stand alone; the word "although" leaves it incomplete).
"The town suffered minimal damage" is an independent clause (can stand alone).
One dependent clause plus one independent clause: this is a complex sentence.
Classify this sentence: "When the bell rang, the students grabbed their bags, and they rushed out the door."
"When the bell rang" is a dependent clause.
"The students grabbed their bags" and "they rushed out the door" are two separate independent clauses, joined by "and."
One dependent clause plus two independent clauses: this is a compound-complex sentence.
Count the independent clauses first, then check for any dependent clause.

One independent clause with no dependent clause is simple; two or more independent clauses with no dependent clause is compound; add any dependent clause to either of those, and it becomes complex (with one independent clause) or compound-complex (with two or more).
) to spot a dependent clause quickly: their presence signals the sentence is at least complex, or compound-complex if multiple independent clauses are also present.
Do not be fooled by compound subjects or verbs.

A sentence with "A and B" as the subject, or "did X and Y" as the verb, is still simple as long as there is only one overall clause: compound elements within a single clause do not create a compound sentence.
#1: Mistaking a Compound Subject or Verb for a Compound Sentence
A compound subject or compound verb within one clause does not make a sentence compound: a compound sentence needs two or more full independent clauses.
"The dog and cat played" has a compound subject but is still a simple sentence, since there is only one clause (one subject-verb unit) overall, not two separate complete thoughts joined together.
Compound sentences join two independent clauses (both can stand alone). Complex sentences join an independent clause with a dependent clause (only one can stand alone).
Look for a subordinating word like "although," "because," or "since": its presence signals a dependent clause, making the sentence complex (or compound-complex), not simply compound.
#3: Missing One Clause Type in a Compound-Complex Sentence
A compound-complex sentence needs all three ingredients: at least one dependent clause, and at least two independent clauses. Missing any one of these makes it a different sentence type instead.

A sentence with a dependent clause and only one independent clause is complex, not compound-complex; carefully count both the independent clauses and check for a dependent clause before finalizing your classification.

lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement / Wastong Gamit ng Salita
lessons.summary: Learn the rules for matching a singular or plural subject with the correct verb form in English and Filipino sentences.

children.text: means the subject of a sentence and its verb must match in number: a singular subject needs a singular verb, and a plural subject needs a plural verb.
A few situations make this trickier than it first looks.
Words between the subject and verb do not change the rule.
fresh," the subject is "basket" (singular), not "apples." The verb must match "basket," ignoring the describing phrase in between.
) name a group but are treated as one singular unit when the group acts together: "The team
practicing." They can take a plural verb only when emphasizing the members acting as individuals, which is rare in most exam contexts.
can be singular or plural, depending on the noun they refer to: "Some of the cake
gone" (cake is singular) versus "Some of the cookies
match the subject closest to the verb: "Neither the teacher nor the students
In Filipino, correct subject-verb agreement is part of
(correct word usage), which also covers matching the correct marker (
) and verb focus to the subject being emphasized in the sentence.
Choose the correct verb: The list of items on the shelf
Find the true subject by ignoring the describing phrase "of items on the shelf."
The subject is "list," which is singular.
The correct verb is "is": "The list of items on the shelf
Choose the correct verb: The committee
"Committee" is a collective noun, naming a group.
Since the committee is acting as one unit reaching a single decision together, it is treated as singular.
Choose the correct verb: Most of the water in the tank
"Most" can be singular or plural, depending on the noun in the "of" phrase that follows.
The noun following "of" is "water," which is uncountable and singular.
The correct verb is "has": "Most of the water in the tank
Choose the correct verb: Neither the manager nor the employees
With "neither...nor," the verb must agree with the subject closest to it.
The subject closest to the verb is "employees," which is plural.
The correct verb is "were": "Neither the manager nor the employees
For long subjects with a describing phrase in between (like "of the items," "along with the group"), mentally cross it out and check agreement with what remains.
"Of" phrases: check the noun that follows.
followed by "of," the noun right after "of" decides singular or plural, not the pronoun itself.
When two subjects are joined by "or" or "nor," only the subject nearest the verb matters for agreement: ignore the farther one.
#1: Being Distracted by Words In Between
The true subject decides the verb, even if other nouns sit closer to the verb in the sentence.
) on the table." Test-makers place a plural noun right before the verb specifically to tempt you into matching the wrong, nearer word instead of the true subject.
#2: Treating All Collective Nouns as Automatically Plural
) are usually singular, since they name one group acting as a unit.
Many students assume a "team" or "family" (multiple people) needs a plural verb. Unless the sentence clearly emphasizes the individual members acting separately, treat collective nouns as singular.
#3: Forgetting Indefinite Pronouns Ending in -body, -one, -thing Are Always Singular
, and similar words are always singular, no exceptions.
Even though "everybody" refers to many people, it grammatically behaves as one singular unit: "Everybody
#4: Matching the Wrong Subject in an "Or/Nor" Sentence
With "or" or "nor," match the verb to the subject closest to it, not the first one mentioned.
late" is correct (matching "teacher," the closer subject), even though "students" (plural) appears first in the sentence.

lessons.title: Tenses and Voice of Verbs (Active vs. Passive)
lessons.summary: Learn how verb tenses show when an action happens and how to tell active voice apart from passive voice.

children.text: shows when an action happens: past, present, or future. Each of these three main tenses also has a "perfect" and "progressive" form for more precise timing.
a letter." (completed at an unspecified past time, still relevant now)
the letter before he arrived." (one past action completed before another past action)

The key skill exams test is tense consistency: verbs in the same sentence (or the same passage, describing the same timeline) should stay in the same tense unless there is a clear reason to shift, like describing an earlier event.
: the subject performs the action. "The chef
: the subject receives the action, and the doer is either introduced with "by" or left out entirely. "The meal
Passive voice is formed with a form of "to be" plus the past participle of the main verb (

Active voice is usually preferred in clear, direct writing, because it is shorter and identifies who did the action. Passive voice is useful when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or intentionally left out ("The window
": we may not know who broke it).
Filipino verbs do not use tense (past, present, future). They use
(aspect), which marks whether the action is finished, ongoing, or not yet started. This trips up students who translate English tense directly. There are three main aspects:
(naganap na): the action is finished. Example:
(magaganap pa): the action has not started yet. Example:
Notice the pattern with the root
: the imperfective and contemplative repeat the first syllable (
(focus), whether the verb highlights the doer (
), which is closer to the active/passive idea in English.
Identify the error in this sentence: "Yesterday, she
The sentence describes actions that happened yesterday, so both verbs should be in the past tense.
"Bought" is correctly in the past tense, but "walks" is in the present tense.
The corrected sentence should read: "Yesterday, she
Identify whether each sentence is active or passive voice: (a) "The dog chased the ball." (b) "The ball was chased by the dog."
(a) The subject "dog" performs the action of chasing: Active voice.
