lessons.title: Word Analogies (Single and Double Analogies)
lessons.summary: Learn how to identify the relationship between a pair of words and apply that same relationship to find a matching pair.

children.text: tests whether you can identify the relationship between one pair of words, then find a second pair with the exact same relationship. Analogies are usually written as "A is to B as C is to D," or in shorthand: A : B :: C : D.

The first step is always to describe the relationship between the first pair in a clear sentence. "Puppy is to dog as kitten is to cat": the relationship is "a ___ is a baby ___." Once you have that sentence, test each answer choice by plugging it into the same sentence pattern.
(a petal is part of a flower)
(a rose is a type of flower)
(a difference in intensity of the same quality)
(a worker and the tool they use)

extends this to involve relationships in both directions or two separate paired relationships within a single question, requiring you to check that the connecting logic holds consistently across all four (or more) words.
Complete the analogy: Pen is to write as scissors is to ______. (A) sharp, (B) cut, (C) paper, (D) blade.
Build the relationship sentence: "A pen is used to write."
Apply the same sentence structure: "Scissors are used to ______."
The word that fits this function relationship is "cut" (B): scissors are used to cut.
Complete the analogy: Author is to book as director is to ______. (A) actor, (B) movie, (C) theater, (D) camera.
Build the relationship sentence: "An author creates a book."
Apply the same structure: "A director creates a ______."
The word matching this creator relationship is "movie" (B): a director creates a movie.
Complete the analogy: Hammer is to tool as oak is to ______. (A) wood, (B) tree, (C) leaf, (D) forest.
Build the relationship sentence: "A hammer is a type of tool" (category relationship).
Apply the same structure: "An oak is a type of ______."
"Tree" (B) fits: an oak is a type of tree. (Note: "wood" describes the material, not the category, so it does not match the same relationship type.)

Complete the analogy: Puppy is to dog as calf is to ______, in the same way that petal is to flower as ______ is to tree. Choose the missing pair. (A) cow, leaf (B) cow, branch (C) cat, leaf (D) horse, root.
First relationship pair: "puppy is a baby dog," so "calf is a baby ______". A calf is a baby cow.
Second relationship pair: "a petal is a part of a flower," so "______ is a part of a tree". A leaf is a part of a tree.
Checking both relationships together (baby-animal pattern, then part-to-whole pattern) against the choices, (A) "cow, leaf" satisfies both relationships correctly.
Always build a sentence linking the first pair before looking at the answer choices.
A clear sentence ("A ___ is a baby ___," "A ___ is used to ___") makes testing each choice mechanical and fast.
Make your sentence as specific as possible.

A vague sentence like "these are related" allows multiple wrong answers to seem plausible; a precise sentence like "a hammer is a type of tool" (not just "hammer relates to tool somehow") narrows down the correct choice quickly.
For double analogies, solve each pair separately first
, then check that your combined answer satisfies both relationships at once.
#1: Choosing a Word That's Merely "Related" Without Matching the Exact Relationship
The correct answer must match the same specific relationship as the first pair, not just be generally associated with the given word.

In the hammer analogy, "wood" is clearly related to "oak," but it does not match the category relationship ("type of") that the original pair (hammer : tool) established. Always test with your specific sentence, not a general association.
#2: Building a Sentence That's Too Vague
A vague relationship sentence lets multiple choices seem to "fit," making it hard to identify the single correct answer.
"Pen and write are related" is too vague; "a pen is used to write" is specific enough to correctly eliminate wrong choices like "paper" (which is used with a pen, not the function of a pen).
#3: Reversing the Direction of the Relationship
Check whether the relationship goes from first word to second word, or the reverse, and apply that same direction to the second pair.

"Author is to book" (author creates book) is different from "book is to author" (book was created by author). While related ideas, keeping the direction consistent between the first and second pairs is essential for a correct match.

lessons.title: Fluid Pressure in Pipes and Containers
lessons.summary: Learn how fluid pressure changes with depth and pipe width, and how to predict flow behavior in connected containers.

children.text: (the force fluid exerts per unit area) follows a few key mechanical reasoning rules that frequently appear in technical reasoning questions, building on ideas from fluid mechanics.

The deeper a point is within a fluid, the more fluid is pushing down from above, so pressure at the bottom of a container is always greater than pressure near the top, regardless of the container's shape or width.
Connected containers settle at the same fluid level.

If two or more open containers are connected at the bottom (like a U-shaped tube), the fluid will settle so that the surface level is the same in every connected container, regardless of each container's width or shape: this is sometimes summarized as "water finds its own level."
Narrower sections mean faster flow (for the same total amount of fluid moving through).

When a fluid flows through a pipe that narrows, the fluid must speed up to keep the same volume of fluid moving through per second (since less cross-sectional area is available): this is why water speeds up when a hose nozzle is squeezed narrower.
Pressure and pipe width in flowing fluid
: in a narrower section where the fluid moves faster, the pressure is typically lower (connecting back to Bernoulli's principle: faster-moving fluid exerts less pressure).
A container is filled with water. Point A is near the surface, and Point B is near the bottom. Which point experiences greater pressure?
Pressure increases with depth, since more fluid is stacked above deeper points.
Point B (near the bottom) has more fluid above it than Point A (near the surface).

A wide container and a narrow container are connected at the bottom by a tube, forming a U-shape, both open to the air at the top. Water is poured in until it settles. Which container has the higher water level?
Connected open containers always settle to the same fluid level, regardless of their width.
Neither container will have a higher level than the other: they will be equal.
The water levels are the same in both the wide and narrow containers.
#3: Predicting Flow Speed Through a Narrowing Pipe
Water flows steadily through a pipe that narrows from a wide section to a narrow section. Compared to the wide section, how does the water's speed change in the narrow section?
The same volume of water must pass through both sections per second (water is not created or destroyed along the pipe).
Since the narrow section has less cross-sectional area, the water must move faster through it to maintain the same volume flow rate.
The water speeds up in the narrow section.
Using the same narrowing pipe from Example 3, how does the pressure in the narrow section compare to the pressure in the wide section?
The water moves faster in the narrow section (as established in Example 3).
By the relationship between fluid speed and pressure (faster flow means lower pressure), the pressure in the faster-moving narrow section should be lower.
The pressure is lower in the narrow section compared to the wider section.
as the single most reliable rule for comparing pressure at different points within the same connected body of fluid.
Remember "connected containers always level out equally"
: container width or shape never affects the final settled water level in an open, connected system.
For flow-through-pipes questions, remember the paired rule: Narrower means faster flow, and faster flow means lower pressure.
These two facts always travel together in fluid-flow reasoning questions.
#1: Assuming a Wider Container Holds Water at a Different Level
Connected, open containers always settle at the same fluid level, no matter how different their widths or shapes are.

A wider container does not settle at a lower level just because it "holds more water" overall: the surface level still equalizes with any connected narrower container, since pressure at the connecting point must balance out equally on both sides.
#2: Assuming Narrower Pipes Slow Down Flow
A narrower section of pipe causes the fluid to speed up, not slow down, in order to maintain the same overall flow volume passing through per second.

Confusing this with everyday intuition (like assuming a "tighter squeeze" naturally slows things down) leads to the opposite, incorrect prediction: the fluid actually accelerates through a narrower opening.
#3: Forgetting That Faster Flow Means Lower Pressure, Not Higher
In flowing fluid, sections with faster movement (like narrow pipe sections) have lower pressure, following the same relationship as Bernoulli's principle in fluid mechanics.
Assuming a narrow, fast-flowing section must have higher pressure (since it "feels more forceful" intuitively) reverses the correct relationship between fluid speed and pressure.

lessons.title: Gear Rotations (Predicting Clockwise vs. Counter-Clockwise Movement)
lessons.summary: Learn how to predict the rotation direction and relative speed of connected gears in a mechanical system.

children.text: are toothed wheels that interlock with neighboring gears, transferring rotational motion between them. The core rule: when two gears' teeth mesh directly together, they always rotate in opposite directions. If one gear spins clockwise, the gear directly meshing with it must spin counter-clockwise, since their touching teeth push against each other in opposite directions at the contact point.

This creates a simple alternating pattern down a chain of meshing gears: gear 1 clockwise, gear 2 counter-clockwise, gear 3 clockwise, gear 4 counter-clockwise, and so on. A quick shortcut: gears in odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th...) all spin in the same direction as the first gear; gears in even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th...) all spin in the opposite direction.
Gear size affects speed, not direction.

A smaller gear meshing with a larger gear spins faster (makes more full rotations in the same time) than the larger gear, because the smaller gear has fewer teeth and must "catch up" to match the same number of teeth passing the contact point per second. Specifically, if gear A has half as many teeth as gear B, gear A rotates twice as fast as gear B (and vice versa): the two gears' rotation speeds are inversely proportional to the number of teeth they each have.
Three gears are connected in a row, each meshing with its neighbor. The first gear turns clockwise. What direction does the third gear turn?
Meshing gears alternate direction: gear 1 clockwise, gear 2 counter-clockwise, gear 3 clockwise.
Since gear 1 and gear 3 are both in odd positions, they turn in the same direction.
The third gear also turns clockwise.
Five gears are connected in a row, each meshing with its neighbor. The first gear turns counter-clockwise. What direction does the fifth gear turn?
Gears 1, 3, and 5 are all in odd positions, so they share the same rotation direction as gear 1.
Since gear 1 turns counter-clockwise, gear 5 (also odd-positioned) turns the same direction.

#4: A Gear System with a Branch

A central gear meshes with three other gears arranged around it (like spokes), each of those three also meshing only with the central gear (not with each other). If the central gear turns clockwise, what direction do all three outer gears turn?
Each outer gear meshes directly with the central gear (but not with each other), so each one individually follows the "opposite direction from its direct neighbor" rule relative to the central gear.
Since the central gear turns clockwise, every gear meshing directly with it turns counter-clockwise.
All three outer gears turn counter-clockwise (since they all mesh directly with the same clockwise-turning central gear, independent of each other).
Use the odd/even position shortcut for a straight chain of gears
: gears in odd positions share the first gear's direction; gears in even positions spin the opposite way. This skips having to trace the alternation one gear at a time.
For gear speed and size questions, remember: Smaller gear (fewer teeth) = faster rotation; larger gear (more teeth) = slower rotation.
The exact ratio of rotation speeds matches the inverse ratio of their teeth counts.
For a central "hub" gear with several separate outer gears attached (a star/spoke pattern), each outer gear independently takes the opposite direction from the central gear
: they do not alternate with each other, since they don't mesh directly with one another, only with the shared central gear.
#1: Assuming All Gears in a Chain Spin the Same Direction
Directly meshing gears always spin in opposite directions: a chain of connected gears alternates, it does not all spin the same way.
Assuming the third gear in a row spins the same direction as the second (rather than correctly alternating back to match the first) is one of the most common gear-direction errors.
#2: Confusing Gear Size with Rotation Direction

Gear size (number of teeth) affects rotation speed, not direction. Direction depends only on whether gears mesh directly (always opposite) or how many gears separate them in the chain (alternating pattern).
A larger gear does not automatically spin the "same direction" or "opposite direction" based on its size alone: direction is governed purely by the meshing/alternating rule, independent of gear size.
Rotation speed is inversely proportional to teeth count: the gear with fewer teeth spins proportionally faster, and the exact ratio must be calculated from the actual teeth counts, not guessed.

Assuming a small gear and large gear "just spin at different speeds" without calculating the precise inverse ratio (based on their actual teeth counts) can lead to selecting an incorrect specific rotation count in numeric gear problems.
#4: Treating Gears in a "Spoke" Pattern Like a Simple Chain

When multiple gears each mesh separately with one shared central gear (rather than meshing with each other in sequence), each outer gear's direction depends only on its relationship to the central gear, not on alternating with its neighboring outer gears.
Assuming outer gears around a hub must "alternate" with each other (as if they formed a chain) misapplies the straight-chain alternating rule to a different gear arrangement where it does not apply.

A single fixed pulley (attached to a stationary point, like a ceiling beam) simply changes the direction of your pulling force (pull down to lift up), without reducing the force needed: you still need to pull with a force equal to the load's weight.

A movable pulley (attached directly to the load itself, moving along with it) does reduce the force needed: with one movable pulley, you only need half the force of the load's weight to lift it, though you must pull the rope twice as far. Assuming a single fixed pulley "makes lifting easier" in terms of force is incorrect: it only makes lifting more convenient by letting you pull in a different direction, while still requiring the full weight's worth of force.
#2: Forgetting the Trade-Off Between Force and Distance
Simple machines like pulleys and levers reduce the force needed but always require moving (or pulling) a correspondingly greater distance: you cannot reduce force without some distance trade-off.
A movable pulley halving the required force also doubles the rope distance you must pull; forgetting this trade-off leads to an incomplete understanding of the mechanical advantage being gained.

lessons.summary: Learn how springs stretch or compress in proportion to the weight attached, and how to compare springs of different stiffness.

children.text: stretches (or compresses) by an amount proportional to the force (or weight) applied to it: this relationship is sometimes called Hooke's Law in physics. In simple terms: Double the weight hanging from a spring, and the spring stretches twice as far (as long as the spring is not stretched so far that it becomes permanently deformed or damaged).

Because stretch is proportional to weight, if you know how far a spring stretches for one known weight, you can predict the stretch for any other weight using a simple ratio: the stretch scales up or down by the same factor as the weight changes.
When comparing two different springs holding the same weight, the spring that stretches more is the looser (less stiff) one, and the spring that stretches less is the stiffer one.

A stiffer spring stretches less under the same weight; a looser (weaker) spring stretches more under the same weight.

It is easy to intuitively assume "stiffer" means "moves more" or "stretches more": in fact, stiffness describes resistance to stretching, so a stiffer spring is precisely the one that stretches the least for a given weight.
#3: Comparing Springs Under Different Weights Instead of the Same Weight

lessons.title: Structural Stability and Center of Gravity
lessons.summary: Learn how center of gravity and base of support determine whether an object stays balanced or tips over.

children.text: is the single point where its entire weight can be thought of as concentrated, balancing perfectly in every direction. For a symmetric, evenly-shaped object (like a uniform ball or box), the center of gravity sits at its geometric center.

is the area on the ground enclosed by its points (or edges) of contact with the ground. A four-legged table's base of support is the rectangle connecting its four feet; a person's base of support is the area between their two feet.

The core stability rule: an object remains stable (will not tip over) as long as an imaginary vertical line dropped straight down from its center of gravity falls within its base of support. If that vertical line falls outside the base of support (for example, if the object is tilted too far), the object becomes unstable and tips over.
This leads to two general principles for improving stability:
A lower center of gravity makes an object more stable (harder to tip), since it takes a larger tilt before the vertical line from the center of gravity can be pushed outside the base of support.
A wider base of support makes an object more stable, since there is more "room" for the vertical line from the center of gravity to stay within before tipping.
A short, wide pyramid and a tall, narrow pyramid have the same weight and are made of the same uniform material. Which one is more stable, and why?
The short, wide pyramid has a lower center of gravity (since it is shorter) and a wider base of support (since it is wider).
Both factors, lower center of gravity and wider base, independently improve stability.
The short, wide pyramid is more stable.
#2: Predicting When an Object Tips Over
A rectangular box is slowly tilted to one side. At what point does the box tip over, rather than settling back down?
The box remains stable as long as the vertical line dropped from its center of gravity stays within its base of support (the bottom edge still touching the ground).
As the box tilts further, this vertical line shifts closer to the edge of the base of support.

The box tips over at the exact moment this vertical line moves beyond the edge of the base of support (falls outside the remaining contact edge with the ground): beyond that point, gravity pulls the box the rest of the way over instead of back down to its original position.
#3: Why Lowering a Load Increases Stability
A moving truck carries cargo either stacked very high or spread out lower (same total weight either way). Which loading method makes the truck more stable while turning corners?
Stacking cargo high raises the truck's overall center of gravity; spreading cargo lower keeps the center of gravity closer to the ground.

A lower center of gravity requires a larger tilt (like from a sharp turn) before the vertical line from the center of gravity could be pushed outside the truck's base of support (the width between its wheels).
Loading the cargo lower makes the truck more stable while turning, since it can tilt further before tipping compared to a high-stacked load.
A person standing normally with feet close together is compared to the same person standing with feet spread wider apart. Which stance is more stable against being pushed sideways?
Spreading the feet wider apart increases the person's base of support (the ground area between the feet).
A wider base of support means the vertical line from the person's center of gravity can shift farther sideways (due to a push) before falling outside that base.
The wider stance (feet spread apart) is more stable against sideways pushes.
Remember the two-factor stability rule together: Lower center of gravity + wider base of support = more stable.
Most stability comparison questions can be answered by checking these two factors against each other.

: imagine dropping a straight line down from the center of gravity to the ground, and check whether that line stays within the object's base of support at the given tilt angle: this mental model directly predicts tipping.

For real-world stability examples (trucks, furniture, people standing), identify what raises or lowers the center of gravity (like stacking cargo high vs. low) and what widens or narrows the base of support (like feet position or table leg spacing).
#1: Assuming Only Height (Not Base Width) Matters for Stability
Stability depends on both the center of gravity's height and the base of support's width: considering only one factor while ignoring the other gives an incomplete comparison.
An object could have a low center of gravity but still be unstable if its base of support is extremely narrow; both factors must be considered together, not just one in isolation.
#2: Assuming a Heavier Object Is Automatically More Stable
Stability depends on the location of the center of gravity relative to the base of support, not simply on how much an object weighs overall.

A very heavy object with a high center of gravity and a narrow base can still tip over easily, despite its large weight: weight alone does not guarantee stability; the geometry (height and base width) is what matters.
#3: Forgetting That Tipping Depends on the Tilt Angle, Not Just the Static Position

An object can be perfectly stable while sitting still, but become unstable once tilted enough that the center of gravity's vertical line moves outside the base of support: stability is not a fixed, permanent property regardless of orientation.

Assuming an object "is stable" as an absolute, unchanging fact (rather than "is stable at this specific tilt angle") misses that further tilting can push any object past its tipping point, given enough tilt.

lessons.title: Figure Grouping (Identifying the Odd-One-Out)
lessons.summary: Learn how to find the shared rule connecting most figures in a group and identify the one figure that breaks it.

children.text: questions present several figures and ask you to identify the one that does not belong with the others. The figures that do belong together share some common rule or feature; your job is to discover that shared rule, then find which figure breaks it.
Since the rule is not stated, approach this systematically by checking figures against a checklist of common shared-feature categories:
: do most figures share the same number of sides, dots, or lines, while one has a different count?
: do most figures have a line of symmetry (can be folded in half so both sides match exactly), while one does not?
: do most figures split their interior into the same number of separate sections, while one differs?
: are most figures made entirely of straight lines (or entirely of curves), while one mixes both or uses the opposite type?
: do most figures share a similar shading rule (like "always exactly one shaded part"), while one breaks it?
The correct approach is to find the rule that makes four (or however many) figures belong to one consistent group, leaving exactly one figure that clearly does not fit that same rule.
Four figures are shown: a square, a rectangle, a rhombus, and a triangle. Which one does not belong, and why?
Check the number of sides: the square, rectangle, and rhombus all have
The triangle is the odd-one-out, since it does not share the "
Four figures are shown: a perfect circle, a square, an equilateral triangle, and an irregular, lopsided blob shape with no matching sides. Which one does not belong?
Check symmetry: the circle, square, and equilateral triangle can all be folded along at least one line so both halves match exactly (they are all symmetric).
The irregular blob shape has no line along which it folds evenly.
The irregular blob is the odd-one-out, since it lacks the symmetry the other three share.
#3: Grouping by Number of Enclosed Regions
Four figures are shown, each a circle with straight lines drawn through it: one circle with
lines not through the center, creating
uneven regions. Which one does not belong?
Check the pattern: the first three figures follow a consistent rule. Lines drawn through the center split a circle into an even number of regions (
The fourth figure's lines do not pass through the center, creating an uneven split (an odd number of regions,

Four figures are shown, each a different shape, but each one contains exactly one small shaded (black) dot somewhere inside it. A fifth figure contains two small shaded dots inside it. Which one does not belong?
Check the shading pattern: four figures share the specific feature of containing exactly one shaded dot, regardless of their outer shape.
The fifth figure contains two shaded dots, breaking that specific count.
The fifth figure is the odd-one-out, since the shared rule here is about the dot count, not the outer shape at all.
Run through the checklist categories systematically
(side count, symmetry, enclosed regions, curve vs. straight, shading) rather than staring at the figures hoping a rule jumps out: a checklist approach finds subtle rules faster than random guessing.
If the outer shape seems to have no shared pattern, check inside the figures
(like dot counts, internal line counts, or shading), since some grouping questions test smaller internal details rather than the overall outline.
Confirm your rule against all the "belonging" figures before finalizing your answer
, not just two or three of them: a rule that fits three figures but fails on the supposed fourth "correct" one is not the actual rule.
#1: Fixating on the Most Obvious Visual Difference
The most visually striking figure is not always the correct odd-one-out: check the actual shared rule carefully rather than picking whichever figure "looks weirdest" at a glance.

A figure that looks unusual in size or orientation might still share the true underlying rule (like side count or symmetry) with the rest of the group, while a more "normal-looking" figure actually breaks the rule.
#2: Assuming the Rule Is About Outer Shape When It's About an Internal Detail
Some grouping rules are about details inside the figures (dot counts, internal lines, shading), not the outer shape at all: check both levels before deciding there's no pattern.
Missing an internal-detail rule (like "each figure has exactly one shaded dot") because you were only comparing outer shapes leads to picking the wrong figure as the odd-one-out.
#3: Choosing a Rule That Only Fits Some of the "Belonging" Figures
A valid shared rule must apply to all the figures that belong together, not just most of them: if your proposed rule fails on one of the supposedly matching figures, keep searching for a better rule.
Settling for a rule that fits three out of four "matching" figures (while ignoring that it does not actually fit the fourth) means you have not yet found the true shared pattern.
