Put these digestive organs in the correct order that food travels through: large intestine, stomach, esophagus, small intestine, mouth.
Recall the path from entry to exit.
Food enters at the mouth, where chewing begins.
It is mixed with acid in the stomach.
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
Water is absorbed and waste is formed in the large intestine.
Order: mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.

Blood leaves the heart, travels to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and returns to the heart. Separately, blood leaves the heart, travels to the leg muscles to deliver oxygen, and returns to the heart. Identify which trip is pulmonary circulation and which is systemic circulation.
Match the destination to the correct circulation type.
The trip to the lungs (to pick up oxygen) is pulmonary circulation.
The trip to the leg muscles (or any other body tissue, to deliver oxygen) is systemic circulation.

Classify each muscle action as voluntary or involuntary, and name the muscle type involved: (a) deciding to kick a ball; (b) your stomach churning food without you thinking about it; (c) your heart beating steadily while you sleep.
Match each action to its muscle type and control type.
(a) Kicking a ball is a deliberate, chosen movement: Voluntary, skeletal muscle.
(b) Stomach churning happens automatically: Involuntary, smooth muscle.
(c) Heartbeat continues automatically, even during sleep: Involuntary, cardiac muscle.
Explain why the pituitary gland is often called the body's "master gland."
Recall what makes the pituitary gland's role different from other glands.
Most glands release hormones that act directly on body tissues (like the pancreas releasing insulin to lower blood sugar).
The pituitary gland, however, releases hormones that control other glands, telling them when to release their own hormones.
Because it manages and coordinates the activity of many other endocrine glands, it earns the nickname "master gland."
Explain, in general terms, what happens to blood as it passes through a nephron in the kidney, and name the two waste products removed.
Each nephron filters blood, removing waste while keeping useful substances (like most water and nutrients) in the bloodstream through reabsorption.
The main waste product removed is urea, which comes from the breakdown of proteins.
Excess water is also removed, together with urea and other wastes, forming urine.
This filtered urine then travels out through the ureters, bladder, and urethra.

A person cuts their finger, and skin plus general immune cells respond immediately to prevent infection. Days later, if the person is exposed to the same specific virus they recovered from years ago, their body fights it off quickly using memory cells from that earlier infection. Identify which response is innate immunity and which is adaptive immunity.
Check the speed and specificity of each response.
The immediate, general response to the cut (skin barrier, general immune cells) is innate immunity: fast, but not targeted at one specific germ.
The response using memory from a past specific infection is adaptive immunity: slower to build the first time, but highly specific and equipped with long-term memory.

For any "which system does this organ belong to" question, match the organ to its one key job: filtering blood (kidneys, excretory), pumping blood (heart, circulatory), releasing hormones (glands, endocrine), or producing movement (muscles, muscular). Most organs belong clearly to just one system.

Remember heart chambers with "A is for Above" (atria are the upper chambers) and "V is for below" is not quite right, so instead remember: atria receive blood coming in, ventricles pump blood out. Blood always flows atria → ventricles → out to the body or lungs.
For muscle type questions, ask "can I choose to do this right now?" Yes: skeletal (voluntary). No: smooth or cardiac (involuntary), and if it is specifically the heart, it is cardiac.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins carry blood back to the heart.

This definition is based on direction relative to the heart, not on whether the blood is oxygen-rich or oxygen-poor (which actually varies depending on whether it's pulmonary or systemic circulation). Anchor it simply: arteries = away, veins = return.
#2: Assuming All Muscle Control Is the Same
Cardiac muscle is involuntary, even though it is striated like voluntary skeletal muscle.

Students sometimes assume "striated" (striped-looking) muscle must be voluntary, since skeletal muscle is both striated and voluntary. But cardiac muscle is also striated, while still being completely involuntary: you cannot consciously stop your heart from beating.
#3: Confusing the Pancreas's Two Different Jobs
The pancreas belongs to both the digestive system (making digestive enzymes) and the endocrine system (making insulin and glucagon).

A question may test whether students realize one organ can serve two different systems. The pancreas's digestive role releases enzymes into the small intestine; its endocrine role releases insulin and glucagon directly into the bloodstream.
#4: Forgetting That Adaptive Immunity Has Memory, But Is Slower At First
Adaptive immunity is slower to respond the first time, but becomes fast on repeat exposure thanks to memory cells. Innate immunity is always fast, but never targets one specific germ.

A choice claiming "innate immunity has memory" or "adaptive immunity is always the fastest response" misunderstands this trade-off: innate immunity trades specificity for speed, while adaptive immunity trades initial speed for precision and long-term memory.

lessons.title: Taxonomy and Classification (Domains, Kingdoms, Binomial Nomenclature)
lessons.summary: How scientists organize and name living things, from the broadest domain down to individual species.

children.text: is the science of classifying living things into organized groups, based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships. This helps scientists around the world talk about the same organism without confusion.
Living things are sorted into a hierarchy of ranks, from the broadest group down to the most specific:
Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Each rank contains one or more of the rank below it. A domain contains many kingdoms; a kingdom contains many phyla; and so on, all the way down to species, the most specific rank.
(both made of simple cells without a nucleus), and
(organisms whose cells do have a nucleus, including all plants, animals, fungi, and protists).
Within Eukarya, life is commonly organized into
such as Animalia (animals), Plantae (plants), Fungi (fungi), and Protista (mostly single-celled organisms like algae and amoebas).
Every known species gets a unique, two-part scientific name, a system called
, created by the scientist Carl Linnaeus in the 1700s. The name has two parts:
name (capitalized), shared by closely related species.
name (lowercase), specific to that one species.
Both words are written in italics (or underlined by hand). For example, humans are named

Binomial nomenclature solves a real problem: common names for the same organism can differ between countries or even regions (a "carabao" in the Philippines is known by other names elsewhere), but its scientific name is the same everywhere in the world.
Arrange these classification ranks in order from broadest to most specific: Family, Kingdom, Species, Phylum, Domain, Genus, Class, Order.
Recall the fixed hierarchy from largest group to smallest.
The correct order, broadest to most specific: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
#2: Identifying the Parts of a Scientific Name
(the lion), identify which word is the genus and which is the species name.
The first word, capitalized, is the genus:
(a genus shared with other big cats like tigers,
The second word, lowercase, is the specific species name:
#3: Why Scientific Names Instead of Common Names?

A biologist studying a certain plant finds that villagers in different regions of the Philippines call it by three completely different common names. Explain why the biologist prefers to use the plant's scientific (binomial) name in a research paper instead.
Consider the purpose of a single, universal naming system.
Common names can vary widely between regions, languages, or even different countries, causing confusion about which exact organism is being discussed.
A scientific name, following binomial nomenclature, is standardized and used by scientists worldwide, so it always refers to the exact same species, no matter who is reading it.
Using the scientific name in a research paper avoids ambiguity, ensuring other scientists anywhere in the world know exactly which organism is being studied.

Memorize the classification order with a mnemonic sentence, matching the first letter of each rank: "Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup" for Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

For binomial nomenclature questions, remember the pattern: capital letter for genus, lowercase for species, both italicized. If a name is written any other way (both capitalized, or neither italicized), it does not follow the proper convention.
The more classification ranks two organisms share, the more closely related they are. Two species sharing the same genus are more closely related than two species that only share the same kingdom.
Domain is the broadest rank; species is the most specific.

Students sometimes list the ranks backwards, especially confusing whether "kingdom" or "phylum" comes first. Anchor the very ends: domain always starts the sequence (broadest), and species always ends it (most specific).
Only the genus name is capitalized; the species name is always lowercase.
" (capitalizing both words) is a common formatting mistake. Correct binomial nomenclature capitalizes only the first word (genus) and italicizes both words together.
#3: Assuming Kingdom Is the Broadest Rank
Domain is broader than kingdom, not the other way around.

Since many students learned the "five kingdoms" system before learning about domains, they sometimes assume kingdom is the top rank. In the modern three-domain system, each domain (like Eukarya) actually contains multiple kingdoms (like Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, and Protista) within it.

To quickly recall neutralization, remember the pattern as a simple word equation: acid + base → salt + water. Every neutralization reaction follows this same basic pattern.
Lower pH numbers mean more acidic, not less.

"Strong" describes how completely an acid or base dissociates into ions. "Concentrated" describes how much of it is dissolved in a given volume: these are different properties.

A dilute solution of a strong acid (small amount, but fully dissociating) can behave very differently from a concentrated solution of a weak acid (large amount, but only partially dissociating). Do not assume "strong" automatically means "a lot" is present.
#4: Assuming Every Reaction Between an Acid and a Base Produces a Neutral Salt
Neutralization always produces salt and water, but the resulting salt solution is not always exactly neutral (

While the core reaction (acid + base → salt + water) is called "neutralization," this term refers to the H+ and oh- combining to form water, not necessarily a guarantee that the final mixed solution's pH will land exactly at

lessons.title: Atomic Structure and Subatomic Particles (Protons, Neutrons, Electrons, Isotopes, Ions)
lessons.summary: The three subatomic particles, how to find them using atomic and mass numbers, and how isotopes and ions differ from ordinary atoms.

children.text: Every atom is built from three
: found in the nucleus, positive charge (
: found in the nucleus, no charge (neutral).
: found orbiting outside the nucleus, negative charge (
Protons and neutrons have roughly the same mass (about
atomic mass unit each) and together make up nearly all of an atom's mass, since electrons are thousands of times lighter and contribute very little mass.

equals the number of protons in an atom. This number defines which element the atom is: every atom of a given element has the same atomic number, and no two different elements share the same atomic number.
equals the number of protons plus neutrons combined.
So, the number of neutrons can always be found by subtracting:
In a neutral atom (no overall charge), the number of electrons always equals the number of protons, since their opposite charges must balance out exactly.

is an atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons, giving it an overall electric charge. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, creating a positive ion (a
). Gaining electrons creates more electrons than protons, resulting in a negative ion (an
#1: Finding the Numbers of Subatomic Particles
An atom has an atomic number of
. Find its number of protons, neutrons, and electrons (assuming it is neutral).
The atomic number gives the number of protons directly:
Find neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.
Since the atom is neutral, electrons equal protons:

Check the atomic number (protons) first, then compare neutrons.

Since they have different numbers of neutrons (
), they have different mass numbers, even though they are the same element.
Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are, by definition, isotopes of each other.

Compare the new electron count to the fixed proton count.
The resulting ion has a charge of

#4: Working Backwards from an Ion's Charge
. How many electrons does it have?
Use the charge to work out how many electrons were lost.

Remember the particle-charge-location trio together: protons (positive, nucleus), neutrons (neutral, nucleus), electrons (negative, orbiting outside). If you know two of the three numbers (atomic number, mass number, or neutron count), you can always find the third with simple subtraction or addition.
For ion charge questions, use one formula both directions: charge = protons − electrons. If given the charge and proton count, just rearrange to solve for electrons: electrons = protons − charge.

Remember which stays fixed and which changes: the number of protons never changes for a given element (changing it would make it a different element entirely). Isotopes vary neutrons; ions vary electrons.
#1: Confusing Mass Number with Atomic Mass on the Periodic Table

The mass number used in isotope problems is a whole number (protons + neutrons for one specific atom). The periodic table's atomic mass is often a decimal (an average across all natural isotopes of that element).
A question giving a specific isotope's mass number (like carbon-
) wants a whole number calculation, not the periodic table's listed atomic mass (about
for carbon, which is an average, not any single atom's actual mass).
#2: Changing the Number of Protons for an Isotope or Ion
Isotopes and ions never change the number of protons: only isotopes change neutrons, and only ions change electrons.

If a proposed answer changes the atomic number (proton count) while calling the result an "isotope" or an "ion," it has actually described a different element entirely (since atomic number defines the element). Protons stay fixed in both cases.
#3: Mixing Up Which Charge Comes from Gaining vs. Losing Electrons
Losing electrons creates a positive ion (cation). Gaining electrons creates a negative ion (anion).

This seems backward to some students, since "gaining" something usually sounds positive in everyday language. Remember: electrons are negatively charged, so gaining more of them makes the atom more negative overall, and losing them (having fewer negatives left to balance the positive protons) makes it more positive.
#4: Forgetting That Neutral Atoms Need Equal Protons and Electrons
Only in a neutral atom do protons and electrons match exactly; ions, by definition, have unequal amounts.

A question might state a proton count and simply assume the electron count matches, even when the object described is explicitly called an "ion." Always check whether the atom or particle is specified as neutral, or whether a charge is mentioned, before assuming protons equal electrons.

lessons.title: Basic Organic Chemistry (Hydrocarbons, Functional Groups, Naming Conventions)
lessons.summary: The basic hydrocarbon families, common functional groups, and how organic compounds get their names.

children.text: is the study of carbon-based compounds. Carbon is special because it can form four bonds and link with other carbon atoms to build long chains, rings, and branches, creating an enormous variety of molecules: everything from plastics to the molecules that make up your own body.
is a compound made of only carbon and hydrogen atoms. The three basic families differ by the type of carbon-carbon bond they contain:
). Called "saturated," since every possible bonding spot is filled with hydrogen. Named with the ending
: contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond (
: contain at least one carbon-carbon triple bond (
). Also unsaturated. Named with the ending

is a specific small group of atoms attached to a carbon chain that gives the molecule its characteristic chemical behavior. Different functional groups create entirely different families of organic compounds, even on otherwise similar carbon chains:
Find the longest continuous carbon chain: this becomes the "parent chain," and its length determines the base name (meth- for
Identify the bond type present (all single, or containing a double/triple bond) to choose the correct ending: -ane, -ene, or -yne.
Number the carbons in the chain to give the lowest possible position numbers to any double/triple bonds or attached groups.

Classify each hydrocarbon based on its carbon-carbon bonds: (a) a molecule with only single bonds between all its carbons; (b) a molecule containing one carbon-carbon triple bond; (c) a molecule containing one carbon-carbon double bond.
Match the described bond type to its hydrocarbon family.
#2: Identifying the Base Name from Chain Length
Name the base (root) part of the name for a straight-chain alkane with
carbon atoms, all connected by single bonds.
Match the carbon count to its base name, then add the alkane ending.
Since all bonds are single (alkane), add the ending "-ane".

A hydrocarbon is described as having every possible bonding position filled with hydrogen atoms, with no double or triple bonds anywhere in its carbon chain. Is it saturated or unsaturated, and which family does it belong to?
Match "every position filled with hydrogen" to the correct term.
Having every possible position filled with hydrogen (no double or triple bonds using up bonding spots) describes a saturated hydrocarbon.
Saturated hydrocarbons, with only single carbon-carbon bonds, belong to the alkane family.
Two molecules have the exact same length of carbon chain, but one has an
group attached (an alcohol) and the other has a
group attached (a carboxylic acid). Explain why these two molecules, despite similar chain lengths, behave very differently chemically.
Recall that functional groups, not just chain length, determine chemical behavior.
group (carboxylic acid) are different functional groups, each with its own characteristic chemical reactivity.

Even with an identical carbon chain length, the presence of a specific functional group is what determines how the molecule reacts chemically (for instance, carboxylic acids are acidic and can donate a proton, while simple alcohols are not acidic in the same way).

This is why chemists classify organic compounds primarily by their functional group, since it is the functional group, not the plain carbon chain, that dictates most of the molecule's chemical behavior.

Remember the three hydrocarbon endings by their vowel, in order of increasing bond strength: -ane (single bond, "a" comes first alphabetically among the three vowel groups used here), -ene (double bond), -yne (triple bond). Matching the ending to the bond type is a fast way to classify or name a compound.
Memorize the first four carbon-count prefixes, since they appear constantly: meth- (
). Everything after generally follows a similar Greek/Latin numbering pattern (pent- for

For "why do these molecules behave differently" questions, always check the functional group first: it is almost always the deciding factor in organic chemistry behavior questions, more so than overall chain length.
Saturated means only single bonds (alkanes). Unsaturated means containing at least one double or triple bond (alkenes or alkynes).

Students sometimes assume "saturated" refers to something being "full" of double bonds, when it actually means the opposite: every possible bonding position is already filled with hydrogen, leaving no room for any double or triple bonds.
#2: Ignoring the Functional Group When Comparing Molecules
The functional group, not just the length of the carbon chain, is usually what determines a molecule's chemical behavior.

Comparing two molecules only by their carbon chain length, while ignoring that one has an alcohol group and the other has a carboxylic acid group, misses the actual reason their chemical properties differ so much.
#3: Mixing Up the Alkene and Alkyne Endings
-ene means a double bond (alkene). -yne means a triple bond (alkyne).

These two endings differ by only one letter, making them easy to mix up under exam time pressure. Anchor them by counting the letters shared with their bond type's name: or simply memorize the pair together as "ene = 2 (double), yne = 3 (triple)," matching the numbers
#4: Forgetting to Find the longest Chain First
Iupac naming always starts by finding the longest continuous carbon chain, which becomes the parent chain, not just any chain that happens to be drawn first.

A branched molecule may have several possible chains to choose from, but only the longest one is used as the parent name; shorter branches are instead named as attached side groups. Picking a shorter chain as the "parent" by mistake leads to an incorrect name.

(b) Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals: Covalent bond.

Match the electron group count (with no lone pairs) to its VSEPR shape.

For quick bond-type identification without checking electronegativity values, use the metal/nonmetal shortcut: metal + nonmetal = ionic; nonmetal + nonmetal = covalent; metal + metal = metallic. This shortcut is accurate for the vast majority of exam questions.

For VSEPR shape questions, count electron groups first (bonding pairs plus lone pairs), then remember that lone pairs still take up space and affect the shape, even though they are not drawn as a "point" of the final molecular shape.

total electron groups, but very different final shapes.
#1: Ignoring Lone Pairs When Predicting Shape
Lone pairs count as electron groups for determining geometry, even though they do not appear as "corners" in the final molecular shape.
A common mistake predicts water's shape as tetrahedral (matching its
total electron groups) without accounting for the fact that
of those groups are lone pairs, which is exactly why the true shape is bent, not tetrahedral.
#2: Confusing Which Type of Atoms Form Which Bond
Metal + nonmetal = ionic. Nonmetal + nonmetal = covalent. Metal + metal = metallic.

Reversing these pairings is a common and costly error. Anchor it to electron behavior: metals easily give up electrons, nonmetals eagerly grab them: put a giver next to a grabber and you get a full transfer (ionic); put two grabbers together and they must share (covalent).
#3: Assuming All Covalent Bonds Share Electrons Equally
Covalent bonds can be nonpolar (equal sharing) or polar (unequal sharing), depending on the electronegativity difference.

A choice claiming "covalent bonds always share electrons equally" ignores polar covalent bonds, like the oxygen-hydrogen bonds in water, where oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer to itself than hydrogen does, creating an uneven, polar distribution.

Quick rule to pick which naming system applies: metal + nonmetal → ionic naming (cation name + anion "-ide," with Roman numerals if needed). Nonmetal + nonmetal → covalent naming (Greek prefixes on both elements).
For writing ionic formulas fast, use the "criss-cross method": take each ion's charge number (ignoring the sign) and use it as the subscript for the other ion. For calcium (

Memorize the "-ate has more oxygen than -ite" rule for polyatomic ions: if you know sulfate is

#1: Forgetting the Roman Numeral for Variable-Charge Metals
Metals that can form more than one common charge (like iron, copper, and most transition metals) need a Roman numeral in their name.

#2: Dropping the "Mono-" Prefix on the Second Element

Polyatomic ions (like sulfate, nitrate, or hydroxide) keep their own special names: do not change them to "-ide," which is reserved for simple, single-atom anions.

You balance an equation by adjusting

Balance elements in this order for the smoothest process: balance any element that appears in only one reactant and one product first, save elements that appear alone (like

For combustion reactions specifically, always balance in this order: carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen last: oxygen's coefficient usually needs to accommodate both

To quickly identify a reaction type, count how many separate substances start on the left and end on the right: one reactant → many products (decomposition); many reactants → one product (synthesis); anything involving

#1: Changing a Subscript Instead of a Coefficient
Only coefficients (numbers in front of a formula) may be changed. Subscripts (numbers within a formula) must stay fixed.
to "balance" an equation actually creates hydrogen peroxide, a completely different substance, not balanced water. Only adjust the whole-formula coefficient, never the internal subscript.
An equation is balanced only when every element's atom count matches on both sides, not just one or two elements.
A student may balance nitrogen correctly but forget to re-check hydrogen after adjusting a coefficient. Always do a final full recount of every element before declaring an equation balanced.
Synthesis combines multiple substances into one. Decomposition breaks one substance into multiple.

These are mirror-image reactions, and it is easy to swap them when reading quickly. Check the arrow direction: many things merging into one on the right is synthesis; one thing splitting into many on the right is decomposition.
Single replacement involves one free element swapping into a compound. Double replacement involves two compounds trading their parts with each other.
If only one reactant is a lone element (like
) and the other is a compound, it is single replacement. If both reactants are already compounds (with no lone elements), and they simply trade partners, it is double replacement.

To pick the right gas law fast, identify which quantity is being held constant: temperature and amount fixed → Boyle's; pressure and amount fixed → Charles's; volume and amount fixed → Gay-Lussac's; pressure and temperature fixed → Avogadro's. If three quantities change and amount stays fixed, use the combined gas law. If moles are given or asked for, use the ideal gas law.

Before calculating, predict the direction of the answer using the relationship type: pressure and volume are inverse (one up, other down); volume-temperature and pressure-temperature are direct (both up or both down together). This catches many arithmetic errors before you even finish computing.
Always convert temperature to kelvin before using any gas law formula. To convert, add
#1: Forgetting to Convert Temperature to Kelvin
All gas law formulas require temperature in kelvin, never Celsius or Fahrenheit.

Plugging in a Celsius temperature directly (especially a negative Celsius value) breaks the proportional relationships these laws depend on, since Kelvin is the only scale where zero truly means "no thermal energy." Always add
#2: Mixing Up Direct and Inverse Relationships
Boyle's Law (pressure-volume) is inverse. Charles's Law and Gay-Lussac's Law are direct.

Applying a direct-relationship setup to Boyle's Law (or vice versa) flips the entire answer. Before computing, briefly reason through the physical intuition: squeezing a gas into less space raises its pressure (inverse); heating a gas makes it expand (direct).
#3: Using the Wrong Gas Law When Multiple Quantities Change
If pressure, volume, and temperature all change together (with a fixed amount of gas), use the combined gas law, not one of the three individual laws.

Trying to apply just Boyle's Law when temperature is also changing ignores an entire variable and produces an incorrect result. Check how many quantities are actually changing before selecting a formula.
#4: Confusing the Ideal Gas Law's Constant with Combined Gas Law Problems

If a problem gives specific values of

lessons.title: History of the Atom and Atomic Models
lessons.summary: How scientists' understanding of the atom's structure changed over time, from Dalton's solid sphere to the modern quantum model.

children.text: Our picture of the atom did not appear all at once. It was built up over more than a century, as each scientist's model was tested by new evidence and then improved or replaced.

: proposed that all matter is made of tiny, indivisible, solid spheres called atoms, and that atoms of a given element are all identical. His model pictured the atom as a simple solid ball, with no internal parts.
, a tiny negatively charged particle, proving atoms are not indivisible after all. He proposed the "
": a positively charged "pudding," with negative electrons embedded inside it, like plums scattered through pudding.

, firing tiny particles at a thin sheet of gold. Most particles passed straight through, but a few bounced back sharply. This surprising result showed that an atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged
at its center. Rutherford's model replaced Thomson's: electrons now orbited around this small central nucleus, more like planets around a distant sun.

: refined Rutherford's model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus only in specific, fixed energy levels (like rungs on a ladder), rather than at just any distance. This explained patterns in how atoms absorb and release light.

, describing electrons not as tiny orbiting planets on fixed paths, but as existing in "clouds" of probability: regions of space where an electron is more or less likely to be found at any given moment. This is the model chemists still use today.
Match each scientist to the correct description of their atomic model: (a) Thomson, (b) Rutherford, (c) Dalton.
(a) Thomson proposed the plum pudding model: negative electrons embedded in a positively charged "pudding."
(b) Rutherford proposed the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.
(c) Dalton proposed the solid sphere model: atoms as simple, indivisible solid balls.

In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most particles passed straight through the thin gold foil, but a small number bounced back at sharp angles. Explain what each of these two results revealed about atomic structure.
Connect each observed result to what it implies about the atom's internal structure.
Most particles passing straight through means an atom is mostly empty space, since most of the fired particles encountered nothing solid in their path.

The few particles that bounced back sharply must have collided with something extremely small, dense, and positively charged (since the fired particles were also positively charged, and like charges repel strongly at close range): this revealed the existence of a concentrated nucleus at the atom's center.

Together, these results overturned Thomson's plum pudding model, which had predicted particles should pass through with only slight, even deflection everywhere, not sharp bounces from a concentrated point.
#3: Why Bohr's Model Improved on Rutherford's
Explain what problem Bohr's model solved that Rutherford's original nuclear model could not explain.
Recall the key limitation of a simple orbiting-electron model and Bohr's fix.

Rutherford's model pictured electrons freely orbiting the nucleus at any distance, similar to planets, but this could not explain why atoms only absorb and release light at very specific, predictable wavelengths (rather than a continuous range).
Bohr proposed that electrons can only occupy certain fixed, specific energy levels around the nucleus, like rungs on a ladder, not just any distance.
This explained the specific light patterns, because electrons jumping between these fixed energy levels absorb or release light of very specific, predictable amounts of energy.

Memorize the five names in order using their nicknamed models: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear/planetary, tiny dense nucleus) → Bohr (fixed energy levels/ladder) → Schrödinger (electron cloud/quantum). If a question describes a specific feature (embedded electrons, fixed energy levels, probability cloud), match it directly to its model's nickname.

For "which experiment revealed X" questions, remember Rutherford's gold foil result in one line: mostly empty space (most particles pass through) plus a tiny dense positive nucleus (rare sharp bounces).
Thomson's model has electrons embedded throughout a positive "pudding." Rutherford's model has electrons orbiting a separate, tiny, dense nucleus.

These two models are the most commonly swapped pair on exams, since both involve a positive charge and electrons. The key distinguishing detail: Thomson's electrons are scattered throughout the positive material, while Rutherford's electrons orbit around a concentrated, separate nucleus.
#2: Believing the Gold Foil Experiment Proved Electrons Exist
The gold foil experiment revealed the nucleus (dense, positive, central); Thomson had already discovered the electron over a decade earlier.

A common error credits Rutherford's experiment with discovering electrons. In fact, Thomson discovered the electron years before, which is what led him to propose the plum pudding model in the first place. Rutherford's gold foil experiment specifically revealed the existence of the small, dense nucleus.
#3: Thinking Bohr's Model Is the Modern, Final Model
Schrödinger's quantum mechanical (electron cloud) model, not Bohr's fixed-orbit model, is the current accepted model.

Bohr's "planetary" model with neat, fixed orbits is a useful simplification often shown in diagrams, but it was later replaced by Schrödinger's probability-cloud model, which better matches experimental evidence. If a question asks for the current scientific model, the electron cloud (quantum mechanical) model is correct, not Bohr's fixed orbits.

lessons.title: Matter (Classification, States, Properties, Phase Changes)
lessons.summary: How matter is classified, the states matter can take, and the difference between physical and chemical properties.

children.text: is anything that has mass and takes up space. Chemistry studies how matter behaves and changes.
(variable composition, made of two or more substances physically combined). Pure substances are further split into
(cannot be broken down into simpler substances, like oxygen) and
(two or more elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio, like water).
(fixed shape, fixed volume, particles vibrate in place),
(fixed volume but takes the shape of its container, particles slide past each other), and
(no fixed shape or volume, particles move freely and spread out). A fourth state,
, is a superheated, electrically charged gas, found in stars and lightning.
Matter can change between states by adding or removing heat energy:
: solid → gas directly, skipping the liquid state (like dry ice).
: gas → solid directly, skipping the liquid state (like frost forming).
Changes that absorb energy (melting, vaporization, sublimation) are
. Changes that release energy (freezing, condensation, deposition) are
: the substance's chemical identity stays exactly the same. Ice and liquid water are both still
can be observed without changing the substance's identity (color, density, melting point, hardness). A
describes how a substance reacts to form a new substance (flammability, reactivity with acid, ability to rust).
does not create a new substance (cutting paper, melting ice, dissolving sugar in water), while a
does create a new substance with different properties (burning wood, rusting iron, an egg cooking).
Classify each of the following as an element, a compound, or a mixture: (a) pure oxygen gas (
); (c) a glass of lemonade (water, sugar, and lemon juice mixed together).
Check whether each substance is made of one element, a fixed chemical combination, or a variable physical blend.
(a) Oxygen gas is made of only one type of atom: an element.
(b) Table salt is two elements (sodium and chlorine) chemically bonded in a fixed ratio: a compound.
(c) Lemonade is water, sugar, and lemon juice physically combined in amounts that can vary (more or less sugar, for instance): a mixture.
Water vapor touches a cold window pane and turns into liquid water droplets. Name this phase change, and state whether it is endothermic or exothermic.
Identify the states involved and the direction of change.
The change goes from gas (water vapor) to liquid (water droplets): this is condensation.
Condensation releases energy (the water vapor loses heat to the cold window): this is exothermic.
#3: Physical Property, Chemical Property, or Change?
Classify each observation: (a) iron is attracted to a magnet; (b) a piece of paper is torn in half; (c) a nail left outside rusts; (d) iron can react with oxygen to form rust.
Check whether a new substance is formed, and whether the description is a property (a description) or a change (an event).
(a) "Attracted to a magnet" describes a trait without forming anything new: a physical property.
(b) Tearing paper changes its shape, but it is still paper: a physical change.
(c) A nail rusting forms a new substance (rust, iron oxide) with different properties than iron: a chemical change.
(d) "Can react with oxygen to form rust" describes a potential for a reaction, not an event that already happened: a chemical property.

For "element, compound, or mixture" questions, ask two quick questions: is it one kind of atom (element) or more than one (compound or mixture)? If more than one, is the ratio fixed (compound) or variable (mixture)?
For phase change direction, remember: going from more ordered to less ordered (solid → liquid → gas) always absorbs energy (endothermic); going the other way always releases energy (exothermic).
For property vs. change questions, look for an action verb describing something that already happened (a change) versus a general description of how a substance would behave (a property).
#1: Thinking a Mixture Must Look Uneven
Mixtures can be uniform-looking (homogeneous) or visibly uneven (heterogeneous): both are still mixtures, not compounds.

Saltwater looks completely uniform, but it is still a mixture (the ratio of salt to water can vary), not a compound. A "looks uniform" test alone cannot distinguish a mixture from a compound: check whether the composition ratio is fixed or variable.
#2: Confusing Phase Changes with Chemical Changes
Phase changes (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing) are always physical changes: no new substance forms.
Water boiling into steam is still
; only its physical state changed. A choice suggesting that boiling water "creates a new substance" is incorrect: the chemical identity never changes during a phase change.
Sublimation skips the liquid phase entirely (solid directly to gas). Evaporation (or boiling) goes from liquid to gas.

Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turning into gas without ever becoming liquid is sublimation, a special and less common phase change. Confusing it with ordinary evaporation misses this key "skipped phase" detail.
#4: Describing a Chemical Property as Something That Already Happened
A chemical property describes what could happen; a chemical change describes an event that did happen.

"Iron rusts when exposed to oxygen and moisture" is a chemical property (a description of a potential reaction). "This nail has rusted" describes an actual chemical change that has already occurred. Exam questions often test this subtle property-versus-change distinction directly.

lessons.title: Mixtures and Separation Techniques (Filtration, Distillation, Chromatography)
lessons.summary: The difference between types of mixtures and how to choose the right technique to separate them.

children.text: is two or more substances physically combined, without any new chemical bonds forming, so each substance keeps its own properties and can be separated back out again.
mixtures are uniform throughout: you cannot see separate parts (like saltwater, or air).
mixtures are not uniform: you can see or detect separate parts (like a salad, or sand mixed with gravel).
Because no new chemical bonds form in a mixture, scientists can use physical methods (not chemical reactions) to separate the components back apart, based on differences in their physical properties.

separates a solid from a liquid (or from another substance), using a material with tiny holes that let the liquid pass through but trap solid particles. Used for a heterogeneous mixture, like separating sand from water.

separates the components of a liquid mixture based on different boiling points. The mixture is heated; the substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first, and its vapor is then cooled back into a liquid and collected separately. Used to separate a mixture like alcohol and water, or to purify seawater into fresh water.
separates the different components of a mixture based on how strongly each one is attracted to a moving liquid or gas (the
) versus a fixed material it travels through (the
). Components that travel faster through the stationary phase are less strongly attracted to it. Used to separate mixtures like ink pigments or plant dyes.
separates a dissolved solid from a liquid by heating the mixture until the liquid turns to vapor and escapes, leaving the solid behind. Used to recover salt from saltwater.
Classify each mixture as homogeneous or heterogeneous: (a) a cup of black coffee (no visible grounds); (b) a bowl of vegetable soup with visible chunks; (c) clean air.
Check whether separate parts are visible or detectable.
(a) Black coffee looks completely uniform, with no visible separate parts: Homogeneous.
(b) Vegetable soup clearly shows separate visible chunks: Heterogeneous.
(c) Clean air is a uniform blend of gases with no visible separate parts: Homogeneous.
A student needs to separate sand from a sand-and-water mixture. Which separation technique is most appropriate, and why?
Identify the physical property difference being used: solid particles trapped versus liquid passing through.
Sand is a solid and water is a liquid; sand does not dissolve in water.
Filtration uses a material with small holes to let the liquid pass through while trapping the solid sand particles.
The answer: filtration, because it separates an undissolved solid from a liquid based on particle size.

A student wants to separate salt from saltwater and does not need to keep the water. A different student wants to separate alcohol from an alcohol-water mixture and does need to keep both liquids separately. Identify the best technique for each student.
Check whether both components need to be collected, or only one.
The first student only needs the solid (salt) and does not care about recovering the water: Evaporation is sufficient, since the water is simply allowed to evaporate away and is not collected.

The second student needs to collect both liquids separately, based on their different boiling points: Distillation is needed, since it collects the vapor (from the lower-boiling-point liquid) in a separate container instead of letting it escape.
Both techniques use heat and boiling, but distillation specifically collects the vapor, while evaporation simply lets it escape.

A student runs black ink on a strip of paper dipped partly into water, and notices that after some time, the black ink has separated into several bands of different colors, some traveling farther up the paper than others. Explain what this shows about the ink's composition, and why some colors traveled farther.
Connect the separation pattern to how chromatography works.
The fact that the single black ink separated into multiple colored bands shows that the ink is actually a mixture of several different colored dyes, not a single pure substance.
The colors that traveled farther up the paper are less strongly attracted to the paper (the stationary phase) and more easily carried along by the water (the mobile phase).
The colors that stayed closer to the starting point are more strongly attracted to the paper, resisting being carried along by the water.
This difference in attraction to the stationary vs. mobile phase is exactly how chromatography separates mixture components.

For separation-technique questions, match the key physical difference being exploited: particle size (filtration), boiling point (distillation), or attraction to a stationary material (chromatography). Identifying which property differs between the components points straight to the correct method.

If a question only cares about recovering one component (usually the solid) and discards the rest, evaporation is enough. If both components must be collected and kept, distillation is needed instead.
Evaporation lets the vapor escape (only the solid is kept). Distillation collects the vapor by cooling it back into a liquid.

If a question specifically asks to recover both parts of a liquid mixture (like alcohol and water), evaporation is not enough, since it does not capture the escaping vapor. Distillation's cooling and collection step is what makes it different.
#2: Assuming Filtration Works on Any Mixture
Filtration only separates an undissolved solid from a liquid: it cannot separate two mixed liquids, or a fully dissolved solid.

Filtration relies on solid particles being too large to pass through the filter's tiny holes. A dissolved solid (like salt fully dissolved in water) has broken down into particles too small for filtration to catch; evaporation or distillation is needed instead.
#3: Thinking Homogeneous Mixtures Cannot Be Separated
Homogeneous mixtures (uniform-looking) can still be separated using techniques like distillation or evaporation: "uniform" does not mean "unseparable."

Saltwater looks completely uniform (homogeneous), yet it can still be separated into salt and water through evaporation or distillation. Being homogeneous only describes appearance, not whether the mixture can be physically separated.

lessons.title: The Mole Concept, Molar Mass, and Avogadro's Number
lessons.summary: How the mole connects the number of particles in a substance to its mass, using Avogadro's number and molar mass.

children.text: Atoms and molecules are far too small and numerous to count one by one. Chemists solve this with the
: a counting unit, just like "a dozen" means
of something, except a mole means an enormous number of something.
One mole of any substance always contains the same number of particles:
. It applies to atoms, molecules, ions, or any other particle you are counting: one mole of water molecules and one mole of table salt formula units both contain exactly
particles, even though they weigh completely different amounts.
is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (

For a single element, molar mass is simply the atomic mass shown on the periodic table, with units of grams per mole instead of atomic mass units. For a compound, molar mass is the sum of the molar masses of every atom in its formula.
Converting Between Moles, Mass, and Particles
Molar mass is the bridge between moles and grams; Avogadro's number is the bridge between moles and particles. The full conversion chain runs:
, always passing through moles in the middle: you cannot convert directly from particles to grams without going through moles first.
#1: Finding Molar Mass of a Compound
Find the molar mass of water (
), given that hydrogen's atomic mass is about
Add up the molar mass of every atom in the formula.
The molar mass of water is
Divide the given mass by the molar mass.
#3: Converting Moles to Number of Particles
How many individual water molecules are in
Multiply the number of moles by Avogadro's number.
How many individual molecules are present in
Since you cannot jump straight from grams to particles, first convert grams to moles, then convert moles to particles.

Think of the mole as the middle stop on a two-step journey: grams and particles never convert directly into each other. Always pass through moles: grams → moles (using molar mass) → particles (using Avogadro's number), or the reverse.

To find a compound's molar mass fast, write out its formula, list each element's atomic mass from the periodic table next to its subscript count, multiply each pair, then add everything together in one pass.
Sanity-check your mole calculations: if the given mass is smaller than the molar mass, you should get fewer than
mole; if it is a whole-number multiple of the molar mass, you get a clean whole (or simple fraction) number of moles.
#1: Converting Directly from Grams to Particles
Grams and particles are never directly convertible: moles must always be the middle step.

Skipping straight from a given mass to a particle count (without finding moles first) produces a badly wrong answer, since it mixes up two completely different conversion factors (molar mass and Avogadro's number) in one incorrect step.
#2: Forgetting to Multiply Atomic Mass by the Subscript
Every atom's contribution to molar mass must be multiplied by how many of that atom appear in the formula.

g/mol) gives an incorrect molar mass of
g/mol. Always check the subscript for each element before adding.
#3: Confusing Atomic Mass Units with Grams per Mole
An element's atomic mass (in atomic mass units, on the periodic table) has the same number as its molar mass (in grams per mole), but they are different units for different purposes.

A single atom's mass is measured in atomic mass units (amu), a tiny unit for a tiny particle. Molar mass describes a mole of that same substance (an enormous number of particles), measured in grams. The numeric value transfers directly, but understanding why (one mole's worth of atoms happens to weigh that many grams) avoids confusion in more advanced problems.
#4: Using the Wrong Number of Significant Figures for Avogadro's Number

lessons.title: Nuclear Chemistry (Alpha, Beta, Gamma Decay, Fission vs. Fusion)
lessons.summary: The three types of radioactive decay and the difference between nuclear fission and fusion.

children.text: studies changes that happen inside the nucleus of an atom, unlike ordinary chemical reactions, which only rearrange electrons. Some nuclei are unstable and spontaneously break down over time, a process called

neutrons). This reduces the atom's mass number by

(one more proton) while the mass number stays essentially the same (since a neutron simply became a proton). Beta particles are smaller and faster than alpha particles, requiring a thicker material (like aluminum foil) to stop them.

: the nucleus releases pure energy, in the form of a gamma ray (a very high-energy type of light), with no change to the atomic number or mass number. Gamma decay usually happens alongside alpha or beta decay, as the nucleus settles down from an "excited" energy state. Gamma rays are extremely penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete to block them.

The key difference to remember: fission splits a big nucleus apart; fusion joins small nuclei together.
A nucleus emits a particle identical to a helium nucleus, and its resulting atomic number decreases by

Match the emitted particle and the resulting change to the correct decay type.

neutrons) is, by definition, an alpha particle.
Emitting this particle matches alpha decay, which also correctly reduces the atomic number by
#2: Finding the New Element After Alpha Decay

The resulting atom has atomic number
#3: Finding the New Element After Beta Decay

The resulting atom has atomic number

Describe which nuclear process is occurring in each scenario: (a) a large uranium nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei inside a power plant reactor; (b) two hydrogen nuclei combine to form a helium nucleus inside the Sun.
Check whether nuclei are splitting apart or joining together.
(a) A large nucleus splitting into smaller pieces: Fission.
(b) two small nuclei combining into one larger nucleus: Fusion.
Memorize the three decay types by their effect on atomic number and mass number in one line: alpha decay drops both numbers (
atomic); beta decay raises atomic number only (
atomic, mass unchanged); gamma decay changes neither number (pure energy released).

For fission versus fusion, remember the everyday meaning of each word: "fission" sounds like "fission-ing apart" (splitting), while "fusion" sounds like "fusing together" (joining). The Sun performs fusion; nuclear power plants typically perform fission.
For penetration-power questions, remember the increasing order: alpha (weakest, stopped by paper) < beta (stopped by foil) < gamma (strongest, needs thick lead or concrete).
#1: Mixing Up Which Numbers Change During Alpha vs. Beta Decay
Alpha decay changes both atomic number (−2) and mass number (−4). Beta decay changes only atomic number (+1), with mass number essentially unchanged.
Confusing these two patterns leads to calculating the wrong resulting element and mass number. Always double check which particle is being emitted before applying a change pattern.
Fission splits a large nucleus apart. Fusion joins small nuclei together.
These two terms sound similar and are commonly swapped. Anchor the memory with real examples: nuclear power plants use fission (splitting uranium); the sun uses fusion (joining hydrogen into helium).
#3: Assuming Gamma Decay Changes the Element
Gamma decay releases only energy, with no change to atomic number or mass number: the element stays exactly the same.

Unlike alpha and beta decay (which transform the atom into a different element), gamma decay simply releases excess energy from an already-changed nucleus settling into a more stable state, without further altering its identity.
Gamma rays are the most penetrating type of radiation discussed here, requiring thick lead or concrete to block, unlike alpha (stopped by paper) or beta (stopped by foil).

A common mistake ranks gamma rays as "weaker" simply because gamma decay causes no atomic changes, confusing "no elemental change" with "less dangerous" or "less penetrating." In reality, gamma rays are the hardest of the three to shield against.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table
lessons.summary: How the periodic table is organized into groups and periods and the trends that repeat across it.

children.text: arranges every known element by increasing atomic number, but its real power is that it groups elements with similar properties together.
. Elements in the same group share similar chemical behavior, because they have the same number of outer (valence) electrons. The horizontal rows are called
Elements are also classified into three broad categories:

Periodic Trends (Electronegativity, Ionization Energy, Atomic Radius, Electron Affinity)
Four major properties change in predictable patterns (

(the size of an atom): Decreases going left to right across a period (more protons pull electrons in closer); increases going down a group (each row adds a whole new electron energy level, making atoms bigger).

(the energy needed to remove an electron): Increases going left to right across a period (electrons are held more tightly); decreases going down a group (outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove).
(how strongly an atom attracts electrons in a bond): follows the same pattern as ionization energy: increases left to right, decreases down a group.
(how much energy is released when an atom gains an electron): generally increases left to right across a period (nonmetals, on the right, tend to gain electrons more readily than metals).

Notice that atomic radius moves opposite to the other three trends: it is largest at the bottom-left of the table (where the other three properties are smallest), and smallest at the top-right (where the other three are largest, ignoring noble gases).
Two elements are found in the same vertical column of the periodic table but in different rows. What can you predict about their chemical behavior, and why?
Connect column position to shared valence electrons.
Elements in the same column (group) share the same number of valence (outer) electrons.

Since chemical behavior is largely determined by valence electrons, these two elements are expected to behave similarly in chemical reactions, even though they are in different periods (rows) and have different atomic sizes.
This is exactly why the periodic table is organized by columns: it groups elements with shared chemical personality together.

Atomic radius decreases moving left to right across a period.

Since sodium is farther left, it has the larger atomic radius.
#3: Comparing Ionization Energy Down a Group
Predict which requires more energy to remove an electron: an atom of lithium (period
Both are in the same group, so apply the down-A-group trend.
Ionization energy decreases going down a group, since outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus and are held less tightly.
Lithium is higher in the group (period
Since lithium is higher up, it has the higher (greater) ionization energy: removing an electron from lithium takes more energy than from potassium.

An element is shiny, conducts electricity well, and is found on the far left side of the periodic table. A different element is dull, brittle, and a poor conductor, found on the far right side. Classify each.
Match the described properties and position to the correct category.
Shiny, good conductor, far left side: this matches the properties and position of a metal.
Dull, brittle, poor conductor, far right side: this matches the properties and position of a nonmetal.

Remember the trend arrows as one diagonal: ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity all increase toward the upper-right corner of the periodic table (fluorine's neighborhood). Atomic radius does the opposite, increasing toward the lower-left corner (francium's neighborhood).

For any "which element has a higher/lower X" comparison question, first check: are they in the same period (compare left-to-right) or the same group (compare top-to-bottom)? Then apply the single matching trend rule.

Remember the metal/nonmetal split with one phrase: "metals lose, nonmetals gain" (electrons), which also explains why metals sit on the side with lower ionization energy and electronegativity, and nonmetals sit on the side with higher values for both.
#1: Mixing Up the Direction of the Atomic Radius Trend
Atomic radius decreases left to right, but increases going down: the opposite direction from the other three major trends.

Since ionization energy, electronegativity, and electron affinity all increase toward the upper right, students often assume atomic radius does too. It is the one trend that runs in reverse, growing largest toward the lower left of the table.
#2: Comparing Elements That Are Neither Same Period nor Same Group
The straightforward trend rules only apply directly when comparing elements in the same period or same group.

Comparing two elements that share neither a period nor a group (diagonal neighbors, for instance) requires combining both trends carefully, and the result is not always obvious from a single rule. Always check position relationships before applying a trend blindly.
Metalloids have properties between metals and nonmetals, but they are not all identical to each other.

The metalloid category is a spectrum along the staircase boundary, not a single uniform behavior. Their most exam-relevant shared trait is being useful as semiconductors (partial electrical conductors), which is neither fully metallic nor fully nonmetallic.

Chemists use several different ways to describe how concentrated a solution is.

#4: Molarity vs. Molality: Why the Difference Matters
Explain why molality, unlike molarity, does not change when a solution's temperature changes.
Compare what each formula's denominator actually measures.
Molarity's denominator is the volume of the solution (in liters). Volume can expand when heated or contract when cooled, due to normal thermal expansion of liquids.
Molality's denominator is the mass of the solvent (in kilograms). Mass does not change with temperature: heating or cooling a substance does not add or remove any matter.

Because molarity depends on a value (volume) that shifts with temperature, a solution's molarity can change slightly as its temperature changes, even though the amount of dissolved solute stays the same. Molality stays constant regardless of temperature, which makes it the preferred measurement for experiments involving significant temperature changes.
Remember the units to instantly identify which formula a question wants: "moles per liter of solution" is molarity; "moles per kilogram of solvent" is molality; "grams per
grams" or plain percentages of mass are percent by mass; percentages of volume (common for liquid mixtures like alcohol content) are percent by volume.
For percent-by-mass problems, always calculate the total solution mass (solute plus solvent) before dividing: a common shortcut mistake is dividing by the solvent's mass alone.

If a problem specifically mentions temperature changes or requires precise, temperature-independent measurements, it is testing molality, not molarity: this is molality's signature real-world use case.
Molarity divides by liters of solution. Molality divides by kilograms of solvent only.

These sound almost identical and are the most commonly swapped concentration terms. A quick check: "molARITY" pairs with "voluме" (both contain similar letter patterns you can associate together), while "molALITY" pairs with "mass" of solvent alone.
#2: Using the Solvent's Mass Instead of the Total Solution's Mass for Percent by Mass
Percent by mass divides by the total solution mass (solute + solvent), not the solvent's mass alone.

#3: Assuming Solubility Is the Same at Every Temperature
Solubility generally changes with temperature: usually increasing for solids as the solvent gets hotter.

A question describing more sugar dissolving as tea is heated is demonstrating this exact temperature dependence. Treating solubility as one single fixed number, without considering temperature, misses this important variable.
"Saturated" specifically means the solution holds the maximum solute it can dissolve at that temperature: it is not just a vague description of "a lot" of solute.

A solution can be saturated with only a small amount of solute if that solute has low solubility, or it can require a very large amount of solute to become saturated if that solute has high solubility. Saturation is always relative to the specific solute's maximum solubility at the current temperature, not an absolute amount.

lessons.title: Thermodynamics and Kinetics (Endothermic vs. Exothermic Reactions, Catalysts)
lessons.summary: Whether reactions absorb or release energy and what factors speed up or slow down how fast reactions happen.

children.text: Chemical reactions involve two separate questions: how much energy is exchanged (thermodynamics), and how fast the reaction happens (kinetics). These are independent: a reaction can release a lot of energy but still happen very slowly, or absorb energy but happen quickly.
reaction releases energy (usually as heat) to its surroundings; the products end up with less energy than the reactants started with. The surroundings feel warmer. Example: burning wood.
reaction absorbs energy from its surroundings; the products end up with more energy than the reactants started with. The surroundings feel cooler. Example: an instant cold pack activating.
Even a reaction that releases a lot of energy overall still needs an initial energy "push" to get started, called the

: the minimum energy needed for reactant particles to collide successfully and begin transforming into products. A higher activation energy means a slower reaction (harder to get started); a lower activation energy means a faster reaction.

is a substance that speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy, without being permanently used up or changed itself in the process. Catalysts do not change how much energy the overall reaction releases or absorbs: they only change how fast the reaction reaches that result.

Several factors can speed up a reaction's rate: Higher temperature (particles move faster and collide more often, with more energy); higher concentration of reactants (more particles available to collide); increased surface area (more exposed area for reacting particles to meet, like crushing a solid into powder); and the presence of a catalyst.
#1: Classifying a Reaction as Endothermic or Exothermic
A chemical hand warmer packet becomes noticeably hot after being activated. A different reaction, mixed in a beaker, causes the beaker itself to feel cold to the touch. Classify each.
Check whether energy is being released (warming) or absorbed (cooling) from the surroundings.
The hand warmer releases heat to its surroundings (getting hot): Exothermic.
The cold beaker reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings (getting cold): Endothermic.

A reaction normally takes several hours to complete at room temperature. When a specific catalyst is added, the same reaction finishes in just a few minutes, and the same final amount of product is formed either way. Explain what the catalyst did and did not change.
Separate what a catalyst affects (rate) from what it does not affect (overall energy change and final product amount).
The catalyst lowered the activation energy needed for the reaction to proceed, making the reaction happen much faster.
The catalyst was not consumed or permanently changed by the reaction (though it may participate temporarily).

Since the same final amount of product formed either way, the catalyst did not change the overall energy released or absorbed by the reaction, nor the total amount of product: only the speed of getting there changed.
#3: Predicting the Effect of Crushing a Solid
A chunk of solid reacts slowly with an acid. If the same solid is instead crushed into a fine powder before adding the acid, predict what happens to the reaction rate, and explain why.
Consider how surface area affects the number of possible collisions.
Crushing the solid into a powder greatly increases its total exposed surface area, even though the total mass stays the same.
More exposed surface area means more particles of the solid are available to collide with acid particles at the same time.
This results in a faster reaction rate, since more successful collisions can happen per second.
A student claims, "Since this reaction releases a huge amount of energy, it must happen instantly." Explain why this reasoning is flawed.
Recall that the amount of energy released and the speed of the reaction are two separate, independent properties.
How much energy a reaction releases (an exothermic amount) is a thermodynamics question, describing the difference between the reactants' and products' energy levels.
How fast a reaction happens is a kinetics question, depending on activation energy, temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts.

A reaction can release a large amount of energy overall, yet still have a high activation energy, making it proceed very slowly without an initial push (like paper, which releases a lot of energy when burned, but does not spontaneously combust at room temperature without an ignition source).
The student's claim incorrectly assumes energy release and reaction speed must always match, when they are actually independent properties.

Remember exothermic and endothermic with their prefixes: "exo-" means out (energy goes out to the surroundings, things feel warmer); "endo-" means in (energy comes in from the surroundings, things feel cooler).
For reaction rate questions, remember the four main "speed-up" factors as one group: temperature up, concentration up, surface area up, and adding a catalyst: all four make a reaction go faster.

Remember that a catalyst affects only the speed (kinetics) of a reaction, never the total energy change or the final amount of product (thermodynamics): these two categories stay strictly separate whenever a catalyst is involved.
#1: Assuming Exothermic Reactions Are Always Fast
Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic (thermodynamics) is independent of how fast it happens (kinetics).

Some exothermic reactions (like the slow rusting of iron) happen very slowly, while some endothermic reactions can happen quickly. Never assume a reaction's speed just from knowing whether it releases or absorbs energy.
#2: Believing a Catalyst Gets Used Up in the Reaction
A catalyst is not consumed or permanently changed by the reaction: it speeds things up without being used up.

Unlike a reactant (which is consumed and turns into product), a catalyst may temporarily interact with reactants, but it is regenerated by the end of the reaction and can be reused. A choice claiming "the catalyst became part of the final product" misunderstands its role.
#3: Thinking a Catalyst Changes the Overall Energy Released
A catalyst changes only the reaction's speed (by lowering activation energy): it does not change the total energy released or absorbed overall.

The overall energy difference between reactants and products (whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and by how much) stays exactly the same with or without a catalyst present. Only the path taken to get there becomes easier and faster.
#4: Confusing Higher Activation Energy with a "Bigger" Reaction
A high activation energy means the reaction is slow to start, not that it releases more energy overall.

Activation energy describes the initial energy barrier a reaction must overcome, which is a completely separate value from the reaction's overall energy change (exothermic or endothermic amount). A reaction can have a small overall energy release but still require a very high activation energy to begin.

lessons.title: Earth's Motions (Rotation, Revolution, Precession)
lessons.summary: The three main motions of Earth and what each one causes: day and night, the seasons, and the slow wobble of the axis.
