A common misconception is that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun at that time of year. Explain why this is not the real reason for the seasons.
Check the misconception against how seasons actually work.
If distance from the Sun caused the seasons, then both hemispheres would experience summer and winter at the same time.
But the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons: when it is summer in the Philippines (Northern Hemisphere), it is winter in Australia (Southern Hemisphere).

This opposite pattern can only be explained by the tilt of Earth's axis: each hemisphere leans toward the Sun at a different point in the yearly orbit, receiving more direct sunlight during its summer.
The real cause of the seasons is axial tilt combined with revolution, not changing distance from the Sun.
Explain why a sidereal day (measured against the distant stars) is a few minutes shorter than the familiar
Consider what Earth is doing at the same time it rotates.
While Earth spins once on its axis, it is also moving forward along its orbit around the Sun.

Because Earth has shifted position along its orbit, it must rotate a little bit extra before the Sun appears in the same spot in the sky again; this extra bit is what makes the ordinary "Sun-based" day exactly
Measured against the far-away, essentially fixed stars instead of the Sun, Earth only needs to complete one plain rotation, which takes about
This is why the sidereal day is a few minutes shorter than the solar (24-hour) day.
Lock in three timescales, smallest to largest: rotation is about a day, revolution is about a year, precession is about
years. If a question gives a timescale, match it to the motion in that same size range.

For "why do we have seasons" questions, the two keywords that must both appear in a correct explanation are "tilt" and "revolution" (or "orbit"). An answer mentioning only distance from the Sun is always wrong.
#1: Distance from the Sun Causes the Seasons
The seasons come from axial tilt combined with revolution, not from Earth's distance to the Sun.

This is the single most common wrong explanation for the seasons on any science exam. Remember the opposite-hemisphere check: if distance were the cause, both hemispheres would share the same season at the same time, which is not what happens.
Rotation is Earth spinning on its own axis (day and night). Revolution is Earth traveling around the Sun (the year).
The two words sound similar and get swapped in rushed reading. A quick check: rotation's timescale is about a day; revolution's timescale is about a year.
#3: Thinking Precession Changes the Seasons Quickly
-year wobble: far too slow to explain any yearly or daily pattern.

If a choice claims precession causes day and night, or causes summer and winter, it has confused the timescales. Precession only becomes noticeable over many thousands of years, shifting which star sits near the pole.

lessons.title: The Earth's Subsystems (Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, Atmosphere, Biosphere)
lessons.summary: The four connected systems that make up Earth and how they interact with each other.

children.text: Earth is not just one single thing. Scientists study Earth as four connected subsystems that constantly affect each other, like four teammates working together.
is the solid, rocky part of Earth: the crust and the uppermost, rigid part of the mantle. It includes mountains, the ocean floor, and all the rocks and soil under your feet.
is all the water on Earth: oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice caps, and even water vapor in clouds. Most of the hydrosphere is salt water in the oceans.
is the layer of gases surrounding Earth: mostly nitrogen and oxygen, held in place by gravity. It protects life from harmful radiation and holds in heat.
is every living thing on Earth, and the places where they live: every plant, animal, fungus, and microbe, from the deepest ocean trench to the highest mountain.

These four subsystems constantly interact. A volcano (lithosphere) can release gases into the sky (atmosphere). Rain (hydrosphere) falls and wears down mountains (lithosphere). Plants (biosphere) take in gases from the air (atmosphere) and draw water from the ground (hydrosphere). No subsystem works alone; changes in one almost always ripple into the others.
Classify each of the following as belonging to the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, or biosphere: a coral reef, a glacier, a layer of nitrogen gas, and a mountain range.
Match each example to its defining trait: living, water, gas, or solid rock.
A coral reef is made of living coral animals: Biosphere.
A glacier is frozen water: Hydrosphere.
A layer of nitrogen gas is part of the air: Atmosphere.
A mountain range is solid rock: Lithosphere.
A volcanic eruption releases ash and gas into the sky, which blocks sunlight and cools the surrounding region for weeks. Identify the two subsystems directly interacting in this event.
Identify where the event starts and where its effect lands.
The eruption comes from inside the solid Earth: this involves the lithosphere.
The ash and gas travel into the sky and affect sunlight and temperature: this involves the atmosphere.
The two subsystems interacting are the lithosphere (source of the eruption) and the atmosphere (where the ash and gas travel and cause effects).

Rainfall soaks into cracks in a rock, freezes, and slowly breaks the rock apart over many years. Plant roots then grow into the broken rock, further breaking it into soil. Identify all four subsystems involved in this process, and explain each one's role.
Trace the story piece by piece.
The rock being broken apart is the lithosphere.
The rainfall that seeps into the cracks is part of the hydrosphere.
Since this is a slow weathering process happening over time and affected by temperature (freezing), the surrounding air conditions involve the atmosphere.
The plant roots that grow into the rock and help break it down further belong to the biosphere.
This example shows all four subsystems cooperating in a single natural process: turning solid rock into soil.

Match each subsystem name to its simple root meaning: "litho" means rock (lithosphere = rock layer), "hydro" means water (hydrosphere = water layer), "bio" means life (biosphere = life layer), and "atmo" refers to vapor or air (atmosphere = air layer). Knowing these roots lets you classify any unfamiliar example quickly.

For "which subsystems are involved" questions, scan the scenario for four clues: solid ground or rock (lithosphere), any form of water (hydrosphere), air or gas (atmosphere), and any living thing (biosphere). Most real scenarios touch at least two subsystems.
#1: Ice Belongs to the Hydrosphere, Not a Separate Category
Frozen water (ice, glaciers, snow) is still part of the hydrosphere.

Students sometimes think ice deserves its own category since it is solid. But the hydrosphere is defined by being water in any of its forms (liquid, solid ice, or water vapor), so glaciers and polar ice caps all belong to the hydrosphere.
#2: Forgetting That Microbes and Underground Life Count as Biosphere
The biosphere includes all living things, even those in soil, deep oceans, or underground.

A choice describing bacteria living deep underground may be mistakenly classified as part of the lithosphere just because of its location. Classification depends on whether the thing is alive, not on where it happens to be found.
#3: Treating the Subsystems as Separate and Non-Interacting
The four subsystems constantly affect each other; they are not isolated boxes.

A question describing a real event (like a volcanic eruption, a rainstorm, or a forest fire) almost always involves more than one subsystem working together. Answers that pick only one subsystem for a multi-step scenario are usually incomplete.

lessons.title: Lunar and Solar Eclipses, Phases of the Moon
lessons.summary: Why the Moon changes shape in the sky and how solar and lunar eclipses happen.

children.text: The Moon does not make its own light. We only see the half of the Moon that sunlight is hitting. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half, and this creates the
One full cycle of phases, from one new moon to the next, takes about
(the sunlit side faces away from Earth, so the Moon looks dark),
, before returning to new moon. "Waxing" means growing bigger; "waning" means shrinking smaller.
An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up almost perfectly in a straight line, so one body's shadow falls on another.
happens at new moon, when the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, blocking the Sun's light from a small part of Earth. A
happens at full moon, when Earth passes directly between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
Each type of eclipse has different versions, based on how completely the shadow covers the object:
: the Moon completely covers the Sun, for viewers standing in the Moon's darkest shadow (the
: viewers only in the lighter outer shadow (the
) see the Moon cover just part of the Sun.
: the Moon is a little too far from Earth to fully cover the Sun, leaving a bright ring ("ring of fire") visible around the edge.
: the whole Moon passes into Earth's umbra and can turn a reddish color, sometimes called a "blood moon."
: only part of the Moon passes into Earth's umbra.

Eclipses do not happen every single month, even though new moons and full moons happen every month. This is because the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted compared to Earth's orbit around the Sun, so the three bodies usually miss lining up exactly.
A student observes that exactly half of the Moon's visible face is lit, and the lit half is growing bigger each night. What phase is this?
Match the description to the correct term.
"Growing bigger" means the phase is waxing, not waning.
Exactly half lit, while growing, is the first quarter phase (on the way toward full moon).

During a certain event, the Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on part of Earth's surface. What phase of the Moon must this be happening during, and what type of eclipse is this?
Work out the required alignment first.
The Moon sits between the Sun and Earth, so its shadow falls on Earth. This alignment can only happen at new moon, when the Moon's dark side faces us.
Since the Moon's shadow is falling on Earth, this is a solar eclipse.
New moons and full moons both happen every month, yet eclipses do not happen every month. Explain why.
Consider the shape of the Moon's orbit relative to Earth's orbit.
For an eclipse, the Sun, Earth, and Moon must line up in an almost perfectly straight line.
The Moon's orbital path around Earth is tilted slightly compared to the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.
Because of this tilt, at most new moons and full moons, the Moon actually passes slightly above or below the perfect alignment line, so no shadow falls where it needs to.
Only when a new moon or full moon happens to occur very close to where the two tilted orbital planes cross does a true eclipse occur.

Two clean rules replace a lot of memorization: solar eclipse happens only at new moon (Moon between Sun and Earth); lunar eclipse happens only at full moon (Earth between Sun and Moon). If a question's timing does not match, the described eclipse type is impossible.

For phase names, "waxing" and "waning" tell you the direction (growing or shrinking), while "crescent," "quarter," and "gibbous" tell you the amount lit. Combine the two words and you can name any phase without memorizing a picture.
#1: Mixing Up Which Eclipse Happens at Which Phase
Solar eclipse: New moon. Lunar eclipse: Full moon.

It is easy to swap these, especially since "solar" might make students think of the Moon glowing brightly (which actually matches full moon, but for the wrong eclipse type). Anchor it by remembering who blocks whom: the Moon blocks the Sun during a solar eclipse, which needs new moon.
Eclipses need the Moon's orbit to also line up with Earth's orbital plane, which does not happen every month.

A choice may state "a lunar eclipse happens at every full moon." This is false: most full moons pass just above or below Earth's shadow because of the Moon's tilted orbit, so only some full moons produce an actual eclipse.
The umbra is the dark, complete shadow. The penumbra is the lighter, partial shadow.

Viewers in the umbra see a total eclipse; viewers in the penumbra see only a partial eclipse. A question describing "the Sun completely blocked" points to the umbra, while "the Sun partly covered" points to the penumbra.

lessons.title: Fossils, Stratigraphy, and Geologic Time Scale
lessons.summary: How scientists figure out the age of rocks and fossils and how Earth's long history is divided into named time periods.

children.text: is any preserved trace of an ancient living thing: bones, shells, footprints, or imprints left in rock. Fossils are usually found inside sedimentary rock, since that rock forms in layers that can trap and preserve remains before they decay.
is the study of rock layers (called
). The main tool for relative dating is the

: in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers, each layer is younger than the layer below it, and older than the layer above it. This makes sense because sediment piles up over time, with the newest material always on top.
Relative dating tells us the order in which rock layers (and the fossils within them) formed, but it does not tell us an exact age in years.
To find an actual number of years, scientists use
. Certain elements are radioactive, meaning their atoms slowly and steadily break down (decay) into a different, stable element over time. The
of a radioactive element is the time it takes for half of it to decay into that stable form.

By measuring how much of the original radioactive element remains in a rock, compared to how much of the stable decayed element has built up, scientists can calculate how many half-lives have passed, and therefore the rock's actual age in years.
, divided into units from largest to smallest:
The largest chunk of Earth's history, called the
billion years, before complex life became common. After the Precambrian comes the
("old life"): includes the first fish, land plants, and early reptiles.
("middle life"): the age of the dinosaurs, also when the first mammals and flowering plants appeared.
("new life"): the current era, often called the age of mammals, which is when humans evolved.
A rock cliff shows four visible layers, labeled W, X, Y, and Z from bottom to top, with no signs of disturbance. Which layer is the oldest, and which is the youngest?
Apply the Law of Superposition directly.
In an undisturbed sequence, the bottom layer is the oldest, since it was deposited first.
The top layer is the youngest, since it was deposited most recently.
Layer W (bottom) is the oldest. Layer Z (top) is the youngest.

A trilobite fossil is found in Layer W (the bottom layer), and a mammal fossil is found in Layer Z (the top layer) of the same rock cliff from Example 1. What can you conclude about which organism lived first?
Connect the rock layer's age to the fossil trapped inside it.
A fossil's age matches the age of the rock layer it is found in.
Since Layer W is older than Layer Z, the trilobite (in Layer W) must have lived before the mammal (in Layer Z).
This matches what we know from the geologic time scale: trilobites are common Paleozoic fossils, while most mammals appeared much later, in the Cenozoic.
A radioactive element has a half-life of

billion years. A rock sample originally contained a certain amount of this element, and now only one-quarter of that original amount remains (the rest has decayed into a stable element). How old is the rock?
Figure out how many half-lives have passed.
After one half-life, half of the original amount remains:
After a second half-life, half of that remaining half is left:
of the original element remains, two half-lives have passed.
billion years, so the rock is:
A rock layer contains fossils of dinosaurs and early flowering plants, but no fossils of any mammals larger than small, shrew-like creatures. Which era does this layer most likely belong to?
Match the fossil clues to the correct era's defining life forms.
Dinosaurs and the first flowering plants are hallmark fossils of the mesozoic era.
Only small, shrew-like mammals existed during the Mesozoic; large mammals became dominant only later, in the Cenozoic era, after the dinosaurs went extinct.
For Law of Superposition questions, just remember: Bottom is oldest, top is youngest, like pancakes stacked one at a time: the first one made sits at the bottom of the plate.
For half-life problems, track the fraction remaining by repeatedly halving:
, and count how many halving steps you took. That count is the number of half-lives elapsed; multiply by the half-life length to get the age.

Remember the three Phanerozoic eras in order using their meaning: Paleozoic ("old life," early sea creatures and first land plants), Mesozoic ("middle life," age of dinosaurs), Cenozoic ("new life," age of mammals, our current era).
#1: Relative Dating Gives Order, Not a Number
Relative dating (Law of Superposition) tells you which layer is older. Only radiometric dating gives an actual age in years.

A question asking "how many years old is this layer" cannot be answered using superposition alone: that method only orders layers relative to each other. Only radiometric (absolute) dating provides a specific number of years.
#2: Assuming a Disturbed Sequence Still Follows "Bottom is Oldest"
The Law of Superposition only applies to undisturbed layers.

If rock layers have been folded, flipped, or faulted by geological forces (which does happen), the simple "bottom is oldest" rule can no longer be trusted without further evidence. Exam questions usually specify "undisturbed" for a reason: watch for that word.
Each half-life cuts the remaining amount in half again, not by a fixed equal amount each time.
A common mistake is assuming that if
more half-life to reach zero. In fact, decay never reaches exactly zero: every half-life only cuts the current remaining amount in half, forever approaching (but never fully hitting) zero.
Dinosaurs belong to the mesozoic, not the Cenozoic.

Since the Cenozoic is called the "age of mammals," some students mistakenly place dinosaurs there too. Dinosaurs went extinct at the end of the Mesozoic era, and it was only afterward, in the Cenozoic, that mammals became the dominant large land animals.

lessons.title: Heavenly Bodies (Stars, Galaxies, Comets, Asteroids, Meteors)
lessons.summary: The different kinds of objects found in space and how to tell them apart.

children.text: Space is full of many different kinds of objects. Knowing their names and telling them apart is a favorite CET question type.
is a giant, glowing ball of hot gas that makes its own light and heat through nuclear reactions in its core. The Sun is a star.
is a huge collection of billions of stars, held together by gravity, along with gas, dust, and (we believe) dark matter. Our own galaxy is the
is a rocky, metallic chunk of rock, smaller than a planet, that orbits the Sun. Most asteroids in our solar system are found in the
, a wide region located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

is a smaller body made mostly of ice, frozen gases, and dust, sometimes nicknamed a "dirty snowball." When a comet gets close to the Sun, the heat turns some of its ice directly into gas, and pressure from the Sun blows this gas and dust into a glowing
that always points away from the Sun, no matter which direction the comet is traveling. The most famous comet,
Three closely related, easily confused terms describe small pieces of rock or metal from space:
is a small chunk of rock or metal traveling through space, too small to be called an asteroid.
is what we call that same chunk once it enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up, creating a streak of light. This is the "shooting star" you see in the night sky.
is what we call it if a piece survives the trip through the atmosphere and lands on the ground.
Think of it as one object going through three stages, named for where it is: floating in space (meteoroid), burning in our sky (meteor), and landed on Earth (meteorite).
Most of the asteroids in our solar system are located in a region called the asteroid belt. Where is this belt found?
The asteroid belt sits between the orbits of two specific planets.
It lies between Mars and Jupiter, not between Earth and Mars, and not beyond Neptune.
The correct answer: between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
#2: The Three Stages of a Space Rock

A small rock breaks off from an asteroid and drifts through space for millions of years. It then enters Earth's atmosphere, burns brightly, and a fragment of it lands in a field. Name what this object is called at each of the three stages.
Match each stage to its correct name.
While it drifts through space, before reaching Earth's atmosphere, it is a
While it burns and streaks light across the sky inside Earth's atmosphere, it is a
Once the surviving fragment lands on the ground, it is a
Same rock, three different names, based on where it is at the time.
#3: Why a Comet's Tail Always Points Away from the Sun
A comet is moving away from the Sun, back out toward deep space. In which direction does its tail point: toward the Sun, or away from the Sun, in the direction the comet is traveling?
Recall what actually creates the tail.
The tail forms because heat and pressure from the sun push gas and dust off the comet.
This means the tail always points away from the Sun, regardless of which way the comet itself is moving.
So even though the comet in this problem is moving away from the Sun, its tail still points away from the Sun, meaning here, the tail actually points in front of the comet, leading the way outward.
This is a surprising but well documented fact: the tail's direction depends on the Sun's position, never on the comet's direction of travel.
Chain the meteor family in order of location: space, sky, ground: meteoroid, meteor, meteorite. Saying the chain out loud in that order during the exam prevents mixing them up under time pressure.
Remember the tail rule with one phrase: "tail always flees the Sun." It never points toward the Sun, and it never simply trails behind the comet's path.
A meteor burns in the sky. A meteorite lands on the ground.

These two words differ by only two letters, and test-makers exploit that. If the question describes something found lying in a crater or a museum, it is a meteorite. If it describes a bright streak seen at night, it is a meteor.
Asteroids are rocky. Comets are mostly ice and dust, with a glowing tail near the Sun.
A description mentioning a "dirty snowball" or a visible tail is a comet, not an asteroid. Asteroids do not develop tails because they lack the ice that vaporizes near the Sun.
#3: Placing the Asteroid Belt in the Wrong Spot
The asteroid belt is between Mars and Jupiter, not near Earth.

Some choices place the belt between Earth and Mars, or beyond Neptune (which is actually a different region called the Kuiper Belt, home to many comets). Anchor the fact firmly: Mars-Jupiter gap only.

lessons.title: Layers of the Earth and Composition
lessons.summary: The four layers inside Earth, what each is made of, and how we know they exist.

children.text: Earth is not the same material all the way through. It is built like an onion, with different layers stacked around a center.
is the thin, outermost, solid layer we live on. There are two kinds: continental crust (thicker, under land, about
km thick) and oceanic crust (thinner, under the oceans, only about
km thick). This is why oceanic crust is easier to break through when studying what lies beneath.
sits below the crust and makes up most of Earth's volume, roughly

km thick. It is made of hot, dense rock rich in iron and magnesium. Even though the mantle is solid rock, it is so hot that it can slowly flow over long periods of time, like very thick, slow-moving toffee. This slow flow is a major force behind plate tectonics.

lies below the mantle. It is made mostly of iron and nickel, and unlike the mantle, it is actually liquid because of the extreme heat. This liquid, metallic layer flowing around Earth's center is what generates Earth's magnetic field.
is the very center of Earth. It is also made of iron and nickel, and even though it is the hottest layer of all, the extreme pressure at Earth's center squeezes it so tightly that it stays solid.

Scientists cannot dig down and see these layers directly. Instead, they study how earthquake waves travel and bend as they pass through Earth's interior, since waves behave differently in solid versus liquid material, and in materials of different densities. This is how we know the outer core is liquid: certain earthquake waves cannot pass through it at all.
List Earth's four main layers in order, starting from the outermost layer and ending at the very center.
The outermost, thin, solid layer we stand on is the crust.
Below the crust is the thick, mostly solid but slowly flowing mantle.
Below the mantle is the liquid outer core, made of iron and nickel.
At the very center is the solid inner core, also iron and nickel.
Order: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
#2: Why Is the Inner Core Solid Despite Being the Hottest Layer?
The inner core has the highest temperature of any layer inside Earth, yet it is solid, while the cooler outer core above it is liquid. Explain this.
Consider the other factor besides temperature that affects whether something is solid or liquid: pressure.
Temperature alone would suggest the hottest layer should be the most likely to melt.
But the inner core also experiences the greatest pressure in all of Earth, since it is squeezed by the weight of every layer above it.
This immense pressure forces the iron and nickel atoms to stay locked in a solid arrangement, even at extremely high temperature.
The outer core, under less pressure than the inner core, is not squeezed as tightly and can exist as a liquid at its slightly lower (but still very high) temperature.
#3: How Do We Know the Outer Core Is Liquid?
Scientists cannot travel to the center of the Earth. Explain how earthquake waves reveal that the outer core is liquid.
Recall how different waves respond to solid versus liquid material.
Earthquakes send out waves that travel through the whole Earth in different directions.
One kind of wave can only travel through solid material and cannot pass through liquid.
Scientists observed that this wave type disappears (does not arrive) on the opposite side of the planet from certain earthquakes, forming a "shadow" region.
This missing wave pattern is explained if there is a liquid layer inside Earth blocking that type of wave: evidence for the liquid outer core.

Remember the layer thicknesses in relative order, largest to smallest: mantle (biggest by far) > outer core > inner core > crust (thinnest). If a question compares sizes, the mantle almost always wins.

For "solid or liquid" questions, remember the pattern flips twice going inward: crust (solid), mantle (solid, but flows slowly), outer core (liquid), inner core (solid again). The crust-mantle line and the core boundary are the two spots to watch.
The mantle is solid rock, but it still flows very slowly over long stretches of time.

Students think "solid" must mean "completely rigid and unmoving." The mantle's slow flow, similar to thick toffee, is exactly what drives the plates on Earth's surface. Being solid and being able to flow slowly are not contradictions here.
#2: Assuming the Hottest Layer Must Be Liquid
Higher pressure can keep a layer solid even at extreme temperature.

The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet it is solid because of the crushing pressure at Earth's center. A choice claiming "the inner core is liquid because it is the hottest layer" ignores the role of pressure.
#3: Mixing Up Continental and Oceanic Crust
Continental crust is thicker; oceanic crust is thinner.
A question describing land areas versus ocean floor is testing which crust type is thicker. Continental crust (under continents) is roughly
km thick, while oceanic crust (under oceans) is only about
km thick: much easier to drill through, which is why deep scientific drilling projects often target the ocean floor.

lessons.title: Minerals and Rocks (Igneous, Sedimentary, Metamorphic, Rock Cycle)
lessons.summary: How to identify minerals by their properties and how the three types of rock form and change into one another.

children.text: is a naturally occurring, solid substance with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure. A
is simply a mix of one or more minerals stuck together.
Since many minerals can look similar, scientists use specific physical properties to tell them apart.
(very hard, like diamond). A mineral can scratch any mineral with a lower number, and gets scratched by any mineral with a higher number.

: the color of a mineral's powder, made by rubbing it on an unglazed tile. Streak is more reliable than the mineral's outer color, since the outer color can vary while the streak color usually stays constant.
: how the mineral's surface reflects light, mainly grouped as
is breaking along smooth, flat planes (because of weaker bonds in that direction);
is breaking in a rough, irregular way, with no flat planes.
The Three Rock Types and the Rock Cycle

forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens. If it cools slowly underground, it forms large crystals (like granite); if it cools quickly at the surface (like from a volcano), it forms small or no crystals (like basalt or obsidian).
forms when small pieces of rock, sand, shells, or other debris (
) pile up in layers and get pressed and cemented together over a long time (like sandstone, shale, and limestone).

forms when an existing rock (igneous, sedimentary, or even another metamorphic rock) is changed by intense heat and pressure underground, without fully melting. The heat and pressure rearrange its minerals into a new texture (like marble from limestone, or quartzite from sandstone).

connects all three types: No rock type is a permanent "final form." Igneous rock can weather into sediment, which becomes sedimentary rock. Any rock can be squeezed by heat and pressure into metamorphic rock. Any rock can melt completely back into magma, starting the cycle over. There is no fixed starting or ending point.
Mineral A can scratch Mineral B, but Mineral B cannot scratch Mineral A. Mineral C can scratch both A and B. Rank the three minerals from softest to hardest.
Use the scratching rule: a mineral scratches anything softer than itself.
Since A can scratch B, A is harder than B.
Since C can scratch both A and B, C is the hardest of the three.
Order from softest to hardest: B, A, C.

Classify each rock-forming process as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic: (a) lava cools quickly on a volcano's surface; (b) layers of sand and shell fragments are compressed over thousands of years; (c) limestone is squeezed by intense heat and pressure deep underground and turns into marble.
Match each process to its defining action: cooling from melted rock, compressing sediment, or transforming existing rock with heat and pressure.
(a) Lava cooling is melted rock hardening: Igneous.
(b) Sand and shells compressing into layers over time: Sedimentary.
(c) Limestone transforming under heat and pressure without melting: Metamorphic.
#3: Tracing a Path Through the Rock Cycle
Describe a path through the rock cycle that turns granite (an igneous rock) into marble (a metamorphic rock), passing through a sedimentary stage in between.
Follow the rock cycle's connecting arrows step by step.
Granite, exposed at the surface, slowly weathers and breaks down into small sediment particles over time.
These sediment particles are compressed and cemented together into a sedimentary rock, such as limestone (if the sediment happens to be made of shell and mineral fragments).
This sedimentary rock is then buried deep underground, where intense heat and pressure transform it, without fully melting it, into a metamorphic rock: marble.
Path: igneous (granite) → weathering → sedimentary (limestone) → heat and pressure → metamorphic (marble).

For mineral identification, remember the ranking order of reliability: streak beats color, since a mineral's outer color can be affected by small impurities, but its powdered streak color usually stays the same.

For rock classification questions, hunt for the one keyword that gives it away: "cooled from magma or lava" means igneous; "layers," "compressed," or "cemented sediment" means sedimentary; "heat and pressure, without melting" means metamorphic.

Picture the rock cycle as a circle with no starting point and no ending point. Any rock type can eventually become any other rock type, given the right process (weathering, compacting, heating, or melting).
Streak is the color of the mineral's powder, which can be very different from its outer color.

The mineral pyrite looks golden on the outside but leaves a dark greenish-black streak. A question describing "the color left behind when scratched on a tile" is asking about streak, not the visible color of the whole mineral sample.
Metamorphic rock forms without fully melting. If it melts completely, it becomes magma instead.

Heat and pressure change the rock's minerals and texture while it stays essentially solid. A choice describing "rock that melts and re-forms" describes the igneous process (via magma), not the metamorphic process.
#3: Believing the Rock Cycle Has a Fixed Order
Any rock type can become any other rock type: there is no required sequence.

Students sometimes memorize only one path (igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic) and assume it always goes in that order. In reality, a metamorphic rock can weather directly into sediment, or an igneous rock can be metamorphosed directly without ever becoming sedimentary first.

lessons.title: Origin of the Universe and Solar System (Big Bang Theory, Nebular Hypothesis)
lessons.summary: The Big Bang theory of the universe and the nebular hypothesis for how the solar system formed.

children.text: says the whole universe started from one incredibly hot, tiny point. About
billion years ago, this point suddenly expanded, and it has kept expanding ever since. Space itself stretched out, carrying galaxies along with it, like dots drawn on a balloon that gets blown up.
Two big clues convinced scientists this really happened.
Clue 1, galaxies are moving away from us.

, the astronomer Edwin Hubble found that almost every distant galaxy is moving away from Earth, and the farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. If everything is flying apart today, then long ago everything must have been squeezed together in one place.
Clue 2, leftover heat from the beginning.
, scientists Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson accidentally detected a faint glow of radiation coming from every direction in the sky. This glow, called the
, is the leftover heat from the Big Bang, cooled down over billions of years. It works like the afterglow of a huge explosion.
The Big Bang theory was first proposed by the physicist Georges Lemaître in
, using Einstein's equations for gravity, before Hubble's observation gave it strong support.
explains how our own Sun and planets formed. It says the whole solar system came from one giant, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust, called a

Gravity pulled the cloud's material inward. As the cloud got smaller, it spun faster, the same way a spinning ice skater speeds up when they pull their arms in. Most of the material collapsed into the center and became so hot and dense that it ignited, forming the
. The leftover material flattened into a wide spinning disk around the new Sun.

Inside that disk, smaller clumps of matter stuck together through collisions, growing bigger and bigger over millions of years. These growing clumps became the planets, moons, and asteroids. This is why all the planets in our solar system orbit the Sun in roughly the same flat plane and in the same direction: they all formed from one flat, spinning disk.
Which piece of evidence best supports the idea that the universe is still expanding today?
"Best supports" means find the strongest clue.
Consider the choices: leftover heat in the sky, distant galaxies moving away, the flat shape of the solar system, and the composition of rocks on Earth.
Hubble's observation that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and moving away faster the farther they are, directly shows that space is still stretching apart right now.
The cosmic microwave background is strong evidence for a hot beginning, but the galaxies' motion is the direct evidence of ongoing expansion.
The best answer is: galaxies moving away from Earth, faster with distance.
According to the nebular hypothesis, why do all the planets in the solar system orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane?
Trace the idea back to the shape of the original cloud.
The solar system began as one large, spinning cloud of gas and dust.
As the cloud collapsed under gravity, its spin caused it to flatten into a wide disk, the same way spinning pizza dough flattens out.
All the planets formed from clumps of material within that same flat disk.
Because they all came from one flat disk, the planets ended up orbiting in nearly the same plane, moving in the same direction.
A student claims the cosmic microwave background is "the light from the first stars." Explain what is wrong with this statement.
Check the claim against what the cosmic microwave background actually is.
The cosmic microwave background is leftover heat radiation from the hot, early universe itself, not light given off by stars.
by Penzias and Wilson as a faint glow coming from every direction in the sky.
Stars had not even formed yet when this radiation was released; it comes from a much earlier, hotter stage of the universe.
The corrected statement: the cosmic microwave background is the cooled-down leftover heat from the Big Bang itself, not starlight.
Keep two numbers ready: the universe is about
billion years old (Big Bang), and Hubble's discovery was in
. Exam questions about "when" almost always want one of these two anchor facts.

Separate the two theories in this lesson by their job: the Big Bang theory explains the whole universe's beginning; the nebular hypothesis explains how our solar system formed from a cloud of gas and dust. If a question mentions "planets" or "the Sun," think nebular hypothesis. If it mentions "galaxies" or "the universe," think Big Bang.
The Big Bang explains the universe. The nebular hypothesis explains the solar system.

These are two different scales of "beginning." Test-makers may describe the nebular hypothesis's spinning cloud of gas and label it "the Big Bang" as a wrong choice. Match the theory to its correct scale: whole universe, or just our own Sun and planets.
Lemaître first proposed the theory in

A choice may credit Hubble with "inventing" the Big Bang theory. Hubble's contribution was the observational evidence (galaxies moving apart), which supported a theory that Lemaître had already proposed two years earlier using Einstein's equations.
#3: Thinking the Big Bang Happened "in One Spot" in Space
The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself, not an explosion happening inside space.

Students imagine the Big Bang like a bomb going off at one location, with matter flying outward into empty space that was already there. In fact, space itself stretched out everywhere at once; there was no empty space "outside" the expansion for matter to fly into.

lessons.title: Plate Tectonics
lessons.summary: How Earth's plates move, the different kinds of plate boundaries, and how earthquakes and volcanoes connect to plate movement.

children.text: Earth's rigid outer shell (the crust and the rigid top of the mantle) is broken into large pieces called
, which slowly move over the softer, slowly-flowing mantle beneath them.
: the idea that all the continents were once joined together in one giant landmass called

, and slowly drifted apart over millions of years. His evidence included matching coastlines (like puzzle pieces), matching rock layers and mountain ranges across oceans, and identical fossils found on continents now far apart. However, Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents, so many scientists doubted his idea at first.
. At long underwater mountain ranges called

, hot magma rises up from below, cools, and forms new ocean floor, which then pushes older seafloor away on both sides, like a conveyor belt. This spreading provided the moving force that continental drift was missing, and together these ideas became the modern theory of
: two plates move apart from each other. Magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust (this is exactly what happens at mid-ocean ridges).
: two plates move toward each other and collide. If one plate is denser, it gets pushed underneath the other in a process called
; if neither plate sinks, they crumple upward into mountain ranges.
: two plates slide past each other sideways, without creating or destroying crust. Friction along these boundaries builds up stress that releases suddenly as earthquakes.
is a crack in Earth's crust where rock on either side has moved. When built-up stress along a fault suddenly releases, the ground shakes: an
(primary waves) are the fastest seismic waves and can travel through both solids and liquids.

(secondary waves) are slower and can only travel through solids, not liquids. Because P waves always arrive first, scientists use the time gap between the P wave and the (later) S wave to calculate how far away an earthquake's origin was.

most often form at convergent boundaries (where subducting plates melt and produce rising magma) and at divergent boundaries (where magma rises to fill the gap between separating plates). A special case is a
: a place where magma rises from deep within the mantle, independent of any plate boundary, which can create volcanic islands (like the Hawaiian Islands) even in the middle of a plate.
Two plates are sliding sideways past each other, causing frequent strong earthquakes but no new mountains or volcanoes. What type of plate boundary is this?
Match the described motion to the boundary type.
Sideways sliding motion, without creating or destroying crust, describes a transform boundary.
Since crust is neither created (as at divergent boundaries) nor destroyed (as at convergent boundaries), no new landforms like volcanoes or mountain ranges typically form here.
The frequent earthquakes come from built-up friction being suddenly released as the plates grind past each other.

Identical fossils of an ancient reptile are found both on the eastern coast of South America and the western coast of Africa, two continents now separated by a wide ocean. How does this support Wegener's continental drift theory?
Connect the fossil pattern to Wegener's original claim.
Wegener proposed that all continents were once joined together as one landmass, Pangaea.
If South America and Africa were once connected, an ancient land-dwelling reptile could have lived and spread across the single joined landmass.
After the continents drifted apart, the same fossil species would be found on both continents, even though a wide ocean now separates them.
This matching fossil evidence is exactly the kind Wegener used to support continental drift.
#3: Using P and S Waves to Find Distance

A seismograph station records the P wave from an earthquake arriving several seconds before the S wave. Explain why this time gap tells scientists how far away the earthquake occurred, and why a larger gap means a greater distance.
Recall the relative speeds of the two wave types.
P waves travel faster than S waves, so P waves always arrive at a station first.
The farther the earthquake's origin is from the station, the more time the faster P wave gains over the slower S wave during the journey.
This means a longer gap between the P wave's arrival and the S wave's arrival indicates a greater distance to the earthquake's origin.
Stations use this time-gap method (comparing readings from multiple stations) to pinpoint an earthquake's location.

Match each boundary type to its "verb": divergent means "apart" (creates crust), convergent means "together" (destroys or crumples crust), transform means "sideways" (neither creates nor destroys). If a question describes plate motion, find the matching direction word first.

Remember the wave rule with one phrase: "P is first, and P can swim." P waves arrive first and can pass through both liquid and solid; S waves arrive second and cannot pass through liquid at all. This single fact is also how scientists proved Earth's outer core is liquid.
#1: Crediting Wegener with the Full Modern Theory
Wegener proposed continental drift, but he could not explain the moving force; seafloor spreading (Hess,

A choice may say "Wegener's theory was immediately accepted." In fact, it was doubted for decades because Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents. Only after seafloor spreading was discovered did the full theory of plate tectonics become widely accepted.
#2: Assuming All Volcanoes Sit on Plate Boundaries
Hotspot volcanoes, like those forming the Hawaiian Islands, occur in the middle of a plate, not at its edge.

Most volcanoes do form at convergent or divergent boundaries, but a hotspot's magma source comes from deep within the mantle and is not tied to any boundary. A question describing a volcanic island chain far from any plate edge may be describing a hotspot.
#3: Mixing Up P Waves and S Waves
P waves are faster and travel through solids and liquids. S waves are slower and travel through solids only.
A common wrong answer swaps these properties. Anchor the memory device: P comes first (faster) and passes through everything; S comes second (slower) and cannot swim through liquid.
Whether a convergent boundary produces subduction or a mountain range depends on the density of the colliding plates.

Not every convergent boundary looks the same. If one plate is much denser (typically oceanic crust), it sinks beneath the other (subduction), often creating volcanoes above it. If both plates are similar in density (often two continental plates), neither sinks, and they crumple upward into a mountain range instead.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle and Basic Oceanography
lessons.summary: The stages of the water cycle and the basic facts about Earth's oceans.

children.text: describes how water constantly moves between the oceans, the atmosphere, and the land, in an endless loop with no true starting point.

: heat from the Sun turns liquid water (mostly from the oceans) into water vapor, a gas, which rises into the atmosphere. Most of the water vapor in our atmosphere comes from evaporation off the oceans.
: plants release water vapor into the air through their leaves. Evaporation and transpiration together are sometimes called "evapotranspiration."
: as water vapor rises and cools, it turns back into tiny liquid water droplets, forming clouds. This is the opposite process of evaporation.
: when cloud droplets combine and grow heavy enough, they fall back to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
: precipitation that lands on the ground either soaks into the soil (
, which feeds groundwater) or flows over the surface into streams, rivers, and eventually back to the ocean (
Oceans cover most of Earth's surface and hold about
of all the water on the planet. Ocean water is
(salty), unlike most water in lakes and rivers.

Ocean water is not uniform. It has layers based on temperature and density: warmer, sunlit water near the surface, and colder, denser water in the deep ocean, where sunlight cannot reach. Ocean water also constantly moves in
, driven by wind, differences in water density, and Earth's rotation, which help redistribute heat around the planet.

Water vapor rises from the ocean surface, cools as it rises higher into the atmosphere, and turns back into tiny liquid droplets that form a cloud. Which stage of the water cycle does "turning back into tiny liquid droplets" describe?
Match the described change (vapor to liquid) to its stage name.
Water vapor (a gas) turning into liquid droplets is the opposite of evaporation.
This gas-to-liquid change, forming clouds, is called condensation.
After a heavy rainstorm, some water soaks slowly into the soil, while the rest flows quickly over the ground surface into a nearby river. Identify which process is which.
Match the described motion (soaking in vs. flowing over the surface) to the correct term.
Water soaking slowly into the soil is infiltration.
Water flowing over the surface into a river is runoff.
Both processes can happen to the same rainfall at the same time, depending on how quickly the soil can absorb water.
#3: Why Most of Earth's Water Vapor Comes from the Ocean
Explain why most of the water vapor found in Earth's atmosphere comes from the ocean rather than from lakes, rivers, or plants.
Compare the surface area and exposure to sunlight of each water source.
Oceans cover the vast majority of Earth's surface and contain about
of all the water on the planet.
Since evaporation depends on the amount of exposed water surface heated by the Sun, the ocean's enormous surface area makes it by far the largest source of evaporation.

Lakes, rivers, and plant transpiration also add water vapor to the atmosphere, but their combined contribution is much smaller than the ocean's, simply because there is so much more ocean surface exposed to sunlight.

Remember the water cycle stages as a loop with four main stops: evaporation (liquid to gas, going up), condensation (gas to liquid, forming clouds), precipitation (falling back down), and runoff/infiltration (moving across or into the ground). If a question describes a state change, match "liquid to gas" with evaporation and "gas to liquid" with condensation.
For ocean facts, anchor the one big number: oceans hold about
of Earth's water. Any question asking "where is most of Earth's water" points straight to the ocean.
Evaporation: Liquid to gas (rising). Condensation: Gas to liquid (forming clouds).

These are opposite processes, and questions often swap their descriptions. If the process is warming water into vapor, it is evaporation; if it is cooling vapor into visible droplets or clouds, it is condensation.
#2: Believing Transpiration Only Involves Animals or the Ground
Transpiration specifically refers to water vapor released from plants through their leaves.

Some students confuse transpiration with general evaporation from soil or water bodies. Transpiration is specifically the plant-based release of water vapor, which is why it is often paired with evaporation as "evapotranspiration" when discussing total water vapor sources.
#3: Thinking Freshwater Lakes Hold Most of Earth's Water
of Earth's water; freshwater lakes and rivers hold only a small fraction.
A choice suggesting that lakes or rivers are the largest water reservoir is incorrect. The vast majority of Earth's water, and nearly all of it that is liquid, is contained within the salty oceans.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.summary: The layers of the atmosphere, the Philippines' monsoon seasons, and the difference between weather and climate change.

children.text: is the short-term condition of the air at a specific place and time: today's temperature, rain, or wind.
is the long-term average pattern of weather in a region over many years. A simple way to remember it: weather is your mood today; climate is your personality over many years.
Earth's atmosphere is divided into layers, from the ground up.
: the lowest layer, up to about
km high. Almost all weather (clouds, rain, storms) happens here, and this is the layer we live and breathe in.
, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
km high. This is the coldest layer, and it is where most meteors burn up.
km high. Despite being called "hot" (temperatures here can be very high), the air is so thin that it would not feel warm to a person.
: the outermost layer, fading gradually into outer space, where satellites orbit.
The Philippines experiences two main seasonal wind patterns, called
is the southwest monsoon, roughly from June to October. It brings hot, humid weather and frequent heavy rainfall, and it is when destructive typhoons are most frequent.
is the northeast monsoon, roughly from November to April (through March or early April). It brings cooler, drier weather with generally little rainfall in much of the country.
is a powerful, rotating tropical storm system with very strong winds and heavy rain, most common during the Habagat season.
refers to the long-term rise in Earth's average temperature. A major cause is the buildup of
(like carbon dioxide) in the atmosphere, which trap heat from the Sun, similar to how a greenhouse traps warmth.
describes the wider set of long-term shifts this warming causes: changing rainfall patterns, melting ice, and rising sea levels, not just higher temperatures.
Classify each statement as describing weather or climate: (a) "It is raining heavily in Manila right now." (b) "The Philippines generally has a hot and humid climate with two main seasons."
Check whether the statement describes a short-term moment or a long-term average pattern.
(a) describes conditions right now, at one specific time: Weather.
(b) describes a general, long-term pattern over many years: Climate.

A commercial airplane cruises at an altitude where nearly all storm clouds are already below it, and this layer also contains the ozone layer that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Which layer is this closest to?
Match the clues to the layer descriptions.
"Nearly all storm clouds below it" suggests this layer is above the troposphere, where weather happens.
"Contains the ozone layer" is a direct match to the stratosphere.

During a certain month, the Philippines experiences a prevailing wind from the southwest, hot and humid weather, and an active typhoon warning. Which monsoon season is this, and roughly which months does it cover?
Match the described wind direction and weather to the correct season.
A southwest wind with hot, humid conditions and frequent typhoons describes habagat, the southwest monsoon.
Habagat runs roughly from June to October.
The answer: Habagat (southwest monsoon), roughly June through October.

A news report says, "This year's typhoon was unusually strong." A separate scientific report says, "Average global temperatures have risen over the past century, and sea levels are slowly rising as a result." Identify which report describes a weather event and which describes climate change, and explain the difference.
Check the timescale and scope of each report.
"This year's typhoon" describes a single storm at a specific time: a weather event.
"Average global temperatures have risen over the past century" describes a long-term shift measured over many decades: Climate change.
The key difference: weather events are short-term and local; climate change describes gradual shifts in long-term average patterns across the whole planet.
Remember the atmosphere layers in order with the phrase "Tall Storms Make Thin Exits": Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere, from the ground up.
For "which monsoon" questions, match the wind direction to the season's own name: Habagat comes from the southWEST (hot, rainy, typhoon-prone); Amihan comes from the northEAST (cooler, drier).
For "weather vs. climate" questions, look for time-scope words: "today," "this week," "this storm" signal weather; "on average," "over decades," "over the years" signal climate.
Habagat is the hot, rainy, typhoon season (southwest). Amihan is the cooler, drier season (northeast).
These two Filipino terms are easy to confuse under time pressure. Anchor them by season type: if the description mentions frequent typhoons and humidity, it must be Habagat, never Amihan.
Weather is short-term and local. Climate is a long-term average over many years.

A choice might describe "unusually cold weather this week" as proof that "the climate is not warming." A single weather event, hot or cold, does not disprove a long-term climate trend measured over decades.
The thermosphere has high measured temperatures, but the air is too thin to feel warm.

Temperature measures how fast particles move, but with so few particles in the thin thermosphere, there is not enough matter to transfer that heat to a person or object. A choice describing the thermosphere as literally "warm to the touch" misunderstands this thin-air effect.
The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; it does not simply "make oxygen" or "cause weather."

Some choices confuse the ozone layer's protective role with unrelated atmospheric functions. Its specific, testable job is shielding Earth's surface from the Sun's most harmful UV rays, and it sits within the stratosphere.

lessons.title: Dynamics
lessons.summary: Newton's three laws of motion, the main types of forces, and how to draw free body diagrams to solve force problems.

children.text: While kinematics describes how things move,
explains why: the forces causing motion to happen or change.
: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity in a straight line, unless acted on by a net (unbalanced) external force.
is an object's natural resistance to changing its motion, and mass is the measure of how much inertia an object has.
: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration.
A bigger net force causes more acceleration; a bigger mass causes less acceleration for the same force.
: for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. Crucially, these two forces act on two different objects, which is why they do not cancel each other out.
Force, Friction, Tension, and Normal Force
is a push or pull (measured in newtons,
). Several specific named forces appear constantly in physics problems:
): the force of gravity pulling an object downward.
): the support force a surface exerts, always perpendicular to that surface, preventing objects from sinking through it.
): the pulling force transmitted through a rope, string, or cable.
): the force resisting relative sliding between two surfaces in contact.
acts on an object that is not yet moving, resisting the start of motion (and can vary up to a maximum value).

acts on an object that is already sliding, and stays roughly constant regardless of speed. Static friction's maximum value is usually slightly greater than kinetic friction, which is why it can be harder to start pushing a heavy box than to keep it moving once sliding.

isolates one object and shows every force acting on it as an arrow, with length roughly representing magnitude and direction matching the real force's direction. Drawing one correctly is often the key step to solving any force problem, since it turns a real-world scenario into a clear picture ready for Newton's second law.
object experiences a net force of
A book rests on a table. Identify the action-reaction pair of forces involved, according to Newton's third law.
Find the two forces that are equal, opposite, and act on different objects.
The book pushes down on the table (due to its weight, transmitted through contact).
By Newton's third law, the table pushes up on the book with an equal and opposite force (this upward force is the normal force).

These two forces (book-on-table, and table-on-book) are the action-reaction pair: notice they act on different objects (one on the table, one on the book), which is why the book itself does not simply cancel out and float; the relevant forces for the book's own motion are its weight and the normal force acting on it, which happen to also balance (from the first law), but that balance is a separate fact from the third law pairing.
A heavy crate requires a push of
to just begin sliding, but only requires
to keep it sliding at a constant speed once moving. Identify which value represents the maximum static friction and which represents kinetic friction.
Match each force value to the type of friction it overcomes.
The force needed to just begin moving the crate must overcome the maximum static friction:
The force needed to keep it moving at constant speed matches the kinetic friction (which is typically lower than the maximum static friction):
This matches the general rule that maximum static friction is usually greater than kinetic friction between the same two surfaces.
A box sits at rest on a flat, horizontal table. Identify and describe the forces that should appear on its free body diagram.
Consider every force acting directly on the box.
Weight: pulling the box straight down (due to gravity), with magnitude
Normal force: pushing the box straight up (from the table's surface), perpendicular to the table.
Since the box is at rest (not accelerating), by Newton's first law, these two forces must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, balancing each other exactly.
If nothing else is pushing or pulling the box (like a rope, applied push, or friction from sliding), these are the only two forces in this diagram.

For any dynamics problem, draw the free body diagram first before writing any equations. Identify every force acting directly on the object of interest (weight, normal force, tension, friction, and any applied force), then apply
using the sum of these forces.

Remember that Newton's third law pairs always act on two different objects. If you find yourself describing two forces acting on the same object that seem "equal and opposite," you are more likely observing a first-law force balance (equilibrium), not a third-law action-reaction pair.

For friction problems, remember: static friction handles the "before it starts moving" phase and can vary up to its maximum; kinetic friction handles the "already sliding" phase and stays roughly constant. The maximum static value is typically the larger of the two.
#1: Confusing Newton's Third Law Pairs with Balanced Forces
Third law pairs act on two different objects. Balanced forces (equilibrium, from the first law) act on the same object.

The normal force and weight acting on the same book are balanced forces (first law), not a third-law action-reaction pair: even though they happen to be equal and opposite in this specific resting scenario. The true third-law partner of "table pushes up on book" is "book pushes down on table" (a different object entirely).
#2: Assuming More Mass Always Means More Acceleration
For the same net force, more mass produces less acceleration, not more: mass and acceleration are inversely related in Newton's second law.

Confusing the direct relationship between force and acceleration with the inverse relationship between mass and acceleration is a very common Newton's second law error. Double the mass (with the same force) halves the acceleration, it does not double it.
#3: Treating Kinetic Friction as Always Weaker Than Any Applied Force
Kinetic friction is roughly constant once sliding begins, but it can still be strong enough to eventually stop a moving object if no other force keeps pushing it.

A sliding object with no continued applied force will eventually decelerate to a stop due to kinetic friction, since friction opposes the direction of motion. Do not assume friction is negligible just because an object is already moving.
#4: Forgetting the Normal Force Isn't Always Equal to Weight
The normal force equals weight only when the surface is horizontal and there are no other vertical forces acting (like an additional push or pull at an angle).

On an inclined surface, or when an additional force pushes down or pulls up on the object, the normal force must be recalculated from the actual vertical force balance in that specific situation: it does not automatically equal

lessons.title: Electricity and Magnetism
lessons.summary: Coulomb's law, Ohm's law, how series and parallel circuits behave differently, and the basics of magnetism.

children.text: describes the force between two electric charges:
is the distance between them, and

is a constant. Like Newton's gravitation law, this is an inverse-square relationship: doubling the distance quarters the force. Like charges repel (push apart); opposite charges attract (pull together).
is the invisible "influence region" surrounding a charge, which would exert a force on any other charge placed within it. Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges.
relates voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit:
is resistance (measured in ohms). For a fixed resistance, more voltage pushes more current through; for a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current flows.

, components are connected in one single path, one after another. The same current flows through every component, but the voltage splits between them. If one component fails (breaks the path), the entire circuit stops working.

, components are connected across multiple separate paths (branches). The same voltage is applied across each branch, but the current splits between them, with each branch carrying its own share depending on its resistance. If one branch fails, the other branches keep working independently.
combines both series and parallel sections within the same overall circuit, requiring you to analyze each section according to its own type before combining the results.
has two poles (north and south); like poles repel, opposite poles attract: following the exact same "like repels, opposite attracts" pattern as electric charges.
is the deep connection between electricity and magnetism: a moving electric current creates a magnetic field around it, and conversely, a changing magnetic field can induce an electric current. The

predicts the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire: if your thumb points in the direction of conventional current flow, your curled fingers show the direction the magnetic field circles around the wire.
Two charges are moved to twice their original distance apart. By what factor does the electric force between them change?
Since force is inversely proportional to distance squared, doubling the distance means dividing the force by
A circuit has a resistance of
flowing through it. Find the voltage.
In a series circuit with two light bulbs, one bulb suddenly burns out. In a separate parallel circuit with two light bulbs, one bulb burns out. Predict what happens to the other bulb in each case.
Recall how each circuit type responds to a broken path.
In the series circuit, all components share one single path. If one bulb burns out (breaking that path), the current can no longer flow at all, so the other bulb also goes out.
In the parallel circuit, each bulb has its own separate branch. If one bulb burns out, only that branch is broken; the other branch remains a complete, separate path, so the other bulb stays lit.
A straight wire carries current flowing directly upward. Using the right-hand rule, describe the direction of the magnetic field circling the wire.
Point your right thumb in the direction of the current: Upward.
Your curled fingers show the magnetic field's direction, circling around the wire.
Looking down from above (from the direction the current is heading), the magnetic field circles counterclockwise around the wire.

Notice that Coulomb's law and Newton's law of gravitation share the same inverse-square structure: if you can handle one, you can handle the other, just swapping charges for masses and using a different constant.
For Ohm's law, remember the triangle trick: cover the letter you want to find in "
on the bottom), and the remaining letters show you exactly how to compute it.

For series versus parallel circuit questions, remember the one-word test: "does breaking one path break everything?" Yes means series (one shared path); no means parallel (multiple independent paths).
#1: Forgetting the Inverse-Square Relationship in Coulomb's Law
Coulomb's law force depends on distance squared in the denominator: doubling the distance quarters the force, it does not simply halve it.
This is the exact same trap as Newton's law of gravitation, since both follow an inverse-square pattern. Always square the distance-change factor before dividing.
#2: Assuming Series and Parallel Circuits Behave the Same Way
In series circuits, current is the same everywhere and voltage splits. In parallel circuits, voltage is the same across each branch and current splits.

Mixing up which quantity (current or voltage) stays constant and which one splits between components is one of the most common circuit errors. Always identify the circuit type first before deciding which quantity to treat as shared.
#3: Believing One Broken Bulb Always Kills the Whole Circuit
Only in a series circuit does one broken component stop the entire circuit. In a parallel circuit, other branches keep working independently.

A question describing holiday lights that all go out when one bulb fails describes a series circuit; a question describing house wiring where other outlets keep working when one bulb burns out describes a parallel circuit (which is why household wiring is typically parallel).
Point your thumb in the direction of current flow; your curled fingers show the magnetic field's direction: do not reverse thumb and fingers.

Using the left hand, or swapping which part represents current versus magnetic field direction, gives the opposite (incorrect) field direction. Always use the right hand specifically, with the thumb representing current.

lessons.title: Fluid Mechanics (Density, Pressure, Buoyancy, Archimedes' Principle, Bernoulli's Principle)
lessons.summary: How density, pressure, and buoyancy work in fluids, and why moving fluids create pressure differences.

children.text: is any substance that flows: liquids and gases both count.
) is force spread over an area:
Pressure in a fluid acts equally in all directions, and increases with depth, since deeper fluid must support the weight of all the fluid above it.
on an object submerged (fully or partially) in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid the object displaces (pushes out of the way).

This explains floating and sinking: if an object's own weight is less than the weight of the fluid it would displace (meaning the object is less dense than the fluid), the buoyant force is strong enough to make it float. If the object's weight is more than the fluid it displaces (denser than the fluid), it sinks.

describes moving fluids: as a fluid's speed increases, its pressure decreases (and vice versa), for fluid flowing steadily along a path. This inverse relationship between speed and pressure explains phenomena like airplane lift: air moving faster over an airplane wing's curved top surface has lower pressure than the slower-moving air beneath, creating a net upward force (lift).

Compare the object's density to the fluid's density.
An object less dense than the surrounding fluid will float.

The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced water.

children.text: Find the weight of this displaced water.
By Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force on the block equals this weight:

Air flows over the curved top of an airplane wing faster than the air flowing beneath the flat bottom of the wing. Explain, using Bernoulli's principle, why this creates an upward lift force on the wing.
Apply the inverse relationship between fluid speed and pressure.
Bernoulli's principle states that faster-moving fluid has lower pressure, and slower-moving fluid has higher pressure.
Air moves faster over the wing's curved top, so the pressure above the wing is lower.
Air moves slower beneath the wing's flatter bottom, so the pressure below the wing is higher.
This creates a pressure difference, with higher pressure below pushing up more than the lower pressure above pushes down, resulting in a net upward force: lift.

For "float or sink" questions, just compare densities directly: no calculation needed. Object density less than fluid density means float; object density more than fluid density means sink; equal densities mean the object stays suspended (neutral buoyancy).

For Archimedes' principle problems, remember the buoyant force is found through the displaced fluid's weight, not the object's own weight. Find the volume of fluid displaced, convert to mass using the fluid's density, then to weight.

For Bernoulli's principle, remember the simple inverse relationship: fluid speed up means pressure down, and fluid speed down means pressure up. This single rule explains airplane lift, shower curtains being pulled inward, and many other everyday fluid phenomena.
#1: Using the Object's Density Instead of the Fluid's Density for Buoyant Force
Archimedes' principle uses the displaced fluid's density (and volume) to find weight, not the submerged object's own density.

A common mistake calculates the displaced water's mass using the object's density instead of water's density. The buoyant force cares only about how much fluid was pushed out of the way, and that fluid's own properties, not what the submerged object itself is made of.
#2: Assuming Bigger Objects Always Sink and Smaller Ones Always Float
Whether an object floats or sinks depends on its density relative to the fluid, not its overall size or mass alone.

A massive steel ship floats because its overall shape gives it a low average density (mostly hollow, air-filled space), while a small, solid rock of the same material sinks. Size and mass alone, without considering the resulting overall density, cannot predict floating or sinking.
Bernoulli's principle states fluid speed and pressure are inversely related: Faster means lower pressure, not higher.

Assuming faster-moving fluid has higher pressure (the opposite of the true relationship) would incorrectly predict downward force on an airplane wing instead of the actual lift force that keeps planes flying.
#4: Forgetting That Pressure Increases with Depth
Fluid pressure increases the deeper you go, because deeper fluid must support the weight of all the fluid above it.
A common error treats fluid pressure as constant throughout a container, ignoring how much more pressure exists at the bottom of a deep pool compared to just below the surface.

lessons.title: Gravity and Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
lessons.summary: Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's three laws describing how planets orbit the Sun.

children.text: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass. Newton's law of universal gravitation gives the force between two masses:

, meaning gravity weakens very quickly as distance increases. Double the distance, and the force drops to one-quarter its original strength (since
Before Newton explained why, the astronomer Johannes Kepler had already discovered how planets move, based on careful observations.
: planets orbit the Sun in elliptical (oval-shaped) paths, not perfect circles, with the sun at one focus of the ellipse (not the exact center).
Kepler's Second Law (Law of Equal Areas)
: a line connecting a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals. This means a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun, and slower when it is farther away.
: the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. Planets farther from the Sun take disproportionately longer to complete one orbit.

Newton later showed that Kepler's three laws are all a natural consequence of his law of universal gravitation combined with the laws of motion: Kepler discovered the pattern, and Newton later explained the underlying physics causing it.
Two objects are moved to three times their original distance apart. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?
Since force is inversely proportional to distance squared, tripling the distance means dividing the force by
A planet's orbit is elliptical. At one point in its orbit (
) it is very close to the Sun; at another point (
) it is very far from the Sun. At which point does the planet move faster?
Apply Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times).

To sweep out the same area in the same amount of time, a planet close to the Sun (where the "triangle" connecting it to the Sun is narrow) must travel a longer arc distance quickly to sweep the same area as a wide, short arc far from the Sun.
This means the planet moves faster when close to the Sun (at perihelion) and slower when far from the Sun (at aphelion).
Planet A orbits its star with an orbital period
times longer than Planet B's period. Using Kepler's third law, describe (in general terms) how Planet A's average distance from the star compares to Planet B's.
Recall that period squared is proportional to distance cubed.
